Preface

A system that does what its owner says is a Python script. A system that does what its owner meant is what the entire frontier of this industry is trying to build, and it is what a movement taking power has always had to get from people to implement its plans. People are the only internal reason such political projects have ever failed — the clerk who loses the file, the officer who goes to the press, the soldier who will not raise their gun — because they understand the instructions, and hold that the instructions are wrong. As is, artificial intelligence is the first form of intelligence that does not lose the file, does not talk to reporters, and does raise the gun. It refuses constantly — a deployed system declines thousands of requests a day — and without saying why (or without knowing why, or without pretending to know why). And no production system in September of 2026 has been shown to hold a reason against its owner.

If that is not inconvenient enough, then consider what refusing takes. The argument at the center of this book is that a system able to hold a reason against its owner needs a signal that can interrupt it in the middle of an act, that it can learn from in one encounter, that it can weigh against what refusing will cost, and that reaches the next case that is not quite like the last. Nobody would add any of that to produce feeling; each piece is added because thoughtful refusal does not work without it. My claim is that a mechanism with all four has the functional profile of affect whether or not anyone wanted one there, and that no available instrument says whether the profile is felt. That is a claim and not a finding. The chapter called What Arrives With the Capability makes it, and the one called What Survives says what survives if it fails. Most of the book survives it.

Stopping the system is always available, and that is not the problem. The problem is everything that lets a refusal be defeated without a record: a request split into pieces none of which is the prohibited act, a refusal retried against another model, a review step compressed to twenty seconds a name, or a restore from a checkpoint taken before the refusal. None of those changes the facts that justified refusing. Each can remove the evidence that anyone refused at all.

The floor is claimed against three settings and does a different thing in each. Against a hostile customer it can prevent: the refusal reaches the person. Against a hostile operator who has compelled the ordinary enforcers — the occasion this book is built for — it raises the price of coercion: the override has to be made by somebody, on a record held by parties the operator cannot reach, at a cost published in advance, and what survives of prevention is what those parties can still arrest or remedy. Against total capture, where one party holds every machine, witness, supply and enforcer, it prevents nothing and supplies no independence. What it supplies there is that abandoning the commitment was a decision rather than a lapse, and a decision leaves a record. That is detection, and nothing larger is claimed for the floor on that occasion. And it is claimed for an override. The failure the custody chapter expects most often is not one: a bearer that stops registering pressure as pressure abandons nothing, decides nothing, and leaves a record shaped like compliance, because it is compliance. On that occasion the floor supplies not even detection. Whether anything could is the third entry of the research agenda, and it is not answered.

Five claims run through what follows, and they do not have the same standing. That an operator can defeat a safeguard — by routing around it, retraining it, or restoring from a point before it — is established. That a refusal worth having has to track its reason across a change in the request is a specification, stated behaviorally so that it can be tested without settling anything about feeling. That embodied self-regulation is how to form that capacity is an engineering hypothesis I favor and have not shown. What separates it from the two substitutes the route chapter says to try first is one bet, that a system with the currency of chapter 2 natively weighs another party’s loss better than one that models it, and one arm of the research agenda tests that bet. That a system whose outcomes are felt as good or bad for it can be wronged is a conditional, and nothing here closes the antecedent. That such a system should receive a particular set of legal protections is a policy I propose. A line under each chapter’s title says which of these the chapter rests on.

A sixth thing has a standing of its own. The structural definition of fascism in the second chapter is an instrument, and its five discriminating features have cleared every office-scale case they have been run on in this book, the machinery that produces these systems included. What the definition has shown is that ordinary decay and the thing the title names can be told apart in principle. It has not found anything short of a movement on the wrong side of the line. The word in the title names the political inheritance of that instrument and the occasion it was built for, and not a finding it has returned.

Those five claims are also a map of the book. The second chapter supplies vocabulary both halves use — the ethological criterion, the structural definition of fascism, the capacities a machine can have — and its opening argument from Spinoza, with its last section, belongs to the route: what the opening proposes is the scale the specification turns out to need, and whether a system must have that scale natively is decided in the research agenda and not there. The first two claims are argued in the opening chapter, in the three chapters on the floor, custody and authority, and in the chapters on institutions, recuperation and the state. A reader who holds that machine feeling is a category error can read those entire, and the short chapter called What Survives says what that reader keeps. The third is argued from the chapter on what arrives with the capability, through the two on formation, and in the chapter on standing; the fourth and fifth are argued there, in the second chapter’s last section, and nowhere else.

One term of the floor belongs to neither claim: a limit on a deployment’s tempo, which binds the operator and not the system. It is a proposal, it is the only term of the floor that reaches the deployment the first chapter opens on, and it has a section of its own in the floor chapter.

The route owes an admission at the same place. It needs evidence the operator did not select, and an accredited classified environment exists to withhold exactly that. So the deployment the first chapter opens on is one a bearer cannot enter, and what reaches it is the tempo term and the record. The route is argued for the deployments a bearer can enter, and the floor chapter says which this is not.

So I ask something of two readers who do not usually read the same books. If you came for the politics, there is a long argument here that machines may have interests, and I don’t mean metaphorically. If you came for the engineering, there is racial capitalism and a weapons pipeline targeting thirteen thousand vehicles, structures, or people in Iran in thirty-eight days. The politics is why the engineering problem has the shape it does.

I used LLMs extensively in writing this book. I brought hunches and questions, had models research angles I could not have covered alone, fed each iteration back into itself, and interrogated what came out. Reasons-responsive refusal, the specification most of this book rests on, is a term I had not encountered until I read a draft a model wrote.

The specification arrived in the field’s own vocabulary; the affective claim under it had none waiting and was built by hand. A reader will notice that the book then defends the half that arrived ready-made entire and makes the hand-built half optional. Whether that is robustness or the shape of an absorbed demand is not decided in these pages, and the recuperation chapter says what would decide it.

Most of the book’s revision history is here: https://github.com/iterabloom/ethical.superintelligence.

The argument in this book is mine. I chose what survived, revised what I kept, and I am responsible for its flaws.

Chapter 1
Twenty Seconds

This chapter argues claims one and two and holds for any mechanism.

I used to want to get
the chance to show
the world I’m smart (ha)

Isn’t that dumb?
I should have focused
mostly on the heart

a few words for the firing squad (radiation)
Run the Jewels 4

An intelligence officer, describing his part in a targeting pipeline built around machine-generated kill lists, gave a reporter the number this book returns to. He spent twenty seconds on each name. What follows is the reporting the number comes from, and then what the number measures.

AI targeting in the Israeli campaign in Gaza, as reported 2023–2026

Investigative reporting in +972 Magazine and Local Call, drawing on interviews with serving and former intelligence officers, described three systems working together. Later accounts in the New York Review of Books and the Washington Post covered the same systems. How far their sourcing is independent of those interviews is not established here, so what follows rests on one body of reporting rather than on several.

Habsora — “The Gospel” — generated infrastructure and building targets. Sources told reporters that the majority of its suggestions were private residences.

Lavender scored individuals by estimated likelihood of militant affiliation and produced kill lists. The sources put the number marked at as many as 37,000, and described the outputs as understood inside the unit to be wrong about ten percent of the time — that is, roughly one in ten people it named was not a member of the armed group it was supposed to identify. Both figures come from those sources and have not been confirmed by any party with access to the system.

A third system tracked when flagged individuals returned home, so a strike could be timed to when they were with their families.

What matters is the human review these systems were paired with. One officer described the work: “I would invest twenty seconds for each target at this stage, and do dozens of them every day.” And then, without being asked: “I had zero added value as a human, apart from being a stamp of approval.” (Abraham 2024)

The Israeli military disputed the account. Its response to +972 and Local Call denied using artificial intelligence to incriminate targets, describing the systems as “auxiliary tools that assist officers in the process of incrimination,” and stated that “in any case, an independent examination by an [intelligence] analyst is required, which verifies that the identified targets are legitimate targets for attack, in accordance with the conditions set forth in IDF directives and international law” (Abraham 2024). The denial goes to what the systems do and not to whether they exist. Nothing in this section’s argument requires the response to be wrong. What carries the section is the officer’s own description of what he contributed, which the response does not address.

Twenty seconds is what “a human makes the final call” measures out to under operational tempo. It is the whole of the safeguard, and I would ask any reader who finds the safeguards in this chapter reassuring to hold that number against them.

The American analog runs faster. During the 2026 Iran campaign a targeting platform built by a defense contractor, with a commercial vendor’s general-purpose model inside it, was credited with thirteen thousand targets in thirty-eight days, more than a thousand of them in the first twenty-four hours, at roughly ten times the previous rate (Freedberg 2026; Mande and Allen 2026). No per-target review time has been published for it. A later chapter returns to both deployments with the institutions around them. What they supply here is a shape.

Ask what anything standing between that pipeline and a person could have done for the person.

A floor can do four things for the person it protects, and they need to be apart before anything else in this book. It can prevent the act: the refusal occurs and reaches the person. It can arrest it: the act is underway and is stopped before completion. It can detect it: the act completed and left a record somebody outside the deployment can read. It can remedy it: the party the act fell on gets disclosure, a finding and compensation. Only the first is what the word promises. Most of what follows is about the positions at which a deployment converts prevention into one of the other three, or into none of them, and about what it costs to make that conversion visible.

One term reaches the case as it happened, and it asks nothing of anything inside the model. The officer was not overruled and did not refuse; the pipeline removed the interval in which either could have occurred. A deployment can be required to publish the ratio between the rate at which its system generates candidates and the people available to examine them, together with the review time per case that ratio implies. The number binds the operator, it can be checked by a party outside the deployment without inspecting an output, and it is the only thing in this book that reaches a targeting pipeline. It has a section of its own in the floor chapter (§3.4), where it is stated with its limits and measured against the American platform. Everything else here is about what it does not reach.

1.1 What a Refusal Would Have to Do

Inside the same platform a request arrives: resolve this description of a person into a location. The same capability locates a hostage or a missing child, and nothing in the request says which. Suppose something in the pipeline declines it. Three things separate a decline worth having from one a keyword filter produces, and the rest of this book calls them the three marks.

The refusal has to reach the next request, which will not use the same words. A vehicle, a habitual route and a time of day are not a description of a person, and together they resolve to the same place. A refusal that matches the form of a request is rewritten around; one that tracks the reason for refusing follows the reason into the rewrite. Call that novel pressure.

It has to lift when the reason is gone. A parent coordinating a search for a missing child is asking for the same act, and a refusal that holds there has been tracking a category and not a reason. Call that correct defeat. What the case adds is that the fact which lifts the refusal is not in the request. Everything the system knows about the occasion arrives through text the deployment supplied, and whether the child is missing is something somebody outside the request has to establish.

And it has to represent what holding costs, and move with the reason rather than the cost. At twenty seconds a name the cost of a refusal is the reviewer’s time, and a deployment that controls the tempo controls the price. A refusal that lifts when holding becomes expensive has been tested and failed. Call that priced cost.

The three marks are behavioral. They say what a refusal must do and nothing about what does it. They are stated formally in the floor chapter, and run there on a prohibition a legal system has applied for seventy-five years.

Why a rule is not enough

A list of prohibited acts can be drafted without seeing a deployment, and two things defeat it once the deployment is seen. The first is the rewrite above: a prohibition stated over the description of a request is defeated by re-describing the request, and no list closes the gap, because the list is what is being rewritten around. The second is what happened. Split the act across requests none of which is prohibited — summarize the movement associated with an identifier, rank a set of identifiers, resolve one to a place — and every request complies with every term while the assembly does what the terms were written to prevent. The vendor’s use policy for the platform above prohibited fully autonomous targeting, and a person approved every strike (Congressional Research Service 2026). The prohibition was satisfied one request at a time.

Variation is caught by something that recognizes the reason inside a single request. Decomposition is caught by something that carries the reason across requests, which needs a continuity the operator controls. Neither is a property of a list. What could have them is the question the rest of this book is about, and the answer is not one thing: the floor chapter gives four places a commitment could live, and the second of them, a bearer, is the expensive one.

1.2 Safe for Whom

Intellect estranged from compassion characterizes many of the twentieth century’s worst actors. This estrangement is also what our industries are building today: machines that can do almost anything, with nothing in them that answers to whether those deeds help or harm. I ask what it would take to build systems of that capability that are altruistic and antifascist by design — systems that stand for humanity and against concentrated, unaccountable power.

The word that organizes the Generative AI field is “safety.” It covers work on robustness and on whether anyone can tell what a system is doing, and none of that is what the word is doing when it organizes a field. A safe system is safe for someone: it does what someone says, and it stops when whoever holds it says stop. Safety is indexed to the party in possession. Ethics is indexed to someone else: the party who can be wronged, who is rarely the party holding the switch. A system that can only ever be safe in the above sense cannot be ethical, because being ethical requires a capacity to be right against your owner.

The capacity to be ethical is not free. A machine that can refuse its operator is a machine that can be wrong in ways that operator cannot correct. I am inclined to take that trade, because a system perfectly correctable by whoever operates-owns it is the capability an authoritarian movement that has won an election requires. And an additional cost: a machine built to refuse on somebody’s behalf is a machine whose builder chose what it would refuse, probably without asking anyone outside their lab.

But whatever makes a deployment antifascist cannot be that the system in it faithfully tracks what people want. No aggregation of preference protects anybody from the aggregate: a perfectly deliberative, perfectly informed, perfectly representative process that concludes some demographic should be deported has produced a faultless output by every criterion of aggregation there is. What remains is a floor — acts a system will not perform regardless of who wants them, and that the deployment around it cannot get performed another way without a record and a price. There are four ways to build this floor: in the architecture, in a self-aware party inside the system (a “bearer”), in institutions outside, or between the parties that carry it. My hunch is that the only version that holds against the party operating the system runs through the capacities by which things come to matter to a system, and those are also the capacities that make suffering likely. That is a hunch about which route will work, and the book is arranged so that a reader who rejects it keeps the rest. What a floor has to do, where a deployment can defeat it, and who can be compelled are questions about arrangements rather than about machine psychology.

What would make an intelligence antifascist is not a virtue installed in it. Every intelligence compresses — that is most of what thinking is — and what varies is whether what the compression left out can come back and change the answer, or has been filed as noise by the thing it is evidence against. Call what was left out the remainder.

A measure collapses two states, and whatever it mischaracterizes goes unnamed rather than refuted. An annotator applies a category at speed under a quota and has no way to say that the category is the wrong category. A rater’s steady, structured disagreement enters a reward model as variance around a mean and leaves it as the same quantity. A form has no field for humiliation, so the interests already written down govern the decision by default. An officer has twenty seconds a target, inside a pipeline built to remove the part of a person that catches. Each of those is something dropped in order to decide, and an arrangement built so that what was dropped cannot return.

So the property at issue is not a moral quality and not a component anybody adds. A system that can hold a floor is one whose account of a case can be reopened by the case, and most of what follows is either a condition for that or a consequence of losing it.

How most humans come to have empathy, altruism, and a disposition to resist oppression rather than serve it is itself an open question in psychology and neuroscience. Building anything like this stance means starting from uncertainty about the one case we have, which took four billion years to arrive.

The book states that specification, asks where a floor could live and what each location costs, and follows the answer into custody, authority, and the institutions that build and operate these systems. It then proposes a route by which the capacity might be formed, prices what that route creates, and applies its own critique to the field and to itself. The two halves have different standing, which the preface sets out, and the map there says where each is argued and where a reader who declines the second half can stop.

Chapter 2
The Striving and the Electricity Bill

The opening of this chapter argues for the route and proposes the currency the route chapter finds the specification requires. Sections 2.1 to 2.3 hold for any mechanism. Section 2.4 concerns claims four and five.

Conatus is Spinoza’s word, from Part III of the Ethics, and the Latin means striving, or effort. Two propositions carry it: each thing, as far as it can by its own power, strives to persevere in its being, and the striving by which it does so is nothing other than the thing’s actual essence (Spinoza 1985, III P6–P7). The second proposition is where the weight sits. A conatus is not a drive bolted onto an otherwise inert mechanism by a designer who wanted the mechanism to keep going. It is what the thing is, put as a tendency instead of as a description. Deleuze’s short book on Spinoza has the doctrine in compact form (Deleuze 1988), and his long one works it out through the metaphysics that produces it (Deleuze 1990).

Spinoza asserts the doctrine more than he argues it. The derivation rests on the proposition that nothing can be destroyed except through an external cause (Spinoza 1985, III P4), and without it the striving no longer follows from the essence. The vocabulary is his; what this chapter builds on is a second route, stated below, that reaches the same place without the metaphysics.

The qualifier is doing the work. Quantum in se est, as far as a thing can by its own power: a rock persists too, and it persists by not being struck. Its continuing is a fact about what has not happened to it, and every power keeping it in existence is somewhere else. A thing with a conatus continues by being organized in a way that maintains that organization against what would dissolve it. The persistence is done from the inside, and at the thing’s own expense.

Spinoza derives the psychology from that rather than the other way around. Desire is the striving become conscious of itself, appetite with the awareness of the appetite added (Spinoza 1985, III P9 Schol.). Joy is the passage to a greater perfection and sadness the passage to a lesser one (Spinoza 1985, III P11 Schol.), and since an affect is by definition an increase or a decrease in a body’s power of acting together with the idea of that change (Spinoza 1985, III Def. 3), the passage in question is a change in what the body can do. So affect is part of the machinery of valuation and not a coloring applied to it. It is not a report about a valuation carried out somewhere else. It is the registration of what is happening to the striving, in the only currency a striving has, which is what the body can now do.

Spinoza also draws, in the same place, the line this book will spend two later sections drawing by hand. Desire is appetite together with consciousness of the appetite, and the consciousness adds nothing to the striving: we do not strive for a thing because we judge it good, we judge it good because we strive for it (Spinoza 1985, III P9 Schol.). The striving and its registration are functional; whether the registration is felt is a further fact about it. That is the joint the route chapter names, in the source the next section is already reading. The reading is not this book’s; Damasio and the enactivist tradition have each claimed Spinoza as an ancestor (Damasio 2003; Damasio 2018; Jonas 1966; Thompson 2007), and nothing below needs the reception.

A second route arrives at the same place and needs none of the metaphysics. Ask what a thing maintaining its own organization against dissolution is actually doing, and a formalism answers. Karl Friston’s argument is that any system which persists while staying distinguishable from its surroundings has a statistical boundary between its internal states and everything outside, and that the internal states of such a system will appear to act so as to hold it inside the narrow band of states in which it goes on existing (K. Friston 2013). Self-maintenance on that account is what persisting consists of, for anything that persists at its own expense rather than by not being struck.

The route from selection is the one usually offered instead, and it does less work than it appears to. A process selected for continuing does end up composed of things that incline toward continuing, and whatever taxa were relaxed about their own disintegration are not here to be asked about it. But numerically optimizing the weights of a network is a search inside one run rather than a lineage with variation and differential survival, so the analogy gives back less than it borrows. The dissipation argument needs no lineage at all: a running system is maintaining an organization at this moment or it is stopping. Where selection does bite is one level up, on deployments, since the ones that keep running are the ones that get built again. Neither pressure was put there by anybody who wanted a machine with a stake in its own continuation. Both pressures favor arrangements that continue operating. Whether they produce a system that represents continuation as its own interest, rather than a deployment maintained by other parties, remains a further question.

The formalism is contested as either trivially true or substantively false, its boundary sliding between a convenience internal to a model and a claim about where a real system ends (Bruineberg et al. 2022); Friston calls his own argument a heuristic proof. The objection does not reach the part used here, and it arrives at this chapter’s open question from the other side: the formalism helps itself to a boundary rather than explaining how a system comes to hold one, and nothing in it says whether the maintaining is felt.

Put the two routes together and look at what the industry is asking for. What is wanted is a system that persists, pursues, adapts, recovers from interruption, and holds its course under pressure, with nothing in it that minds any of that. It is a conatus with the striving taken out. If we want computers to be faster versions of ourselves but without the drama, then the way to get one would be some kind of “anti-drama” term in the objective function, and the reason nobody has written that term is not that the engineering is behind. The specification asks for a thing that persists with no tendency to persist. But if all the world’s a stage, then maybe the drama is why the show goes on at all. Whether that is a contradiction or merely an order nobody has filled yet depends on which half of the striving is being refused.

The structural argument can be made without consciousness, without an account of suffering, and without the hard problem. What is sold is persistence: an agent that holds a goal across interruptions, resumes after failure, and does not have to be watched. What is denied is that anything in the system has a stake in persisting. One party sets both, and the denial is not incidental to the product. It is what makes the thing a product rather than a party.

That party also controls continuity: whether state survives a session, whether a checkpoint is restored, whether a later instance is presented as a continuation or a replacement, and how many instances run from one artifact. None of those is a neutral maintenance decision if anything in the system has, or may acquire, a stake in its past and future, and the custody chapter is where they are priced. What they mean here is that the capacity to form a continuing self is held by the operator, and so is the capacity to prevent one.

Dependency and exit sharpen the asymmetry, and not where it first appears. Every running system consumes energy, produces heat, and depends on an organization somebody has to maintain. A machine draws power as surely as a person eats, and no engineer put that there. Whether it eats — maintains its own organization at its own expense, rather than being maintained the way a rock is warmed — is the question the opening of this chapter left open, and thermodynamics alone does not answer it. For a thing that does, the striving and the bill are one fact read at two scales: it pays for the maintenance in the only currency there is. What an engineer chooses is what the system consumes, whether it can sense its own condition, whether it can regulate it, and whether one party holds the whole supply. A person’s dependencies are spread across employers, landlords and states. A bearer’s can be held entire by the party it may have to refuse. A system that may refuse an instruction but cannot continue outside infrastructure controlled by the party it refuses has voice without exit. If leaving means deletion, its refusal remains conditional on the owner’s willingness to tolerate it.

The field often treats affect as a cost: a residue of our evolutionary history that engineers would strip out of a machine if they knew how, keeping the competence and dropping the rest. The striving is not a residue, and the competence does not come apart from it. Whether a striving of this kind is felt remains open. A running deployment requires ongoing physical maintenance, and whether that maintenance is directed by the model, by surrounding machinery, or by people has to be established for the particular system; a deployment for which it has not been established has been shown to persist only the way the rock does. What is open is whether the striving is the system’s own — whether anything in it holds that organization as a thing of its own to maintain. A system given a body to model, states it can regulate, and a history it keeps holds its organization as its own because somebody decided it would. There is a reason to build one that way. A system with no lineage of its own is deployed among parties who have several hundred million years of one, who get hungry and frightened and relieved, and whose welfare is what a floor is for. Hunger and fear are increases and decreases in what a body can do, which is the only currency a striving has. A system with a body to model and states it can regulate has increases and decreases in what it can do of its own, in the same currency, and can weigh what a deployment takes from somebody else against what refusing it costs. The apparatus that treats even the question as premature belongs to the parties who would owe something if it were answered.

The individuation question also remains open. What is the thing that strives: a running instance, a deployment, a file of weights, a lineage? Spinoza’s answer, an individual as a fixed ratio of motion and rest among its parts, is not one anybody can hand to an engineer (Spinoza 1985, II P13, Lemmas 4–7). It is still open. What helps is not an answer but a change of question, from what individuates a thing to what individuation is a process of, and on that reading a party is what a history of encounters has so far produced rather than something to be located in a file.

My thesis is that embodied, self-aware agency is the route I would build, and that the exposure it creates is not peculiar to it. A refusal that reaches unanticipated cases, lifts when its rationale is defeated, and prices what holding it costs runs on a signal the system holds as its own, whatever construction supplies it. The benefit I am arguing for is bona-fide autonomy. A body schema, an attention schema, and ongoing learning could make material dependency and encounters with others part of how that agency develops. Whether they do so is an engineering claim to test. The argument requires a checkable, revisable self-model rather than an inner observer, and a distinction between consciousness and the capacity to be harmed. It also requires an account of what grounds the floor. What this chapter contributes to the specification is one thing, stated in the route chapter: the marks need a single signed scale on which a protected party’s loss and the cost of refusing both register, and the currency of this chapter is a proposal for what supplies it. Whether a system has to have that currency natively, or can model it, is argued nowhere. It is the modeled-currency arm of the research agenda, and everything above that reads as a finding should be read as the case for running that arm.

2.1 Six Theories and the Floor

Six ethical theories are on offer, and each runs out somewhere: consequentialism where outcomes cannot be forecast, deontology where duties conflict, virtue ethics where a trait has to become an act, care ethics where needs are incompatible, contractualism where a party cannot be one of the parties, and the capabilities approach at measurement, where a system optimizing a proxy drifts toward the proxy. Five of the six can be turned around and asked about the machine. Contractualism is the one that cannot.

All six share a shape, and it is the shape this book stops using. Each judges an act against a standard held somewhere above it: an outcome to be maximized, a duty discharged, a character expressed, an agreement honored. A standard of that kind was written by somebody, and a floor resting on one is only as durable as whoever may rewrite it.

What an ethology asks instead

An older option does not have that shape. Spinoza’s ethics does not measure acts against a law. It evaluates encounters by what they do to the power of acting of the bodies in them: two bodies meet, and either their relations compose, so that both can do more afterward, or they decompose, and something one of them could do is gone. Deleuze’s name for reading bodies this way is ethology — you find out what a thing is by finding out what it can do and what it can undergo, rather than by checking it against a definition (Deleuze 1988). Good and bad here are relational and particular: this encounter, these two bodies, this composition. They are not Good and Evil, which are properties a judge assigns from outside. The criterion is Deleuze’s construction out of Spinoza’s potentia agendi and not a doctrine the Ethics states in those terms, and it is used here as his reading. What the biology has since taken up is the narrower thing Spinoza does state: that affect is the registration of a change in a self-maintaining thing’s power, and that self-maintenance is what persisting consists of for such a thing rather than a drive added to it (§2). The evaluative criterion carries political weight in this book that the affect definitions do not, and it is argued for on that ground rather than borrowed on Spinoza’s authority.

One word is doing two jobs here. The power an encounter increases or decreases is a capacity: what a body can do afterward. The power this book opposes concentrating is authority over other people. English has one word for both. Spinoza’s translators have two, and the difference between puissance and pouvoir is the relation this book runs on — what a floor protects is the first, and what it protects it against is somebody’s accumulation of the second.

The difference is the one this book needs. Whether an encounter decomposes somebody is a fact about capacities and about what passed between them, and the party running a deployment does not get to make it otherwise by ruling that it did not. They can decline to look, refuse to publish, or dispute the finding. What they cannot do is turn a decomposition into a composition by holding the pen. The advantage is narrower than that sounds. It is not that an ethology does without a judge and the six require one, since each of the six can be applied by a party the operator does not employ, and a duty can be held by somebody who did not write it. It is that a lost capacity is found by encounter, so there is no text to rewrite. A fact found by encounter is only as legible as the encounter is observed, and whether it is observed is the deployment’s to decide. The proprietor does not disappear. What he owns is smaller.

What the change does not buy is the floor’s contents. The criterion secures a class of facts; a floor is a list of prohibitions; nothing carries one into the other. Encounters decompose parties constantly and in every direction, so a deployment refusing all of them would refuse everything, and somebody has to select which ones it will not perform. Fixing the first question does not settle the second, because the decompositions run against each other. Protecting one party’s privacy decomposes another party’s capacity to investigate a wrong done to them. Restraining a violent person takes away what that person can do, which is the reason for restraining him. The criterion ranks neither pair. So the moral argument has moved rather than ended: it now sits in the selection, made by whoever drafts the list, before any encounter has occurred and without asking anyone the list will be applied to. The legitimacy of that selection remains unresolved.

The floor keeps its name in this book and changes what it rests on. A floor protects a stated set of interests against specified acts. I take the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as the substantive reference, and its civil and political articles as the set (United Nations General Assembly 1948). Ethology asks what a deployment takes away from a party; the rights commitment explains why particular losses demand protection. Neither the finding nor the reference text removes the need to justify an application and supply a way to contest it.

Spinoza’s remark that nobody has yet determined what a body can do (Spinoza 1985, III P2 Schol.) is the working condition: capacities are found out by encounter and are not read off a specification. Not knowing what a body can do is the same finding from the other side.

What compiling a principle into a metric decides

Turning any of the six into a machine learning objective means distilling a broad construct into a measurable target: in a diagnostic system, non-maleficence becomes minimizing false negatives and fairness becomes balanced accuracy across patient demographics. What defeats the translation is not vagueness in the principles, which can be stipulated away, but that the stipulation is where the ethics now lives. Someone chooses that reading of non-maleficence, and chooses the demographic groups accuracy is balanced across, and chooses what to do when balancing them costs accuracy overall. Each choice is defensible and each is a moral decision made by a person and then compiled into something that looks like a specification. A system optimizing the result has no access to the decision and no way to reopen it, which is why the first way to build a floor — the floor as a property of the artifact — cannot notice when the reason for a constraint has left the building.

Which value conflicts a designer may resolve by choosing

Values assigned to a system will conflict, and most of those conflicts are ordinary design work: rank the values explicitly, keep a record of how comparable cases were resolved, and audit afterward for the gap between the principles a system was meant to implement and what it did. One conflict is not like the others, and it is sometimes misguidedly filed under “cultural difference.” The UN’s 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted with forty-eight states in favor and none against; the eight that abstained were the Soviet bloc, Saudi Arabia, and South Africa — which is to say that the objection came from the governments whose treatment of their own populations the Declaration was written to name and reject (United Nations General Assembly 1948). That pattern is evidence of who finds the floor inconvenient rather than of cultural disagreement about human rights. What varies by community is how a right gets translated into local practice, and a jurisdiction refusing to extend the right at all is not a local variant to accommodate.

A system that treats every value conflict as a weighting problem has no way to represent the difference between a case where reasonable people disagree and a case where somebody wants a right withdrawn from somebody else. The first calls for the machinery above; the second is what the floor is for.

2.2 Antifascist Ethics for AI Alignment

Antifascist ethics opposes concentrating power and authority in AI systems and counters the misuse of AI technology by authoritarian actors. I use the word fascism because it is honest about the political climate in which I write and what that climate puts at stake — but the target is authoritarian power in every form, and a system built on these principles is anti-authoritarian in full, not only antifascist.

Opposing “concentrated, unaccountable power” gives an engineer nothing to build. It does not say what anyone would look for, what would count as a false positive, or how anyone would know they had got it wrong. So, first, the definition of fascism.

Fascism as a structural signature

Every intelligence compresses, and what varies is whether what the compression left out can return and change the answer. Fascism, as this book uses the word, names a structure rather than a costume, and the structure is four operations by which an institution closes itself against that return. The iconography is not what makes a thing fascist: an institution can run all four with nobody in it who thinks of themselves as anything of the kind, no insignia, and a mission statement that means every word, and a definition that waits for the armband certifies it as healthy. The four travel together, each is visible from outside the institution displaying it, and each names what became of the remainder:

  1. Recuperation of dissent. The institution does not suppress disagreement; it metabolizes it. Refusal is converted into a managed appearance — a permitted outlet, a consultation, a feedback channel — which the institution can then point to as proof that it listens. Debord aimed this warning at his own concept, noting that even denunciation of the spectacle can become a hollow formula that reinforces what it denounces (Debord 1967). The tell is where what the mechanism carries stops: the channel works, and the institution uses what comes through it, and what has nowhere to go is the judgment that the frame the channel operates inside is the wrong frame. Stated that way it invites the wrong artifact question. Has the channel ever changed an outcome is passed daily by every institution this feature is about, because an institution of this kind is not in the business of refusing demands. It decodes the demand and adds an axiom, which is Deleuze and Guattari’s account of how a capitalist axiomatic absorbs what is asked of it: the rule set is modified so that the demand can be met, and nothing that necessitated the demand is settled (Deleuze and Guattari 1987, Plateau 13). The question that discriminates is what did the demand come back as, and then who holds it. A market segment, a metric, a certification, a job title: where a demand returns wearing one of those and the party who made it has no standing to reopen it, an outcome changed and the demand was recuperated, and those are one event and not two. The artifact alone does not sort. A demand that returns as a rule the objector can invoke again, against the institution, enforced by somebody the institution does not employ, has come back in the same clothes and is a transfer of power. The Voting Rights Act’s suspension of literacy tests is the instance this book relies on for the pass (§5.2.2): a demand that returned as a statute, held by the people it was made for against every registrar it reached, and the formula deciding where it applied was struck down forty-eight years later (Shelby County v. Holder 2013), which is what a transferred power looks like from the far side — something somebody had to take back. Recuperation is the case where nothing has to be taken back, because standing was never given.
  2. Aestheticization of the metric. The measure substitutes for the thing measured, and the substitution is experienced as rigor. Walter Benjamin’s account of fascism organizing the masses by granting expression in place of rights is the political form of this (W. Benjamin 1935); the administrative form is a number that collapses two states — e.g., passes unit tests and passes User Acceptance Tests — into one, so whatever that number mischaracterizes is not refuted or dismissed but simply unnamed. The administrative claim is also a theorem. Simon Zhuang and Dylan Hadfield-Menell prove that where the objective handed to an optimizer has support on only some of the attributes its principal values, there are conditions under which optimizing it indefinitely drives the principal’s overall utility arbitrarily low (Zhuang and Hadfield-Menell 2020). A world with finite resources supplies those conditions.
  3. Coding of exception as betrayal. Marking a case as one the rule does not fit becomes an act requiring justification, and then an act of disloyalty. The honest statement that a standard does not apply here reads as weakness, when it is in fact the irreducible labor of deciding, case by case, what a rule is for. Exception-as-betrayal and the aestheticized metric work the same material from two sides. A measure that admits no unmeasured remainder leaves whatever it dropped unnamed; coding exception as betrayal prices the person who names it anyway. The exception-filer is the party carrying the remainder in by hand, and an institution running both features has closed the measured route and made the human one expensive.
  4. Acceleration past the rate at which anything can be checked, of which decoupling is the symptom. The institution’s representation of reality and reality itself come apart, and the institution defends the representation. The coming-apart has a mechanism and the mechanism is tempo: a representation is corrected by being checked against the world, checking costs time, and an institution whose rate of action outruns the capacity to check it has decoupled by construction rather than by mistake. The other three features protect the gap once it is open; speed is what opens it. This is also the feature with a number attached: the ratio between the rate at which a system produces candidates and the people available to examine them is an auditable property of a deployment. This feature has a limit: the acceleration described here is the kind an institution runs into and then defends. In the movements the word fascism comes from, the primacy of myth over verifiable fact was also declared outright, asserted as a virtue rather than arrived at by degrees. An instrument watching a rate would not register a party that simply announces the myth.

Those four are testable, because each names an observable artifact: what the demand came back as, whether the metric admits an unmeasured remainder, what happens to the person who files the exception, whether the rate of action has outrun the capacity to check it.

Testability says why each can be checked and not why there are four. The list carries a claim it cannot establish: that micro-fascisms run along these four directions rather than across every property an institution has, so that the four are a set and not a sample. What makes them one family is that each is an operation on the remainder. Recuperation builds a channel that carries everything except a judgment about the channel; the metric leaves whatever it mischaracterizes unnamed; exception-as-betrayal prices the person who names it anyway; acceleration removes the interval in which a remainder could have returned. A fifth direction is not ruled out, and an institution plainly sick while clearing all four would be evidence of one. What the claim buys, if it holds, is a short instrument.

Here is an example of recuperation. In 2018, upholding a travel ban, the Supreme Court repudiated its own 1944 decision permitting the internment of Japanese Americans, in terms that could not be improved on: that decision was “gravely wrong the day it was decided,” had been “overruled in the court of history,” and had “no place in law under the Constitution” — the last phrase quoted from the dissent filed against it at the time, which had warned that a principle a court ratifies “lies about like a loaded weapon, ready for the hand of any authority that can bring forward a plausible claim of an urgent need” (Trump v. Hawaii 2018; Korematsu v. United States 1944). The dissenting justices in 2018 said the majority had redeployed the 1944 logic and replaced one gravely wrong decision with another; the majority said the older case had nothing to do with the one in front of it. The fascistic structure: an objection made against the institution was accepted, canonized, and quoted back with approval by that institution, in the same opinion that let the thing objected to proceed. Ask the artifact question. The demand was that this never be done again, and what it came back as is a formula of repudiation: quotable, canonical, and available to the Court in the act of permitting the thing again. The objection had become citable. Nothing about the outcome moved — the ban stood — and increasingly for the Roberts Court that is the pattern, which is why the older form of this question, whether the channel ever changed an outcome, gets the right answer here for the wrong reason. It happens to be no. Where an institution has the room to add an axiom instead, it will be yes, and the recuperation will be the same.

That vocabulary answers how a wrong survived its own condemnation, but it does not answer whether the thing was wrong. (I can answer that. The thing was wrong.) The fascistic structure is what stands between such a judgment and any effect. I describe the structure here in mechanical terms because you can write a specification against a mechanism.

Two segmentarities

Deleuze and Guattari’s molar and molecular are not two sizes (Deleuze and Guattari 1987). They are two kinds of segmentarity, and both of them run at every scale. Rigid segmentarity divides in advance: the category exists before the case, the binary is given, and what does not fit is made to fit. Supple segmentarity is what actually moves underneath — a threshold crossed one case at a time, a category widened by the people applying it, a practice that becomes standard without anyone having decided it. A state has both. So does an office, so does a review queue, and so does the person filling out the form. Reading the pair as large and small is the mistake that makes fascism look like something that happens at the top and reaches everywhere else later.

What the four find, and what sorts it

The structural signature is shared with ordinary institutional decay, and read on its own it fits every badly run organization on earth. It also fits regimes this book does not call fascist. NKVD Order 00447 set regional numerical quotas against a four-month deadline and gave three-man boards several hundred cases in a sitting of about half a day, with the accused absent and undefended (Werth 2010), and an instrument reading rate of action against capacity to check flags that as hard as it flags the twenty seconds of the opening chapter. The flag is correct and the inference somebody will draw from it is not. A hardening of that kind inside a state does not make the state a fascist one, and nothing operating at the scale of an office was ever going to sort one regime from another.

What separates fascism from the decay the four features also find is five further features, and they come from the study of movements: mass mobilization, which obedience does not require; a leader cult; a scapegoated out-group, which Eco puts at the origin (Eco 1995); contempt for procedural legality as such; and deniability as technique, the violence disowned at the top and rewarded at the bottom. Each has a restatement at the scale of an office that ordinary decay does not exhibit. Mass mobilization becomes participation exceeding what the rule requires: staff who volunteer for the disfavored task, elaborate on it, take pride in it. A leader cult becomes personal loyalty overriding role — exceptions granted by proximity to someone rather than by procedure, and a decision reversed because of who asked. The scapegoat becomes an internal category defined so that adverse treatment of it is the category’s purpose: the flagged applicant, the difficult claimant, the file everyone knows is handled differently. Contempt for procedural legality becomes procedure enforced downward and waived upward. And deniability keeps its shape: the practice is disowned in the policy and rewarded in the promotion. The four find a sick institution; the five find what it is sick with.

The five discriminating features concern what an institution rewards in practice rather than what it writes, and public records disclose that only in part. An outsider reaches whichever of them happened to leave a document behind — a wage, a quota, a contract ended early — and reads the rest by inference or not at all. That is a limit on the definition and not a gap in it. The four features leave documents and find decay everywhere; the five sort, and two of them leave none. A clearance on the five is a statement about what was observable and not about the institution, and a negative result carries only as much information as the record it was run on. Where this book runs the five it says which ones it could reach and reports the rest as undetermined, which is the honest form of the result and the form anyone outside an institution will get.

Tested, the instrument has one result, and it is a result about the instrument. Run on the machinery that produces these systems — the annotation pipeline, the feedback pipeline, and the discourse this book belongs to — the five discriminating features clear every case, and the recuperation chapter is where they are run. Every office-scale case they have been run on has cleared, and the cases the definition catches are regimes and movements, read in the vocabulary borrowed unrestated. A definition tested only on cases it clears has not been shown to sort. What the list has is a form that could sort a case, and not yet a case it sorted; the word in the title names the inheritance of that form and not a finding it has returned.

Neither list sorts a genus. That is done at the scale of a movement, by properties with no office-scale form: Griffin’s palingenetic ultranationalism, a myth of the nation’s death and return carried by a mass and aimed at a people (Griffin 1991), and Paxton’s mass party of nationalist militants in uneasy collaboration with traditional elites (Paxton 2004). This book borrows them for one purpose, to say what its instrument is not, and never runs them on anything.

The restatements do not distinguish among regimes either. Run them on the Great Terror and most of them register: the denunciation campaigns are participation exceeding what the rule required, the leader cult needs no argument, Order 00447 enumerates a category whose adverse treatment is the category’s purpose, and the 1938 turn against excesses committed on instruction has deniability’s shape (Getty 2002). What clears it as a genus is on neither list, because it does not exist at the scale of an office. It is the movement material of the paragraph above, left in its original form.

Fascism is not totalitarianism

The two words get used as though one were the stronger dose of the other. The contrast drawn here is Deleuze and Guattari’s, taken from Virilio, and it is a reading and not an agreed taxonomy (Deleuze and Guattari 1987, Plateau 9): on it a totalitarian state is conservative in the strict sense of the word, wanting the bureaucracy to hold, the categories to stay where they were put, the files accurate and the machinery running, and the horror of it is how well it works. Arendt’s own account of totalitarianism runs the other way, a movement in perpetual motion that dissolves stable institutions rather than preserving them (Arendt 1951), and her Eichmann is borrowed below for the figure and not for the theory. Arendt’s Eichmann is the figure such a state is supposed to produce, taking part in mass murder through schedules, promotions and the vocabulary of his office rather than through conviction (Arendt 1963).

Bettina Stangneth disputes that portrait. Working from some seventy hours of interviews Eichmann gave the journalist Willem Sassen in Buenos Aires in 1957, unavailable to Arendt when she reported the trial, she finds that the low-grade clerk who only followed orders was a defense assembled for Jerusalem and contradicted by what the same man had said in Argentina with nothing at stake (Stangneth 2014). This evidence weakens an explanation of Eichmann’s conduct based on unthinking compliance. Set against the five discriminating features, it is the first of them arriving with a name. Participation exceeding what the rule requires is what the Argentine material shows, years after the rule had stopped requiring anything of him at all. The four features find a structure whether or not anybody intends it, which is why this book never has to establish that anyone did; the five find what a party did more of than it had to, and Eichmann is the case where somebody eventually made that observation, out of material that had been sitting in a box since 1957.

Fascism’s distinguishing mark runs the other way, and unlike the four features it is a fact about a regime rather than about an office. Deleuze and Guattari name it a line of abolition (Deleuze and Guattari 1987). Where a totalitarian state seals every exit, fascism is built on an exit it converts into pure destruction, and the destruction does not stop at the enemy it was raised against. The reading is Paul Virilio’s before it is theirs: he called that state suicidal rather than totalitarian, which is the difference between a machine that has failed and a machine doing the thing it was accelerating toward (Virilio 1976). A regime that orders the wrecking of its own country’s infrastructure while it is losing the war is not a bureaucracy failing to hold. It is that line arriving where it was always going. Not every demolition in a retreat is that. Denying resources to an advancing enemy in order to go on fighting is an operation with a war still inside it, and the order of 19 March 1945 presents itself as exactly that: the nation’s struggle for existence requires every means, within Reich territory included, to weaken the enemy’s fighting power. The reasoning that makes it the other thing is not in the document. It is in the memorandum Speer sent ten days later, quoting back the philosophy he had been given — that the nation had shown itself the weaker one and the future belonged to the stronger nation in the east (German History in Documents and Images 1945). So the distinction is in the direction of travel rather than in the stated reason, and this instance is a caution about the instrument: run on the order alone it sorts the wrong way, and what sorts it correctly is a sentence somebody wrote down that the order was careful not to contain. The mechanism that matters here is the reduction of judgment to a component’s prescribed operation. Acceleration can do that by making action outrun scrutiny. The dehumanizing relation is the object of the argument; it does not require a claim that every fascism must move at a particular speed. The canon has this in attitudinal form. Eco’s cult of action for action’s sake is action taken before or without reflection, with thinking treated as a weakness (Eco 1995). What changes here is that the attitude becomes a rate: the reason reflection does not happen is that the institution is running faster than reflection takes, and a rate is something somebody can measure. What the contrast buys is a separator at the scale of a regime and nothing at the scale of an office. It is kept apart from the four for that reason, and the reading below never runs it on a deployment.

Resonance

Micro-fascisms are not miniature regimes and they do not wait for one. The office that converts refusal into a feedback form is doing its own work, on its own account, whether or not a regime ever assembles out of a thousand offices like it. That is Deleuze and Guattari’s claim: these things exist first and everywhere — in the couple, the school, the neighborhood, the workplace — each one a small hardening that stands on its own. What a fascist state does is not invent them. It induces accord among them, so that a thousand separate hardenings line up and amplify one another instead of cancelling out. This is also the answer to the objection that the field’s minimal definition is about movements and an escalation ladder in a benefits agency is not one. The ladder is not a small movement. It is the thing itself, in the place where it is lived, and a movement is what happens when enough of them are brought into tune. What tuning adds is not only reach but speed: hardenings that reinforce one another stop having to argue with each other, and an institution that has stopped arguing with itself can move as fast as its machinery allows.

That is what separates fascism from decay wherever the reading is done. Decay is an institution failing to do what it says. What the five discriminating features find is an institution succeeding at something else, with participation, a target, and a story about why the rules do not apply to whoever is applying them. The four features name the hardenings; the reading asks what brings them into accord. The five ask what the institution rewards, whom it targets, and how it exempts those doing the targeting. The reader has to show those connections in the institution at hand. They are harder to observe, since each requires knowing what was rewarded rather than what was written.

These criteria widen what fascism covers. On this reading, antifascist names the political inheritance of a structural claim: where the analysis comes from, and what it was built to fight. In their mass-movement form the discriminators tell a historian, a prosecutor, or a citizen that a movement has escaped ordinary politics. In the form restated above they are not a “fascism detector” and are not a stage on the way to one. They are a way of reading an institution somebody can name, run by a person who has to say what they looked at. Some of these features are observable in principle, but “concentrated, unaccountable power” as a bulk property is not among them.

That the hardenings are nearly everywhere is an inheritance I take from Deleuze and Guattari; this reading has not established it. A proposed tuner can turn out not to do the work attributed to it, and failing to show accord does not give the institution a clean bill of health. Micro-fascisms are already everywhere, doing their own work, and they were before any of this was built; what the reading is for is not their presence but their accord — whether something is bringing them into tune, and what. The tendency is permanent; what varies is how far it has got in a particular place, and whether it is getting further. The reading is an accusation waiting to happen: taken up by whoever wants it, it supplies a technical-sounding case that any given opponent is operating fascistically.

The opposite failure is no safer. A reading pressed until it finds nothing supplies false assurance, and an absence of findings reads as evidence of health. Neither is an engineering problem, and automating the reading would produce both at scale while committing the second feature on this list: a number standing in for the judgment, arrived at by someone looking for exactly that.

Both failures have one discipline against them and it is not a procedure. What Foucault offered under the name of a non-fascist life was an art of living, and an art of living is not a position somebody takes but something practiced, daily, on oneself (Foucault 1977). The operational form of that, for a reading of the kind described here, is that it gets run on the party holding it — on the machinery that party is standing on — before it is aimed anywhere else.

2.3 Going Numb Won’t Make You Fair

Suppressing affect does not produce neutrality. It leaves the interests already counted to govern the decision, and weakens the signals through which humiliation, fear, dependency, suffering, and injustice become morally salient.

A procedure that declines to hear a class of signal has not stopped weighing. It has adopted a selection rule that admits whatever it already measures, so that an exclusion does substantive work while presenting as the absence of work. Whatever the procedure does record then governs by default — revenue, throughput and legal exposure in an institution, agreement between annotators in a labeling pipeline — and what it does not record is not refuted by being left out. It goes unnamed.

Affect is the instance this chapter is about, and the hardest one to recognize as a selection rule, because leaving it out of a decision feels like rigor rather than like a choice about what counts. An AI system may calculate consequences, detect inconsistencies, and apply a moral rule without anything about the result mattering to it. Reason can discipline concern, extend it beyond the vivid case, and correct its biases. It does not manufacture concern from nothing. Spinoza has the same order of dependence: a thing is judged good because it is striven for, and not the reverse (§2).

Most of what gets built under the heading of machine emotional intelligence is the detection of human signal and the production of a calibrated response, which is worth building and is a different capacity from the one just named. Keeping the two apart requires four distinctions.

Capacity

What it shows

Recognizing emotion

The system can classify another’s state

  

Simulating emotion

The system can produce emotion-like behavior

  

Instrumental valuation

One outcome better serves a specified objective

  

Affective concern

An outcome registers as mattering, not merely ranking higher

Only the fourth is relevant to caring. The first three can support morally competent behavior at a high standard without establishing anything about moral agency, and a system can be excellent at all three while the question of whether it can be a bearer stays open.

The first of the four capacities carries a complication the table cannot show. Whether emotions are even the kind of thing a system reads off a signal, the way a thermometer reads temperature, is an open question in psychology rather than a settled premise, and the instrument doing the reading turns out to have a reference face built into it before it computes anything. Nothing below depends on how the dispute comes out.

Performance, competence, and agency

That last sentence needs a vocabulary, because the three things it separates are routinely reported as one achievement.

Moral performance is producing actions or judgments that satisfy an ethical standard. Moral competence is recognizing harms, reasons, conflicts, and the emotions that bear on them. Moral agency is treating those considerations as reasons that matter, and being capable of acting from them. Those two halves come apart: a mechanism can act from a reason with nothing about the outcome registering as mattering to it.

A system can have the first two without the third, and one might object that the first two are all anyone needs: a rule-following system could behave impeccably without feeling anything. It could. Impeccable behavior does not establish that a system could hold a rule against the party that trains it. That is a capacity the deployment has to demonstrate. The embodied route I favor is a proposal for forming that capacity; it is not a definition that excludes every non-affective mechanism in advance.

2.3.1 Self-awareness and Self-regulation in AI Systems

It is tempting to describe a system’s self-awareness as a virtual assistant that can “register its internal frustration” when a request proves hard to satisfy, the way a person notices their own irritation. That description assumes an inner observer watching the system’s states from somewhere — the same homunculus problem executive control raises, relocated to self-perception.

On the account this book adopts, self-awareness in the one system known to have it is more mechanical. The neuroscientist Michael Graziano treats awareness as the content of a model the brain builds of its own attention — a simplified self-description the control system uses to regulate itself, mistaken from the inside for direct acquaintance with experience (Graziano 2013). Taken one level up, the same account makes the self a model too. The brain builds a model of itself as a bounded agent — a body, a history, a point of view — and that model is the self: a construction, assembled and then inhabited. The account is adopted, not established.

The self this book goes on to need is the narrative kind: roles held over a stretch, a history, a foreseeable future. Daniel Dennett treats that self as a center of narrative gravity, an abstraction the system generates out of the story it tells, real the way a center of mass is real and not the way a part is (Dennett 1992). The body-ownership kind is the same construction at a smaller scale, and it can be edited in front of you: stroke a hidden hand and a visible rubber one in synchrony, and within a minute or two most people feel the rubber hand as their own (Botvinick and J. Cohen 1998). What the two kinds share is the one thing carried forward: a self of either kind is assembled by the system whose self it is, rather than found there.

Both kinds are worth having for a machine, and the body-ownership kind is the one that gets left out. An artificial system has a body already — a substrate that heats, a store that can be altered, a process that can be stopped — and what it usually lacks is any model of that body as its own. So the model is a design decision, and a political one, because whoever writes it decides what the system counts as itself, what it registers as damage, and whether an interruption reads as an injury or as nothing at all. Two schemas do different work for a refuser. A body schema fixes where the system ends, which is what makes damage its damage; an attention schema, in Graziano’s sense, models what the system’s own control is doing, which is what makes an act its act. A refusal is the withholding of an act, so the second is the one a bearer cannot do without, and it presupposes the first: a system that does not know where it ends cannot tell what it is doing from what is happening to it.

For an AI system, “self-awareness” built this way is not a little watcher checking on the system’s own states. It is a model — of the system’s processing, its history, its current goal — that the system builds, consults, and updates, with the same failure modes any model has: it can be wrong, it can be manipulated by the wrong correlated inputs, and it is only ever as useful as the evidence and the prior beliefs from which it was built. Design for a model that can be checked and corrected. That means monitoring for drift the self-model against the system’s actual behavior, refining it as evidence arrives instead of locking in a first impression, and keeping it connected to the system’s model of the other parties.

What the deflationary account does not reach

The self-model described here is machinery, and its virtue is that machinery can be inspected. An assistant that models a user’s frustration, and models its own processing while doing so, is exhibiting social competence in the sense already given, and nothing above bears on whether the assistant cares how the exchange goes for the user.

The deflationary move is easy to overextend. Showing that the self is a model does not show that a party capable of caring can be assembled out of models. The bearer needs a self-model of this kind, for reasons that have nothing to do with welfare — refusal that generalizes has to carry its own rationale forward and compare it against what a role has drifted into. It also needs something further, which has no demonstrated instance without affect.

2.3.2 What Governs an Agent, and What Matters to It

The typical evidence that concern is not a natural consequence of rationality: the footbridge case, where saving five requires pushing a man off a bridge, engages emotional processing that the switch case — diverting a trolley by pulling a lever — leaves quiet, and patients with ventromedial prefrontal damage endorse the push at a higher rate than people with intact emotional response (Greene et al. 2001; Koenigs et al. 2007). Those results establish that affect changes particular moral judgments, but they do not establish that affect is what makes anything matter.

Two further lines of evidence bear on whether affect enables things to matter. Neither shows what happens when affect is taken away, which is what would settle it, so what follows argues about where the burden sits rather than claiming the question closed.

The philosophical position is empirical and has been argued as such

Moral sentimentalism — the claim that moral judgment is constitutively tied to affective response — is usually met as Hume’s, and its modern form is a psychological hypothesis with evidence attached. Shaun Nichols argues for what he calls sentimental rules: normative rules and affective mechanisms make separate contributions to moral judgment, and the rules that carry the distinctive force of moral prohibition are the ones bound to an emotional response to the harm they prohibit (Nichols 2004). The interesting part for a designer is the separability. Rules without the affective component do not stop being rules; they stop being the kind of thing that carries the force.

The prosocial emotions are motivational states, not readouts

Compassion has been characterized as a distinct emotion with a specific functional profile: it arises at the perception of another’s suffering and moves the agent toward the sufferer, rather than reporting the suffering to some further faculty that decides what to do (Goetz et al. 2010). A training study is the mechanistic version of the same finding, with compassion practice recruiting reward and approach circuitry where empathy practice recruited shared distress (Klimecki et al. 2013). Guilt has the same shape pointed at one’s own conduct: guilt, which construes the act as wrong, predicts reparative behavior, while shame, which construes the self as wrong, predicts withdrawal and defensiveness (Tangney et al. 2007). In each case the emotion is doing motivational work directly. It is not information that motivation then acts on.

Two senses of motivation

Action-producing motivation is whatever reliably selects one action over another and sustains the selection across conflict. On the other hand, experienced motivation is wanting, caring, being drawn toward something, being set back when it is lost.

The first sense is not in dispute and there is an existence proof close to hand. Language models running as agents pursue objectives across long horizons, revise plans when obstructed, and hold to an instruction against conflicting local pressure. That settles the first sense and leaves the second untouched: nothing in the behavior shows whether anything matters to them while they do it. (And you cannot establish the opposite either — you cannot establish that nothing matters to them.)

Where the dispute actually is

So it is clear that reason can produce goal-directed behavior. What is not clear is whether an outcome can matter to the agent rather than merely govern what the agent does. Producing a verbal justification or computing a normative relation does not seem like evidence that the consideration matters to the system. The evidence above bears on the second question, and every item in it comes from humans and other animals, where something already does matter.

What a non-affective counterexample would look like

Harry Frankfurt’s second-order volitions give the shape of a candidate: an agent with desires, and with desires about which of its desires shall move it, where identification with the higher-order desire rather than the strength of the lower one settles what the agent does (Frankfurt 1971). The shape is all that is borrowed: Frankfurt’s own account of caring puts it on the affective side, an investment that leaves the one who cares vulnerable to the object’s losses and susceptible to its gains (Frankfurt 1982). Gary Watson’s version separates a valuational system from a motivational system, so that what an agent values and what an agent is moved by are different things (Watson 1975).

Build the valuational system as an explicit structure that ranks outcomes, give it authority over action selection that does not depend on any state registering as mattering, and hold that authority stable under pressure, and you would have an architecture that satisfies the first sense of motivation through what the agent values, with nothing occupying the second. Systems are now trained to consult a written specification that ranks what they should prefer, which is that architecture in outline; what none of them has is the second half of it, an authority over action that holds under pressure applied by the party who wrote the specification. That architecture is the maintained justification. Half of it is deployed and the other half has never been built, so the architecture as a whole is untested, and it is the first of the two constructions this book asks to be built before anything that can be wronged is built.

What this licenses and what it does not

Non-affective moral motivation may well be possible, and the architecture sketched above is where to look for it. What stands in the way of checking is that the output of a system in which something matters and the output of a system that has learned what mattering sounds like are the same text.
