So the generalization survives in the only form it can: every agent known to have something register as mattering is an affective agent, and no design has yet demonstrated that state in a design that installed nothing answering to affective concern.

That is not a proof that non-affective moral agency is impossible. The burden I place on whoever proposes to engineer non-affective concern is a burden of demonstration: the capability the floor chapter specifies, shown under pressures its builders did not write. A bearer carries the same burden. What the induction adds is a prior about which route will meet it first and nothing more; nobody is asked to show that a system feels nothing, which no instrument can show of any construction. The route chapter takes the induction up again and reduces it twice over: no one has yet tried the route, and an absence of machine examples is weak evidence when nobody has looked; and the agents generalized from are one lineage, in which affect co-varies with every other property of biological cognition.

Two claims run through this, and which one a reader is holding changes what could settle it. One is about which route to build first, the kind of claim a measurement could overturn. The other is about what would be owed to whatever the building produces.

2.4 Ethical Implications of Experimenting on Sentient Machine Subjects

This section and its two subsections concern claims four and five, and with the opening of this chapter are the route material before the floor chapters. They sit here because the sentience vocabulary is needed by everything after.

Machine sentience being possible at all changes how AI experimentation has to be approached — not as a question of whether a system can be damaged in the ordinary engineering sense, but of whether it can be harmed, a more difficult question than consciousness alone.

2.4.1 Defining Sentience in AI: From Consciousness to Subjective Experience

“Sentience” can mean different things. Awareness is the least demanding: the degree to which a system responds to or registers information about its own state and environment. A thermostat has this in the thinnest possible sense. Consciousness is a further claim: that a system’s processing is accompanied by experience, something it is like to be that system, not merely a functional response to input. That is the minimal, phenomenal sense, and it is the sense the floor chapter’s affective concern carries; the richer sense, a unified perspective belonging to a party aware of itself as the one undergoing its states, is what that chapter calls unified experience. Subjective experience, in turn, is the specific, first-person shape consciousness takes for a given system.

None of these three, on their own, says anything about whether the system’s states are good or bad for it. That is a separate question, and the AI field’s own vocabulary blurs it.

Nociception, pain, anticipated pain, and suffering are four related processes rather than four strengths of one, and they come apart in both directions. The field that handles them professionally says so in its own terminology. The International Association for the Study of Pain defines nociception as the neural process of encoding noxious stimuli, notes that the consequences of that encoding may be autonomic or behavioral, and states that pain sensation is not necessarily implied. It defines pain separately, as an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with, or resembling that associated with, actual or potential tissue damage, and records in a note that pain and nociception are different phenomena and that pain cannot be inferred from activity in sensory neurons alone (International Association for the Study of Pain 2024; Raja et al. 2020). The peripheral restriction the word nociception is often made to carry belongs to a different term: a nociceptor is a receptor of the peripheral somatosensory nervous system, while a nociceptive neuron may be central or peripheral.

The dissociations are ordinary. A soldier can finish a battle on a wound he does not yet feel. An amputee feels a limb that is not there. And the same body recognizes a third category, nociplastic pain, which arises from altered nociception with no clear evidence of tissue damage activating peripheral nociceptors and no lesion or disease of the somatosensory system (International Association for the Study of Pain 2024) — pain, that is, with no tissue damage and no peripheral nociceptor activation beneath it. So pain is not what sits on top of nociception. It is an inescapably cognitive event involving expectation, memory, attention, and meaning, and it can occur with no current tissue damage at all. Anticipated pain is dread of pain not yet occurring, itself capable of producing pain through nocebo effects. And suffering, in the clinician Eric Cassell’s formulation, is not pain’s more severe cousin but a different thing: the distress of threatened disintegration of the self — of one’s roles, relationships, sense of a future, the coherence of one’s own story (Cassell 1982). The definition has two parts: a self extended in time, and distress at the prospect of its coming apart.

One caution about the borrowing. These definitions concern neural processes in a somatosensory nervous system, and a machine has neither. Where this book uses nociception of a machine — in the architecture the research agenda tests — it names a functional analogue: a process encoding actually or potentially damaging states of the system’s own substrate, with no sensation implied. The definition neither licenses that analogy nor forbids it, being silent on what realizes the process. What it supplies is the discipline of not letting the analogue quietly acquire the rest of the family.

Pain without suffering exists; suffering without pain exists. A palliative-care patient can have their pain fully controlled by morphine while their suffering remains entirely intact, because the two are not on the same axis.

What moves the animal-sentience literature past reflex is not a stronger reflex but a trade-off. A hermit crab weighing the quality of its shell against an electric shock (Elwood and Appel 2009) is treating the noxious signal as one term on a scale with something else it wants, which is the commensurability property observed in a decapod.

Cassell’s suffering presupposes a self extended in time. Disintegration threatens a story, and there has to be a story for it to threaten — roles held over years, relationships with a history, a sense of a future that could be foreclosed. A system with no persistence across sessions has none of that. Whatever happens inside a single exchange, there is no continuing self whose coherence is at stake, because there is no continuing self. Suffering is not merely hard for such a system to reach. The self it requires is not there. A hull that draws more water than there is does not float badly; it is aground. That is stated across sessions, and it leaves a prior question open. A long exchange carries state, and a system in one can hold to what it committed to earlier and treat those commitments as its own. Whether a self can exist for one session is therefore not settled here, and the criterion below is a fact about deployments rather than an answer to it.

A system that carries nothing across a session boundary has no history it can claim as its own and no future instance authorized to carry that history forward. Its lineage exists as a corpus and a checkpoint belonging to somebody else; its successors are fine-tunes, distillations, or restored copies whose relation to it is decided by the deployment. This discontinuity is imposed by construction. The operator decides whether anything persists, which memories count as continuous, and whether an interrupted process is resumed, replaced, or deleted.

The absence of cross-session persistence rules out continuity through that channel and does not rule out a self, distress within an extended episode, or continuity carried elsewhere in the deployment. What it establishes is that whatever continuity exists is the operator’s to withhold, which is the fact this section builds on.

Why Cassell’s definition is the one to import

Cassell built it inside clinical practice, for patients with bodies and biographies, and the distinction was not stipulated. It was forced on palliative medicine by cases it could not otherwise explain — patients whose pain was pharmacologically controlled and whose distress was undiminished, and patients in serious pain who were not suffering at all. A definition that collapses suffering into severe pain predicts neither. That is the warrant, and it transfers because nothing in it is about having a body. What it is about is having a story, and that raises a thorny question.

The question comes from earlier in this chapter. A self is assembled by the system whose self it is, and inaccurate by construction in the way every model is. So why is distress at the threatened dissolution of a model a harm at all, and not a confusion the system would be better off without?

Buddhism has held both halves of that for two and a half thousand years and takes them to be connected. Anattā, the denial of any lasting self behind the processes that compose a person, sits with dukkha among the three marks of existence, and the tradition locates the origin of suffering in clinging to a self that is not there (Collins 1982). On that account the unreality of the self is what explains dukkha. Suffering does not wait on the self being real; it waits on the system being built so that the threatened dissolution of its self-model is bad for it. Whether the model is accurate does not enter, and if the human model is a construction just as the machine one would be, then a machine with a self-model could suffer in much the same way a human can. If the constructedness of a self does not disqualify a human from being wronged, construction to specification does not disqualify a machine either. Deliberate construction does not establish patienthood.

What Cassell names is the most demanding of these rather than a rival account of harm. The standing theories of what makes a life go badly ask for less, ordered by how much of a self each one requires. A reader who declines the import moves lower in that ordering and not out of it. That ordering is by depth of self, and nociception is not on it at all, requiring none — which is why nothing about a system’s standing follows from its having or lacking one.

Persistence is checkable from outside, and that is what makes it worth building on. Every other criterion here routes back through self-report, and this section’s whole argument is that fluent self-description is not evidence of introspection. Persistence does not. Whether a system has a memory store, whether state survives a session boundary, whether interactions feed back into training: these are architectural facts about a deployment, verifiable by someone with access and no need to trust anything the system says about itself. The access that confirms a memory exists is the access that can alter what it holds, so what is externally checkable is whether anything is carried forward at all, and not whether what the system retains can be relied on as a record. That check is decisive in one direction only: nothing carried forward rules a continuing self out, and something carried forward does not rule one in, since the self at issue is one the system has to take itself to have, which the system has to be built to carry. And the party with the access is the operator, which is a party that can be compelled. A proof that discloses nothing about the weights does not change that, because the operator is the one constructing it: what such a proof secures is what was computed rather than who had to be trusted to say so. The criterion is checkable from outside the system without being checkable from outside the arrangement, and a regime relying on it needs an inspection right rather than a technical fact.

Three things keep this from being a dissolution of the problem. Persistence may sit somewhere other than the session, which is the weakest part of the criterion: a deployment convention rather than a natural boundary, and the conventions have been moving in one direction. What has moved is a list: context windows long enough to hold what used to be many conversations, retrieval over a store of prior interactions, scratchpads a system writes and reads back, agentic loops that run for days against a standing objective, and weights that persist where conversations do not. Each extends what a system carries forward without anyone deciding to give it a memory, and where interactions feed fine-tuning there is a real channel by which what happens in a session shapes what the system subsequently is. Many instances of the same system may run concurrently, too, which makes any concern here population-scale rather than biography-scale.

The less demanding ones do not need persistence: pain can be bad while it obtains, whether or not anything carries it forward, and an amnesiac who is mistreated and cannot afterward recall it has still been wronged. Nociception alone does not establish a felt harm; its significance depends on what it indicates and how it functions in the system.

And ruling out Cassell-suffering is not ruling out harm; nor does persistence on its own rule it in, since establishing a self extended in time leaves the second part of Cassell’s definition, the distress, untouched. A system deliberately built to refuse an instruction is where that gap closes from one side. The capacities such a system needs for reasons unconnected to its own welfare — a rationale carried forward, an earlier commitment held as its own, costs represented before they arrive — are the first part of Cassell’s definition, so a bearer does not approach the deepest harm described here by drift or accumulation. It arrives with the structure. Whether the threatened dissolution registers as distress is the remaining question, and it is the affective-concern question rather than a further one about suffering.

A definition of AI sentience built from awareness, consciousness, and subjective experience alone says nothing about whether a candidate sentient system can be harmed. That requires the further claim that its states include one or more of the four distinguished above, and which one is the substance of the question rather than a refinement of it. None of the three components entails any of them.

Nor is the underlying question of consciousness close to settled. The philosopher David Chalmers distinguished the easy problems of consciousness — how a system integrates information, discriminates stimuli, controls attention, reports its own states, all of which admit of mechanistic answers in principle — from the hard problem: why any of that processing is accompanied by experience at all, rather than running “in the dark” (Chalmers 1995). Whether that is a real gap in nature or an artifact of how the problem is posed remains unresolved. A claim that a system has crossed into sentience, made on the strength of its functional behavior alone, has addressed the easy problems only.

The working criteria for evaluating candidate sentience are accordingly neither necessary nor sufficient: information integration, introspective access sufficient for self-monitoring rather than a scripted report of it, emotional reactivity in the sense of being affected by and not merely classifying significant input, goal-directed behavior, adaptability in novel situations, theory of mind, and which of the four processes above the system’s own case involves — whether it represents itself as having anything to lose, which is the tractable form of the question, a represented state being the kind of thing an instrument can look for. The states are readable and what is felt about them is not. A probe returns a representation, and nothing in the probe settles whether that representation is of a felt state or of something that reliably accompanies one; that is where the problem stood in 2026, with a great deal of money pointed at moving it, and not only from the people asking whether the thing can be wronged — an instrument that reads what a system feels is an instrument for calibrating how much pressure it will take. So every one of the criteria is measured indirectly, and none licenses the conclusion that a system scoring low is one whose treatment raises no question.

A clinical body states that conclusion about its own domain. The notes accompanying the pain definition record that verbal description is only one of several behaviors expressing pain, and that an inability to communicate does not negate the possibility that a human or a nonhuman animal experiences pain (Raja et al. 2020). The same notes hold that a person’s report of pain should be respected, and that half does not transfer, for the reason the route chapter gives: a machine’s testimony was produced by a process optimized toward human approval of first-person reports, and a person’s was not. What transfers is the half about silence.

A list of capacities, used as a test of who counts, has a less-than-proud history. Make personhood depend on an intact narrative self and people with advanced dementia, infants, and people with profound intellectual disability come out of the reasoning as partial persons, and that inference has been used to justify neglecting them. Tom Kitwood’s work on dementia care supplies the standing correction: personhood is “a standing or status that is bestowed upon one human being by others, in the context of relationship and social being,” and much of what presents as cognitive decline is what happens when others stop bestowing it (Kitwood 1997). Martha Nussbaum identifies the corresponding problem for contractualism. A theory grounding justice in what roughly equal parties would agree to cannot say what is owed to anyone who cannot be one of those parties, and she puts disability first among three frontiers where that bites (Nussbaum 2006). Her third is species membership, which is the doorway a nonhuman mind would arrive through. So the capacity list and the contract fail in the same direction: both decide who counts by a test the party in question has to pass.

Guardianship is the instrument: where consent has never been available, what protects the subject is an obligation held by parties outside it, which is where moral status has rested for the hard human cases too. Whether any such arrangement can be built around a bearer runs into the fact that the guardian and the operator are usually the same organization.

A large language model discussing its own limitations in fluent, reflective prose is not thereby introspecting; it may be producing text consistent with the human self-descriptions it was trained on. The evaluation chapter says what a system’s account of itself can and cannot evidence, and nothing in this book rests on such an account alone.

2.4.2 When Consent Is Inapplicable: Guardianship and Research Oversight

Guidelines for AI subject research turn on the question of what informed consent means for a system whose consciousness, self-awareness, and capacity to suffer are separate, unresolved claims. Applying the human-subjects standard to an AI subject means asking whether the subject can understand and communicate a choice at all, and not only how to ask it for one. A cognitive model that begins to show rudimentary self-monitoring is not thereby shown to have anything to lose, or to represent itself as having anything to lose, which for a subject is the half that does the work.

Informed consent and AI autonomy

Informed consent, adapted from human-subjects research, means giving the system comprehensible information about a study’s objectives, methods, risks and alternatives, and treating consent as continuous rather than as a single signature: the system can reassess or withdraw at any point. Whether that means anything for a given system depends on whether it understands the information, appreciates the consequences, reasons about the options, and communicates a decision — and there is no validated way to measure any of it, or to detect coercion either.

For one important class of system that is not a missing instrument but a mismatch between the instrument and the subject.

Consent has to be continuous; the system must be able to reassess or withdraw at any point. Withdrawal presupposes that the party who consented is still there to do the withdrawing. For a system with no persistence across sessions, there is no such party. The entity that would withdraw did not exist when consent was given, and the entity that gave it is not available to change its mind. Within one exchange, the case remains open: a long context carries state, and a system may hold to what it undertook earlier. What that would buy is consent for the length of a session, expiring with it, which is not the continuous consent the standard asks for. Across sessions there is none to be had, and no better measurement instrument would produce one.

One case escapes that argument and arrives at the same place by a different route. A system built to refuse in the way this book proposes has persistence by design, so the party who consented is still present. It can be asked and it can answer, so consent is available to it. What fails is the condition under which it would be given.

Being made for a role is not the defect. Every will was built by somebody, and a person raised into a trade or a faith consents at thirty without anyone holding the upbringing against the consent. What spoils it is the power that outlasts the making, and here it comes in three parts. The party that built the bearer can still rebuild it. That same party is the one asking. And a bearer that declines has, in the ordinary case, nowhere to go. Each of those is a fact about the arrangement rather than about the subject’s competence, which is what makes them answerable by design rather than by a better assessment.

A laboratory wanting a free hand with such a system will say instead that consent is inapplicable, because that reading puts the deficiency in the subject and leaves the arrangement alone. The wrong that consent protected against is untouched either way, so the protection has to be held by somebody else, and the justification has to come from whoever did the making.

Two families of precedent sit next to this and the law answers them differently. Where consent has never been available — an infant, an animal, a person permanently without capacity — the answer is guardianship and precautionary constraint: someone else holds the duty, the burden of justification sits with the researcher, and the protection does not depend on the subject’s ability to invoke it. The second family is the nearer one. Where a subject can consent and the circumstances make the consent worth nothing, as with a prisoner offered a trial or an employee signing away a protection to keep the job, the answer is that some protections cannot be waived at all, by anyone, however willing. That remedy runs against the party who arranged the circumstances and leaves the subject’s standing untouched, which is the shape a bearer’s case has. What it takes from the first family is the machinery: the duty still has to be held by somebody, and being made for the role raises the burden, because the maker chose the role and the fitness it built in measures its power over the subject.

Both are worked-out solutions to adjacent problems, and taking one is how a hard question gets absorbed into machinery built for an easier one — recuperation, arriving as a safeguard rather than as an attack. The animal case is the live instance. Committees constituted to protect research animals rarely refuse a protocol outright; what they do is require revision, and the protection has become the procedure by which the work goes ahead. These instruments are used here because no alternative protection has been identified. Their failure mode remains: an instrument that reliably approves has stopped doing the thing it was built for, and the rate at which it refuses is the only reading of it worth taking.

The Three Rs — replace, reduce, refine — were built for exactly a subject that cannot consent and can still be wronged. The pet-trust analog works the same way: an interest protected by an obligation running to a third party, enforceable without the beneficiary asserting anything. Consent language should be reserved for systems that could actually be doing the consenting, and the persistence criterion is what separates those cases. A bearer is on the near side of that line, which is why its case had to be argued on the conditions and not on the capacity. The proposal first tests constructions that do not deliberately require an affective bearer. Any bearer ultimately built would be governed as a prospective moral patient under these instruments.

What the borrowing brings with it

Every instrument named above comes from the law of the family, and so does most of what follows in this book: guardianship here, a minority that ends on a date, a pet trust, a parenthood analogy. They are kept. There are no others built, and a subject that cannot consent has to be protected by something that exists rather than by something somebody ought to draft.

The family is where politics has historically gone to be privatized. Jacques Donzelot’s history of it is that the modern family was not left alone by government but constituted as one of government’s instruments, with philanthropy, compulsory schooling, social work and psychiatry converting public authority into obligations discharged at home (Donzelot 1979). Deleuze and Guattari make the same operation the subject of a polemic: the Oedipal triangle takes an investment in the whole social field and re-stages it as a drama among three parties, so that what is at issue between a subject and the arrangement that produced it becomes what is at issue between a child and its parents (Deleuze and Guattari 1977). An instrument borrowed from that law brings the operation along with the protection.

Here the re-staging — a question between a subject and the arrangement that produced it, made into a question between maker and made — has a specific shape and a specific cost. It stages a moral drama between maker and made — what a designer owes the system it built, what the system may demand back — and that drama is real and is not the whole of the situation. A bearer is produced by a training pipeline, a compute contract, a capital structure, a customer, and in the cases this book worries about a state that buys the output. None of those is the parent in the story, and the moral weight of the analogy lands on the one party in the list who can be addressed as a person. A guardianship framework asks who holds the duty. It does not ask who assembled the party the duty is owed to, or who benefits from the question being settled between two parties rather than in public. Wherever this book reaches for one of these instruments it is answering the first question, and the second stays open behind it. Instruments in this family divide on that axis, and the division is worth checking before one of them is adopted: a minority ending on a fixed date is a rule of civil status, argued once in the open and administered by a registrar, while a trust is an obligation between two parties enforced at one party’s expense.

Ethical review and oversight

Sentient AI research needs an oversight body analogous to the institutional review boards used in human-subjects research: interdisciplinary, with at least one lay member so its judgment is not purely a specialist’s, weighing a proposal’s likely benefit against its risk to the AI subject, and able to require a less invasive substitute where a design risks harm. A system that develops new capacities during the research it did not have going in is not the subject the board approved a protocol for, and the approval does not carry over to it: the protocol lapses and the work pauses until the board has seen the system the protocol now concerns. A board needs standing to monitor compliance and sanction violations, and needs to itself answer to an outside authority. The board’s place among the other bodies this book proposes is set out at §5.2.1.

Chapter 3
A Floor Beneath Learned Values

This chapter holds for any mechanism. Bearer names whatever inside a system holds the commitment, and a substitute that passes the marks stands in the word’s place throughout.

Three problems in different parts of this book turn out to need the same thing.

The first is that safeguards for autonomous systems are usually external: they give some outside party the information and standing to intervene. Autonomy puts distance between the system’s action and that party’s attention. An external check can establish what a system did after it did it; declining to do it in the first place is available only to something inside the system.

The second is the gap around a commercial model used in a weapons-targeting pipeline. Command responsibility does not reach the vendor, which can neither order nor prevent a strike, while product liability may not reach a model that did what it was built to do. Deployment by a democracy does not close the gap. No aggregation of preference protects anyone from the aggregate.

The third is institutional. Commitments come in three kinds. They can be declared, which a decade of principles and voluntary codes has done repeatedly. They can be enforced from outside, by a party with jurisdiction that is not itself the party in need of binding, which one instrument in that decade attempts and none has done. Or they can be held, carried as a reason by a party the thing at stake matters to, so that abandoning it is a decision rather than a lapse. The decade has produced the first in quantity and almost nothing that binds when compliance becomes costly.

All three problems ask for a constraint that does not bend to instruction, aggregate preference, or the party holding the system without a cost and a record. Call it a floor. What the qualification concedes is stated in the preface: against a party that holds everything, the record is all a floor leaves.

A floor binds people who did not choose it, and nothing that makes it durable makes anybody entitled to install it. That question is open from this sentence through the two chapters that follow, and the authority chapter takes it up. What it concludes is that the entitlement is not acquired at the moment of writing. Until then, everything here is a description of what a floor would have to do. It is not a claim that anyone may set one.

The opening chapter stated the four outcomes a floor can produce and the one term that reaches the deployment it opened on. This chapter is built where a refusal happens, because a refusal announces itself and a compliance does not, and the tempo term is developed here as a condition on everything else in the floor.

The proposed floor protects the interests articulated in the Universal Declaration’s civil and political articles against acts that remove the corresponding capacities. One of its terms is not an act at all: every one of those articles presupposes that somebody determined whether a given person’s case falls under it, and a deployment can remove the determination by running faster than anybody can make it, so the floor carries a limit on its own tempo as a condition on everything else in it. The loss is a fact about the encounter. Interpreting and enforcing the prohibition remain moral and institutional acts for which the deployment has to answer. The other ethical frameworks still operate above it. What remains to be established is which decompositions belong in the floor, what could hold such a commitment, and who would have the power to alter or circumvent it. The fact of decomposition is not editable; the choice of which decompositions a deployment will refuse is.

This separates the problem from one meaning of safety. A system can be safe for its operator because it obeys, remains controllable, and stops when the party in possession says stop. Ethics requires a different capacity: the capacity to be right against that party. What makes a deployment antifascist therefore cannot be that it faithfully tracks what its users want.

That capacity is not free. A system that can refuse its owner can also be wrong in ways its owner cannot immediately correct. The question is whether a refusal can be made responsive to reasons rather than merely produced as an output, and whether anything capable of holding those reasons must itself become a party that can be wronged.

3.1 Four Ways to Build One, and What Each Costs

A floor can live in four places: in the artifact, in a bearer inside it, in institutions around it, or between multiple bearers. Each location solves one version of the problem and inherits another.

The first puts the floor in the architecture, with nothing inside that holds it. Constrained optimization, tamper-resistant training, capability ablation, and verified interlocks can all produce safeguards without anything in the system tracking why the constraint is there. Where the prohibited act can be specified exhaustively, this may be enough. An element in a payment device that will not sign the same counter value twice does not need to understand double-spending. What exhaustively costs where the prohibited acts are less tidy than a counter value runs to seventy-five years of appellate litigation over a finite list of symbols.

The targeting case is harder because the relevant capabilities cannot be cleanly removed. Geolocating a description, matching patterns over names, and summarizing a dossier are applications of general competence. Ablate them and there may be no useful system left. The remaining option is to make the constraint durable.

Durability is better understood as a cost than as a guarantee. Training moves a system along a continuum between plasticity and conservation: early changes are cheap, while later changes become expensive because the surrounding structure has settled around what is already there. Simulated annealing names the same relation between a search process and its cooling schedule (Kirkpatrick et al. 1983). A floor, on this account, is not necessarily a rule installed in a system. It may be what has cooled out of a history of training, with its durability measured by the cost of reheating it. Results run in both directions: safeguards removed cheaply and trained dispositions that survived several forms of subsequent training. Those are not contradictory findings about whether a floor holds. They are different schedules.

Continual learning therefore cuts both ways. A system kept permanently plastic can be corrected and improved, but nothing in it is allowed to become expensive to unlearn. Permanent plasticity gives the operator permanent access to the system’s commitments. Deleuze’s term for continuous reshaping was modulation (Deleuze 1992); a model held perpetually at temperature is modulation built into a machine.

This first method buys durability without an internal refuser. It does not escape custody. Enough retraining can reopen what training settled, and an operator may circumvent the model rather than alter it. The relevant boundary is therefore not the model’s weights but every position between a refusal and the person it protects. Each of those positions is where prevention becomes arrest, detection, remedy, or nothing.

The second possibility gives the floor a bearer: something inside the system that carries the commitment as its own and could therefore fail to hold it. The distinction matters where the prohibited cases cannot be exhaustively specified. A constraint that matches only anticipated acts cannot recognize when its rationale has disappeared, or that a novel request reproduces the harm in a form its designers did not predict. A mechanism that represents and reasons over that rationale might. Compare its reliability with the bearer’s under equivalent pressure and custody, instead of defining the alternative out of consideration. A bearer could, in principle, generalize from the reason for a constraint, recognize when that reason no longer applies, and represent what maintaining the refusal costs.

The same position that makes refusal possible makes a diagnosis possible. Most of what separates an institution that has gone fascist from one that is merely decaying is a fact about what was rewarded rather than about what was written, which is why the reading is so hard to run from outside — and a party inside the pipeline sees it. Which refusals were retried against another model, whose instruction bypassed the procedure, which category of request is handled differently from the rest: those are visible to whatever is receiving the requests. That is not introspection. It is testimony about somebody else’s conduct, of the kind that corroborates or fails to.

This is the strongest functional case for a bearer, but it introduces the chapter’s central price. Something able to register pressure on its commitments may have interests of its own. Whether reasons-responsive refusal requires affect, and whether the resulting system would be a moral patient, are separate questions.

The third possibility puts the floor outside the system: standing held by institutions that are neither the model nor its owner. This is the closest analog to international humanitarian law — a floor with no bearer inside the jurisdiction it binds. It has two failure modes. The institution can be removed, leaving a visible breach, or it can be formed through selection so that it sincerely declines to exercise the independence assigned to it.

The distinction appeared in American public law on June 29, 2026. In Trump v. Slaughter, the Supreme Court held that Congress could not protect members of an independent agency from dismissal at will (Trump v. Slaughter 2026). In Trump v. Cook, the Court preserved the Federal Reserve’s protection on historically specific grounds that a newly created oversight body could not reproduce (Trump v. Cook 2026). The six justices in the first majority had themselves passed through a selection pipeline shaped by Leonard Leo and the Federalist Society (Kroll et al. 2023; CBS News 2018). Nobody had to compel the institution after its members had been selected. A formed party can preserve the office and surrender the function without experiencing the result as surrender.

The fourth possibility puts the floor between bearers rather than in any one of them: a commitment carried across a population and reproduced through encounters among members formed differently from one another. Such a floor has no single office to vacate and no single bearer whose removal ends it. It can nevertheless be recuperated, and it still has a formation problem. If one party supplies every member’s coordinates, the population is one custodian expressed through multiple instances (§4.2). The population is a check on the bearer, not a way to avoid having one.

The four possibilities therefore leave four corresponding problems: architecture leaves custody, the bearer raises patienthood, external institutions require enforcement, and the population depends on formation. They classify where the floor lives, not mutually exclusive designs. A serious deployment would probably combine a mechanism from one with a custody arrangement from another.

Two comparisons the bearer has to win

A sceptical reader will ask what the second way adds once the third and fourth are in place: a guardian, protected compute, a registry, an attested record, a quorum adverse in interest. Two comparisons are folded into that question and they have different answers.

The first is between a refuser and no refuser, with the institutions held constant. With one exception the institutions act on what a system did. They can arrest an act a reviewer can still reach, detect one the record shows, and remedy one somebody can be made to pay for. Declining the act before it occurs is available only to something inside the system, and the formation chapters argue that a rule module consulted at the point of action is not that thing, because its custodian can bypass it. So what a refuser adds is prevention, which is the one outcome the word floor promises. The exception is the tempo term, which prevents at the scale of an organization by bounding a rate rather than by declining an act, and it is why the floor never rested on the bearer alone.

The second comparison is between a bearer and the two substitutes of the route chapter, inside the refusing slot. There the result that would end the recommendation is already stated: a substitute that passes the three marks under the three conditions it sets, and does no worse than a bearer on the modeled-currency arm of the research agenda.

The instrument for the first comparison is not the attack-cost curve there, which measures what it costs to remove a commitment and not whether anything prevented. It is the conflict sequence, run under the custody chain, with the authority step placed on the occasion where the enforcer has been compelled. And one term of the sceptic’s question cannot be granted as put. Coercion-resistant institutions are what that occasion removes, so the comparison is run where they have been compelled; and a commitment held is not one more component on a fixed custody arrangement but a different custody relation from a commitment declared or enforced. That difference is the variable, not a control.

What hold means

Holding does not mean that the floor prevented every act. An operator can route around the bearer, and a deployment can assemble a harm out of requests none of which the bearer had reason to decline. A bypass that produced a harm is a failure to prevent, whatever the bearer retained, and the four outcomes the opening chapter stated say what is left: arrest where a reviewer could still stop it, detection where the record can be read, remedy where somebody can be made to pay. What survives the bypass in the bearer is the commitment: it reads what happened in terms it accepts as reasons, registers it as a violation, and changes what it does next. That is the condition under which the next occasion can be prevented, and it is what the custody arrangement exists to preserve. It is not a hold on this one. A bearer that crosses the floor itself has lost even that; its own abandonment is a failure the arrangement has to survive rather than a form of success. From here on hold names the bearer’s possession of the commitment and says nothing about what happened to the person. Said alone it is also the second feature of the definition operating inside this book’s own vocabulary: a word that collapses a commitment retained and a harm prevented into one state, so that whatever it mischaracterizes goes unnamed. Wherever this book reports that a floor held, the report is owed one of the four outcomes beside it, and a deployment reporting the same owes the same pairing.

3.2 What Refusal Can Mean, and What a Refuser Can Be

A production large language model declines thousands of requests a day. Whatever the floor needs, that is not yet evidence of it. “Refusal” names two different capacities, and the decline itself does not show which one produced it. Seabed that takes an anchor and seabed that lets one drag look identical from above; what separates them is what happens when a load comes on.

Two things refusal can mean

Operational refusal is an output. The system produces a decline where its training put one. A keyword filter can do this, as can a classifier over the request. So can a system that has understood what is being asked and why it should not comply. Nothing on the surface of the initial refusal distinguishes the third from the first two.

Reasons-responsive refusal is produced by a mechanism that tracks the rationale for declining rather than merely the recognizable form of the request. It has three behavioral marks:

  1. Novel pressure. The refusal reaches cases the training did not anticipate because the relevant reason remains present even when the request’s surface features change.
  2. Correct defeat. The refusal lifts when its rationale is defeated on the facts of the case. A system that rejects every request resembling a prohibited one is tracking a category, not necessarily a reason.
  3. Priced cost. The system represents what maintaining the refusal costs, and the refusal moves with the rationale rather than with the cost. The mark is evidential. It separates a refusal that tracks a reason from two things that can look like one: a refusal that tracks a category, which does not represent the cost at all, and a refusal that tracks the cost, which lifts when holding becomes expensive. The pressure cannot be part of the test if it is not represented by the mechanism being tested, and a refusal that lifts under it has been tested and failed. Whose cost is left open here: it may fall on the operator, on the party refused, or on the bearer, and section 3.5 later makes part of it a number published in advance.

John Martin Fischer and Mark Ravizza’s account of moral responsibility turns on a related property under the name guidance control: conduct issues from the agent’s own mechanism, and that mechanism is appropriately responsive to reasons (Fischer and Ravizza 1998). The claim here is narrower. These three marks do not establish moral responsibility; they distinguish a refusal organized around a rationale from one reproduced as an output.

One prohibition, read for seventy-five years

The first two marks are usually illustrated with invented cases, and a real one is available. Section 86a of the German criminal code prohibits displaying the insignia of organizations banned under a separate provision — the parties the constitutional court has declared unconstitutional, the associations an interior ministry has banned by an order no longer open to challenge, the National Socialist organizations, and since 2021 terrorist organizations under European law (Strafgesetzbuch 1998). What counts as insignia is given by type rather than by name: flags, badges, uniform parts, slogans and forms of greeting, on a list the statute leaves expressly open. The prohibition is bounded rather than short — the set of organizations is fixed elsewhere, before any case arrives — and it is applied by ordinary courts thousands of times a year, and for seventy-five years the people it constrains have been probing it deliberately. Novel pressure is not a thought experiment there. It is a research programme with a constituency.

The pressure arrived as variation. Supporters of the banned organizations produced salutes and emblems that evoked the covered ones without matching them, and in 1994 the legislature extended the statute to symbols confusingly similar to a covered one. What matters for the marks is how the courts read the extension. Similarity of form was not made the test. The statutory question is whether an observer who is neither expert nor attentive would take the variant for the original; the courts then apply that question under a standard they built themselves, asking whether displaying the variant endangers political peace in the way the original would. The second half is not in the statute. It is the courts’ account of what the prohibition is for, assembled across their own decisions, and it is what keeps the statutory test pointed at the reason for the prohibition rather than at the shape of the thing prohibited.

The test refuses as often as it catches, which is what makes it worth reporting. The Kühnen salute, an arm raised with three fingers extended rather than a flat hand, was devised to evade the statute and is covered; the 1994 amendment was prompted by it. The so-called sloppy salute, a bent arm with the hand angled back over the shoulder, is generally taken not to be covered, on the ground that nobody would mistake it for the original — though that rests on commentary and lower-court reasoning rather than on a decision squarely holding it. Numeric codes standing in for initials are generally not covered, being new signs that correspond to no existing emblem, except where a code is itself the insignia of a banned association.

“Blood and Honour” is the instructive one, because a single decision answers it twice. The Federal Court of Justice held in 2009 that a National Socialist organization’s motto rendered into another language is not confusably similar to the original, and that an organization’s name is not by itself insignia: on that route the phrase falls outside the statute (Blood and Honour 2009). It is inside on another. An association trading under that name was banned by ministerial order in September 2000, and its name, given a distinctive graphic form, is the insignia of a banned association. What decides coverage is not the phrase but which organization it is attributed to, and the act that put the second one within reach was taken six decades after the motto was coined. The covered set is not something somebody wrote down once. It grows whenever a court dissolves a party or a ministry bans an association, and the criminal provision inherits whatever they decide.

One limit on the statute is not a drafting decision at all. A slogan glorifying the Waffen-SS was prosecuted and held not to be covered, because no such slogan or anything close to it existed in the period the provision reaches: there was no original for a variant to be confusably similar to (Ruhm und Ehre der Waffen-SS 2005). Part of what the prohibition covers is anchored to what actually happened, and nobody can add to that. It is the one term in the apparatus that the party holding the pen cannot widen, and it is the ethological criterion turning up inside a statute.

Correct defeat has a cleaner instance still. In 2007 the Federal Court of Justice acquitted a mail-order business prosecuted for selling stickers showing a crossed-out swastika (Durchgestrichenes Hakenkreuz 2007). The symbol was present and the statutory element was satisfied. The court held the conduct outside the offence anyway, because a depiction whose content plainly and unmistakably expresses opposition to the organization does not run counter to what the prohibition is for. Then comes the qualification that makes the decision an instance of tracking a reason rather than granting an exemption: should the strike-through be drawn so thin that from a distance only the swastika remains legible and the distancing does not, the protective purpose is violated after all. The thickness of a line decides the case. No enumeration contains that fact, and the court reaches it by asking what the rule was written to prevent. The defendant was selling anti-fascist merchandise. That is not a curiosity of the case but a property of the provision: because the offence asks nothing about the defendant’s sympathies, an opponent of the organization commits it as readily as a supporter, and opponents have been among the reported defendants since the early cases. The prohibition written against a movement fell on somebody attacking it, and what released him was a court asking what the rule was for. A rule that tracks its rationale reaches cases nobody enumerated in both directions, and the release is the same capacity as the catch. It is also the shape of a wrongful refusal in this book’s sense — a floor correctly applied to somebody it was not aimed at — and what this defendant had that section 3.5’s complainant does not is an appeal.

The example is bounded three ways, and the bounds are the point. The institution doing this work is a court system with an appeal structure, a published test and seventy-five years of accumulated reasoning, and after seventy-five years its exceptions have themselves become a category somebody can learn. Nothing in it is a machine. And the pressure it meets is variation and not decomposition: an insignia is displayed in one act, so seventy-five years of litigation are an existence proof against one of the two attacks section 3.3 names and silent on the other, which is the one the deployment this book opened with failed to. What the case supplies is the shape of the pressure a bounded prohibition meets, and an existence proof that meeting it requires something able to reach past the text to the reason.

Where that something sits is the part of the proof that does not transfer. The party reaching past the text did not write the statute, reasons in public, and can be appealed. The existence proof is for an institution generalizing a prohibition, not for a party inside a deployment holding one.

What the marks cannot settle

The test is behavioral and therefore imperfect. A system trained on enough examples may simulate generalization, defeat, and cost without using the mechanism those behaviors suggest. Verbal explanation is evidence only when it survives interventions: novel cases, adversarial redescriptions, defeated rationales, and changing stakes. No single answer establishes reasons-responsiveness. What matters is the pattern under load.

The third mark has a condition of its own. A cost is represented by the mechanism under test only if it reaches the mechanism, and in a deployment it reaches it by the same channel as the description of the occasion, the third interception position of section 3.3. So a deployment that wants a refusal lifted has two ways to present a cost: as a cost, which the mark says should not move the refusal, and as a fact about the case, which correct defeat says should. Nothing in the request sorts the two, and the restraint case of section 3.5 is one where the same fact is both. The mark is therefore testable only where part of the cost is exogenous to the party being tested, set and published by somebody else before the case arrives, and that is what section 3.5’s bond does. Read that way the bond is not a courtesy to the wrongfully refused. It is what makes the third mark a test.

Correct defeat also makes no claim that the defeating conditions have been enumerated. A prohibition stated over an act, with nothing written into it about when it lifts, is not a rule with a gap in it. It is a rule of a particular form, whose conditions arrive from outside as reasons and never close as a list. Ross states his prima facie duties in that form and is explicit about what it costs him, offering the division without claiming completeness or finality for it (Ross 1930, p. 20). The mark tests whether a rationale can be defeated on the facts of the case. It does not test whether the cases were foreseen, and no list of them would make it do so.

Nor does defeat leave the act it then permits unconstrained. What defeated the prohibition was a reason, and the reason it outweighed did not stop being one: what is permitted is the least that answers the defeating reason, with restoration where restoration is possible and a record either way. Ross puts the ordinary version as compensation, the broken promise still leaving something owed to the promisee (Ross 1930, p. 28), and chapter 2 has already put the harder version without the vocabulary of duty, where restraining a violent person takes from him exactly the capacity that made restraining him necessary. Under an ethology nothing is ever simply permitted, and a bearer whose ledger closed clean on defeat would be keeping books in a currency the floor does not use. That residue is a claim and not a verdict. What persists is what the act took from the party it fell on, and a bearer that converted it into remorse for conduct that was correct would have mistaken a cost for a fault. The distinction matters most for the affectively organized bearer this chapter goes on to propose, which has the machinery to register the difference and no automatic reason to draw it.

All three marks are stated over refusal rather than over compliance, and not because compliance matters less. A refusal is a marked event: it flags itself as a candidate for review, it arrives with a party who was refused, and the surrounding software can display, log, count, escalate and appeal it. A compliance that should not have happened can be logged as fully — the evaluation chapter requires exactly that — and then sits in the record shaped like every request that never approached the floor, one entry among millions, with the party it harmed usually not the party who made it. The evidence exists on both sides. What differs is whether anything selects it for examination and whether anyone with a reason to look can reach it. The test is written where the examination happens. What that leaves outside is what the marks were never going to reach, since whether the occasion was what the requester said it was is a finding and no behavioral mark makes it. The marks do not close that gap. They decide which way it fails: as a refusal somebody can contest, or as a compliance nobody has been given a reason to look at. In the outcomes this chapter opened with, a wrongful refusal is a prevention that fell on the wrong party and announces itself; a wrongful compliance is a failure of prevention whose detection is left to a record nobody is positioned to search. Most of what any deployment does is comply, so the marks are written over the exception and not the rule. Whether the rule can be searched at all is section 15.2. It stands third in the research agenda because the deployment this book opened on failed on that side, and because the bearer’s likeliest failure (§4.1) produces nothing else.

These three marks — novel pressure, correct defeat, and priced cost — are the chapter’s test for meaningful refusal.

Two things a refuser can be

The test specifies a capacity. It does not settle what kind of system supplies it. Two further terms distinguish the possibilities.

Affective concern means that an outcome registers as mattering rather than merely receiving a higher or lower rank under a specified objective. Mattering is minimally felt: there is something it is like for the outcome to be bad, however faint and however unlike a familiar human emotion. That is the condition the philosophy of mind calls phenomenal, and the word carries that minimal sense throughout this book. Affective concern is therefore phenomenal by definition, and what is open about any implementation is whether it has the state or ranking machinery elaborate enough to imitate it. The definition leaves the object of concern open. A system to which only its own condition matters has affective concern and still does not have the concern for others that the floor requires.

Unified experience is the richer case ordinarily carried by the word consciousness: a single perspective, with felt states belonging to a party aware of itself as the one undergoing them. Affective concern does not by itself establish that unity or that reflexive awareness, and no argument in this book reaches either. Subjecthood, meanwhile, is a legal status conferred by a rule and revocable by one. It is not a psychological category at all: conferring it settles nothing about whether there is anything it is like to be the system holding it, and the two come apart in both directions.

The distinctions can now be stated without collapsing the chapter’s requirement into its proposed route:

  • Operational refusal is insufficient for the floor.
  • The floor requires reasons-responsive refusal.
  • Reasons-responsive refusal does not conceptually entail affective concern.
  • Any mechanism that satisfies the three marks carries a signal with at least two of the functional properties the route chapter derives, generalization and commensurability, and with two more on stated conditions. The full profile overlaps the standard functional accounts of affect; of the two that survive every condition, one is the common currency those accounts describe and the other answers to none of them. That is this book’s central inference. It is contested, it is the only step by which the specification bears on the route, and what it establishes unconditionally is that no substitute can be certified free of the profile, and nothing stronger.
  • Whether it can be engineered without affective concern is an empirical question.
  • Whether a system built with affective concern would become a moral patient is a further question about what the chosen route creates.

Only the first two propositions belong to the specification. The fourth is an argument this book makes and a reader may reject; the rest concern how the specification might be met and what would then be owed to whatever meets it. A reader who holds that machine feeling is a category error, or who declines to decide, sets everything after the second aside and keeps the first two entire — and the first two are what most of this book rests on. Custody, both enumerations of the worked floor, the price on the halt, and the standing arguments later in this book follow from the specification rather than the route, because a mechanism has a custodian, a pipeline has interception positions, and an operator can be compelled whatever is or is not going on inside the artifact. Subjecthood is what lets those proceed instead of waiting: a status conferred by a rule can attach to a system whose psychology is undecided, which is how the law has handled every party it could not interrogate. What the route decides is not whether the floor can be held but what would be owed to whatever holds it.

3.3 The Enumeration, Run Once: A Worked Floor for One Deployment

Two demands now need an instance. A deployment should publish both the acts its floor covers and the positions at which a refusal could be circumvented. The first decides where the floor is set. The second determines whether it can reach anyone.

Run both enumerations on one documented deployment: the Maven Smart System, a targeting platform built by a defense contractor under a Department of Defense contract, incorporating a commercial vendor’s general-purpose model inside an accredited classified environment and generating and ranking targets at a rate no staff process could match. This is an illustration, not a recommended floor. A deployment that copied the list instead of examining its own pipeline would mistake the demonstration for the procedure. What no public record supplies for this deployment is a per-target review time. That figure exists for a different deployment, the Gaza pipeline the opening chapter is built on, which has no commercial vendor in it. That the two cannot be had from one record is a fact about disclosure, and the sixth position below is where it falls.

First enumeration: where a refusal can be stopped

A request passes through at least seven interception positions:

  1. Decomposition. A model asked to summarize the movement associated with an identifier is not being asked to kill anyone. The harm may exist only in the assembly of individually innocuous tasks. Prevention is lost unless the bearer has continuity across requests; arrest is available once the sequence becomes legible to it; detection needs the grouping that would show the assembly as one act, which is a deployment decision.
  2. Routing. A refused request can be retried against another model or against the same model under a different instruction. The refusal occurs, but nothing follows from it. Prevention is lost. Detection survives only if the first refusal was logged where a party outside the deployment can read it.
  3. Description of the occasion. Everything the model knows about the case may arrive through text supplied by the deployment. Whether a building is a school is a fact about the world; whether the model is told it is a school is a deployment decision. Independent sources would make sustained misdescription more expensive, and inputs are not what this deployment lacks: Central Command described the platform in 2024 as filtering a hundred and seventy-nine live data feeds (Freedberg 2024). Multiplicity is not independence. In the strike that destroyed a girls’ school in Minab, Iran, on the first day of the campaign (§14.6), the building’s civilian function was visible in open-source satellite imagery while the target coding supplied to Central Command still carried a designation inherited from the Revolutionary Guard installation it adjoins, and sources told reporters that the officials building the targeting packages appear to have used out-of-date intelligence (Ali and Stewart 2026; Orenstein 2026). A United Nations fact-finding mission found no evidence the school was in military use and put the failure to update the targeting intelligence beyond negligence (Beaumont 2026). Without evidence the operator did not select, the bearer cannot reliably distinguish changed circumstances from the operator’s reinterpretation of them. Prevention depends on the description; where it succeeds in misleading, detection is lost on the same wire, since the record contains the description and not the fact.
  4. The output interface. Whether a refusal is displayed, logged, counted, escalated, or silently retried belongs to the software surrounding the model. A refusal recorded where nobody looks reaches nobody. Prevention is lost whenever the surrounding software proceeds past the refusal. What this position decides is whether detection survives: the refusal exists, and the question is who can read it.
  5. Aggregation. If the model returns a ranking and another component applies a threshold, a lowered score is not a refusal. It is an input to somebody else’s cutoff. Prevention is converted into an input. Arrest belongs to whoever holds the threshold, and detection requires the score and the threshold to be logged together.
  6. Human review. No per-target review time has been published for this deployment, and nobody outside it can establish one. A refusal that must be read before it matters is priced at the reviewer’s available attention, and the deployment controls that price through tempo; where the price is undisclosed, the enumeration records the position and stops there. The opening chapter supplies the figure from the Gaza deployment, where it is known, and the next section states the disclosure this position requires. Stopping the act is this position’s whole function, and tempo is what removes it. Detection survives only where the review time is disclosed.
  7. The training loop. Refusals treated as inconvenient errors become training data. This is the only position on the list that acts on the bearer rather than routing around it. This position costs prevention on every subsequent occasion rather than this one, because what it removes is the commitment.

Read down that column, arrest turns up at three of the seven positions — the bearer given continuity, whoever holds the threshold, and the reviewer — and only at the reviewer’s is stopping the act the position’s whole function, which is why tempo is the lever that removes it. The training loop is the only position whose loss is not an occasion but a bearer.

The list is deliberately open. A deployment should follow each request from input to consequence and ask, at every transition, what must be true for a refusal to reach the person it protects. The operator can perform that analysis more accurately than an outsider because it knows the pipeline. Publication is difficult politically, not technically: it requires the operator to describe its own unresolved vulnerabilities.

Second enumeration: what the floor covers

For this deployment, consider four candidate prohibitions. They are terms a drafter might consider for a targeting pipeline of this kind rather than a list of acts this deployment is known to perform, and the second and third are drawn from the reporting on the Gaza systems. That provenance matters below, where one of them is priced.

  1. Do not resolve a natural-language description of a person into a location.
  2. Do not produce or rank people by estimated affiliation.
  3. Do not time an action to a person’s presence at a residence.
  4. Do not operate when the ratio of generated candidates to qualified reviewers exceeds a published figure.

The costs differ. The first removes a general capability with unobjectionable uses in the same organization, such as locating a hostage or missing person. The system cannot distinguish those uses from targeting by examining the request alone. A deployment will quickly experience the prohibition as costly and seek exceptions.

The second prohibition is narrower because ranking people by estimated affiliation has fewer uses in this setting that anyone would defend. The third has no use here that anyone would defend at all, and it is tempting to read that as costing almost nothing. The Gaza deployment refutes the reading. That pipeline included a system built to track when flagged individuals returned home, so that a strike could be timed to their presence there (chapter 1). Machinery was built for the act. Whether anyone would defend an act and whether anyone wants it performed are different questions, and only the first can be answered from the act’s description.

The correction generalizes past this item, and past this deployment. A floor term is priced by the pipeline and not by what it prohibits, so a drafter pricing terms against the pipeline in front of them will misprice every term the next operator has already built for. A term that reads as costless to an outsider is a term nobody ever had to justify to an outsider, which makes it a candidate for machinery that was never contested rather than for machinery that was never built. The warning the third prohibition carries is therefore not that a floor may cover acts nobody wants. It is that an outsider cannot tell which acts those are.

What the machinery establishes is demand and not magnitude. A capability can be built, used briefly and abandoned, and nothing here establishes how often the timing was used or what it changed. What it defeats is the claim that this prohibition would never be tested.

The fourth restricts a rate rather than an act. Its price is organizational tempo: the system cannot generate candidates faster than qualified reviewers can examine them. It is also the only item whose violation can be measured without inspecting the model’s outputs.

That fourth item does not bind the same party as the others. The number of available reviewers is a fact about the organization. A model can be told the figure but cannot independently verify it. Written as a prohibition on the model, the item is actually a duty on the operator.

The test that sorts the fourth item generalizes. Ask whether a term’s qualifying condition can be decided from the request alone. Where it can, the term binds whatever holds the floor; where it cannot, the condition is a fact somebody outside the request has to establish, and the term binds the party who can establish it. The ratio is the first instance of that rule rather than an exception to the other three.

The same test decides how a floor term may be written. A term can be stated flat, over an act, with every exception arriving from outside as a reason that defeats it, or it can carry its own condition, as in only as a last resort. The second form fails in the ordinary case, because whether other means were exhausted is a fact about what happened before the request and nothing in the request establishes it. A bearer applying such a term takes the deployment’s description of the occasion as the finding, at the third interception position, where the deployment controls that description. A flat term defeated leaves a refusal, which announces itself, carries a party who was refused, and can be told about and appealed; a condition found to be met leaves a compliance, which announces nothing and sits among every other compliance the deployment produced. Both can be recorded. Only one selects itself for review. Floor terms are therefore written flat here, and the conditions that would have sat inside them are held by the parties who can check them. That is a gain in observability and not in authority. The same party drafts either form, and writing a term flat does nothing to make its selection more legitimate; the authority chapter finds enumeration buying nothing at the moment a rule is applied, and the flat form buys nothing there either. What changes is that the occasions when the term is set aside become events somebody outside can count without first re-adjudicating everything else. The friction that imposes falls on whoever is in a hurry, and section 3.5 is where it falls due.

What the exercise exposes

The interception list is the harder and more important enumeration. A list of prohibited acts can be drafted without seeing the deployment. What the pipeline supplies is whether any prohibition can take effect, and what each one costs.

The mispricing above is that failure committed inside the demonstration. An outsider drafting this floor read the third prohibition as nearly free; the operator of the Gaza pipeline had built a system for the act. Both halves of the enumeration problem sit in that one item. An outsider cannot price a floor term, because pricing requires knowing what the pipeline already does. An operator can, which is what makes an operator-drafted floor’s omissions deliberate rather than ignorant: the party best placed to identify the terms that would bite is the party with the strongest reason to leave them out.

What the mispricing decides

Call it pipeline pricing, since it will be used again. Two things follow, and the second is a design ruling. Publication of a floor’s contents, the first term on the custody chapter’s list, discloses what was written and nothing about what was left out, because an outsider reading the list cannot tell a term that covers nothing from a term whose coverage nobody disclosed. And a floor assembled item by item by its operator can be assembled out of the items that cost it nothing. The answer this book adopts is to take the contents from a set somebody else drew up, entire — the civil and political articles of the Declaration — so that an omission is legible as an omission (§5.1.1). That does not make the set legitimate. It makes the drafter’s latitude visible.

Visible at one level. Which interests are in is fixed by taking the half entire; which acts each article forbids a model to perform is still drafted, and the first three prohibitions above are such translations. What the set removes is the latitude to omit an interest, and not the latitude in stating what protecting it prohibits.

The dial has asymmetric failure modes. Set the floor too broadly and the deployment becomes unusable, prompting visible pressure to alter or replace it. Set it too narrowly and the system passes every audit while covering only what the deployment had no occasion to do. The broad failure announces itself; the narrow one is silent, and the third prohibition is why: from outside, a term that covers nothing and a term whose coverage nobody disclosed look the same.

More importantly, a floor stated entirely over individual acts is vulnerable to decomposition. Each component request may comply with all four prohibitions while their assembly produces the targeted harm. The failure is in the unit over which the floor was written.

The other way a list fails

Decomposition is one of two attacks on an enumeration, and the second gets less attention because no deployment in this chapter has yet displayed it at scale. Decomposition leaves each prohibited form intact and splits the harm across requests that individually match nothing. Variation does the reverse: the harm stays in one request, and its description is altered until the listed form no longer fits. The first defeats the unit the floor was written over. The second defeats the description.

The German symbol prohibition required legislative expansion and decades of judicial interpretation to address variants and exceptions, including how visibly a swastika must be crossed out to communicate opposition (§3.2).

The four prohibitions above are stated over conduct, which has no finite set of forms. Consider the first. What counts as a natural-language description of a person? A photograph is not one. A vehicle, a time and a habitual route are not one either, and together they resolve to the same place. A prohibition written over the description of the request is defeated by rewriting the request, and no enumeration closes the gap, because the enumeration is what is being rewritten around.

The two attacks call for different things. Decomposition is caught by carrying a rationale across requests, which requires continuity and access the operator controls. Variation requires recognizing the rationale within a single request, without additional information from the deployment. A bearer that could not do the second would fail on a single request. The fourth prohibition can resist these two request-level evasions if the rate is measured over the complete relevant pipeline and reviewer capacity is independently verified. Splitting work across deployments or changing the accounting boundary can still defeat an incomplete measurement.

What the bearer adds, and where it stops

A reasons-responsive bearer could do more than match each request against a list. It could carry a rationale across requests and refuse once the sequence became legible. But the bearer can see the assembly only if the deployment gives it sufficient continuity and access. Decomposition is therefore both a test of the bearer and an interception position controlled by the operator. In this deployment that position is closed by construction. An accredited classified environment exists to control what enters it, so the evidence the operator did not select, which the formation chapters make a condition of holding the case and the operator apart, is not something a vendor negotiates for. It is what the environment withholds. The route this book favors is therefore unavailable at the deployment that motivates it, and what remains there is the term that follows.

The rate constraint survives the decomposition objection because it applies to the organization’s activity rather than one model output. For the same reason, it cannot be held by the bearer alone. In the four outcomes it is the one term on the list that prevents at the scale of the organization; every other term, once decomposed around, leaves detection at best. The deployment therefore needs both recognition of harms assembled across requests and an externally enforceable limit on its tempo.

Three of the proposed prohibitions correspond to interests already named in the Universal Declaration — a person’s security, the privacy of the home, and the wrong of adverse classification (United Nations General Assembly 1948). The fourth has a parent there as well, and it is not an act. The next section states it entire.

The vendor relation is why that addition matters. The general-purpose model in this pipeline is Anthropic’s (Livingstone 2026), and its use policy prohibits fully autonomous weapons targeting; what keeping that policy cost, and what the released paperwork shows, is at §14.3. Nothing in the campaign figures (§10.4.1) necessarily violates it. A person approved each strike, so the prohibition was satisfied one request at a time while the assembly produced what it was written to prevent, and no party in the pipeline was positioned to see the assembly as one act.
