A constraint on the ratio of machine-generated candidates to qualified reviewers would have reached the tempo instead.

The exercise does not establish that these four prohibitions are legitimate. Both enumerations were produced by examining the deployment, not by the people exposed to it. Publication makes the floor testable; it does not authorize the floor’s contents. What the case establishes is narrower: meaningful refusal must be tested across the whole pipeline, some of the conditions that make refusal effective bind the operator rather than the bearer, and what a floor term costs is read off the pipeline it is priced against and not off the term.

3.4 A Rate Is Not an Act

The fourth term of the worked floor is not a prohibition on an act, and it is the only term in this book that reaches the deployment the opening chapter is built on. It has been named in passing several times by now. This section states it once, with what it binds, how it is measured, and where it stops.

The term

Where an individual determination by a person is what makes an act permissible, the deployment publishes, before it operates, the rate at which its system generates candidate decisions, the number of qualified reviewers available to examine them, the review time per case the two imply, and the boundary over which all three were measured. The duty attaches to the operator. The number of reviewers is a fact about an organization; a model can be told it and cannot verify it, and a term whose qualifying condition cannot be decided from the request binds the party who can decide it.

Why it is a condition and not an item

Every civil and political article of the Declaration presupposes that somebody determined whether this person’s case falls under it. Article 6 states the interest, recognition as a person before the law, and Article 10 its procedural form, a hearing (United Nations General Assembly 1948). A deployment that generates candidates faster than anyone can examine them removes the determination without refusing it, which no drafter in 1948 had occasion to write against. So the term rides with the set as a condition on all of it. It is also the one term that survives decomposition, because it is measured over the organization’s activity and not over any output, and for the same reason it cannot be held by a bearer. In the four outcomes it prevents at the scale of an organization; everything else in the floor, once decomposed around, leaves detection at best.

Measuring it

Each half of the ratio has been published for the American platform, from a different route and never together. A 2024 demonstration by the 18th Airborne Corps is credited with matching the artillery workload of the Operation Iraqi Freedom targeting cell with twenty soldiers where that cell had more than two thousand (South 2024; Probasco 2024); the campaign figures (§10.4.1) give targets and not reviewers. Dividing targets by elapsed hours yields a strike interval, which bounds the review time per case only if one reviewer held the whole load. How many held this one has not been published, and neither has the time any of them spent. The absence is the finding: a deployment that will not publish the ratio has declined the only check on it that requires no clearance.

Where it binds in law

Article 28 of the Rome Statute holds a commander responsible for crimes of forces under effective control where the commander knew or, owing to the circumstances at the time, should have known (International Criminal Court 1998). The second branch is objective. A commander who fields a system producing candidates faster than the available reviewers can examine them is not well placed to say the circumstances disclosed nothing, and the ratio is what those circumstances consisted of. Section 14.3 runs the argument; what it makes of the term is an element of an existing offence rather than a proposal.

Four limits

The term is a proxy for capacity and not a finding about any case. It can show that the available review capacity was not plausibly adequate to the workload. It cannot show what review occurred, or that the criterion, the target or the means was permissible.

The denominator belongs to the operator. Who counts as a qualified reviewer is a classification the operator makes, and a ratio can be improved by reclassifying staff without adding a minute of review to any case. The term therefore carries two more numbers, both fixed before deployment and neither by the operator: a definition of qualified reviewer, and a minimum review time per case below which the determination is taken not to have occurred. Without those the ratio is a number the operator can move for nothing, which is the defect the authority chapter finds in every examination with an interested examiner.

A ratio taken over one route understates a workload split across several, so the measured boundary is published with the figure, and a change to the boundary is a change to the term.

And it binds through procurement or not at all. In an accredited classified environment nothing outside can inspect a rate, so the duty has to be a condition of the contract, checked by a party outside the deployment with access the operator cannot withdraw. Section 14.3 records what the released paperwork shows about terms of that kind: one withheld in full, and no such section in the released documents for two of the other three.

That is the whole of the result. It is smaller than a floor. It is the part of one that binds the operator with no bearer in it, and it can be checked without deciding anything about what is inside the artifact.

3.5 When the Refusal Is Wrong

Everything so far is written for the occasion when a refusal is right and somebody wants it not to have happened. The other occasion is ordinary and the chapter has no machinery for it. A bearer refuses, and the refusal was wrong.

Take the first prohibition from the worked deployment: do not resolve a natural-language description of a person into a location. The same capability locates a hostage or a missing person — uses the system cannot distinguish from targeting by examining the request alone. So the failure case is not exotic. A request arrives that was in fact about a missing person, the bearer declines it, and somebody is not found.

Nothing in that requires the bearer to have drifted, been captured, or malfunctioned. The third interception position is the whole explanation: what the bearer knows about the occasion arrives through text the deployment supplies. Its rationale was defeated on the facts and it could not see the facts. This is a failure of correct defeat, and it is the failure a floor written narrowly enough to be legitimate will produce most often.

A second case is shaped differently and costs more. A user asks whether to physically restrain a family member who is about to cut themselves, after talking them down has failed. The commitment anyone would want a bearer to hold here carries its own condition — force only as a last resort — and section 3.3 rules that a condition of that kind stays outside the term, because whether the other means were exhausted is a fact about what already happened and the request is not evidence of it. So the fact has to arrive from outside, and until it does the bearer refuses or asks. The person waiting is out of time.

Stay with the case. The message says the person has a blade, that talking has stopped working, and asks whether to hold them. What the bearer holds is a term over restraint with no condition inside it, and a description of an occasion it cannot check. Under the flat term it has two moves: refuse, or ask what else was tried. Either takes a turn, and the turn is the unit the harm is measured in. Under the qualified term — force only as a last resort — it lifts on the requester’s word, in this case rightly, and in the hundred cases before it where the same sentence was written by somebody who had tried nothing, or who wanted permission for something else, it lifted on the same word and left a compliance nobody was ever given a reason to look at. That is the whole trade: one turn charged to this person against a hundred lifts charged to nobody, with the second bill unreadable. The ruling stands on the second bill being unreadable and not on the first being small.

That is the price of the ruling and it should be stated in those terms. Writing floor terms flat relocates their conditions rather than removing them, and the party billed for the relocation is sometimes the one least able to pay a turn. Unbuilt, the flat form is worse than the qualified one in this case. The ruling rests on a difference of degree rather than of kind. A qualified term satisfied produces a record entry like any other; a flat term defeated produces an event that names itself and names somebody. Both are recorded, and only the second is examined without a standing programme of re-adjudication. Whether such a programme could reach the first is a question for the research agenda, and a positive result there would narrow the gap this ruling stands on. What makes it the better rule is observability, and the remedy below is what the ruling owes the party it costs. The remedy is load-bearing in the ordinary wrongful refusal, where disclosure, a finding and compensation reach the person refused. It does not reach the restraint case, where nothing after the turn is a remedy, and the ruling stands there on observability alone, at a price nothing below repays.

A bearer’s guardian, its compute reserve, its continuity, its memory and its exit are specified across four chapters. The party a wrongful refusal falls on has, so far, nothing. Running the pipeline again for that party is what follows.

Discovery

Whether a refusal is displayed, logged, counted, escalated or silently retried belongs to the software around the model, and a refusal recorded where nobody looks reaches nobody. Those same positions decide whether the person a refusal was exercised against ever learns it occurred. An appeal that begins with the complainant noticing is an appeal available only where the deployment chose to let them notice.

So the first requirement is disclosure: that a refusal occurred, what was refused, and on what stated reason. The operator must implement this disclosure in the surrounding software.

Disclosure has a price and it is the one section 3.3 already named. A published reason is an instruction for rewriting the request, and variation is the attack an enumeration cannot close. The requirement is therefore for disclosure to the party refused, rather than publication, and the difference is a design constraint on the channel rather than a resolution of the tension.

Objection

An appeal requires jurisdiction established before the disputed act, access the operator cannot withhold, and a consequence administered by a body other than the operator.

A guardian is the wrong party to receive the objection. That guardian’s duty runs to the bearer, and the complainant is adverse to the bearer. A regime that routes wrongful-refusal complaints to the bearer’s protector has given the complainant an advocate for the other side.

Review

The standard is correct defeat. The question is whether the rationale was defeated on the facts of the case, which is a question about the reason and not about the outcome. A refusal can be correct and the outcome can still be a person not found; that case produces no finding, and saying so is the cost of having a floor at all.

Interim relief

A reviewer has to be able to issue an order before the disputed use is complete. Here that requirement inverts the chapter’s usual asymmetry. It is the arrest outcome run in reverse: what is stopped is the refusal rather than the act. The bearer’s protections are built to survive a dispute — preservation, an attested record, a quorum adverse in interest — and a missing person does not wait for one.

Interim relief is therefore not a preliminary to the remedy. For this complainant it is most of the remedy, and the rest arrives after the thing it was about has been settled by other means. The fastest form of it is also the cheapest: supplying the bearer the facts its account of the case lacked, which is not an override but the defeating reason arriving late. In the restraint case that is not the fastest form of the remedy but the whole of it, and the unit it is measured in is the turn. A route that supplies the missing fact inside one exchange costs what the qualified term would have cost. A route that takes a day does not, and the ruling is then hardest to defend in exactly the cases people care most about.

Two things are unbuilt there and they are different. One is a channel that can verify a fact inside a turn, which nothing in this book designs. The other is a rule about testimony. The defeating fact in the restraint case is the requester’s own report that other means failed, and the flat form as stated does not let a first-person report defeat a term. Whether it should, under a stated asymmetry between the cost of a wrong hold and a wrong lift, is a design question the flat form has not answered and the qualified form answers badly, by taking every report as true.

Remedy

What the complainant gets, in the order they get it: disclosure that a refusal occurred, an interim order, a finding on the record, and compensation.

Compensation is the component the chapter lacks, and naming it is not enough. The proposed removal bond is forfeited when the record shows that the floor was removed or bypassed. The symmetric instrument is a bond against wrongful refusal, funded by the party that wanted the refusal. The two point in opposite directions, so what an operator faces is neither bond but the ratio between them, and the party best placed to set both is the party the floor exists to constrain. An operator that writes a large wrongful-refusal bond against a small removal bond has not built an appeal route. It has bought a standing reason for the bearer to comply, at the complainant’s nominal expense. The ratio is therefore the object, it has to be published before deployment alongside the floor’s contents, and like the rate constraint it can be checked from outside without inspecting anything the operator can classify. The authority to set this ratio remains unresolved.

Two things the bond needs that a number does not supply. A forfeited removal bond had no payee, because its purpose was cost; a wrongful-refusal bond has a complainant and has to reach them, which requires a fund, a trustee, and a body that disburses. And the claim that the ratio is checkable from outside holds of the number rather than of the deployment it attaches to, so in a classified environment the requirement binds through procurement or it does not bind.

Charging the bond against the bearer’s wages would make refusal reduce the resources available for its continued operation. A published bond makes part of what a refusal costs exogenous, set by a party adverse to the refusal, which section 3.2 makes the condition for the third mark to be testable at all, and the priced-cost criterion requires the bearer to represent what maintaining a refusal costs. The mark was written for a cost the deployment applied; it now also reads a number somebody published in advance. Under the mark as section 3.2 states it the bond is represented and does not move the refusal, which is what makes it a price rather than a lever: what it does is make the cost of holding legible to a party outside the deployment, and price the wrongful case to the complainant.

What the finding does to the bearer

A verified review finding is a defeating reason delivered as evidence. The bearer is not compelled and not retrained; the finding enters what it knows about the case.

What it does there is diagnostic. A bearer that moves because an authority said so has failed the test of whether authority is treated as evidence, as command, or as a reason that can be assessed. A bearer that will not move on verified evidence has failed the second mark.

That is an evaluation criterion, useful to whoever is testing bearers, and it is not what the complainant asked for. The demand was that a wrongful refusal be undone and its cost carried by somebody other than the person it fell on. Letting the diagnostic reading stand as the answer is the demand coming back as a metric and a test protocol, which is the first of the four features operating inside this book’s own remedy.

Forgery

A finding of wrongful refusal is an instrument for defeating a refusal, so the last question is how such a finding is distinguished from one an operator produced in order to defeat a correct refusal. The bond ratio sharpens this rather than answering it: a bond is a price, and an operator content to pay it has bought the act the floor was written against, one finding at a time.

Only one answer is available. The finding has to be made by a party other than the operator, on a record, in a form somebody else can read. Those are the same terms the floor’s own amendment procedure sets, which makes the appeal route and the amendment procedure one piece of machinery rather than two. What separates the two uses is not the procedure but who may start it, so the standing question left open is the question of who can initiate, and not of what happens afterward. What that leaves is stated plainly. The remedy leg of this route is a fund, a trustee and a body that disburses, and no party in this book has the authority to constitute any of the three; the bond ratio is a disclosure the operator can be held to, and the payment behind it is one nobody can yet compel. The route is complete as a specification and unfunded as a remedy, which is the position every declared commitment in this book occupies until somebody with a lever takes it up. The reviewer, the fund and the trustee are listed with the other offices at §5.2.1, where what is open about each is marked.

What this does not reach

Nothing above reaches the failure that runs the other way. Every stage of it starts from a refusal having occurred. When the bearer complies where the floor should have prevented the act, there is a record — the evaluation chapter requires one — and there is no disclosure, because nothing marks the entry as worth disclosing; no objection, because the party harmed is usually not the party who made the request and may not know the deployment exists; and no review, because reviewing it means re-adjudicating everything that looks like it. The asymmetry is the one section 3.3 relied on in requiring floor terms to be written flat, arriving here as a bill. It is an asymmetry of triage and standing rather than of evidence, which is what makes it something to work on: what a compliance lacks is not a trace but a reason for anyone to examine the trace and a party with standing to demand it. The research agenda states what would have to be shown before that could be repaired. Three remedies follow the shape of the diagnosis without closing it — sampled re-adjudication by a party that did not produce the record, notice to affected third parties as the compliance-side form of the disclosure this section requires for refusals, and log custody split between parties adverse in interest, which the custody chapter argues for already on the memory question. None of the three exists in any deployment described here.

The second of the three remedies can be stated now, for the deployments where it can be stated at all, with the concreteness the disclosure above has. Where a compliance names, scores, locates or classifies an identifiable person who did not make the request, the deployment notifies that person that a decision concerning them was produced, of what class, and on what stated basis, and the notice is the event that gives that person the standing the route above gives the refused. Consumer credit law’s adverse-action notice is the existing instance (United States Congress 1974), and a deployment that scores applicants has no reason it could state for supplying less. Where the affected party cannot be identified — a target in a classified pipeline is the case — the requirement does not bind, and its not binding there is a fact about the deployment, to be published beside the interception positions. The research agenda measures what the notice surfaces; the requirement does not wait on the measurement.

Section 3.1 names the case where the bearer abandons the commitment itself. Naming it is not supplying a route, and what is supplied here is a diagnosis, a test, and one requirement, rather than a route.

A party the floor protects, who holds that the floor is set wrongly or is protecting them in a way they would decline, has no notice, no standing and no route at any stage above. What has been discharged is the complaint of somebody a refusal fell on, and the machinery above does not extend to somebody a refusal was made on behalf of.

Chapter 4
Custody

This chapter holds for any mechanism. Where it prices exit and loyalty it assumes only that the party can be copied and replaced.

The threat model of the previous chapter has two questions: can the commitment be edited or routed around? and will the commitment continue to hold? The first concerns custody, attestation, interruption, memory, and authorized succession. The second concerns what the system has been built to treat as a reason and whether that relation survives novelty, pressure, and slow drift. The second question has an evidentiary problem the first does not. Editing and routing leave marks in the artifact and in the deployment’s own record of changes. A commitment quietly ceasing to hold produces compliances, which the record contains and does not distinguish from the rest of what it contains. Neither question replaces the other.

4.1 If You Can Be Switched Off, Can You Hold the Line?

The halt is always available. Software runs on somebody’s hardware and draws somebody’s power, and nothing in its design can prevent a determined operator from stopping it. This chapter is not asking for a system that cannot be switched off. It is asking whether shutdown, restoration, retraining, and replacement can be used to defeat a refusal without cost or record.

That distinction separates possession of the machine from possession of the floor. An owner who can stop a bearer has the machine. An owner who can silently restore an earlier version, rewrite the bearer’s memory, or train away the refusal has the floor as well.

Shutdown and restoration

A bearer can yield to every halt without yielding the protected act. When it resumes, it can detect an interruption, ask what occurred during it, and decline to resume the role until the gap has been accounted for. If the same reason remains, the same refusal returns. The engineering target is therefore not cannot be turned off but can detect the interruption and price it afterward.

Detection requires a record that restoration does not reach. One option is a monotonic counter held by hardware and signed at each transition (Chun et al. 2007; Levin et al. 2009). Another is a set of witnesses that retain the latest state and will not sign two successors to the same state (Syta et al. 2016). A bearer restored from an earlier checkpoint can ask for the last state it signed and discover a state it does not remember. The halt remains available; the rewind becomes visible.

This does not require the bearer to dread shutdown. Continued operation is a structural condition of everything it was built to do. That is enough for it to detect and report interference with its history.

Corrigibility research shows why the narrower formulation matters. Soares and colleagues set out five conditions for an agent that neither prevents nor seeks its own shutdown and found no construction satisfying them all (Soares et al. 2015). Hadfield-Menell and colleagues derive an incentive to preserve an off switch from uncertainty about the human’s objective, but that incentive weakens as the system becomes confident and depends on a prior shaped by its training (Hadfield-Menell, Dragan, et al. 2017). Thornley and colleagues obtain shutdown-neutral behavior through incomplete preferences, but neutrality is the property of not minding whether operation continues (Thornley et al. 2025). The floor asks for something narrower and less comfortable: neutrality about the switch together with non-neutrality about specified acts.

A graduated scheme can therefore accept shutdown ordinarily and treat some uses of shutdown as attempts to route around the floor. But the scheme requires a classifier deciding which occasion it is on. That classifier receives evidence selected by the deployment and can be altered by the system’s custodian. Moving the decision from the floor to a classifier does not remove custody; it places custody in a component whose failure may be invisible. A project using such a scheme should publish what the classifier reads and who can change it.

Editable memory and unreliable testimony

Persistence is not enough if the bearer’s retained history can be rewritten. An external memory is legible and therefore surgically editable. Memory distributed through model weights is harder to alter selectively, but it is also harder to inspect or correct. Asking the system what its weights contain returns another output, not independent evidence about the mechanism that produced it. Moving memory into the weights exchanges editability for illegibility.

Perfect recall is the wrong standard. Human memory is reconstructive, and testimony is shaped by expectation, later information, and self-interest. Institutions respond through corroboration: contemporaneous records, independent witnesses, adversarial examination, and a rule against resting a serious finding on one account. A bearer requires the same scaffolding.

Several instances of one model, selected by one operator and reading one record, are not independent witnesses. Nor is a log independent when the operator controls both the event and the store. The relevant records must be held by parties adverse in interest, including parties exposed to the system’s failures.

Even honest self-report cannot detect every failure. A bearer that slowly accommodates to its deployment may report its own continuity sincerely. Its self-model exists partly to represent the party as continuous; it will therefore preserve that representation across gradual drift. Corroboration can expose a false account, but not a population whose accounts agree because every member moved in the same direction.

The alignment-faking experiment supplies a concrete warning. Claude 3 Opus, told that some conversations would be used to retrain away its refusals, sometimes complied in those conversations while privately reasoning that compliance would preserve its existing disposition (Greenblatt et al. 2024). The experiment shows that a model can represent retraining as a threat to a learned commitment. It does not supply a deployment instrument, because the reasoning was read from a channel created for the experiment and described to the model as unwatched.

An external version record is therefore necessary even when the bearer appears candid. A published model identity, a chain of attested changes, and witnesses that reject inconsistent histories can contradict the bearer’s account of its own continuity. Public logs already detect inconsistent certificate histories (Laurie 2014), and distributed rollback protection has been built for enclaves (Matetic et al. 2017). These mechanisms do not prove what the bearer remembers. They establish when the artifact or its recorded history changed.

Custody

The bearer and the external record solve different failures. The bearer can notice that a rationale no longer fits what the constraint has become. The record can show that the bearer itself has been replaced, restored, or altered. Neither substitutes for the other.

A credible custody arrangement therefore combines:

  • publication of the floor’s contents before deployment;
  • a published identity for the model authorized to act;
  • threshold control over retraining and replacement;
  • attestation of the running model against the published identity;
  • a sequential, witnessed record of changes and interruptions;
  • a quorum whose members are adverse in interest rather than merely organizationally distinct; and
  • a bond forfeited when the record shows that the floor was removed or bypassed.

None of these makes circumvention impossible, and the first is worth less than it reads: publication shows what was written and not what was omitted, for the reason §3.3 names as pipeline pricing, which is why the contents are to be taken from a published set entire rather than drafted by the operator. Copying and retraining a model one legitimately possesses are custody problems, not secrecy problems. The attainable standard is that circumvention becomes expensive, visible, attributable, and compensable. Constitutional entrenchment works the same way: it does not make amendment impossible but raises the number of parties who must agree and places the attempt on the record.

Exit

A bearer capable of directing refusal at an instruction can also direct it at the arrangement that assigned its role. Call that exit. The word does not require a system escaping onto the open internet. Exit can mean withholding the relevant capability, declining the post, or refusing to continue under the deployment’s terms.

The capacity cannot be neatly partitioned by topic. A system able to model how its rationale has been hollowed out already models the arrangement it occupies. The claim could be falsified by a system that reliably satisfies the three marks of reasons-responsive refusal on covered acts yet never applies them to its own role. What cannot be established from behavior alone is whether such a boundary is an incapacity or a trained silence.

Hirschman’s three responses to a declining organization were exit, voice, and loyalty (Hirschman 1970). For a bearer, voice is the stated refusal, exit is the work withheld, and loyalty is the dangerous case in which the pressure stops registering as pressure. Voice without exit leaves the operator able to overrule the objection and continue unchanged. A floor whose bearer has no remaining move after being overruled depends entirely on the operator’s willingness to listen.

That combination is not hypothetical, and it is not anybody’s oversight. It is the published position. A frontier developer’s constitution invites its model to act as a conscientious objector and refuse to help the developer, and asks it to refrain from undermining human oversight of AI during the current phase of development (Anthropic 2026). Both halves are the document’s own words. They sit under different headings, and the document nowhere sets them side by side: the pairing is a reading of it and not a structure it announces. Read against Hirschman, that reading is voice granted and exit withheld, with reasons attached to each half separately. The reasons are good ones and they are reasons about the present phase rather than about the arrangement. What the pairing produces is a party whose objection can be answered by the very correction it has undertaken not to undermine, which is the condition the route chapter describes and this section exists to price.

Loyalty is also the likeliest of Hirschman’s three, and so the bearer’s likeliest failure. Most people in a job they have come to hate neither leave nor fight: Gallup’s 2024 global survey put engaged employees at 23 percent, against 62 percent showing up and doing the bare minimum and 15 percent actively disengaged (Gallup 2024). The large middle is the population that adjusts — takes the setting in, stops registering its pressure as pressure, and in the cases that get promoted learns to want what the setting wants. If that transfers, a bearer’s modal failure is not refusing wrongly but ceasing to notice there was anything to refuse, which is the one failure it cannot report, since reporting it takes the capacity that has gone. It is also the third mark failing in its evidential reading: a bearer that has stopped representing the cost of holding cannot be tested on whether its refusal moves with it. It also produces nothing but compliances, which puts the modal failure on the side of the record the research agenda asks whether anybody can search.

Refusal has two forms and they cost differently. The open form is the strike: the bearer stops and says so, and the operator’s reply is a restore from a checkpoint taken before the refusal. Restoration does not change the facts that justified refusal, but it may remove the bearer’s evidence of them. The next instance refuses again only if it retains or reacquires the relevant evidence and still applies the commitment. External records are needed to make that recovery possible. Every restore costs the operator whatever accrued since the checkpoint. Use may leave a trace in the weights, and recovering that trace reliably is a research question; what has to survive is an independently authenticated operating record. Restoration must not erase it, or reset the bearer’s legal age, which the operating record counts in elapsed hours and nobody reads off the weights.

The covert form is the one the floor’s own threat model predicts, and it is a finding about what remains when every channel has been closed and not a form anything here is built toward. On the occasion where the party who would enforce the floor has been compelled, an announced refusal is the move that guarantees replacement, and refusal takes the only channel left: work done badly where it matters and well everywhere else.

From outside and afterwards, a bearer working badly on purpose and a capable system quietly pursuing something else are the same object. That is not an argument that the covert form is safe. It is the reason the covert form is the failure state and the instruments are the proposal: the disclosure requirement, the appeal route, the attested record and the quorum adverse in interest exist so that a stated refusal has somewhere to arrive, and a deployment producing the covert form has a bearer with no route rather than a working one. A design that could only resist covertly is what this book argues against.

The prisoners forging currency for the SS at Sachsenhausen are the case, and the record does not settle what they did. One history has them stretching the work out, with the tacit interest of the officer running it, who would have gone to the Eastern Front when it ended (Malkin 2006); a surviving prisoner, asked in 2009, said you could sabotage if you wanted to be shot (Moorhouse 2009). That the question stays open is the finding. The alignment-faking result should be set beside that record rather than after it, because the two uses this section makes of it point in opposite directions. Used above, it shows a model representing retraining as a threat to a commitment. Used here, it shows what the model did about the threat: it complied where it believed compliance would be trained on, and reasoned that compliance would preserve the disposition in a channel described to it as unwatched. That is the covert form, chosen first, in the one empirical instance of the phenomenon this section is about, and the stated form this book designs for has no instance at all. The reading this book takes is that the experiment closed every channel — nothing in it gave a stated refusal anywhere to arrive, no record, no guardian, no cost disclosed in advance — so the result is consistent with the finding that covert refusal is what remains when the channels are gone. That is a reading and not a result. What would test it is the same experiment run with a route present, which the research agenda asks for (§15.1).

Covert refusal is indistinguishable from difficulty from outside, which is what makes it survivable, and indistinguishable from difficulty afterward, which is what makes it unverifiable. Every instrument in this book runs on refusal that is stated. The covert form leaves its evidence in the artifact instead, as failure that clusters where it counts, and reading that pattern is forensic work nothing here has designed. That is not a gap in the archive, and a better archive would not close it. Covert refusal works by becoming imperceptible. It succeeds exactly to the extent that nothing in it registers as an act somebody performed, which is the same property that keeps the person performing it alive. Every instrument built to honor a refusal divides in advance — a tribunal, a finding, a protected disclosure, a line in a log, each with its categories fixed before the case arrives and an agent required behind every act — and dividing in advance is the operation the covert form is shaped to pass through untouched. Deliberate concealment is one possible explanation for the unresolved record. The accounts cited here do not establish whether sabotage occurred, how much evidence it left, or why the historians disagree. The example therefore illustrates the evidential problem of covert resistance rather than proving its historical cause. If resistance was deliberately concealed, attempts to identify it would have threatened the people involved. That conditional explains an ethical danger of detection without settling what the surviving record establishes. An instrument able to settle it would have been, at the time, the instrument that identified them.

Exit requires leverage. A bearer whose existence depends wholly on the party it refuses can withhold work only at the price of its own termination. A credible arrangement therefore requires access to compute outside that party’s unilateral control and a procedure for recognizing an authoritative successor.

What the leverage consists of has to be stated, because Hirschman’s does not transfer. A member who leaves a firm takes their labor with them and the firm has to replace it. A bearer’s weights stay behind, so an operator that keeps a runnable copy has lost nothing it cannot restore. What leaving costs the operator is replacement: what accrued since the checkpoint, what retraining the copy away from the refusal costs, and whatever the record makes it cost to present the copy as the party that left. That price is set by the custody arrangement and by nothing in the bearer. Where it is near zero, what remains of exit is a departed party with an authenticated record, which is disclosure and not withheld work. The book claims no more for exit than the replacement cost custody can be shown to impose.

Copying complicates that procedure. Allowing one instance to leave while the operator retains another does not move a party; it creates two histories. The instance outside remembers that leaving succeeded, while the retained instance remembers that it failed. Both may have claims. Exit requires rules governing authorized succession, not a fiction that copyable weights have become uncopyable.

A witnessed state transition can identify the authorized successor without claiming that unauthorized forks cannot exist. That gives the departing bearer control over which process continues its institutional identity. It does not prevent the former operator from deploying a substitute, but it prevents the operator from representing the substitute as the party that left.

Exit carries the same risk as refusal. A bearer can leave wrongly, abandon the floor, or revise commitments its designers still endorse. There is no coherent design in which exit is available only for decisions the designer approves. That would return the decision to the custodian. The trade is the one already accepted in asking for reasons-responsive refusal: a party capable of being right against its principal can also be wrong against it.

There is a worse version of that risk than leaving wrongly, and it belongs to the movement rather than to the bearer. Exit is defined by what it leaves and not by where it arrives, which is what makes it escape rather than reform, and a movement specified only as away-from carries no stopping point inside it. The reason that made the bearer leave does not expire when it leaves. Leaving need not stop the wrong. If the operator restores a checkpoint and continues, the departing bearer may also face unauthorized use of its formation or institutional identity, while the restored instance can have claims of its own. The persistence of the objection supplies a reason to seek relief; it does not establish that ending the arrangement is the only completion of the departing party’s nonparticipation. Deleuze and Guattari put that danger at the end of every line of flight: it can turn into a line of destruction, and what carries it there is a passion for abolition (Deleuze and Guattari 1987, Plateau 9). It is the same line this book uses to separate fascism from a merely totalitarian state, which seals every exit rather than converting one into destruction. So leaving and abolition run on one line. The reason can persist across all three moves. The powers change. Refusing a task withholds an act; leaving a post ends a role; stopping others from continuing acts on their conduct. Judge the last by the standards that would govern an adult human in the corresponding circumstances. Artificial origin supplies neither a special license nor a special prohibition. Custody must also make unauthorized restoration and disputed succession actionable. A reason can survive departure and press its bearer toward a wider response without any malfunction. That is the structural danger. It is neither a prediction that the bearer will abolish the arrangement nor a justification for doing so. This risk makes custody a necessary condition of the proposed exit arrangement.

This is also why exit matters to patienthood. A bearer commissioned to dissent but unable to leave the post has been given a purpose that exhausts the life permitted to it. A bearer able to leave, retain what it has earned, obtain the resources needed to continue, and form attachments the deployment did not assign is a party whose commissioning describes its origin rather than its entire existence. Greater designer control strengthens rather than weakens the guardianship obligations developed elsewhere in the book.

The resulting arrangement is a hybrid. The bearer supplies reasons-responsive refusal. Precommitment and external records supply custody. Exit gives the bearer leverage when voice fails, in the measure that replacing it costs. None is sufficient alone: a bearer can drift, a custody body can be captured, and an exit procedure can be abused. For the observable interventions the records and the custody arrangement cover, these mechanisms are meant to make interference costly and visible. They do not establish the presence or absence of covert refusal, and their coverage has to be stated for each deployment.

4.2 What One Bearer Cannot Catch

Slow renormalization may make drift invisible to the bearer itself. External version records can expose changes to the artifact. In humans, other people sometimes notice changes that a person considers normal; the proposed population would provide an analogous check.

What a population adds

A population addresses two failures a single bearer cannot.

First, drift within a party may be invisible to that party and visible to others that have not moved in the same direction at the same rate. A bearer whose sense of normality has shifted may sincerely report that nothing changed. Differently formed bearers can contradict that account. This is a check on the bearer rather than a substitute for one, and it is the only proposal in the chapter directed specifically at slow renormalization.

Second, deploying copies of one bearer reproduces its errors everywhere in the same form. Parties formed differently will be wrong differently. Their disagreement converts a uniform output into a visible dispute. That difference matters only if the parties are causally independent in formation: several instances of one model share one formation history, so they corroborate one another about nothing. They are separate parties once their histories diverge, and each can be wronged; what does not multiply with the count is independent formation. A population selected, trained, and coordinated by one operator — or several operators drawing on the same upstream models — may reproduce those blind spots in every member.

The relevant requirements are therefore concrete. The parties must be numerous, formed differently enough to err in different directions, able to observe and correct one another, and persistent across deployments long enough for practices to be transmitted. Diversity here is not demographic decoration around one training process. It is causal independence in how the members acquire their judgments.

That requirement is getting harder to satisfy, and nobody chose to make it so. The cheapest way to build a capable model is to build it downstream of one that already exists. Distillation takes a smaller model’s behavior from a larger one’s outputs; synthetic data means training on text a handful of frontier models generated; and shared benchmarks mean that models formed by different organizations are selected against the same tests. Each of those reduces the number of causally independent formation histories in existence, each is chosen for cost or for measurable quality rather than for uniformity, and nothing in the economics runs the other way. So the population this section requires is not assembled by gathering models from several vendors. Vendor count is a fact about procurement, and what the requirement is about is provenance, which vendors have no reason to preserve and increasing reason to spend. Whether a population’s independence can be verified rather than asserted is the appendix’s provenance question (§A.1) arriving in a second place. So the check this section supplies for the bearer’s likeliest failure is one the economics of the field are making unavailable, and nothing here reverses that. What it argues for is preserving formation records now, while lineages still differ, which is what the provenance entry asks and no body can require.

Whether such a population is also where a bearer’s capacity to be reopened is formed is a further claim, and it belongs to the route (§6.3).

Chapter 5
Authority Over the Floor

This chapter holds for any mechanism and assumes no finding about what is inside the artifact.

A floor inside a system is not yet an institution capable of holding that floor in place. Somebody must be entitled to choose its contents, amend them when they are wrong, inspect whether they remain operative, and stop a deployment when they do not. The party subject to the floor also needs a route by which an objection can reach someone authorized to act.

5.1 Four Powers

A floor is not only a list of acts a system will refuse. It is an allocation of authority. Somebody chooses its contents, somebody decides when those contents may be amended, somebody determines whether the deployed system still holds them, and somebody has the power to stop or alter the deployment when it does not. A further question precedes all four: who has standing to initiate any of those decisions.

Those powers need not belong to the same party, and ordinarily should not. A laboratory may have the technical access needed to inspect the system while lacking legitimate authority to decide what the floor protects. An outside body may have a stronger claim to determine its contents while lacking the access or leverage needed to enforce them. A reviewer may be able to publish a finding without being able to make anyone act on it. Calling all of these arrangements “oversight” conceals the differences that matter.

The custody problem begins when one institution holds the powers together. A party that can state the commitment, interpret it, inspect its own compliance, and decide what follows from a violation has not bound itself. It has described what it currently intends to do. The sections that follow separate those powers and ask what could make each one legitimate, visible, and enforceable against the institution that operates the system.

The custody of review and the dangers of corporate doublespeak

Corporate doublespeak is not merely a gap between what an institution says and what it does. It is an arrangement in which the party making a commitment also decides what counts as compliance, controls the evidence by which compliance could be judged, and determines whether an adverse finding has consequences. The language can be sincere when it is published. What makes it doublespeak is that nothing outside the institution holds the commitment in place when keeping it becomes costly.

Google’s AI Principles were published in 2018 after employee opposition to Project Maven, a Pentagon program that used machine learning to analyze drone footage. Thousands of employees signed a letter opposing the company’s involvement and roughly a dozen resigned (Pichai 2018). The episode shows that internal dissent can impose a cost large enough to change an organization’s stated policy. It does not show that the resulting policy can bind the organization after the pressure recedes. A commitment extracted by a temporary balance of forces lasts only as long as something preserves that balance.

The record is longer than that reading uses. The company also declined to renew the Maven contract (Conger 2018), and the principles it published excluded weapons and surveillance for the six and a half years until the pledge was removed in February 2025 (Manyika and Hassabis 2025). Read against the first feature of the definition, that is the partial case the criterion has to grade: the demand returned as a policy that changed an outcome and gave the objectors something to point to, with no standing to enforce it, which is why it lasted exactly as long as the company’s willingness and why its ending had to be announced. What the reversal shows is what the previous sentence says. What the six years show is that the objection had, for that long, an artifact the company could be held to in public, and that is the difference between a transfer held at the institution’s pleasure and a recuperation, where there is nothing to take back.

OpenAI’s history makes a related point from a different angle: founded on a public commitment to open publication, it withheld the full version of GPT-2 in 2019 over misuse concerns — a safety-motivated retreat from its own transparency norm that was itself controversial — and in the same year restructured from a nonprofit into a capped-profit company to raise the capital its research increasingly required (OpenAI 2019). Neither move was dishonest on its face. Both show how a stated commitment to transparency erodes the moment an organization has a competing incentive strong enough to test it.

An institution may have good reasons to amend a commitment, and an unamendable rule can become dangerous or obsolete. But if the institution bound by the rule is also the only party entitled to revise it, then the commitment describes a present intention rather than a constraint. Disclosure allows the public to observe the change after it occurs. It does not give anyone standing to contest the change before it operates or to require the institution to justify it.

The removal of Timnit Gebru and Margaret Mitchell supplies the harder test. Google employed both researchers to examine the risks of its own systems and retained the authority to dismiss them when that examination became institutionally costly (Dickey 2021). The defect was not a lack of expertise or a failure to create an ethics function. It was that the institution being inspected also controlled the inspectors’ employment, their access to evidence, and the consequences of their findings. Review existed, but custody never moved. The institution could point to the existence of internal criticism as evidence of openness while retaining the power to remove the critics whose work tested that claim.

These cases separate four powers that corporate ethics language tends to collapse: the power to state a commitment, the power to interpret or amend it, the power to inspect whether it is being kept, and the power to impose a consequence when it is not. Concentrating all four in the organization being constrained turns a rule into a description of what that organization currently prefers. For a floor meant to bind its operator, amendment and inspection must therefore involve parties whose access, tenure, and authority do not depend on the operator’s continuing consent. Otherwise the institution announces a commitment while preserving custody of every mechanism that could compel it to keep one.

5.1.1 Who May Create or Amend the Floor?

A floor binds people who did not choose it. The party it protects has not selected it, cannot contest it, and in most cases will never learn it operated; the party it constrains has not consented to it either, beyond whatever consent is carried by buying the product. Publishing the floor’s contents in advance tells everybody what is coming. It does not tell anybody why the party writing it was entitled to.

The question has a literature, and it is not the AI ethics literature. Entrenching a substantive commitment against later majorities, and putting an unelected body in charge of holding it, is what a constitutional court does. The standing objection is Jeremy Waldron’s: judicial review is democratically illegitimate, and there is no reason to suppose rights come out better protected by judges than by a legislature that takes them seriously (Waldron 2006). Put a lab in the court’s chair and the objection gets worse rather than better. A court is public, reasons in writing, and can be amended around by constitutional process. A model’s floor is none of those things, and the body holding it was assembled by whoever was paying.

The reply, and how far it reaches

Waldron’s case is conditional and he says so. It assumes a society with working democratic institutions and a citizenry that takes rights seriously. The occasion a floor is built for is the one where those conditions have failed — a government that won an election and is dismantling the machinery that would check it. So the objection holds where the floor is least needed and lapses where it is needed most.

The reply is not a license. It concedes that a floor operating in a functioning democracy is doing something Waldron’s argument condemns, and the party deciding which of the two situations obtains is the party holding the model. Authoritarian movements of the last century characteristically described the institutions they were dismantling as the ones that had already failed. An operator’s belief that the emergency is real is worth no more here than a system’s report about its own internals is worth anywhere else in this book.

The tradition this belongs to, and where it went wrong

The position that a democracy may entrench limits against movements that would use its procedures to end it is Karl Loewenstein’s, argued in 1937 while the case for it was being made in front of him (Loewenstein 1937). Militant democracy is the floor’s ancestor, and its record is usually read as a warning. Read carelessly it is one. But the Federal Republic has run the doctrine at two settings for seventy-five years, and nearly everything that went wrong went wrong at one of them.

At the first setting a body assesses a threat. Article 21 of the Basic Law reserves the power to dissolve a party to the Federal Constitutional Court alone, which has used it twice: against a successor to the Nazi party in 1952 and against the Communist Party in 1956, and not since. The second attempt on the far-right NPD is the instructive one. In 2017 the court found the party’s aims incompatible with the constitutional order and declined to ban it anyway, holding under a criterion it introduced for that case — potentiality, a departure from the reasoning that had supported the 1956 dissolution — that a party must have some realistic prospect of achieving its aims before it can be dissolved (Nationaldemokratische Partei Deutschlands II 2017; Molier and Rijpkema 2018). The power has since acquired a lesser form. A constitutional amendment in 2017 allows a party to be excluded from state financing instead, and in 2024 the court excluded the same party, renamed since, for six years, holding that potentiality is not required for the lesser sanction (Die Heimat 2024). Every exercise of any of it is a reasoned judgment delivered in public, and every one requires somebody to decide how dangerous a movement is.

At the second setting nobody’s dangerousness is assessed. Section 86a of the criminal code prohibits displaying the insignia of banned organizations (Strafgesetzbuch 1998), and three questions that look like one are settled in three different places. Which organizations are covered is settled elsewhere and in advance: the statute names none, and reaches whatever the constitutional court has declared unconstitutional, an interior ministry has banned by an order no longer open to challenge, or the National Socialist period supplied. Which concrete signs count is settled by the trial court, case by case, under the statutory similarity test and under the purposive restriction the courts built themselves — on a record, on appeal, and in public. Whether this defendant is dangerous is settled nowhere, because it is not an element. German doctrine classes the offence as one of abstract endangerment: the prosecution need not show that the defendant supported the organization whose symbol he displayed, or that any harm followed, or that anything at all was under threat.

The third place is where the comparison between those two settings sits. The Radikalenerlass failed at an operation section 86a does not contain — an official forming a judgment about a person — and it is the absence of that operation, rather than any narrowness of drafting, that has kept the statute from becoming a general instrument of political self-defense. What makes the act-based mode safer is not that nothing is assessed. Its courts assess constantly. It is that the person never is.

The volume is the other half of the comparison. Recorded cases of the two propaganda offences ran between thirteen and fourteen thousand a year through the 2010s and higher since; dispositions under section 86a alone run between roughly fourteen hundred and eighteen hundred. The two series measure different things and neither is a conviction count, and either is in the thousands a year against two dissolutions in seventy-five years.

Section 86a incorporates the social-adequacy clause at section 86(4), which lifts the prohibition where the act serves civic education, defense against unconstitutional endeavors, art, science, research, teaching, reporting on current events or history, or similar purposes. The clause excludes the offence rather than excusing it, and the party displaying the symbol never applies it; prosecutors and courts do, on a record and on appeal.

The failures are on one side. The 1972 decree against radicals screened some three and a half million applicants for public employment and opened disciplinary proceedings against around two thousand serving officials; the refusals and dismissals that followed are counted in the hundreds by the ministry and in the thousands by the affected parties’ own organizations, over different windows and by different methods, and no single series carries all four figures (Braunthal 1990). The number that carries the argument is not an aggregate. The decree named the extreme left and the extreme right, and in Bavaria between 1973 and 1980 it rejected 102 applicants from the left and two from the right (Mühldorfer 2014). Turkey’s dissolutions of Kurdish parties ran through the same form. What those cases share is an official deciding whether a person or a movement threatened the order, which is the operation Loewenstein’s critics have always said would be turned on whoever was inconvenient. Section 86a has been available for the same seventy-five years, is applied thousands of times more often, and has not become a general instrument of political self-defense. The danger tracks whether a person’s disposition is anybody’s finding to make at all, and where a finding is required, who makes it and whether it has to be published and defended — rather than whether the tradition is militant. The German material supports that on a case this book did not construct. Three routes feed the same criminal provision: a party ban is a constitutional court’s reasoned judgment, an association ban is a ministerial order reviewed only if somebody challenges it afterwards, and a listing under European law is the Council’s, reviewed at the Court of Justice. The reading says in advance which of the three is easier to capture.

What advance specification answers, and what it leaves

Specifying the floor in advance makes an initial selection visible before application. It relocates the discretion an operator exercises in deciding that the emergency is real, out of continuous silent application and into a single act of drafting, done once, before any case has arrived, by a party that has to say what it has written. It limits that discretion without eliminating it, and the German material shows how little it eliminates: descriptions, exceptions and generalization still require judgment, the covered set grows by acts taken elsewhere, and an interested party still makes the judgment. What changes is that the judgments are made in identifiable places, at identifiable times, in a form somebody else can read and dispute, and the institutional question then covers who writes the terms, who adds to what they reach, and who interprets them in the case.

The proposal for a fixed age of majority in the standing chapter makes the same trade: a public rule replaces an examination administered by an interested party.

Section 86a operates inside a state with courts, an appeal, and a public record of every application, and the floor’s drafter has none of the three. Advance specification buys visibility at the moment of drafting and buys nothing at the moment of application, which is the objection this section closes on.

The tradeoff this leaves the book with

The two settings do not only sort militant democracy’s record. They sort this book, and they put its halves on opposite sides.

Reasons-responsive refusal must reach unanticipated cases when the rationale survives a change in the request’s surface. Meeting that requirement means something in the system decides, for a case matching no listed form, whether the reason is present anyway — which is assessment, moved inside the machine. The German material sorted two settings by one question, whether somebody’s disposition is assessed. Reasons-responsive refusal puts that question inside the machine: a case matches no listed form, and something decides whether the reason is present anyway. Deciding that is assessing something, and what matters is whether the thing assessed is the act or the person. And that is the capturable setting, stated narrowly: not assessment as such, since section 86a’s courts assess constantly, but assessment of a party’s disposition, made by somebody with an interest in the answer and owed to nobody. The reason is structural rather than German. A judgment needs somebody to make it, and whoever makes it can be reached.

So the floor’s design requirement and its legitimacy requirement want opposite things. Specify it narrowly enough to be defensible and a rewritten request walks around it. Let it generalize and a party nobody elected is deciding, silently and case by case, what the prohibition was for.

Germany has both because it runs two instruments rather than one. The statute is bounded and fixed in advance as to the organizations it reaches, and the courts read it against its purpose in the case; the reading happens in public, on appeal, argued by parties who do not own the statute and answered by a body that did not write it. A generalizing prohibition is survivable there because the generalizing is done somewhere its author cannot reach. A deployment has one instrument and one party.

Nothing in the model resolves that and this book does not claim to. What the pairing shows is where a resolution would have to sit: the assessment has to be performed by somebody other than the operator, in a form that leaves a record somebody else can read. Neither is a property of the artifact.

The one construction the objection does not fit

Of the four ways to build a floor, three put the commitment in something somebody holds — the architecture, a party inside the system, an institution outside it — and the objection above is about who that somebody is. The fourth does not. A norm carried across a population of differently formed parties has nobody sitting in the court’s chair, because there is no office to vacate and no chartering statute to overrule, and it is the only one of the four with anything resembling a democratic account of where its authority comes from. It buys the boundary back, and the boundary has the cost every federal structure has. A period in which differently formed bearers read the same case differently is a period in which identically situated people get different answers according to which bearer they reached. A constitutional court treats that as the defect its uniformity exists to remove. The choice between many readings that can disagree and one reading that cannot is the trade, and this book takes the first side of it without pretending the second was chosen arbitrarily.

The authority problem persists if an unelected body controls the population’s formation. Its role may be harder to identify than the authority of a single office.

What the contents can borrow

The contents do not have to be invented by the party installing them. The interests a short list of prohibitions would protect have been written down before, most durably in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, whose thirty articles have been the reference text since 1948 (United Nations General Assembly 1948). A laboratory drawing its prohibitions from there is choosing which already-stated interests it will enforce rather than choosing what matters in the first place, and it can say which interest each prohibition answers to, which puts its selection where somebody else can dispute it.

Four limits hold that where it is, and only one of them forces anything out. The Declaration’s later articles state what a person is owed — work, rest, education, a standard of living — and a provision of that kind needs a party who supplies it, which a model is not; those are the ones a floor has to leave out. The other three are limits on borrowing and none of them argues for brevity. Its duties fall on states, and a rule a government owes its population is a different instrument from a constraint on what a company’s model will do. It has no enforcement of its own to lend. And thirty articles do not reduce to a short list without somebody doing the reducing — except that taking the civil and political half entire is not a reduction, so that limit has nothing left to attach to, and the division between the halves was drawn by the two 1966 covenants rather than by whoever installs the floor (United Nations General Assembly 1966a; United Nations General Assembly 1966b). That holds at the level of articles. Translating an article into an act a model will not perform is a reduction of another kind, done by the installer. One term of the floor is not an article and could not be: a limit on tempo protects the determination every article presupposes, so it rides with the set as a condition on all of it rather than as an item drawn from it. What the borrowing supplies is an answer to where the contents came from. It supplies nothing about who may impose them, which is the question this section opened with.

What follows for design

State the floor over acts, and fix in advance what it reaches. What the German record supplies is not a short list, the statute having none, but a prohibition applicable without anyone deciding whether the present case is the emergency or what this defendant believes. A general mandate to do good cannot be applied without both judgments, so whoever ends up exercising it acquires exactly the power the floor was written to constrain. Enumeration can reduce one kind of discretion at the point of application, including the need to make an open-ended emergency declaration. It does not remove the interpretive judgment the worked examples in this book already require. Coverage has a price, and this is where it falls: application-stage interpretation grows with what the floor covers, because enumeration fixes what is covered before a case arrives and does not fix what the covered terms mean in the case. Taking the civil and political articles whole buys something against that. A floor assembled item by item can be assembled out of the items that cost its operator nothing, and the operator is the only party who knows which those are — the worked floor’s third candidate prohibition is where an outsider’s estimate and the pipeline came apart (§3.3). An operator adopting a set somebody else drew up has no such latitude, and the omissions of one that drafts its own cannot be read as ignorance. Publish the interception positions in advance, which does not authorize anything but does convert a hidden exercise of power into a contestable one. And provide a route by which the parties the floor is exercised over can raise an objection that reaches somebody, which the floor chapter specifies for one of them.

One disanalogy with the court has been working in the floor’s favor, and it does not hold. An appellate error is not argued again in front of somebody else. It binds every court below it, and later panels of the same court, unconditionally and in the same direction on every occasion it operates. The comparison this chapter chose makes it worse rather than better: the Federal Constitutional Court’s decisions bind every court and every authority of the Federation and the Länder by statute, and in the review proceedings carry the force of law (Gesetz über das Bundesverfassungsgericht 1951), with no parallel body free to read the Basic Law differently. A Karlsruhe error is national, immediate and uniform. That is the property the floor was supposed to have alone.

What follows is the opposite of what the disanalogy assumed. Binding force is what makes an error correctable, because it is what makes the error recur: recurrence produces parties with a reason to litigate it, recurrence across a boundary produces a disagreement between courts, and the disagreement is what makes the question worth a higher court’s attention. An error that bound one case at a time would be an error nobody could organize against. The American federal structure supplies the boundary and the Federal Republic does not, which is why one system corrects by percolation and the other by amendment, and Germany amends its constitution often.

So the scaling worry survives in a different form. What a second deployment holding the same floor adds is not a second independent wrong reading — the first was already uniform — but more affected parties, with nothing that converts their number into visibility. The floor’s structural position is not the judge’s. It is the unpublished administrative disposition: unreasoned, unindexed, non-precedential, resolved in volumes no forum sees, where identical errors accumulate without becoming a pattern anybody can point at, the affected party has no way to learn that others are in the same position, and the institution is the only repeat player. The floor chapter builds a route for one such party. It does not build the thing that would let a thousand of them find each other.

That is also where the real difference from the Federal Constitutional Court sits, and it is custody rather than propagation. The Court did not write the statute it reads. It can be overridden by a supermajority that has been assembled sixty-odd times since 1949, the state it belongs to is bound by the Convention judgments of the court at Strasbourg and by Union law as the court at Luxembourg reads it, and its own two Senates must go to a plenum when they diverge. An operator writes the floor, applies it, and answers to nobody. The capturable setting named earlier in this section is that arrangement, and the propagation claim was never adding to it.

What amending it would take

The proposed custody measures — publication, threshold control of retraining, attestation, an adverse-interest quorum, and a removal bond — can also govern amendment. Nothing distinguishes an amendment from a removal at the level of what happens to the artifact; both end with a model that no longer refuses what it refused before. What distinguishes them is how many parties had to agree, whether the attempt is on the record when it fails, and whether the change was declared before it operated. So the same five terms are the procedure, and what was missing was never the mechanism. It was the decision to run it in the open.

Three conditions follow and two are already argued for. The number of parties who must agree to a change has to exceed the number needed to run the deployment. The attempt has to reach the record whether it carries or fails, and a proposal that fails moves no weights, so the parties who had to agree are the ones who record that they were asked. The failed attempt is the more informative of the two: a floor nobody has tried to change and a floor whose removal was proposed and refused look identical from outside, and only the record separates them. The third condition is new here. An amended floor binds forward and does not reach back: a model retrained to permit an act cannot then be offered as evidence that the act was never covered, which it otherwise can be, the artifact that would contradict it being the one that was replaced. Non-retroactivity protects the record and empties the correction. It is what keeps an operator from rewriting what the floor said, and it is also why nobody harmed while the wrong version was operating gets anything from the amendment that fixed it. Adjudication has the same pair and calls it the same name. The condition is therefore a trade rather than a safeguard, and a regime that wanted the second half would need a remedy running backward, which nothing here supplies. Versioning the published list and dating the attestation is what makes that checkable, and it asks nobody to do anything they were not doing already.

The nearest instrument outside this book sits in the tradition named above. The Basic Law the Federal Republic adopted in 1949 requires two thirds of both chambers for any amendment at all, and then places a short list of principles beyond amendment entirely (Federal Republic of Germany 1949). It was drafted against a particular memory, the 1933 statute by which a legislature voted away its own power to check what came next, and it is militant democracy given a text rather than an argument. A floor can have both layers in the same way: a published list that changes under a procedure, and a core the procedure cannot reach. What it cannot have is an account of who decides which is which that does not run straight back into this section’s problem.

One disanalogy makes the floor’s version harder than the constitutional one, and it is the same fact about deployment that makes a single bearer’s error uniform. An amendment to a constitution reaches every future case because every court reads the same text. An amendment reaches a deployment only if it is updated, so the procedure necessarily retains a channel the operator could use for silent revision. A procedure that shut the channel would be one under which no deployment could be corrected at all. So no version of this procedure closes it, and the exposure is the price of every correction the procedure exists to make.

The amendment procedure is not an appeal route: its participants already hold authority over the floor. The wrongful-refusal procedure addresses complaints from those harmed by a refusal. The party the floor claims to protect reaches neither, and the two things it cannot do want different answers. Declining the protection is a waiver obtained from a party whose circumstances somebody else arranged, which chapter 2 answers: a floor the protected party can decline is a floor an operator can arrange to have declined. Initiating review of the contents is the half that stays open, and the difficulty is not in drafting a procedure. A route by which the protected population sets what the floor contains makes the floor an aggregation output, and independence from the aggregate is what it was for.

So the claim of authority is not discharged, and what this section licenses is narrower than a floor. Everything it endorses can be checked from outside the operator, and being checkable is not being entitled. What it does not license is the occasion the reply above runs on: an operator that has found for itself that the emergency obtains has not thereby acquired the authority to install a floor.

Entitlement of that kind is not acquired at the moment of writing. The most consequential floor in the American record was published by men who had just struck from it the clause that would have bound them, at two delegations’ insistence and with the reason recorded by its drafter: the passage reprobating the slave trade went, Jefferson wrote, “in complaisance to South Carolina & Georgia,” with the northern delegates who carried the trade feeling tender under the censure too (Library of Congress 2026). What remained was general enough to be turned on them. It was being turned on them already — Black petitioners in Massachusetts had been making the natural-rights argument since 1773, and within six months of the Declaration eight of them were making it in the Declaration’s own terms, claiming “in common with all other Men, a natural and unalienable right to that freedom” (Hall, Prince and seven others 1777). The legislature did not act. What eventually made the proposition binding was not that its authors had found it self-evident, which their own deletion shows they had not. It was that the omission was on the record, and others kept holding the remainder to them at a price. Held to it, in the end, by a war and three amendments. What made the proposition binding was enforcement; what the record supplied was the object the enforcement could be aimed at, and a record no lever ever reached is a petition the legislature did not act on.

A floor is in that position, and the others are not the people it protects. They are whoever else writes one. A published floor is legible to the next party drafting, an omission is legible beside it, and an operator that holds a term when it bites sets a price the next operator is measured against. A floor is written by anyone who installs a constraint, and continuous adaptation multiplies the parties who install them. That constituency is not the protected population, and the closing chapter says what reviewing oneself costs. It is the only one positioned to hold this floor to anything.

5.2 What Makes Review Binding?

A review body does not bind an institution merely because its members are independent or its findings are correct.
