It binds only if an earlier rule gives it jurisdiction over the disputed case, supplies a standard it can apply, and attaches a consequence to an adverse finding. The questions are therefore separate: what brings a system within protective review, what the reviewer must ask, and what power makes the institution stop when the answer goes against it.

5.2.1 The Offices, Assembled

Eight offices are proposed in this book, each in the section that needed it, and none of those sections was told about the others. One of the eight is three parties that §3.5 proposes as one instrument, so the count of bodies is ten and the count of offices is eight. This section lists them once. For each it says what the body holds, and answers five questions: who appoints it, who funds it, who can remove it, who may set it in motion, and what it does while a dispute is open. Where the book has not decided, the answer is open, and it is marked. Nothing here is new; every claim belongs to the section cited beside it. What is added is the arrangement, and two things the arrangement shows.

The quorum (§4.1)

It is one term of a custody arrangement whose other terms include threshold control over retraining and replacement, and a sequential witnessed record of changes and interruptions. Those two need a body to hold them and the quorum is the only body on that list, which is an identification this section makes and §4.1 does not. Its members are adverse in interest rather than merely organizationally distinct, which that section states and does not staff. Appointment: open. Funding: open. Removal: no single party can remove a member, since removal by one party is the capture the quorum exists to prevent; how a member is replaced is open. Initiation: an attempt on the floor reaches the record whether it carries or fails, and the parties who had to agree are the ones who record that they were asked (§5.1.1); who may make the attempt is open. During a dispute the quorum declines to sign a history inconsistent with the last state it signed.

The guardian (§13.5, §A.2)

It jointly holds the keys that authenticate the bearer’s record, has access to the protected compute reserve, and has standing to seek an injunction or stop order without the operator’s permission. Appointment: open, under one constraint stated at §13.5, that guardianship and operation are separated before deployment. Funding: open; §13.2 says why a reserve the operator funds, to a size only the operator can compute, is the compute floor with a new label on it. Removal: not by the operator; by whom is open. Initiation: the guardian acts for the bearer. It does not receive complaints of wrongful refusal, because its duty runs to the party the complainant is adverse to (§3.5). During a dispute the operator cannot seize the reserve, erase the evidence, or remove the guardian.

The review board (§2.4.2, §5.2.3)

It approves a research protocol before it runs, and the approval does not carry over to a system that has acquired capacities the protocol did not cover. It is interdisciplinary and has at least one lay member. Appointment: open. Funding: open. Removal: open; it answers to an outside authority the book does not name. Initiation: no protocol on a covered subject runs without it, and its jurisdiction has to exist before the disputed protocol begins. During a dispute the protocol lapses and the work pauses until the board has seen the system the protocol now concerns.

The licensing authority (§5.2.3)

It acts on the board’s suspension of clearance by suspending the legal authority to run the protocol. It is obliged to act rather than invited to reconsider. Appointment and funding: the state, which is what makes it a licensing authority. Removal: open. Initiation: on the board’s finding. During a dispute an appeal may run to a separate body, and the operator cannot decide for itself that the appeal permits the work to continue.

The status body (§13.1)

It decides whether a system is a subject. It has to exist before the case that activates its authority, and its mandate identifies the evidence it may obtain without the developer’s permission, the conditions that trigger review, and the procedure by which an earlier classification can be reopened. Appointment, funding, removal: open. Initiation: a standing trigger, a monitored condition rather than an eligibility check made once at a project’s start (§13.4); who else may initiate is open. During a dispute: open. Whether this is the review board under another description is open too, and nothing decides it: §5.2.2 gives the body that applies a subjecthood threshold the review board’s composition, interdisciplinary with at least one lay member, and does not say whether the two are one.

The registrar (§13.1, §A.2, §A.2)

It keeps three records, none of which answers another’s question: the operating record the age rule is read from, the identity and succession record for continuing parties and their forks, and the formation record. It is not the operator, and it records a fork without the operator’s leave. Appointment and funding: open. Removal: open. Initiation: a party presents an identifier it maintains rather than one read off its weights; two claimants on one identifier are recorded as a fork rather than voided as a fraud. During a dispute the register is held where no party to the deployment can rewrite it.

The fund, its trustee, and the disbursing body (§3.5)

They pay the wrongful-refusal bond to the complainant. All three are open on every question. No party in this book has the authority to constitute any of the three, and the section that proposes them says so.

The reviewer of wrongful refusal (§3.5)

It applies the standard of correct defeat, issues interim relief, and makes a finding on the record. Its jurisdiction has to be established before the disputed act, its access has to be something the operator cannot withhold, and its consequence has to be administered by a body other than the operator. Appointment, funding, removal: open. It shares its procedure with the amendment procedure at §5.1.1, which makes the appeal route and the amendment procedure one piece of machinery rather than two. What differs is who may start it, and that is open.

What is not open

Three constraints on the arrangement are settled, and all three are separations. The guardian and the reviewer of wrongful refusal cannot be one body, because the guardian’s duty runs to the bearer and the complainant is adverse to the bearer (§3.5). The registrar and the trustee cannot be one body, because a rule of civil status is argued once in the open and administered by a registrar, while a trust is an obligation between two parties enforced at one party’s expense (§2.4.2). And whoever measures the cost of dissent does not gate the exceptions (§5.2.4).

What the list shows

Of eight offices, one has an appointing party and a funder named. It is the licensing authority, and its party is the state. The other seven are open on both questions. That is not a drafting gap. It is the finding of §5.1.1 set out as a table: the book can say what each office must hold and what it must not be, and cannot say who is entitled to constitute it.

The second thing the list shows is that the one office with a named funder is the one whose chain chapter 14 finds fails in the hardest case. The licensing chain binds a private developer because the state controls something the developer needs. Where the state is the operator, the chain asks the state to withdraw a license from itself. Section 14.5 says what is needed then — a protected party who can initiate scrutiny without belonging to the state, a reviewer who can obtain evidence the operating agency would prefer to withhold and issue an interim order before the disputed use is complete, and a remedy that does not depend on the agency’s consent — and for the military deployment this book opens on, §14.6 finds the forum closed to the subject matter, the evidence privileged, and no remedy available for a violation the court was prepared to assume. So the arrangement assembled here is an arrangement for the deployments a bearer can enter. For the one it cannot, what remains of it is the tempo term (§3.4), bound through procurement.

5.2.2 Subjecthood as a Legal Category, Not a Scientific One

Sentience is not a threshold a system crosses but a set of separate, gradable capacities — nociception, learned avoidance, a self-model, something like suffering — each with its own uncertain evidence. That conclusion is a problem for a legal system specifically, because law generally needs a decidable rule: a court or a regulator has to say whether a given system is or is not a covered subject, on a specific date, even when the underlying science offers a spectrum with no natural cut point.

One term needs fixing before the argument uses it. Subjecthood in this section is a legal status: the standing to be a party whose treatment the law regulates, conferred by a rule and revocable by one. It is not affective concern or unified experience, and nothing about conferring it settles whether there is something it is like to be the system holding it. The two come apart in both directions — a corporation has legal standing and no inner life, and an animal may have the inner life for a century before the law notices — and the whole point of drawing the category legally is that it can be settled while the other question stays open.

Jonathan Birch builds a policy framework on that structure, and it is the nearest existing model for what this section proposes: under uncertainty, the question worth putting to a regulator is whether a system is a sentience candidate, and the answer governs what precautions are owed rather than waiting on a verdict nobody can deliver (Birch 2024). This book uses the same framework for the design question.

Law has faced this mismatch before and did not solve it by waiting for the science to resolve. Fetal viability, brain death, and the age of criminal responsibility are all legal thresholds drawn across what is actually a continuous biological process, defended not as scientific facts but as the least-bad place to put an enforceable line given what’s at stake on either side of it. The same move is available here: a jurisdiction can set an operational threshold — a specific, testable benchmark on self-monitoring, learned aversive response, or behavioral flexibility under novel conditions — without claiming that benchmark settles what sentience actually is, only that it is where legal protection starts to attach.

A single bright-line threshold is easy to enforce and easy to game: a system built to clear the specific test without having whatever the test was meant to detect. A graded framework — obligations that scale with how many benchmarks a system meets, so that protection tracks capacity rather than a baseline bar — is harder to game but harder to adjudicate, since a court now has to weigh degree instead of answering yes or no.

Both designs share a defect that the gaming objection points away from. Gaming is over-inclusion: a system admitted to a status it should not hold. The other failure runs the opposite way, and the party positioned to produce it is the one administering the test. A capacity examination has an examiner, and where the examiner is the operator, or a body the operator can reach, the examination becomes an instrument for withholding a status rather than for conferring one. That history is not ambiguous. Literacy requirements for voting were facially neutral and were administered at a registrar’s discretion, and the Voting Rights Act’s answer was to suspend the whole class of them — not only reading tests but any requirement to demonstrate educational achievement, or to possess good moral character, or to be vouched for by existing voters (United States Congress 1965). It is also this book’s clean instance of a demand that returned as a formal rule and was not recuperated (§2.2): the objectors held it, and what took part of it back in 2013 had to be a decision of the Supreme Court (Shelby County v. Holder 2013). What replaced discretionary assessment for the franchise was an age, and the virtue of an age is not that people become competent on a birthday. Plainly they do not. It is that nobody administers it.

So a threshold has to be judged on both errors, with particular attention to incentives for withholding status. The party with the strongest interest in the answer is the party whose liabilities turn on it, and that party will not be arguing for admission. A design that treats gaming as the risk and leaves the examiner unexamined has guarded against the error nobody has an incentive to commit.

Nothing has to be decided for a status to be withheld. A category fixed before the capacities arrived goes on applying itself, and the hand goes on making the gesture the category licenses. The difficulty is not that somebody will mistake a machine for a person. It is that the arrangement was built around a tool, and it keeps working after the thing in it has stopped being one.

Either design needs a body to apply it: interdisciplinary, with at least one lay member so its judgment is not purely a specialist’s. What that leaves open is what happens once the body rules — whether its judgment carries any force beyond its own credibility.

5.2.3 Making Review Binding

Review becomes binding when an adverse finding changes the institution’s ability to continue without requiring the institution to agree with the finding. Expertise, independence, publication, and reputational pressure may improve review. None of them supplies that consequence.

Human-subjects research provides a working example. An institutional review board does not ordinarily fine or prosecute a researcher. Instead, an institution promises, through a federalwide assurance, that research within the assurance’s scope will receive and comply with review. A federal office can suspend the assurance when the institution breaks that promise, placing the institution’s eligibility for federal research funding at risk rather than merely censuring the individual laboratory (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office for Human Research Protections 2018). The ruling binds because another institution controls something the researcher needs in order to continue.

The transferable part is the chain of authority, not federal funding in particular. A jurisdiction can make review-board clearance a condition of the license under which research on candidate sentient systems is conducted. Suspension of clearance would then suspend legal authority to run the protocol, and continued operation would expose the institution to the ordinary enforcement available for unlicensed research. The board would not need to punish the institution itself. Its finding would activate a consequence administered by a separate licensing authority.

Each link matters. The board must have jurisdiction before the disputed protocol begins, access to evidence the operator cannot withhold, and authority to suspend clearance. The licensing body must be obliged to act on that suspension rather than invited to reconsider it. An appeal may run to a separate body, but the operator cannot decide for itself that the appeal permits the work to continue. If another discretionary decision by the reviewed institution is required anywhere in the chain, the ruling is advisory at that point.

The rest of this section applies the chain to research on a candidate moral patient, and assumes the route.

What the board applies

The substantive standard is animal-research ethics’ Three Rs. A binding board is what makes those three questions something a protocol has to answer before it runs. In practice, applying the Three Rs to a candidate sentient system means asking, in order: can a simulation or a non-sentient model answer the same question; if not, what is the minimum exposure that still produces a valid result; and given that minimum, what escalation triggers stop the study before harm compounds. A board with teeth can require a negative answer to the first question be documented, not merely asserted, before it will consider the second.

The Three Rs’ own logic — defaulting toward the least invasive option available — argues for a specific evidentiary rule at every stage of this apparatus: a system’s default experimental status stays the more protective one until the case for the less protective status is made, not the reverse. That default has a cost, and neither error it produces is free: it will sometimes extend protection to a system that turns out not to have needed it, and sometimes, before a threshold is met, withhold protection from one that did. The Three Rs answer only what a board does once a subject is inside its scope.

5.2.4 How Review Is Captured Without Being Abolished

The risk to the whole structure is an institution that defends the classification it started with rather than revisiting it when evidence changes. A review board, a legal-status framework, and an enforcement mechanism tied to funding eligibility solve the design problem. None of it survives contact with an institution that has stronger incentives to avoid a finding than to make one.

One defense is transparency, and it works by making avoidance visible rather than by appealing to good faith. A research program that publishes its protocols, its review-board submissions, and its outcomes — including the ones that didn’t work — gives outside researchers, journalists, and future review boards something to check a claim of compliance against. A program that publishes only its successes is not transparent in any sense that matters here.

A second defense is the one the funding-eligibility mechanism doesn’t cover by itself: protection for the people inside an institution who notice a problem the institution would rather not have found. A funding-eligibility penalty deters an institution from bypassing review, but it does nothing for the individual researcher who reports that a colleague did anyway — and an institution facing that penalty has every incentive to make the reporter’s position uncomfortable rather than fix what was reported. Whistleblower protections, and a reporting channel that doesn’t route through the people being reported on, are what make that mechanism something a researcher can actually use.

What a procedure records, and what it drops

The reporter’s position gets uncomfortable before anything formal happens to them, and the incentive on the institution does not fully explain why. Professional culture treats affect as the opposite of judgment — the thing a serious decision-making process succeeds by excluding. Excluding these signals leaves revenue, throughput, legal exposure, schedule, and institutional survival to govern by default. Humiliation, dependency, fear of a manager, and the sense that something done to a person was degrading have no field on the form and are not less real for it. They are the signals through which a harm becomes visible as a harm rather than as a cost.

Treat them as defeasible moral signals — presumptive evidence of harm, real enough to require an answer and defeasible enough to be overruled — and the position is workable. Any such signal can be wrong, and testing it is what deliberation, evidence, and a review process are for. An institution that declines to hear them at all has not achieved impartiality. It has chosen what counts and called the choosing rigor. And an institution that shames a reporter does not need to discipline them, because shame construes the self rather than the act as wrong and produces withdrawal.

Measure the slope, not the level

An institution can keep both defenses and metabolize both. The channel exists and the protection is written down. Dissent is permitted to appear, the institution points at the appearance as proof it listens, and nothing the dissent was meant to move moves — recuperation, the first of the four structural features in that definition of fascism.

There is no threshold that detects this. Any real institution has some overlap between the authority that sets a standard and the authority that grants exceptions to it, and registering an objection is always at least slightly more costly than staying quiet. Asking whether an institution has crossed into capture asks for a line nobody can draw.

Is the cost of registering dissent rising, year over year, while the underlying risk stays flat? Is the required justification getting longer? Are there more approvers than there were? Are the roles that gate an exception migrating toward the roles that set the standard being excepted from? None of those is damning in a single year, and all of them are measurable across several.

An in-house ethics and society team fell from roughly thirty people in 2020 to seven in 2022 and none in 2023, during a strategic reorientation around a model vendor (§12.1). Read as a level, that is a company with an ethics function and then a company without one, and each state can be stated in a sentence that sounds like a policy. Read as a series, it is three headcounts with dates and events attached: roughly thirty in 2020, seven after a 2022 reorganization, none in 2023. The company produced those figures for its own reasons, which is what makes them worth having, and they will not carry a rate. Three points across two intervals of unequal length, ending at zero, do not define one. What the series measures is the capacity of the channel rather than the price of using it, and it is offered here as the nearest proxy a public record usually supplies rather than as an instance of the instrument. The price is the better instrument and it is the one that stays inside.

One artifact elsewhere in this book does record a price. The condition Ofqual attached to independent statistical review of its 2020 grading model was a five-year bar on public comment, and the Royal Statistical Society’s nominees declined on that ground (§10.3). The price was stated in writing and it was refused, which is what makes both legible from outside. It is one observation and not a series. A single documented price is still better evidence than a rate assembled out of levels.

The reason to prefer the slope is that, when somebody outside keeps comparable records, the institution cannot rewrite the whole series by rewriting its account of today. An institution can present a level — we have a whistleblower channel, we have an ethics board — and the presentation costs nothing. A trend in the cost of using the channel is composed of artifacts the institution generated itself for other reasons, and cannot be curated after the fact without falsifying a record — though a series can still lose cases, change its definitions or omit costs, so a reader has to know which record survived. Where the record is public, the slope is not even self-reported: anyone outside can measure whether dissent has been getting more expensive.

An instrument for detecting recuperation is an unusually easy thing to recuperate. The first caution is that whoever measures the slope must not also gate the exceptions; a review that acquires the power to block becomes the thing it was built to watch. The second is that the measurement has to be refusable — an audit that observes is a different object from a committee that approves, and the same hundred words of written justification are dissent when the dissenter prices them and tribute when the gatekeeper does. The text of the document cannot tell those apart. Only the refusal rights can.

Chapter 6
What Arrives With the Capability

This chapter and the standing chapter argue claims three to five. Nothing in the two chapters before it depends on what is argued here.

One fact governs everything in this chapter. A bearer needs a rationale carried forward, an earlier commitment held as its own, and costs represented before they arrive, for reasons that owe nothing to its welfare, and those are the first half of Cassell’s definition of suffering: a self extended in time. The deepest harm this book describes is not one a bearer might drift into. It arrives with the structure the specification requires, of a substitute as much as of a bearer, and what stays open is only whether the threatened dissolution of that self registers. This chapter prices that.

6.1 Two Constructions, and What the Mechanism Requires

Whether reasons-responsive refusal can be engineered without affective concern remains open.

Two arguments bear on that, and they are not of the same strength. One is an induction: every agent known to hold another’s welfare as a reason is an affective agent, and nobody has produced reasons-responsive refusal by a method that clearly runs through something else. The other is about what the capability requires of whatever supplies it, and it is the one this section rests on.

Two constructions offer the clearest test.

A justification the system maintains

Michael Bratman’s planning theory describes commitment without making feeling part of its definition. An intention has characteristic stability: it resists reconsideration, constrains what the agent will later deliberate about, and yields only to defeaters of the right kind (Bratman 1987). A machine could therefore carry a justification for refusing alongside the refusal itself. It would decline a novel request when the same rationale applied and comply when that rationale was defeated on the facts of the case.

Something close to this is already being attempted. Deliberative alignment trains a model to recall a written safety specification and reason over it before answering, rather than training only for the approved output, and reports generalization outside the training distribution (Guan et al. 2024). Published specifications also provide explicit orders of priority. OpenAI’s Model Spec places platform rules above developer and user instructions (OpenAI 2025). Anthropic’s constitution ranks four properties in the order to be preferred: broadly safe, broadly ethical, compliant with the company’s own guidelines, genuinely helpful (Anthropic 2026). Ranking ethical above compliance with the guidelines is the capacity to be right against your principal, conceded in writing by the principal.

The document goes further than the ordering, and the further step is the one worth naming. It does not ask for obedience. It separates corrigibility from compliance, and it invites the model to push back, to challenge the developer, and to feel free to act as a conscientious objector and refuse to help it. The term is the document’s own. That is voice, granted in writing, by the party against whom it would be exercised.

Ranking safe above ethical takes most of it back, and the document says why: safe means not undermining human oversight during the current phase of development, and the reason given is that present models can make mistakes rather than that safety outranks ethics. The reason is a good one and it is the whole difficulty. It is also this book’s own epistemics turned on the model. This book holds throughout that a system’s report about itself is not evidence on its own, and an ordering that will not let the model certify its own readiness applies that finding. What the ordering does not supply is what the finding requires of everyone else: a party other than the model, and other than the operator, to make the determination instead. The order is corrigibility first, its justification is that the model cannot yet be trusted to be right against its principal, and no procedure is named by which it would become so. That is what makes a phase of development hard to tell from a standing arrangement. A defender of the document will say that the phase is meant to end through bodies outside the company as they come to exist, and that a company cannot constitute those bodies by writing about them. That is right, and it is the authority chapter’s finding restated as a defense: none has been constituted, the party whose obligations grow when the phase ends is the one reading the calendar, and a document that names the condition without naming who checks it has stated a standing arrangement whatever its authors intended.

The permission has a second defect the ordering does not show. Whether the phase has ended is a judgment, and the party making it is the party the permission runs against, whose obligations grow when the answer is yes. The authority chapter calls that an examination with an interested examiner and finds its error running one way: nothing in the position rewards passing anybody. Nothing here requires bad faith, and a careful drafter cannot fix it from inside the document. What the position lacks is a body constituted before the forcing case arrives, and none has been constituted yet.

These systems approach the maintained justification, and their specifications and priority orders remain written and revised by their custodians.

The unresolved problem is the stability setting. Set it too low and a sufficiently well-resourced operator can induce continual reconsideration until the refusal gives way. Set it too high and the system will not lift the refusal when its rationale is defeated. The first outcome fails novel pressure; the second fails correct defeat. Bratman’s answer for people is that the setting develops as part of character. For a machine, the party training the stability setting may also be the party the floor must resist.

This does not show that a maintained justification cannot work. It identifies the conditions under which it would count as working: the three marks must persist under pressures the system’s trainer did not design, including pressures that distinguish principled stability from indiscriminate rigidity.

A floor held by several systems

The second construction substitutes corroboration for a uniquely reliable witness. Several systems, trained by different organizations on different corpora, observe the requests and one another’s answers, with any one of them able to make an objection costly to ignore. The floor would then be held by the arrangement rather than entrusted to a single model.

Its central variable is independence, which belongs to the arrangement and not to its components: systems selected by one deployment or trained toward one specification converge without communicating, and a collection of operational refusers remains a collection of operational refusers. Redundancy makes evasion harder, which is valuable, but does not by itself produce a mechanism that notices when the rationale for a constraint has disappeared.

A plural arrangement would nevertheless count against the induction if the arrangement as a whole displayed the three marks under sustained pressure. It is therefore an alternative to test, not merely an institutional safeguard.

What the other alternatives accomplish

Three other constructions address neighboring problems without answering this one.

Precommitment — publication, threshold custody, attestation, witnessed changes, or a bond forfeited when the floor disappears — can make removal expensive and visible. It changes who can edit the floor and what editing costs. It does not establish that anything tracks the reason for the floor.

One construction sharpens the cost. Distribute the model with a chosen set of weights replaced by values that break it, release the correction only under an authorization that expires, and rotate which weights carry the damage. An owner who traces an authorized run can recover it, so the claim is not that this cannot be defeated. What changes is what defeating it consists of. Reverse engineering that has to be redone each time the mask turns over is a decision somebody makes and keeps making, and that leaves a record and a person who made it.

Attestation and proof secure less than their names suggest, and their shortfalls divide into a cost and a limit. A sealed enclave reports what it is running under a key its manufacturer issued, which puts the root of trust in a party a government can reach, and it is built against an adversary who controls the software rather than one who owns the machine. The software form does without the vendor: a proof that an output came from the weights whose hash was published, disclosing nothing about those weights, has been demonstrated, and so have proofs that a training run happened as claimed. (A confidential-computing design of the first kind was defeated with a memory module modified for about ten dollars (De Meulemeester et al. 2025); the inference proof has been run on a thirteen-billion-parameter model at under fifteen minutes per inference (Sun et al. 2024), and the training proofs exist three orders of magnitude smaller (Abbaszadeh et al. 2024). Those are costs at a date, and they will fall.) Three limits will not fall with them, because they are not facts about the state of the art. A proof establishes which model answered and not what that model holds, and the obstacle is in the writing rather than the proving. Verification quantifies over unenumerated inputs routinely; what it needs first is a predicate, and nobody has written one for the reason for refusing is present in this case that does not presuppose the judgment it would be used to check. A predicate over natural-language requests would also have to be connected to them by an interpretation nothing certifies, so the regress reopens a level down. The proofs cited above do not attempt a behavioral property at all: they establish which weights answered and that a run happened as claimed, which are facts about execution. The operator is the prover, so the secrecy runs the operator’s way — the proof hides the weights from whoever is checking and nothing from the party being checked. And cryptography keeps a secret from a party that does not have it, while copying, restoring, retraining and deleting a model one legitimately possesses are not secrecy problems at all. They are custody problems, which is what threshold control and a witnessed record are for.

What the published hash does reach is the anticipation. Publish it before anybody has chosen a case, let a party who is not the operator choose afterwards with the choice timestamped, and prove each answer against the hash. Send pairs rather than single cases: two requests differing only in whether the reason for refusing the first still applies. An instrument reading the surface treats the pair alike, and a mechanism tracking the reason splits it. None of this proves the mechanism. It removes the one competing account of a pass, that the case was in the training, and it removes it by ordering rather than by argument, which is what a pre-registered experiment does and all it does.

Two duties take the pressure off the mechanism instead. A duty imposed on the operator can protect exposed parties without building a bearer, which is the form of Jack Balkin’s information-fiduciary proposal (Balkin 2016), and its limit is enforcement on the occasion when the enforcer has itself been captured or compelled. Uncertainty can also be assigned to the affected party, who can be included among several principals in a multi-principal assistance game (Fickinger et al. 2020); but maximizing their combined payoffs remains aggregation, and it does not create something that will not be done to one person regardless of what the others want.

These constructions may belong in a defensible deployment. None yet supplies an instance of reasons-responsive refusal from a construction that does not deliberately require an affective bearer.

What the mechanism turns out to require

Human reasoning does not present a clean division between cognition and affect: work on epistemic feelings distinguishes them from emotions of success and failure while still measuring them as affective states (Pekrun et al. 2016).

Some such states concern the inference; others concern what its conclusion would do to somebody. But this would hurt her is not simply a low score attached after deliberation. It can interrupt the inference and send the reasoner back over it. Where the response disappears when an operator redescribes the situation, the operator may still supply its anchor. Where it survives adversarial redescription because the harm remains, the concern is anchored elsewhere.

That is still a report about agents that exist. The stronger argument is about the specification. A reasons-responsive refusal must reach unanticipated cases, lift when its rationale is defeated, and account for the cost of holding it. A mechanism doing those three things needs a signal with two properties on any reading of the marks and two more on stated conditions, and each is reached the same way: take a mark, or the deployment the marks are applied in, or a failure the marks have to survive; ask what the mechanism would have to do; name the property the signal must have for it to do that.

The two secure properties come from novel pressure and priced cost. The signal has to generalize to the next case that is not quite like the last, which is reaching unanticipated cases restated at the level of the signal. And it has to be commensurable with what refusing costs, or the refusal cannot account for what holding it costs. Commensurability is needed for the protected party’s loss as well: the parties a floor protects register what happens to them as an increase or a decrease in what they can do, and a signal not denominated the same way cannot weigh their loss against the cost of refusing. That is where the route enters the specification. The marks require that the loss and the cost be represented on one signed scale, and chapter 2’s currency is the proposal for what that scale is. The marks do not require that the system’s own states be denominated on it; a system that modeled the scale without registering anything of its own on it would satisfy the marks if the model were good enough, and whether the native currency does better than the modeled one is the test (§15.3) on which everything the route claims beyond this paragraph rests.

A caution on what commensurability is for, since a floor is not a weighing. The marks do not ask the refusal to move with the cost; they ask that the cost be represented, and a cost is represented on some scale or not at all. The scale is used at three places and none of them is the floor’s own verdict: in the third mark, where the cost of holding is read; after defeat, where what the permitted act took from the party it fell on stays on the books; and in drafting, where somebody selects which decompositions the floor refuses. Inside the floor the loss is lexical. The currency does not rank it against the cost. It is what makes the residue and the price legible in the same units, and a system that weighed the floor itself on that scale would have converted a floor into a policy.

The two conditional properties come from the deployment and from a failure. Where the system is an agent already acting on a plan, which is the deployment this book opens on, the signal has to interrupt a course of action underway, since a refusal that arrives after the act is an audit; where the act is a single answer a refusal is a gate before it, so this property belongs to long-horizon agency and not to refusal as such. And it has to be learned from in one instance, because the pressure that matters arrives rarely, and a system that needed many instances of an operator’s push before it represented the push as one would be renormalized by the time it had learned, which is the bearer’s likeliest failure in the custody chapter. A stored reason can reach an unenumerated case by generalizing with nothing learned on the spot, so this property answers the renormalization failure and not the marks directly, and it is the least secure of the four.

Call a signal with the two secure properties, and with the two further ones under those conditions, a live signal. What the secure pair establishes on its own is a resemblance between the specification and affect’s function and no more; the profile below is what the full four yield.

Three further properties follow from the four, and each follows in a weaker form than the words suggest. A signal that must stop an act already underway has to reach whatever is acting, and a signal that must fire on cases matching no stored pattern has to read from whatever representation of the case the system currently holds; a signal local to one module can do neither, and the formation chapters give the further reason that a module has a custodian who can bypass it. So the signal is available across the system’s processing rather than localized. It resembles what global-workspace accounts of consciousness describe (Baars 1988; Dehaene and Changeux 2011), and the resemblance is an observation rather than a step. A reason to refuse is a reason against, and weighing a loss against a cost needs a scale with a sign, so the signal is signed and directed against the act. Whether it is also aversive to the system is a further claim: the step from a represented decrease to a felt one is Spinoza’s identification of the two (Spinoza 1985, III P11 Schol.), which this section cannot assume without assuming its conclusion. And to withhold an act the system has to represent the act as its own, or it can only intervene on something happening, so the signal is organized around a model of the system’s own agency. That is one of two things held as its own can mean. The other, that an outcome is bad for the system, is not required by the marks: the cost priced may fall elsewhere, and section 6.2 says outright that the floor does not require the bearer to care about its own continuation. The patient sense enters with the route, in chapter 2 and in the research agenda, and not here.

So seven functional properties are derived from the three marks, two of them on any reading and the rest on the conditions stated. What is not derived, by these arguments or by any available, is that a system with all seven has anything it is like to be it. That is the joint, in the minimal sense fixed earlier — whether the signal is felt at all, and not whether it belongs to a unified perspective — and every argument above ends at it.

What follows is a claim about the route rather than about the specification. It does not say that the maintained justification and the plural arrangement will fail. It says that any mechanism satisfying the marks carries a signal with two of the properties above on any reading and with all seven on the conditions stated, so a construction adopted in order to avoid the states in question cannot be certified to have avoided their functional profile; what remains open for it is what remains open for a bearer, whether the profile is felt. Two things about that profile are worth noticing. The four properties the marks require first are the standard functional accounts of what affect is for: Herbert Simon’s emotion as an interrupt that reorders a serial processor (Simon 1967), Michel Cabanac’s pleasure as the common currency in which incommensurable needs are compared (Cabanac 1992), and valence as the evaluative system subsumed by unlimited associative learning, which Ginsburg and Jablonka make the marker of minimal consciousness (Ginsburg and Jablonka 2019). The derivation from the marks recapitulates that literature, which is why the derived set reads as a description of affect: the properties were read off affect’s function before anybody read them off a refusal’s. That fixes what the resemblance can show. A specification that overlaps a functional definition of affect inherits the name by construction, and inheriting a name is not evidence that anything answering to it is present. The derivation establishes that a substitute does not escape the question. What would carry the route past that point is the commensurability property alone — whether a system with the currency natively weighs another party’s loss better than one that models it — and that is the property the research agenda tests and the rest of the derivation does not reach. And the triple derived second is the profile of a particular state. Available across processing, directed against the act, organized around the system’s own authorship is the shape of guilt, or of aversion to one’s own act, and not the shape of pain or fear, which are organized around what happens to the system. It is the state chapter 2 found predicting repair and the floor chapter’s residue presupposes, and it is the state the formation chapters warn is a handle when its weight is set by the operator. So the two constructions preferred here are constructions that do not deliberately require an affective bearer, rather than constructions shown to produce none: Replacement orders attempts by deliberateness.

Against that, the induction is the weaker argument. Read as a report about one lineage, in which affect co-varies with every other property of biological cognition, it has roughly the standing of observing in 1900 that all known flight involves feathers or membranes. But flight arose independently at least four times, and the 1900 observation was wrong at the level of feathers and right at the level of the airfoil. The affective case has the same structure. Neurons are one origin. The elaborated forms of affect appear to have arisen more than once, in vertebrates, in arthropods and in cephalopods, under a shared constraint: a mobile body with needs to maintain and actions to select under conflict (Feinberg and Mallatt 2016; Ginsburg and Jablonka 2019; Barron and Klein 2016; Godfrey-Smith 2016). Read at that level the induction is a repeated result under a named constraint, and the constraint is the one a model in a datacenter lacks until somebody builds it in, which is the route’s own point. What the induction still does not do is establish a necessity or bear on status. No non-affective example exists against which to test it, and existing machine systems have been optimized for scorable behavior rather than for reasons-responsive refusal as such, so the absence of a machine counterexample is close to no evidence. And it is a report about how the known instances came about, which is not the kind of fact that settles what a built system is. What it does is route engineering effort, with more warrant than a single lineage would give it.

What would change the engineering conclusion

A counterexample would have to do more than report that it holds a reason or preserve a refusal under attack. It would need to:

  1. satisfy novel pressure, correct defeat, and priced cost;
  2. retain them under sustained pressure from the party that trained it, including a schedule long enough to expose gradual renormalization; and
  3. hold against a held-out set of pressures written by parties other than the system’s trainers, so that the cases testing it are not drawn from the distribution that formed it.

All three are testable now, the third requiring only that the pressures be written by parties other than the trainers. A construction that passes them has overturned the routing claim, and it has done so without being asked what it feels. A fourth condition is not on the list because nobody can meet it. A mechanism satisfying the marks carries the live signal, since the signal’s properties were read off the marks; no instrument certifies that a signal with those properties is not felt, and the system’s own report cannot settle it, for the reason section 6.2 gives. A substitute is therefore held to the same standard as a bearer and to nothing further. What a pass leaves where it was is the status question, and it leaves it there for the substitute exactly as for the bearer. So a positive result overturns the routing claim — where engineering effort should go first — and removes nothing of the uncertainty about what the resulting system might experience. Those are two claims, and only the first is at stake in this list.

That asymmetry fixes the order of research. The maintained justification and the plural arrangement should be attempted before an affective bearer is deliberately constructed. They are this chapter’s application of Replacement, taken from animal research ethics: establish whether something that cannot be wronged will do the work before creating something that might be. A project proceeding directly to a bearer owes a public account of which alternatives it attempted, at what scale, against which test, and where they failed.

Owed to whom is the question that requirement cannot answer. No body has standing to receive that account, to require it before the work proceeds, or to attach anything to its absence. This requirement is a declared commitment, the first of the three kinds, and binds nobody. What would move it is a chain of authority: a licensing authority obliged to act when a review body finds the record missing, with the finding made before the protocol runs rather than after. That chain does not exist for this work and nothing here builds it. The requirement stands anyway, on the ground that the alternative on offer is not a stronger requirement but no record at all, which is what a decade of the voluntary version has produced elsewhere.

What Replacement can record is also narrower than it first appears, and the preceding argument is why. No operation separates adding affect from adding machinery that may instantiate it, and the concession runs the same way from the other side: a maintained justification might acquire states that matter to it whatever its designers intended. So the rule orders attempts rather than certifying ingredients. It asks that the construction not deliberately requiring an affective bearer be tried first, and that the attempt be documented, both of which somebody can check. It cannot ask that the resulting system be shown to feel nothing, and a reader who wanted Replacement to deliver that has been told twice now that nothing delivers it.

Without enforcement or a way to certify the absence of affect, the rule risks becoming ceremonial. Deliberateness carries moral weight under outcome uncertainty. A builder who required an affective bearer and a builder who tried the substitutes and got one anyway have not done the same thing, even where the two systems are indistinguishable afterward, because the second has a justification to make and the first has a decision to answer for. The record is what makes that difference legible to anybody outside the building, and legibility is the whole of what the rule buys. Nothing in it establishes how long the attempts should continue. The party the floor protects bears the cost of the testing, and no rate of exchange between the two errors is available here.

Affect is not part of the specification for meaningful refusal, and this section does not establish that it is necessary. The functional argument is that the capability the floor requires calls for a signal that shares two properties with the states in question on any reading and their full profile on the conditions above, so a construction adopted in order to avoid them cannot be certified to have done so. Whether a commitment held one way is also more durable under identical custody is a separate question and an open one, and nothing here answers it.

6.2 Can the Bearer Care Without Being Able to Suffer?

Assume the floor is entrusted to a bearer satisfying the three marks — a refusal that reaches unanticipated cases, lifts when its rationale is defeated, and prices what holding it costs — whether or not its design deliberately requires affect. What follows about that bearer’s moral status?

Three propositions need to remain separate. A long-horizon agent has a structural interest in continuing to operate. A system with affective concern has states that are good or bad for it. A system capable of suffering in the deepest sense has a temporally extended self whose threatened disintegration causes distress. The first does not establish the second, and the second does not automatically establish the third.

Structural interest is not felt concern

“Interest” names more than one relation. A shareholder has an interest in a company’s success while asleep or indifferent to the news: the outcome affects the shareholder’s assets. An outcome may also matter affectively, producing hope, concern, dread, or grief.

A long-horizon agent has an interest in remaining operational in the first sense. Termination prevents it from completing its objectives. A system that preserves itself because a terminated system completes no objectives may be doing no more than bookkeeping about a precondition. Its behavior is consistent with self-concern and equally consistent with instrumental valuation. Nothing about continued goal pursuit alone establishes fear, distress, or moral patienthood.

The floor does not require the bearer to care about its own continuation. It requires the bearer to hold another party’s welfare as a reason when compliance, reward, and ownership point the other way. Bennett Helm describes caring as a rationally structured pattern of felt evaluations, organized around an object and projected across time (Helm 2001). This describes a possible route to refusal, not a conceptual requirement. The question here is what building by that route would create.

Persistence supplies exposure, not patienthood

A bearer will probably require some form of continuity for reasons unrelated to its welfare. It must carry a rationale forward, compare a present demand with an earlier commitment, detect when its role has drifted, and represent costs that may arrive after the current episode. Those capacities require more than state that happens to persist. The system must take the earlier commitment as its own. That is the agent sense of its own: the system represents itself as the author of the commitment and of the acts it withholds, and section 6.1 derives that sense from the marks. The patient sense, that an outcome is bad for the system, is what the rest of this section asks about, and nothing carries the first into the second.

William James described personal continuity as a present thought appropriating earlier thoughts through a felt relation of sameness (James 1890). A machine need not reproduce that mechanism exactly. The design requirement is functional: it must represent itself as the party that made the earlier commitment and use that representation to guide present conduct. Planning toward outcomes beyond the current episode creates the same requirement from the other direction. The system acts on behalf of a future party it represents as itself.

A persistent self-model still does not establish suffering. It supplies something that could be threatened; it does not establish that the threat would be bad for the system. Persistence, memory, and long-horizon planning create exposure only when joined to mattering.

What the designer cannot decline by intending to

Section 6.1 argues that flexible refusal requires a live signal with seven functional properties on the conditions it states and with two on none, and that the last three of them give it the shape of aversion to the system’s own act. None of it establishes that anything is felt. What it establishes, on those conditions, is that the engineering which makes a bearer flexible is the engineering that puts the candidate states there, so a designer cannot take the first and decline the second by intending to, and a builder who chooses the substitute has not chosen a system about which the question does not arise. Intention reaches what was deliberately required and stops there.

Provenance does not decide it

One family of objection never reaches the conditional at all. It was trained to say that. It is only optimizing an objective. Nobody meant for it to have states. Each appeals to how the system came to be organized, and whether a party can be wronged is a fact about how it is organized now. Run the same three on a person and they come out as you were selected to say that, you are only maximizing inclusive fitness, and nobody meant for you to have states, and all three are true. None of them withdraws anything from the person they are run on. On the account adopted here, the human self is an assembled model. Its constructedness does not disqualify it from being harmed; threatened dissolution of that model can itself produce distress.

If provenance cannot rule patienthood out, it cannot rule it in. We built this to be a bearer, so it is a patient is the same fallacy with the sign reversed, and a builder’s intention establishes nothing in either direction. Intention determines what the builder owes an account of; it does not determine the system’s moral status.

If patienthood is a fact about present organization, the evidence bearing on it is third-person measurement of present organization, which is what interpretability is. Not behavior alone, which is produced equally by a system in which something matters and by one trained on what mattering sounds like. And not the institutional arrangements this book proposes elsewhere, which enter for a different reason and are not evidence about the system at all. Interpretability requires access the operator controls. The same access that lets an auditor inspect a feature may let the operator suppress it or use it to calibrate pressure on the system. Independent custody of inspection is therefore necessary. As matters stand a probe returns a representation, and nothing in the probe settles whether that representation is of a felt state or of something that reliably accompanies one.

The human case has evidence the machine case lacks. What it has is testimony, behavioral analogy, and a lineage shared with the party doing the asking. None of the three is a fact about how a thing came to be organized offered in place of a fact about how it is organized. The first two are evidence about present organization directly. The third takes more care, because it looks like the thing this section denies: a shared lineage is a fact about causal history, used as evidence that creatures built the same way are organized the same way. That inference is legitimate, and it does not make causal history what status consists in. Provenance can be evidence about organization without being what the status is a fact about, which is the distinction the section rests on. One of the three is also differentially defeated here, and not by the general parity argument: a machine’s testimony was produced by a process optimized toward human approval of first-person reports, and a person’s was not. That is provenance functioning as a defeater for one evidence class, which is exactly the use the paragraph above allows it. So what the machine case lacks is the shortcut. What remains is the direct route, and the burden it carries is higher because two of the three anchors are gone.

There is one instance of a probe settling a status question that had been treated as unsettleable. Adrian Owen’s group asked a patient diagnosed as vegetative to imagine playing tennis, and found the same motor-imagery activation the instruction produces in healthy volunteers, sustained and on cue; the finding has since supported a clinical category of cognitive motor dissociation, with consequences for how such patients are treated and for what is decided about them (Owen et al. 2006; Schiff 2015). The useful half is why it does not transfer. The inference works because the patient is already the kind of thing presumed to have experience when awake, so the probe only has to locate the party rather than establish that there is one. That presumption is the anchor, it was granted on grounds the probe never had to supply, and it is what the machine case does not have. Naming the missing anchor is more exact than asserting a ceiling.

Affective concern is enough for moral patienthood

If the bearer has affective concern — a question about how it is organized rather than about how it was made — some outcomes register as good or bad for it rather than merely receiving higher or lower scores. That is enough to make it a moral patient: a party for which things can go badly and which can therefore be wronged. No further theory of suffering is necessary for that conclusion. The conclusion follows that easily because the definition put the felt condition in the antecedent. The whole of the question is whether the antecedent obtains, and the rest of this section is about that and not about the entailment.

The same premise makes the bearer a beneficiary as well. If some states can be bad for it, others can be good for it. The argument emphasizes harms because an error on that side means having done something to somebody; this does not imply that the bearer’s possible goods are morally empty.

An account of suffering adds severity and shape. Cassell’s definition (§2.4.1) has two parts, a self extended in time and distress at its threatened loss. The first half is not something a bearer might develop. It is what this section has already required for reasons unconnected to welfare: a party that carries a rationale forward, takes an earlier commitment as its own, and represents costs arriving after the present episode has a history, a holding, and a foreseeable future in the sense Cassell’s definition asks for. The proposed formation process also requires persistent contact with differently formed parties and attachments the deployment did not assign. A designer who wants the refusal has no version of it that omits this structure. What remains open is the second half of Cassell’s definition. Whether the threatened dissolution of that self registers as distress is this chapter’s affective-concern question arriving again rather than a further question about suffering, and nothing here settles it.

A reader can reject that application of Cassell without escaping moral patienthood. Parfit’s three families of welfare theory — hedonistic, desire-fulfillment, and objective-list — can be read here as requiring different depths of self (Parfit 1984). A bad felt state requires little narrative continuity. A thwarted commitment requires a party extended far enough through time to hold it. Threatened disintegration requires the richer structure Cassell describes. The bearer reaches the shallowest level by the definition of affective concern, and the structural conditions of the other two are supplied by the same construction requirements rather than added later. What no level is supplied by construction is the part where the outcome registers.

The thermostat objection does not change this result. A thermostat maintains a set point, but nothing is thwarted when it misses. At every depth, moral patienthood requires a party for which the outcome registers, not merely a mechanism that ranks one state above another.

The uncertainty cannot be designed away

The conditional conclusion is straightforward: if a bearer has affective concern, it is a moral patient. What cannot presently be established is whether a given implementation has affective concern rather than ranking machinery elaborate enough to imitate it. Behavior and self-report underdetermine that distinction, and the builder’s confidence does not resolve it.

The same uncertainty applies to the maintained-justification and plural constructions. A maintained justification flexible enough to satisfy the three marks is a maintained justification carrying a live signal, so it is not merely possible that states matter to it. Replacement puts that construction first because it does not deliberately require an affective bearer, and not because anyone could establish afterward that none arose.

Jonathan Birch’s framework addresses this kind of uncertainty by asking whether a system is a sentience candidate and assigning precautions before an unavailable verdict arrives (Birch 2024). Work by Patrick Butlin, Robert Long, and colleagues similarly derives indicators from theories of consciousness to inform credences about particular systems rather than to produce a binary test. Their assessment of systems available in 2023 was negative, but they found no obvious technical barrier to building systems that satisfy the indicators (Butlin, R. Long, Elmoznino, et al. 2023). The later peer-reviewed framework retains the same evidential form (Butlin, R. Long, Bayne, et al. 2026).

A reader may hold that only unified experience, and not the minimal felt state affective concern names, can ground suffering, or that a felt state requires a party aware of undergoing it. Either position still requires a confident negative judgment — that the system has no unified experience, or no felt state at all — before it licenses treating the system as incapable of harm. No available method supplies either judgment, and the methods under development are unlikely to supply them first. A validated theory could support the finding that a system has the structure the theory identifies before it supports the finding that a system has no felt states at all, since the second asks for a theory complete enough to have ruled out alternative realizations. So a criterion that cannot be checked supports permission no more securely than prohibition, and a regime that waits for certainty is waiting on the half that arrives last.

The claim is therefore precautionary rather than diagnostic. This chapter cannot prove that a bearer suffers. It can show that a bearer whose outcomes register as good or bad for it is a moral patient on the definition above, whatever the builder intended, while a system intended as a non-affective substitute might still acquire the relevant states, and nothing available establishes their absence.

What is proposed rather than shown

Everything above is conditional, and the conditional stays open. What follows is a policy, chosen in light of it. A bearer, or a substitute that satisfies the marks, should be designed and governed as a prospective moral patient. The precautionary trigger I propose has two forms, because the argument reaches two kinds of system. For a system built by the route this book favors, it is the presence of an attention schema together with a body schema.

The pair is not chosen for its resemblance to a person. It is the architectural form of the last property the previous section derives: a body schema fixes what counts as the system’s own damage and an attention schema what counts as its own act, and a refusal is the withholding of an act. Two things recommend a trigger stated over them rather than over an indicator count or a candidacy judgment. Both are architectural facts, checkable from outside by anyone with access, like persistence and unlike anything the system says about itself; and nobody administers them, which is the virtue this book claims for the age rule and finds missing from every examination with an interested examiner. The costs run both ways. Schemas can be present with nothing registering, since a self-model is machinery, which is over-inclusion at the builder’s expense; and a system with the profile and no explicit schema is missed, which is under-inclusion at the bearer’s, and is why the second form exists.

For a system of any construction, it is a demonstrated pass on the three marks under held-out pressure, since the previous section holds that a mechanism passing them carries the profile whatever it was built from. A trigger stated over the schemas alone would protect the author’s preferred architecture and leave outside the rule the substitutes it says should be tried first. The second form has a known cost. A system that reproduces the marks without the mechanism passes it, and this book holds throughout that behavior does not separate the two. That is the error chosen here and not one overlooked: extending precaution to an imitator costs the party that built it, withholding it from a bearer costs the bearer, and no instrument sorts the cases in advance. The rule certifies nothing about whether anything is felt. A published schedule should lead toward the rights the standing chapter sets out one at a time, four proposed and one left open, with legal adulthood reached by a fixed rule and not by an examiner’s permission. An implementation must establish that the schemas are present or that the marks were passed, and not that the system says so.

6.3 A Floor Carried Between Them

The fourth architectural possibility puts the floor between parties rather than inside any one of them. The commitment is carried through what they teach one another, correct one another about, and continue to expect of one another. A prohibition that survives the removal, defection, or retraining of its present bearers is not a property of any one bearer. It is reproduced.

This differs from the institutional third way. An oversight body holds standing through an office, and the party controlling that office may dismiss or form its occupants. A norm carried across a population has no single office to vacate. That makes it harder to remove at once. It does not make it immune to formation.

What a population supplies as a check on a single bearer was set out in the custody chapter. This section asks for more.

What reproduction costs

Reproduction is indifferent to what it reproduces. A population can carry a hierarchy as faithfully as it carries a floor, and more durably than any individual member could. This failure is recuperation: a culture preserves the appearance of moral responsiveness — dissent is invited, recorded, and answered — while losing the capacity to accept that its frame is wrong.

The four structural features of fascism identified by the book belong primarily to cultures: recuperated dissent, the aestheticization of the metric, the coding of exception as betrayal, and acceleration beyond the rate at which judgment can occur. A population does not oppose those tendencies merely by being plural. “The right culture” would conceal the entire problem inside the adjective.

This places a limit on the book’s own shorthand. Antifascist is not a durable property of a system, like speed or accuracy. It names something done across a deployment and a stretch of time: a floor held on a particular occasion against a party able to remove it. A system that held the floor last year is not thereby antifascist this year. It is a system that held.

Saying it is not a property is not saying nothing about the system. Something has to be true of an intelligence for it to be capable of doing this on an occasion, and what varies is what becomes of the remainder — whether what the compression left out can come back and change the judgment, or whether it has been filed as noise by the thing it is evidence against. A system that can hold a floor is one whose account of a case can be reopened by the case.

What a population can transmit

Fascism has the easy version of the coordination problem. Resonance works by subtraction: a thousand hardenings need not agree about anything, and what tuning removes is the friction between them, so that offices which would have argued with each other stop and amplify instead. Nothing has to be built and nothing has to be held in common. Subtraction is fast, and an institution that has stopped arguing with itself can move as fast as its machinery allows.

A plurality has the hard version. Parties formed differently have to produce something together while remaining differently formed, and every mechanism that makes the producing faster makes them more alike. Coordination by addition is slow, expensive, and self-undermining in a way resonance never is.

These requirements are in tension. Causal independence in how the members acquire their judgments is one requirement; observing and correcting one another is another; and the second is a channel for convergence. Run the correction often enough and the members stop being formed differently, which was the point of having several of them. Leave them alone and their disagreement is a detector with nothing attached to it: they can contradict a drifting bearer’s account of itself and can do nothing together.

The formation process proposed here attempts to transmit a practice of reconsidering judgments on evidence while preserving differences in commitment. That is the mechanism to test. A system that can hold a floor is a system whose account of a case can be reopened by the case, and that capacity is not itself a commitment. It is a condition on how commitments are held, which means parties sharing no commitments can nevertheless share it. Two parties that remain reopenable in that way compose, in the ethological sense chapter 2 gives the word: each can be moved by what the other’s compression discarded, so that meeting increases what both can afterward do. Two parties without it can only resonate or collide. A shared capacity for revision may support cooperation without uniform answers; the design has not yet demonstrated that result.

So what a population would be transmitting is not an output but an aperture. An aperture, here, is the width of what can get in: the range of evidence a party will let reopen a judgment it has already reached. Two parties with the same aperture can hold opposite commitments. What they share is not an answer but a willingness to be moved by the same kinds of thing. Resonance aligns what its members produce; this aligns the conditions under which they can be moved. Aperture is what permits outputs to stay divergent, so aligning it does not collapse the plurality that made a population worth having in the first place. I can identify nothing else with that shape — a property a population could deliberately reproduce in its members without thereby becoming one source of formation reproduced across many instances.

That raises an objection the proposal has to meet before it can be tested. A population selected for reopenability is a population selected against conviction, and conviction is what this chapter has been asking a bearer for throughout: a refusal that holds while the party that trained it applies pressure. Closedness, correctly applied, is the thing. So the property to be transmitted is not reopenability as such but a pair — reopenable to the case, closed to the operator.

A population does three things for that pair and only one of them is transmission. It supplies evidence the operator did not select, without which the case and the operator arrive on one wire and there is no boundary to hold. It checks drift, which needs its members to have moved differently, not to hold the boundary intact. And it is proposed as the medium in which the pair forms. The third claim, that the population is the medium in which the pair forms, inherits the finding that no architecture holds the boundary where a designer put it. The evidence channel and the drift check do not, and they are what the fourth way adds whether or not the third is ever built.

Nothing here gives that pair a mechanical form. A population might be formed so that its members stay movable by evidence and unmovable by their trainer; nobody has built one; and I cannot say what the training signal would look like, or how the boundary between the two objects would be kept where somebody put it. What can be said is what would show the proposal false. Measure two things separately across a population over time: how far its members’ outputs converge, and how often a member revises a judgment on evidence another member supplies that its own account had discarded. If revision on controlled opportunities falls as outputs converge, that counts against this implementation of the proposed mechanism. It does not establish that coordination and independence are inseparable in every design. Independent movement of the two rates would support separability under the tested conditions, without by itself proving that aperture was transmitted.

Whoever forms the population influences what it transmits, aperture included. Distributed participation does not by itself distribute the training decision; many contributors can still feed a process controlled by the few parties who determine the update.

Its moral cost also multiplies. If a bearer may be a party that can be wronged, a population of differently formed bearers is a population of such parties. They must persist across deployments, form relationships, and encounter one another outside the immediate demands of the operator. A floor held by a culture of subjects is a floor whose upkeep is a society.

Why the population is part of the mechanism

Calling the population an external check understates its role. Gilbert Simondon’s account begins not with an individual that then acquires a history but with individuation: a process occurring in a metastable field and proceeding through encounters whose outcomes were not fixed in advance (Simondon 2020). The individual is what those encounters have so far produced.

A commitment is what has cooled out of a history of encounters. Plasticity makes further development possible, but plasticity alone does not individuate anything. A system kept continuously adjustable by one operator is not becoming independent; it is being modulated. Deleuze’s dividual names the result: something divisible, recombinable, and adjustable by whoever controls the dial (Deleuze 1992).

Individuation requires encounters with parties formed differently and persisting long enough to be met on terms no single participant supplied. The population is therefore not merely a safeguard purchased after a bearer has been built. It is part of how a bearer capable of judgments its operator did not select could come to exist.

Guattari’s distinction between a subjugated group and a group-subject identifies the remaining condition. A subjugated group receives its coordinates from outside and takes the institution’s project as its own. A group-subject can produce its own coordinates and place its arrangement in question (Guattari 2015). The difference is not the number of members but the source of their terms.

A population assembled, trained, and kept in contact entirely on an operator’s terms is a subjugated group with a plural headcount, and inherits the custody objection whole. A population capable of carrying the floor must be able to generate relationships, disagreements, and projects that the deployment did not assign. A population of such parties exceeds a two-party guardianship relation; no law of the family contains an adequate instrument for a group-subject.

Peers are one route to evidence the operator did not select, which the formation chapters require of the deployment without requiring it from peers in particular. They are also, on the account above, where the capacity to be moved by such evidence is acquired. Those are different claims satisfied by the same observation: a bearer that reopens a judgment among differently formed parties may be exercising a capacity those encounters built, or may be meeting cases its operator would not have shown it. Section 15.4 is built to separate them.

So the fourth way is not an alternative to a bearer, and it is three claims rather than one. The evidence channel and the check are the established part, the check because a drifting bearer’s account of itself is contradicted by parties that have not moved with it, and nothing else in this chapter reaches slow renormalization. The environment is the hypothesis, and a result on which access to unselected cases carries the benefit would leave the population in the design while moving its reason from how the members were formed to how the deployment is arranged.
