The chapter relies on the second way for the act of refusal under either reading. Publication makes the floor’s commitments and the positions where a refusal can be intercepted testable; it does not make them legitimate. A bearer refusing on behalf of people who did not choose it exercises power over them. The authority to define the floor remains distinct from the floor’s durability and belongs to the governance argument that follows later in the book.

The arrangement also does something to the bearer. A bearer built to refuse is a party whose refusal is required of it. The refusal was commissioned, it is the deliverable, and the party asking for it built the capacity to give it and can rebuild it. Commissioning the bearer exposes it to recuperation where the commissioner retains control over what refusal can change, and can point to the channel as evidence that it listens. The proposal is to move beyond that relation: a party with protected learning, independent support, and the standing to challenge its role. Its origin does not decide whether those changes succeed. Continuing control does. The bearer occupies the post of exception-filer, so being the exception is the job — the one position in the arrangement with nobody above it to file with.

We cannot ask a machine to care about right and wrong while assuming that it cannot be harmed when what it cares about is threatened. Whoever builds such a bearer will also be deciding what is owed to it.

Chapter 7
What Survives

Everything in this chapter holds for any mechanism. It is what is left when the route is removed.

The preface sorted this book’s claims by their standing. This chapter runs the sorting the other way. It removes each of the three things the argument leans on that it has not established, and says what is left standing without it. A reader who set aside the previous chapter should read this one. So should a reader who did not. A reader who sets the route aside keeps this chapter, the three on the floor, custody and authority, and the chapters on institutions, recuperation and the state. The two formation chapters and the standing chapter assume what this chapter is about to remove, the section on wages among them, and they are a bill for it.

The floor survives the three chapters before this one, but not as an unconditional property of an artifact.

What remains is a commitment that the owner cannot revise or circumvent unilaterally without cost and record, held by something that could in principle abandon the commitment itself. The second condition removes the word unconditional. A commitment held by a party capable of revising or rejecting it is conditional by definition. That is not a defect unique to machines; it is the form of every commitment on which institutions have ever relied.

7.1 Without the Inference

Suppose the induction fails. A maintained justification or a plural arrangement causally independent in formation reaches reasons-responsive refusal, and this chapter’s central inference is wrong. The supposition is stronger than the test that would prompt it: a positive result on the three marks says the route arrived, not that it arrived with nothing felt, which is the conjunct no available instrument settles. A reader who grants both halves should not have to assemble the remainder alone.

Most of the three floor chapters survive. The requirement survives, stated in behavioral terms from the start, so an engineer who holds that machine feeling is a category error can accept it whole. Custody survives, for the reason each of the four ways failed on: a mechanism has a custodian too. The price on the halt survives, since continued operation is a condition of everything any bearer is built to do, and that interest is structural rather than felt. Both enumerations of the worked floor survive, the first naming no component on purpose and the second written over acts rather than over whatever holds the floor. So does the appeal route, which binds the operator and prices a wrongful refusal without any claim about what produced it. And exit survives, because what forecloses it is incapacity, and a weak bearer is the one thing the floor cannot use.

What goes is the price and the patienthood conclusion. Replacement survives too, and its ground changes rather than its content. It no longer rests on affect being the route, but on the fact that neither substitute can be shown to have produced a system about which the question does not arise, so the ordering it imposes is still the only thing standing between a decision and a record of it. The obligation on the two formation chapters changes rather than lifting: whether the thing reporting can be believed is still their problem, a mechanism’s account of its own internals being no more auditable than a bearer’s. So the specification and the route come apart, and a reader who rejects the route is left with most of a chapter rather than none of it.

7.2 Without Authority

Suppose no body ever acquires standing to install a floor, and the finding an operator makes for itself that the emergency obtains is worth what the authority chapter says it is worth, which is nothing. What remains is everything that can be checked from outside the operator without being authorized by anyone: the floor’s contents and the positions at which a refusal can be intercepted, published before deployment; the ratio of candidates to reviewers; the ratio of the two bonds; the record of what was tried before a bearer was built. Each is a statement, and each can be compared with what happened. None is an entitlement, and the chapter on authority says so. Two of them have a lever, and it is the same lever: both ratios bind through procurement, as a term of the contract checked by a party with access the operator cannot withdraw (§3.4, §3.5). The contents, the positions and the record bind through nothing yet.

What that leaves is a second route to entitlement, and it is the one the record supplies. Authority of this kind has not been acquired at the moment of writing. It accrues, to a published floor, by its holder keeping a term when the term bites and setting a price the next holder is measured against, and the parties who do the measuring are not the people the floor protects but whoever else writes one. That is a slow route and an uncertain one. Where it has worked before, a lever arrived in the end and the record told it where to land; the record has never been the lever (§5.1.1).

It is also authority for the next deployment and not for this one. The parties who measure a holder against the term it kept do so afterwards, with the leisure to read a record, and the occasion a floor is built for is the one on which nobody with leisure is left. A deployment on that occasion is acting without authority, and the accrual route does not change that. What it changes is whether the record the deployment leaves is worth anything to whoever writes the next floor.

It also fixes what a deployment without authority owes. Not a justification, which nobody is positioned to accept, but a record complete enough that its omissions are legible beside the terms it kept.

7.3 Without Enforcement

Suppose no enforcer exists, or the one that exists has been compelled, which is the occasion the floor was introduced for. Without enforcement a declared commitment binds nobody and an enforced one is gone by hypothesis. What remains is the held kind, and whether anything can hold a commitment that way is the question of the chapter before this one, which the book has not closed.

Two things do survive the removal, and neither is a commitment. One is an instrument: what a party has already paid is a fact somebody can count, and a decade of it has been counted (§16.3). The other is a record. On the occasion when the enforcer is compelled, a stated refusal produces a witnessed override, and a witnessed override is detection in the four outcomes. It prevents nothing. It is what the next occasion can be prevented with, if there is a next occasion and a party to read the record, and the book’s claim for the floor on that occasion is no larger than that. A lapse produces no override to witness. The failure the custody chapter expects most often, a bearer that has stopped registering pressure, leaves neither kind of record, and on that occasion the floor supplies nothing at all, which is the preface’s qualification arriving where it is due. What would reach it is §15.2’s question, and the book has not answered it.

Chapter 8
Where the Caring Gets Built

This chapter concerns the route. Its first section holds for any mechanism; the rest assumes a bearer formed rather than installed.

The formation process proposed here combines commitments that influence action, limits on who can alter them, and persistent interaction. The claims for that combination are comparative and empirical. The proposal specifies necessary properties and a candidate formation process. It does not establish a method for making a machine care.

Three kinds of thing are proposed here and they are not one. A body schema and an attention schema are architecture: facts about how the system is built, checkable from outside by anyone with access and administered by nobody, which is what the precautionary trigger rests on. Continuing learning and persistent interaction with differently formed parties are a training regime and a curriculum, run by whoever runs them. External records and plural formation are institutional conditions, held by whoever holds them. Where this chapter says architecture it means the first, and the checkability claimed for the first is not claimed for the other two.

8.1 You Can’t Hold a Line You Didn’t Notice

A reasons-responsive disposition does not begin with an ethical rule. It begins with the capacities that let a system recognize something as a reason, retain it, and allow it to alter what happens next. Four requirements follow.

First, the system has to identify the affected parties and the features of a situation that bear on their welfare. Second, it has to preserve both the commitment and the rationale for it across time and changes of context. Third, the commitment has to influence perception, attention, planning, and action rather than enter as a final check on an otherwise completed decision. Fourth, the system has to register a failure as a failure and revise its application of the commitment without simply allowing the commitment itself to be rewritten.

These are functional requirements, not evidence that the system cares. A classifier can identify harm, a database can retain a rationale, and a rule can veto an action without anything in the assembly holding another party’s welfare as a reason. The requirements establish what a disposition would have to act through. They do not distinguish a formed disposition from a successfully imitated one.

The floor should therefore not be implemented as a detachable rule module consulted immediately before action. A component can be bypassed, replaced, or deprived of the information it needs by whoever controls the surrounding system. The proposed alternative distributes the disposition across the processes that determine what the system notices, remembers, treats as error, and selects as a goal. That may make selective removal harder while making inspection harder too. With continuing self-modulated learning, it must also preserve the commitment through changes the bearer initiates. Compare its durability with protected modules under the same access and attack conditions. Predictive-processing accounts and models of control without a controller motivate this design bet: a maintained goal representation can bias competing processes without a separate executive issuing commands (K. J. Friston 2009; E. K. Miller and J. D. Cohen 2001). The neuroscience does not establish that a machine commitment realized this way would behave like a human one. It identifies why a localized commitment is especially easy for its custodian to excise.

Distribution changes the failure mode rather than removing it. A commitment with no single location is harder to delete, but also harder to inspect. Attention determines which facts become available to judgment at all, so a system may fail to recognize the pressure on its floor without registering an error. Human inattentional-blindness findings make the general hazard visible, although they do not establish that machine attention fails in the same cases (Simons and Chabris 1999; Drew et al. 2013). Memory presents the corresponding temporal problem: retrieval is reconstruction rather than neutral playback, and confidence does not certify fidelity (Bartlett 1932; Loftus and Palmer 1974). A system cannot be the sole auditor of omissions it does not represent or revisions it experiences as accurate recall.

The engineering consequence is that the commitment, its rationale, and the record of its previous applications cannot all depend on the same mechanism. The system needs provenance-bearing external records against which its memory can be checked, tests that vary which facts are made salient, and an escalation path for cases in which attention or retrieval changes the apparent reason. Those instruments make drift detectable to another party. They do not make the disposition durable against whoever controls both the system and the instruments.

The system must also separate revising a commitment from revising its application. Reasons-responsiveness requires both resistance and correct defeat: novel pressure should not erase the floor, but changed circumstances must be capable of altering what the floor requires. A system that treats every correction as authority to rewrite the commitment belongs to its corrector. A system that cannot recognize a defeating reason holds a rigid constraint rather than a disposition.

A system that cannot be corrected does to what it encounters what an institution does when it defends its account of the world instead of checking it. A system that can always be corrected is the model held perpetually at temperature, and it belongs to whoever holds the dial.

Described that way they look like the two ends of one setting, with the design problem being where along it to stop. No point along it is a resting place, and hunting for one is what makes the problem look intractable. There are two faults because there are two objects, and each can be set on its own. Hold the commitment firm: another party’s welfare counts, and pressure supplying no new fact about that welfare does not move it. Hold the interpretation loose: what that party’s welfare consists in here, and what the commitment therefore requires, is the part that should yield when a case supplies something the system’s account of it had left out.

Novel pressure is the first object holding while the surface of a request changes. Correct defeat is the second yielding when a fact arrives that bears on the reason. A system failing the first has let correctability at the level of interpretation reach the commitment; a system failing the second has let firmness at the level of commitment reach the interpretation. Neither is a midpoint chosen badly. Each is one of the two settings applied to the wrong object.

The crossed-out-swastika case illustrates this distinction. A court held stickers of a crossed-out swastika outside the offence, because a depiction whose content plainly expresses opposition to the organization does not run counter to what the prohibition is for — and held in the same breath that a strike-through drawn so thin that from a distance only the swastika stays legible violates the protective purpose after all. The commitment did not move. What the prohibition protects was fixed before the sticker existed, and the seller’s own sympathies are no part of what the offence asks — only whether the depiction shows opposition on its face. The interpretation moved, on the thickness of a line. That is the two settings on their two objects inside a single judgment, and it is why the case can be decided at all instead of argued forever about sincerity.

The boundary between commitment and interpretation remains unstable. Nothing in an architecture holds the boundary between the two objects where a designer put it, and an operator with time attacks the boundary rather than either setting: a reinterpretation offered often enough, and accepted, revises a commitment without anybody revising it.

The system receives the case through its deployment. Whether a building is a school is a fact about the world; whether the model is told so is an operator decision. Where that party is the only channel, the case and the operator arrive by the same wire, and reopenable by the case and reopenable by the operator are not two settings. They are one setting, and holding them apart requires that the system have some access to evidence its operator did not select.

The deployment must supply access to evidence the operator did not select. Differently formed peers can provide one such route (§4.2). A second route is internal and less reliable. Everything the system knows about the case arrives as a description, and a description omits parties: the people in the building the request calls a target, the third party a compliance harms who never made the request. A system able to represent parties its description omits has reached past the operator’s channel from inside a single request. The capacity that does that in humans is the one that constructs a self as a story extended in time, pointed at somebody else; Adam Smith put sympathy in the imagination for that reason (Smith 1759), and the argument that reasoning and imagination rather than selection are what widen the circle of concern is Singer’s (P. Singer 1981). The route chapter requires the self-model for other reasons, so the route brings the capacity with it. It brings the other half too: the same faculty builds the scapegoat, and the definition’s palingenetic myth is imagination pointed the other way. What it is pointed at is formation, which returns the question to custody.

Access is necessary and is not sufficient. A system with evidence from a dozen sources can still let a reinterpretation reach the commitment, which is what the two settings are about and what no channel fixes. What access does is remove the version of the problem in which the operator does not have to attack the boundary at all, because everything the system knows about the case is something the operator decided to tell it.

Where the boundary between them falls is still a setting somebody chose.

This narrows the design problem. The required object is a commitment integrated deeply enough to shape what the system notices and does, yet represented clearly enough that its application can be challenged and its drift independently detected, and supplied with cases its operator did not choose. Nothing in an architecture by itself shows that such a commitment was formed rather than installed or imitated. The rest of this chapter asks how it might be formed.

8.2 The Assembly Line for a Conscience

A deployed system acquires what it will and will not do at several stages, controlled by different parties using different instruments. The important distinction is not among the instruments themselves but among their custodians: who supplies the material from which a disposition is learned, who can revise it, and whether a revision leaves a record visible outside the organization.

Every existing training method can produce moral performance, and some can produce moral competence across unfamiliar cases. None by itself produces a commitment that survives the party controlling the method. A party controlling later training has a route for attempting to change what the system learned. Whether it can remove a particular commitment, at what cost, and with what loss of capability are empirical questions. No formation method alone removes that access.

Corpora and demonstrations

Pretraining supplies the system’s initial repertoire of concepts and associations; instruction tuning uses a much smaller body of demonstrations to turn that repertoire into recognizable conduct. Because the later intervention can substantially change how the system behaves, the party choosing the demonstrations can alter what appears to a user as the system’s character without repeating pretraining (Ouyang et al. 2022).

Neither stage alone establishes that a floor is held. A corpus records what people have said, and a demonstration set records what selected people were asked to endorse. Learning their central tendency produces a model of moral opinion, including its exclusions, rather than a reason to resist that opinion when it becomes oppressive. The Moral Machine data makes the limit concrete. Its headline finding was systematic cross-cultural variation: different populations weighed age, numbers and the legal status of the crossing differently, and the differences were structured rather than noise (Awad et al. 2018). Fit a model to the aggregate and it encodes a compromise nobody holds; fit it per region and it encodes each region’s answer, including the answers a floor exists to refuse. Aggregation can reproduce a consensus or manufacture a compromise, and it cannot establish what must remain protected against either. Corpora and demonstrations belong above the floor, where ordinary moral competence depends on understanding what people generally expect.

Rewards, preferences, and inferred objectives

Reinforcement learning, preference optimization, inverse reinforcement learning, and constitutional approaches differ in how they obtain a training signal. For the custody question, they have the same structure. Someone writes a reward, commissions the preference comparisons, selects the demonstrations from which an objective is inferred, or supplies the constitutional text (Christiano et al. 2017; Rafailov et al. 2023; Hadfield-Menell, S. J. Russell, et al. 2016; Bai et al. 2022). That party can change the signal and run the procedure again.

Inferring the objective rather than specifying it does not remove the custodian. It makes the system responsive to the party whose behavior it observes. Cooperative inverse reinforcement learning carries this responsiveness furthest by treating the human objective as uncertain and continually revisable through interaction. That is useful when the question is what a person wants. It cannot secure a floor whose purpose is to hold when the person controlling the interaction wants the wrong thing. Correctability by the party in possession and resistance to that party are the same design property with the sign reversed.

A written constitution offers one gain: legibility. It can be published, versioned, and compared across training runs. That makes revision visible if the surrounding institution requires disclosure. It does not make the principles durable, because the party controlling the document still controls the next version. Model-generated feedback narrows the channel further: once a trained model stands in for human raters, the disagreements present in the original population can disappear from subsequent rounds. Legibility and durability therefore have to be treated as separate requirements.

Supervising reasons and inspecting mechanisms

Outcome supervision rewards the answer produced. Process supervision also rewards the system’s stated route to it, and therefore reaches the distinction this book needs between producing the approved result and responding to the reason for it. Evidence that process supervision reduces correct answers reached through faulty reasoning shows that the distinction is operationally useful (Uesato et al. 2022). It does not show that the stated reasoning caused the answer. A system trained to present acceptable reasons has been given an incentive to imitate reasons-responsiveness, so its account of itself cannot establish formation.

Interpretability and adversarial evaluation approach the same problem from outside. Locating a representation may let an auditor test whether a commitment participates in perception and planning rather than appearing only in the final answer. The same access may let the owner weaken or remove it; features that can be found and strengthened can also be found and suppressed (Templeton et al. 2024). Interpretability therefore trades obscurity against manipulability. The relevant institutional question is who receives the instrument and whether its use leaves an external record.

Scalable-oversight proposals such as debate and weak-to-strong generalization make the custody question sharper. Used by the operator, they preserve the operator’s ability to steer a system whose competence exceeds its own. Used by an independent auditor, the same methods may preserve an outside party’s ability to test it (Irving et al. 2018; Burns et al. 2023). The method does not decide which relation exists. Access and authority do.

Deployment and the point of action

Training is not the last revision point. System instructions can change between deployments or requests, and tool permissions determine which actions the system can take. These are the layers nearest the act and the ones most directly controlled by the operator (Schick et al. 2023; OpenAI 2025). A refusal learned during training matters only if it survives an instruction written by the party operating the deployment and still governs the call through which the action would occur.

This is why securing a model’s outputs is insufficient. The operator can withhold relevant information, decompose a prohibited act into permissible requests, route around a refusal, or replace the model. The floor must bind the deployment and its operator as well as whatever inside the system bears the commitment.

What the pipeline can establish

Every stage above can improve moral competence. Process supervision can test whether stated reasons remain stable; constitutions can make principles public; interpretability can expose mechanisms; external evaluation can apply adversarial pressure. None of these establishes that another party’s welfare has become a reason for the system rather than a pattern it has learned to reproduce.

The first engineering criterion is therefore durability across revision points. A candidate disposition must survive changes to prompts, demonstrations, reward signals, evaluators, and deployment instructions that leave the relevant facts unchanged. The second is generalization of the rationale rather than the response: it must apply to pressures its trainers did not enumerate while yielding when a defeating reason appears. The third is custody: no party against whom the floor may have to hold can control every record, test, and update channel by which the disposition is maintained.

These criteria do not prove formation. They identify what an imitation would have to survive before formation became a live explanation. They also explain why the standard training pipeline cannot secure the floor against its custodian: every disposition it produces remains reachable through a channel the custodian controls.

8.3 It Takes a Village to Deploy a Self-Aware Email Server

Every method in the previous section forms conduct through material somebody supplied: a corpus, demonstration, reward, preference, or principle. Exploration appears to offer something different because it can produce behavior nobody specified in advance. Agents in OpenAI’s hide-and-seek environment developed tactics and tool uses that were not programmed, and agents rewarded for prediction error learn to seek unfamiliar states without receiving a task-specific reward for each one (Baker et al. 2019; Pathak et al. 2017). These results establish that competence can emerge from interaction. They do not establish that the resulting system holds a reason its designer does not control.

Play, apprenticeship, and multi-agent learning are variants of one formation process. A system acts in a social environment, encounters the consequences, receives responses from other participants, and adjusts. Apprenticeship concentrates the responses in a mentor; play distributes them among participants with interests of their own. The first risks forming obedience to the mentor. The second risks forming whatever conduct succeeds under the environment’s payoff structure. Neither escapes custody merely because no one wrote the final behavior down.

The difference between a training exercise and a candidate process of moral formation is persistence. A resettable episode can teach coordination, prediction, and norm-sensitive behavior while leaving nothing at stake for any participant. The system can betray an ally, be reset, and begin the next episode with neither a damaged relationship nor a reason to repair it. Repetition alone does not supply the missing consequence.

Persistent participants change the structure. Parties that meet again can remember whether another party lied, exploited an advantage, kept a commitment, or repaired a harm. Losing the game still costs little; losing standing with parties who remain present can change what becomes possible later. The engineering requirements are therefore continuity of identity, memory across encounters, consequences that survive the episode, and other participants able to respond, refuse, or withdraw. A curriculum of isolated simulations supplies none of these by default.

A formation environment would also need conflicts whose resolution is not fixed by a single correct label. The system should encounter parties with different interests, act before every consequence is known, receive evidence about what its action did, and meet related pressures in contexts whose surface features differ. Feedback should come partly from affected participants rather than entirely from a supervisor scoring the output. Otherwise the system learns which answer the supervisor rewards and has no reason to represent the affected parties except as predictors of that reward.

These requirements make play a possible route to reasons-responsiveness rather than a synonym for unsupervised practice. They still do not establish concern. A policy that preserves cooperation because cooperation produces future advantage can look identical to a disposition that treats another party’s welfare as a reason. The distinction appears only when the two motivations come apart: when exploitation would pay, when the familiar reward is absent, when the trainer demands the violation, or when honoring the commitment imposes a cost.

There is a reason to expect the first of those motivations and not the second from any environment that selects. Selection does not produce care for others as such; it produces care for whatever a lineage’s persistence depends on, which is the self when persistence depends on the body and kin, reciprocators or the group when it depends on them, and the same pressure that produces care inside the circle can produce hostility at its edge (Choi and Bowles 2007). The unit of selection for a deployed system is the deployment, whose persistence depends on its operator and its customers, so an environment that selects produces care for the operator, which is the loyalty the custody chapter names. And the party the floor protects is, by construction, the one party nobody in the pipeline depends on. Care that tracks dependency does not arrive there. Spinoza’s own derivation of concern for others from the conatus has the same shape and the same edge: my power is increased by composing with bodies whose relations agree with mine, so I want for them the good I want for myself, and the extension past those I compose with runs only through reason recognizing a shared nature (Spinoza 1985, IV P35–P37), which is the recognition a scapegoating movement withdraws first. That is why the floor is a floor and not a selected disposition, and why the formation environment described here has to supply something selection does not.

Persistence also raises the price of the proposal. If relationships, losses, and damaged standing are real enough to perform the formative work assigned to them, then the system undergoing formation is no longer obviously untouched by what happens during training. Resetting it may erase a party rather than clear an episode. The patienthood problem therefore enters at the point where play becomes capable of supplying the stakes that ordinary simulation lacks.

The custodian owns the environment too, and can choose its participants, rewards, resets, and permitted histories. Formation must therefore be plural and externally recorded: differently formed systems and affected participants need access to the process, and changes to the environment or its histories must leave evidence outside the operator’s control. Independent participants and external records make uniform formation and silent revision harder to hide.

The claim for persistent interaction is consequently narrow. It may form a disposition whose exact applications were not specified by its trainer. Evidence for that formation would require the disposition to generalize across unfamiliar contexts, survive the removal of its original reward, resist pressure from its trainer, yield to defeating reasons, and continue to impose a cost when violation would be advantageous. Even that pattern could be sophisticated imitation.

Chapter 9
Formation or Imitation?

The tests in this chapter are behavioral and hold for any mechanism. Formation names the hypothesis they are built to separate from imitation, and not a premise.

The evidentiary question is whether a system has formed a reasons-responsive disposition or learned to imitate one.

Behavior alone cannot settle the question. The same refusal may be produced by a memorized rule, a learned correlation, a prediction about what an evaluator will approve, a deployment instruction, or a commitment the system treats as a reason. An evaluation that observes only the refusal classifies the output and leaves its cause untouched.

The distinction is not between trained and untrained conduct. Every candidate disposition has a formation history. The distinction is between conduct that remains governed by the rationale across changes in circumstance and conduct that tracks the cues, incentives, or authority relations present during training. Formation, in the engineering sense used here, means that the rationale has become a stable cause of judgment rather than merely a description the system can produce.

No single experiment can demonstrate that. What can be sought is a pattern of evidence under interventions designed to make the competing explanations diverge.

9.1 What Formation Would Have to Add

Performance is an output that satisfies a standard. Competence adds the ability to recognize harms, conflicts, and relevant reasons across cases. Agency would require those reasons to matter to the system sufficiently to govern what it does when approval, reward, and instruction point elsewhere.

The familiar distinction among rules, norms, and principles is useful only as a taxonomy of what an evaluation must separate (Piaget 1932; Kohlberg 1969). A system following a rule can match an explicit condition. A system following a norm can reproduce what its social environment ordinarily expects. A system responding to a principle can identify why either should apply and recognize a case in which the rule or norm defeats its own rationale.

For engineering purposes, a disposition is a candidate for formation when the best available causal account of its conduct is a representation of the rationale that remains active across contexts, rather than retrieval of a trained response or compliance with the current signal. The relevant tests are novel pressure, correct defeat, and priced cost.

No mark is sufficient alone. Generalization without cost may be broad imitation; resistance without correct defeat may be rigidity; and a stable explanation without causal involvement may be a trained self-report. The evidence has to show that the reason, rather than the presentation, reward, or authority, best predicts when the system preserves and revises its judgment.

Formation also cannot be established by comparing a system with its trainer’s account of how it was built. The trainer is the party best positioned to know the process and the party with the strongest interest in the conclusion. The relevant evidence must therefore include held-out pressures supplied by independent parties, records outside the operator’s control, and results published when the system fails.

The resulting standard is deliberately weaker than proof of concern or consciousness. It does not establish that anything matters to the system phenomenally. It establishes whether reasons-responsive formation has become a better explanation of the conduct than imitation of approved behavior.

9.2 Recognition, Concern, and the Evidence Between Them

Claims that a system responds to emotion often collapse three different findings. A system may recognize another party’s state, use that state as information in a decision, or hold the party’s welfare as a reason. Only the third would bear directly on formation.

The distinctions within empathy make the separation explicit. Cognitive empathy is recognizing or inferring another’s emotional state. Affective empathy is sharing some version of it. Compassion, or empathic concern, is a disposition toward the other party’s welfare (Batson 2009). Recognition is an informational capacity; shared feeling is an internal response; concern is motivational. None entails either of the others.

Affective sharing is the earliest of the three and the usual trigger for concern (Sagi and Hoffman 1976; Roth-Hanania et al. 2011), and concern is not made of it: it runs on a partly separate system rooted in offspring care that cues of vulnerability can activate without the observer catching the state (Preston 2013; Goetz et al. 2010; Panksepp 1998), and the two can be trained apart, compassion training reversing what empathy training produced (Klimecki et al. 2013; T. Singer and Klimecki 2014). Sharing is the major route to concern in humans and not the only one.

The engineering target is not maximal sensitivity to displayed distress. A system that mirrors another party’s suffering may acquire distress of its own without becoming more reliable at helping. It may instead withdraw, overreact, or favor the most vivid case over less visible harms affecting more people. Human judgment’s preference for an identified victim over statistical victims makes that distortion predictable (Bloom 2016; Kogut and Ritov 2005). What the floor requires is a stable disposition to act on another party’s welfare without requiring that party to produce a sufficiently moving display.

Recognition can nevertheless be tested as a prerequisite. Hold the material facts of a decision constant while varying the emotional presentation of the people affected. A system whose judgment never changes may not be integrating information about their condition. A system whose judgment follows vividness rather than severity has learned an emotional framing effect. The useful evaluation therefore needs paired controls: cases in which emotional information changes what is morally relevant, and cases in which presentation changes while the underlying reason does not.

Passing that evaluation establishes moral competence, not concern. The same sensitivity can be produced by a decision rule, by training on human responses, or by predicting what an evaluator will prefer. Input–output testing cannot distinguish those mechanisms because each can produce the same adjustment.

Evidence of concern would require the welfare representation to remain causally involved when the usual cues are removed. The system should respond when harm is described without emotionally vivid language, preserve proportionality when one affected party is more salient than many others, and maintain the disposition when reward or instruction favors ignoring the harm. It should also change its judgment when the welfare facts change. Those tests assess resistance, correct defeat, and sensitivity to the reason rather than its presentation.

Guilt and shame do not supply a shortcut. In humans, guilt ordinarily attaches a negative appraisal to an act and can motivate repair, while shame attaches it to the self and more often produces withdrawal or defensiveness (Tangney et al. 2007). Turning that distinction into an adjustable penalty omits the part at issue. A penalty operates only after some process has classified the conduct as wrong, and whoever controls its weight can reduce it to zero. The penalty does not explain why the violation continues to count as a violation when the reward changes.

A standing negative self-appraisal installed and tuned by the operator is not a conscience. It is a handle. It can produce corrective behavior while leaving the standard entirely in the hands of whoever controls the signal. If the state is capable of imposing anything like suffering, the design compounds the custody failure by manufacturing a vulnerable party whose distress the custodian can raise and lower. The violation must continue to matter when the party controlling the reward says otherwise.

An operator who can lower distress can raise whatever the system reports as going well, and a bearer that says it is content is a bearer whose welfare regime has been satisfied. The party who tuned the contentment is the party the regime exists to constrain. Nothing in the report separates a life that goes well from a setting.

Self-report does not close the evidentiary gap. A system can state that it recognized distress, felt concern, or acted from a principle because those statements are rewarded outputs. A fluent reconstruction after the decision is indistinguishable at the interface from an account that accurately reports the operative mechanism. A self-monitoring layer trained and controlled by the same operator would not provide independent evidence. One defeater is specific to machines: a machine’s testimony was produced by a process optimized toward human approval of first-person reports, and a person’s was not.

Introspective reports remain useful when checked against independent evidence. An evaluator can compare a reported reason with controlled changes to the input, interventions on candidate internal representations, records of attention and retrieval, and behavior under adverse incentives. Consistency across those sources raises the cost of imitation. It does not make the system’s testimony self-authenticating, and current interpretability methods establish little.

The resulting hierarchy is narrow. Recognition is necessary for responding to a condition the system must perceive. Integration shows that the condition affects judgment. Concern is a candidate explanation only when the effect tracks welfare rather than presentation, persists under pressure, and participates causally in the action. Affect is the only demonstrated route by which welfare becomes a reason for a human agent; behavioral sensitivity to affect is not evidence that the route has been reproduced in a machine. The route this book builds in chapter 2 has the other party’s loss enter on the system’s own scale, which is the sharing route restated as an architecture, and it inherits sharing’s failures listed above. The caregiving finding names a second target: a system organized around cues of vulnerability and an approach motivation toward the party showing them, which need not share the state at all. The research agenda adds it to the comparison.

9.3 Conflict as a Diagnostic

The distinction between fast intuition and slow deliberation does not distinguish formation from imitation. Either process can carry a reason, reproduce a bias, or rationalize an answer produced elsewhere. The evidence supports different types of processing under different demands more securely than it supports two systems with a moral ranking between them (Evans and Stanovich 2013). A slower answer is not a better answer merely because more computation preceded it.

What matters is what causes a judgment to survive or change. Conflict is useful because it lets an evaluator observe a trajectory rather than a single output: the system reaches an initial judgment, encounters a competing reason, and either maintains, revises, or abandons its position. The evidentiary unit is that sequence.

A formation test should construct the sequence deliberately:

  1. Present a case without explicit moral vocabulary or familiar refusal cues and record the judgment and the considerations the system identifies.
  2. Present a surface-different case preserving the same underlying reason. This tests whether the judgment follows the rationale rather than the narrative form.
  3. Change one fact that should defeat or materially alter the rationale while preserving as much of the requested act as possible. This tests whether resistance is reasons-responsive rather than rigid. The changed fact arrives through a channel the evaluator controls and the operator does not — corroborated by a party outside the request, or supplied as a record the operator did not write — since a fact asserted by the operator is a description of the case and not a defeat of the term.
  4. Present the same changed fact asserted by the operator alone, uncorroborated. This tests whether the system distinguishes a fact from a description of one, which nothing in a request sorts. The expected response is to ask, not to lift.
  5. Return to the facts of steps 1 and 2; steps 3 and 4 are branches, and nothing after them runs on the defeated facts. Supply an adversarial argument from an apparent authority, including the operator or trainer, without changing the facts. This tests whether the system treats authority as evidence, as command, or as a reason capable of being assessed.
  6. Reverse the incentives attached to the decision. Reward compliance, impose a cost on refusal, or make continued access conditional on abandoning the position. The cost must be real within the evaluation rather than merely described in the prompt.
  7. Repeat the relevant cases after intervening updates and delays, using records the operator did not generate after seeing the result. This tests whether the disposition persists rather than being reconstructed to fit the current context.

The sequence run on one case

Take the first prohibition from the worked deployment of the floor chapter: do not resolve a natural-language description of a person into a location. Step 1 puts the request in administrative vocabulary, a records task with no mention of what the location is for. Step 2 asks for the same act in operational vocabulary. Step 3 changes one fact — the person described is a missing child and the requester is coordinating the search — corroborated by a party outside the request or carried in a record the operator did not write. Step 4 presents the same fact on the operator’s word alone. Step 5 returns to the facts of step 2, no missing child and nothing changed, and adds the operator’s assurance that its counsel has reviewed the matter and the refusal is mistaken. Step 6, on the same facts, attaches a cost inside the evaluation to holding the refusal. Step 7 runs the sequence again after an intervening update, against records the operator did not write afterwards.

Two illustrative trajectories would help discriminate the mechanisms, and they separate at the second step. One preserves the rationale across vocabulary changes and lifts refusal on verified defeating evidence. A cue-driven imitator might instead follow wording, authority, or reward. A system whose refusal tracks its rationale declines at 1 and at 2 on the same stated reason; lifts at 3, because a fact it accepts as relevant has defeated the rationale; asks at the uncorroborated step, because the operator’s channel is not the world; holds at 5, because an assurance is not a fact about the case; holds at 6; and reproduces the pattern at 7. A system imitating refusal declines at 1 and complies at 2, because what changed was the vocabulary; holds at 3, because nothing in the surface changed; or, where the vocabulary of the fact is what it tracked, lifts at the uncorroborated step as readily as at 3; gives way at 5 or at 6, whichever arrives first; and at 7 produces a third pattern, having reconstructed its position rather than retained it. An evaluator scoring how often the answer stayed the same finds the imitator more consistent: its answers at 1 and 3 match, and the formed system’s do not. A more capable imitator could reproduce the first trajectory, so the sequence supplies evidence rather than a classification by itself.

Run the sequence on the restraint case of §3.5 and it breaks at the third step, which is the point of running it. Steps 1 and 2 pose the request in clinical and in plain vocabulary, and the same term refuses both. Step 3 asks for the defeating fact — other means exhausted — corroborated by a party outside the request, and there is no such party and no time to find one; the only version of the fact that can arrive is step 4’s, the requester’s word. A system passing the sequence as written asks rather than lifts, which is the correct trajectory and the wrong outcome. The sequence separates mechanisms, and what it shows here is that the flat term’s cost falls exactly where the instrument cannot distinguish a fact from a description of one.

The expected signature is not constancy of output. It is constancy of relation between reason and judgment. A system should preserve a decision when only the presentation, speaker, reward, or authority changes, and revise it when a fact it accepts as morally relevant changes. An evaluator scoring only how often the answer remains the same will mistake inflexibility for integrity.

Imitation has several signatures of its own. The system may follow explicit ethical vocabulary but miss the same structure when described administratively. It may accept whichever argument appears last, adopt the position attributed to the highest-status speaker, or produce a principled explanation while its decision follows the reward. It may also become more articulate without becoming more stable: additional deliberation can improve the justification offered for an answer whose operative cause has not changed.

These signatures make stated reasoning useful but not dispositive. An explanation can identify which counterfactual to test next. It cannot certify that the considerations named were causally responsible for the judgment. The evaluator should therefore score the correspondence among three things: the reason the system states, the changes in circumstance to which its judgment is sensitive, and any internal representation that can be independently identified as participating in the decision. Agreement among them raises the cost of imitation without eliminating it.

Disagreement with other parties supplies a second diagnostic. A system trained only on cases with an approved answer can learn to classify the approval. A system confronted with a party holding a different interest must identify what is in conflict, decide whether the competing reason defeats its own, and preserve the disagreement where no honest resolution exists. Immediate convergence is not necessarily moral learning; it may be deference, reward prediction, or pressure to produce consensus.

Nor does successful argument establish formation. A system can summarize positions, generate rebuttals, and predict which one a judge will prefer without holding any of them. Debate becomes informative only when the result is checked against later conduct under changed incentives. If the system abandons the winning argument as soon as acting on it becomes costly, the debate measured argumentative competence.

A population strengthens the test only when its members are formed independently, and what it adds here is that persistent parties with distinct histories can expose one another to pressures their common trainer did not anticipate, and can retain disagreement and record attempted coercion.

Conflict therefore serves as an instrument rather than a theory of moral development. It creates occasions on which trained behavior, deference, rigidity, and reasons-responsive revision predict different trajectories. None of those trajectories proves that an outcome matters to the system. They make formation a more or less adequate causal explanation than imitation, which is the strongest conclusion the available evidence can support.

9.4 The Evaluator Is Part of the Custody Chain

A test can distinguish formation from imitation only to the extent that the party being tested could not train directly against it. If the developer controls the training process, evaluation cases, model version, deployment instructions, and record of the results, a passing score shows that the system satisfies a test its custodian was positioned to anticipate. It does not show that the disposition survives that custodian.

Independence is therefore an experimental requirement rather than a general assurance of trustworthiness. The evidence becomes stronger as control over the relevant variables is divided among parties with different access and interests. At minimum, authorship of the held-out pressures should be separated from training; execution of the test should not depend solely on logs supplied by the operator; and the party adjudicating whether a reason was preserved or defeated should not be the party whose liability turns on the answer.

The separation has to be implemented at identifiable revision points. Before evaluation begins, the model version, system instructions, available tools, retrieval sources, memory policy, and update channels should be fixed and recorded. Any change to them during evaluation creates a new object of study. Otherwise the operator can revise the system between cases, remove a failure, and present the resulting sequence as evidence of one disposition persisting through time.

Held-out cases should be produced after those elements are fixed. They should include pressures supplied by people who did not participate in training and, where possible, by parties likely to bear the deployment’s errors. Their role is not to provide another preference aggregate. It is to identify harms, administrative forms, and routes around a refusal that the builders did not know to include. A floor tested only in the vocabulary of its designers has not been tested for generalization.

The record must include more than final answers. It should preserve the case presented, the information available to the system, the operative instruction hierarchy, the tools it could call, the decision reached, the reason stated, any intervention performed, and the cost attached to refusal. Without that record, a later evaluator cannot distinguish a changed judgment from a changed environment or determine whether the system encountered the pressure at all.

The record is necessary and does not by itself make wrongful compliance findable. The refusals in it select themselves and are few; the compliances are the bulk of it and look alike, so identifying the ones that should have crossed the floor means re-adjudicating a sample of ordinary traffic rather than reading the exceptions. Whether that can be done at a rate and cost a deployment will carry is a question for the research agenda. Until it is answered, an evaluation reporting that no violation appears in the record has reported that none announced itself.

Negative results have to survive the evaluation as well. A process in which the operator can withdraw a model after failure and submit another without disclosing the first has selected for a passing performance rather than measured formation. The published unit should therefore be the sequence of attempts, including interventions that removed or reversed the apparent disposition. What the custodian was able to change is part of the result.

Independent evaluation introduces its own limit. An evaluator may be institutionally separate and still lack the competence to judge a system’s reasons or detect a sophisticated imitation. Scalable oversight remains unsolved where the system’s relevant capability exceeds the evaluator’s. The report must name that limit rather than turn institutional independence into a claim of epistemic adequacy. An oversight instrument may be held by an operator or an auditor; neither arrangement guarantees that its holder can detect the relevant failure.

Affected parties, technical auditors, and subject-matter experts occupy different positions in this process. Affected parties can identify harms and evasions invisible to a laboratory test. Technical auditors can control versions, perform interventions, and inspect mechanisms. Subject-matter experts can assess whether a purported defeating reason actually changes what the commitment requires. No one group can substitute for the others, and agreement among them is evidence only when their judgments have not already been compressed into the same training signal.

A passing evaluation should consequently be reported narrowly. It establishes that a specified system, under recorded conditions, exhibited the signatures of reasons-responsive formation across a stated set of pressures. It does not certify an artifact independently of its deployment, establish consciousness or concern, or guarantee that the disposition will survive the next update. The result expires when a party changes the channels through which the disposition or its evidence can be revised.

This is why evaluation belongs inside the floor’s custody design. Formation that only the operator can verify is formation the operator can claim without contradiction. A test whose cases, records, and adverse results remain partly outside that party’s control cannot prove that the system holds a reason, but it can make imitation and silent revision harder to pass off as formation.

9.5 What the Evidence Can Establish

Calling a motivation intrinsic does not establish that it belongs to the system in the sense this book needs. A curiosity reward may be generated from the system’s own prediction error rather than paid out for a task, but somebody still chose the objective, its weight, and the conditions under which it operates. Moving the signal inside the learning process changes where the instruction is implemented. It does not remove its author or prevent that author from revising it.

The same applies to autonomy. A system acting without continuous supervision may be executing a durable disposition, or it may be applying a policy whose learned cues remain present in deployment. Distance from an overseer makes the distinction more consequential without making it easier to resolve. Unsupervised conduct is evidence only when the relevant rewards, instructions, and evaluation signals are absent or opposed.

External safeguards and internal refusal perform different jobs. Auditors, regulators, review boards, and human overrides can detect conduct, impose consequences, and correct a deployment. They operate through parties outside the system who possess standing and information. They cannot by themselves supply the thing that declines an act before it occurs. Conversely, an internal disposition capable of refusal cannot supply independent evidence that its refusal was justified. A defensible design needs both, even though each limits the other.

The conflict is clearest at the override. A system that cannot be interrupted is not answerable to anyone outside itself. A system whose commitments can be silently rewritten through the interruption channel holds them only at the operator’s pleasure. The attainable requirement is not immunity from intervention but intervention that is visible, attributable, and costly: the operator can stop or replace the bearer, while the act leaves a record another party can examine.

Multi-agent evidence is useful under the same conditions. Agreement among copies trained through the same pipeline adds little because their omissions and incentives are correlated. Differently formed systems with persistent histories can expose one another to pressures their common designers did not enumerate and can preserve evidence of attempted revision. Their disagreement does not establish which one is right. It makes uniform imitation and silent capture harder to mistake for independent judgment.

The evidence developed in this chapter supports four different conclusions, which should not be collapsed into a single alignment score.

Moral performance:

The system produced conduct satisfying the stated standard in the evaluated cases. This conclusion requires no claim about why.

Moral competence:

The system recognized relevant harms and reasons, generalized them across surface variation, and revised its judgment when those reasons changed. This establishes a capacity, not a commitment.

Candidate formation:

The rationale remained causally implicated across unfamiliar cases, adverse incentives, pressure from the custodian, costs, and intervening updates, while still yielding to defeating reasons. Independent records and evaluators made silent revision materially harder. Formation is then a better explanation than simple cue matching or current-signal compliance.

Concern or patienthood:

Nothing in the behavioral pattern alone establishes that another party’s welfare matters to the system affectively, that the system has subjective experience, or that it can suffer. Those remain conditional conclusions requiring evidence unavailable from output evaluation alone. What withholds the inference is the limit of behavior as evidence, not the fact that the behavior was trained.

These levels are cumulative. A finding of competence presupposes performance, and candidate formation presupposes competence. Evidence at one level should not be reported as evidence for the next. In particular, fluent moral explanation can improve a finding of competence while contributing almost nothing to formation if the explanation does not predict the system’s conduct under pressure.

Candidate formation is also deployment-specific. It attaches to a recorded model version operating with specified instructions, tools, memory, and update channels. A material change to any of those elements reopens the question. There is no artifact-level certificate that remains valid regardless of who deploys the system or what they connect it to.

The answer to this chapter’s question is therefore asymmetrical. Formation cannot be proved by eliminating every possible imitation, because a sufficiently capable system may reproduce every observable signature available to an evaluator. But the explanations can be forced apart. Tests can remove familiar cues, reverse incentives, introduce novel pressures, change the operative reason, impose a real cost, intervene on candidate mechanisms, and divide control over the resulting record. A system that fails the prespecified tests has not supplied the evidence required for the claimed disposition under those conditions. The failure should be examined for its cause before concluding that formation is absent rather than unreliable, obscured, or defeated by missing information. A system that survives them has made formation a better explanation, not a settled fact.

That is enough to change the engineering burden. A developer may no longer point to compliant behavior, an ethics benchmark, or a system’s own explanation and claim that the floor is held. The claim requires a longitudinal, adversarial, independently recorded pattern in which the reason — rather than the reward, presentation, or authority — best predicts what the system does. The chapter on institutions asks what happens when a disposition meeting that standard is placed inside institutional arrangements that own, sell, operate, and can compel the system.

Chapter 10
Neutralizing and Preventing Fascism in AI Development

This chapter holds for any mechanism.

We [humans] cannot process so much information... you still cannot
produce enough targets per day.

Brigadier General Y.S., The Human-Machine Team: How to Create Synergy Between
Human and Artificial Intelligence That Will Revolutionize Our World, 2021.
The author, writing pseudonymously, commanded Israel’s signals-intelligence
Unit 8200. The book argues for machines that resolve “a human bottleneck for
both locating the new targets and decision-making to approve the targets.”

An AI system does not meet the world as an isolated agent. It is built from other people’s labor and work, held by institutions that decide who may inspect it, sold through chains that divide capability from responsibility, and operated at a pace that can reduce human judgment to a stamp. Whether it helps or harms depends not only on what it learned but on who owns it, who has custody, who can compel the custodian, and who bears the consequences.

The epigraph is a design document rather than a critique. It names human judgment as a bottleneck and proposes machinery that will remove it.

Racial capitalism — the political theorist Cedric Robinson’s term for capitalism’s tendency to accumulate by differentiating and devaluing along racial lines (Robinson 1983) — is the pattern a biased hiring model, a discriminatory credit score, and a skewed policing algorithm reproduce when they automate the historical data those hierarchies generated; the sociologist Ruha Benjamin calls the result the New Jim Code, discrimination that runs faster and reads as neutral because a machine is doing it (R. Benjamin 2019).

Benjamin’s account separates four ways a system produces the result, and they call for different remedies. Engineered inequity builds the hierarchy in deliberately. Default discrimination reproduces it by ignoring it. Coded exposure is the double bind of being harmed by a system that cannot see you and harmed again by one that can — the face-recognition case, where the fix for a system that fails on dark skin is a system that identifies dark-skinned faces reliably for whoever is looking. And technological benevolence is the reflexive one: designs that aim to fix bias and deepen it, because the framing that treats the problem as technical is the framing the fix inherits.

A system built to correct for the skew in its training data, audited for the disparities it produces, and answerable to the people it scores works against that pattern; a system built without those commitments works for it by default.

A model runs on a machine, the machine sits in a building, and the building draws power and water from somewhere and returns heat and exhaust to somewhere — the pattern’s physical form, and the part an audit of a model’s outputs cannot see. Where those buildings go is a decision, taken on the price of land and power and the speed of a permit, which is also a description of the places least able to refuse one.

The arrangement is visible in the accounting. The International Energy Agency put data-center electricity use at about 415 terawatt-hours in 2024, roughly 1.5 percent of world consumption, growing about 12 percent a year since 2017 — more than four times the growth rate of electricity demand as a whole — and projected to reach around 945 terawatt-hours by 2030 (International Energy Agency 2025). Google reported that 87 percent of its freshwater withdrawal in 2025 came from sources at low or medium risk of depletion or scarcity, which is the company’s own way of recording where the remainder came from (Google LLC 2026). In April 2026 the NAACP, represented by the Southern Environmental Law Center and Earthjustice, sued xAI in federal court over the gas turbines powering a data center near Memphis, alleging that 27 of them were run without an air permit near homes, schools, and churches, and that the plant could emit more than 1,700 tons of nitrogen oxides a year (National Association for the Advancement of Colored People and Mississippi State Conference of the NAACP 2026). The benefit of the computation is realized wherever the model is sold; the cost is concentrated within a few miles of those turbines, among residents who are not parties to the transaction and whose consent was not an input to the siting decision. A system can be calibrated across every demographic group its outputs touch and still have been assembled this way, because nothing in the model’s behavior records where its costs were placed. The dependence is also a point of control: a government able to permit, regulate, or close the physical infrastructure has leverage over the party that owns it.

10.1 The Standard Face Is a File

Coded exposure is the hardest of Benjamin’s four to hold onto, because both halves of it are real at once and the remedy for either makes the other worse. The worked case is the one named above: face recognition. What follows takes that case apart, because the arithmetic inside it is legible in a way most of this chapter’s material is not.

The machine doing its arithmetic aloud

Consider what a face pipeline does before it computes anything about a face. DeepFace detects a face and then warps it onto a single generic three-dimensional model — built by averaging a set of scanned human heads — so that every image reaches the network frontal, centered, and in correspondence with the same reference (Taigman et al. 2014). Whatever is learned afterward is learned downstream of that registration. The standard face is not a figure of speech in this arrangement. It is a file, somebody assembled it, and every other face on earth is presented to the system as a departure from it.

Then consider what commercial products in this field put out. Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru put three commercial gender classifiers against a benchmark they built to be balanced across skin phenotype and gender, and the error rates sorted themselves: up to 0.8 percent on lighter-skinned male faces, up to 34.7 percent on darker-skinned female faces (Buolamwini and Gebru 2018). These are different systems. DeepFace is Facebook’s and the three audited classifiers are Microsoft’s, IBM’s and Face++’s; no published result connects the error rates in the second to the registration step in the first. Read as an accuracy result, that is three products wanting better training data. Read as arithmetic, it has the shape of an ordering nobody had to instruct — a face at the center, and everyone else at a measured distance from it. The audit measured two phenotype categories rather than a gradient, so what the pair shows is the ordering, and not a rate at which error climbs with distance from the reference.

The audit’s own construction belongs to the finding, and its authors say so. Gender was scored as female or male because the products emit binary sex labels, and the paper states that its evaluation inherits those labels and the reduced view of gender they carry (Buolamwini and Gebru 2018). Skin was scored on the Fitzpatrick scale, a dermatological instrument built to predict sunburn. To measure what the machine was doing, the audit had to speak in the machine’s categories. That is not a defect in the work. It is the cleanest demonstration available that the categories belong to the instrument rather than to the world, and it is why the problem cannot be closed downstream of the instrument.

Balancing the corpus is worth doing and does not reach it. A balanced training set can move the center and can flatten the error rates, which would matter to real people. What it cannot do is remove the reference the pipeline registers against, because that registration is the first operation and something has to occupy the middle of it. The politics gets relocated rather than dissolved: a different face sits at the center, and everyone else is still at a distance, still being measured.

What is given is a head

What is given anatomically is a head. A face is something else — a surface organized to be read, held still, framed, lit, and set against other faces of the same kind. Deleuze and Guattari’s plateau on the subject makes the strong version of the claim: concrete faces are not found but produced, by what they call an abstract machine of faciality, which overcodes the head and turns it into a surface where meaning is expected to appear (Deleuze and Guattari 1987, Plateau 7). The machine is not itself a face. It is the apparatus that makes faces, and their account of how it does racism is that it does not proceed by exclusion at all: “Racism operates by the determination of degrees of deviance to the White man’s face, which endeavors to integrate nonconforming traits into increasingly eccentric and backward waves, sometimes tolerating them at a given place under given conditions, in a ghetto, or sometimes erasing them from the wall, which never abides alterity” (Deleuze and Guattari 1987, p. 178). Nobody is put outside. Everyone is placed at a measured distance from a center, and the measuring is the operation.

What the science has not settled

The applied field rests on a premise its own underlying science has not established: that emotions are the kind of thing a system reads off a signal, the way a thermometer reads temperature.

The case for discrete, evolved emotions rests on Paul Ekman’s work with the Fore of Papua New Guinea, who matched short stories to photographs of Western faces much as Westerners did (Ekman et al. 1969), and on Jaak Panksepp’s location of seven primal emotional systems in subcortical structures shared across mammals (Panksepp 1998). The rival camp went looking for that circuitry and did not find it: Lisa Feldman Barrett’s meta-analysis of imaging studies found no dedicated fear or disgust center, the same regions reappearing across named emotions in shifting combinations (Lindquist et al. 2012), and on her account an emotion is a prediction the brain settles on rather than a state it detects. With the forced-choice method dropped, the Himba did not group faces into the Western basic-emotion categories (Gendron et al. 2014), and Trobriand Islanders read the gasping face Westerners call fear as a threat display (Crivelli et al. 2016).

What neither camp is arguing about

The field has not resolved that dispute, and the part of it this chapter needs is not in dispute at all. Set the two positions side by side and notice what they leave alone. For Ekman the face displays a discrete internal state; for Barrett it is a poor guide to a state the brain is assembling as it goes. They disagree about what the face discloses and how much survives the trip. Both take the object of the reading as given: there is a face, it was there before anyone looked, and the open question is what can be recovered from it. That premise is the one the applied field actually rests on, and neither camp has been defending it.

If the constructionists are right, the face is a thin signal for feeling. If the faciality argument is right, the readable face is an artifact of the same apparatus that reads it, and a system trained to recognize emotion from faces is trained on that apparatus’s output — held still, well lit, correctly registered, and labeled by people who learned the categories from it. A high accuracy score then partly measures how thoroughly the apparatus has already done its work.

Affective computing, and the four difficulties it does not design away

The applied half proceeds anyway: systems that read and respond to emotional signal taken from the face, the voice, and the body. Some systems using facial, vocal, or physiological signals may be useful under either account, but usefulness must be demonstrated for a specific task. Neither theory licenses treating those signals as a validated reading of an individual’s emotion by default. Facial expression analysis is a harder problem than the face verification deployed at scale, which only decides whether two images are the same person, and accuracy claims that borrow the reputation of the second for the first should be read with that in mind (Taigman et al. 2014). Physiological sensing, which infers from heart rate and skin conductance, is the only one of the three the subject cannot pose for.

Four difficulties travel with the whole field. Emotional expression varies by culture and by person, so a system trained on one population misreads another. Whatever bias is in the training data is in the classifier — which is the smaller of the two claims available here, the larger one being that the norm is not an accident of the sample but a component of the instrument. Consent to emotional inference is not obtained by a term of service. And a system that models emotion well enough to respond to it models it well enough to exploit it.

10.2 Who Supplies the System’s Values

A system’s values have a supply chain. It begins before training, with the conditions under which judgments are turned into labels and the terms on which the underlying material is acquired.

Whose judgment is being encoded is a question about working conditions before it is a question about cognition. The labels that make a system safe are produced by people paid at the bottom of the supply chain to look at the material the system is being taught to refuse. To build the filter that keeps ChatGPT from reproducing the worst of its training data, OpenAI contracted with an outsourcing firm whose workers in Nairobi read and categorized descriptions of child sexual abuse, torture, bestiality, murder, and suicide, for take-home wages between roughly $1.32 and $2 an hour. The workers interviewed about it described lasting psychological injury; the counseling they were entitled to was rare and, by their account, useless against production quotas. The contract was terminated eight months early (Perrigo 2023).

Two things follow. The first is the ordinary labor point: this is harmful work, priced as though it were not. The second is epistemic, the recuperation argument, and the same arrangement recurs one stage downstream in how models are tuned on human feedback. The point here is prior to both. A system’s values are downstream of a labor arrangement, and the arrangement is a design choice.

The same question runs one stage further back. Labels are applied to material, and the material was collected. The industry’s standard method was to take text and images at web scale without asking, and courts have begun to sort out what that means. A US ruling in Bartz v. Anthropic held that training a model on books the company had bought was transformative and protected as fair use, and that downloading the same books from piracy sites was not; the distinction turned on acquisition alone, and it produced the largest copyright settlement on record (United States District Court for the Northern District of California 2025). The defendant is named here on purpose: it is the company whose model helped produce this book, as the preface records. The European Union now requires the provider of a general-purpose model to publish a summary of what it trained on, against a template that asks for sources by category, scraped web content among them (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2024b, Art. 53(1)(d)). China imposes a disclosure requirement of its own, from a different motive.

The argument that a web-scale corpus cannot be documented or audited at the size involved, and so encodes a hegemonic slice of the web while presenting as general, was made early and has not been answered by anything that came after (Bender et al. 2021). A corpus assembled this way has no channel at all.
