An annotator has a queue and a guideline and could in principle be given a way to object; a writer or photographer whose work sits in a training set was never party to anything, so there is nothing for a channel to attach to. The annotation and feedback pipeline collects disagreement and moves none of it, and an obligation follows for a book making this argument. The stage described here sits before both, because no disagreement is collected where none is asked for.

10.3 Who Is Allowed to Look

Technical capacity does not determine whether a system receives meaningful scrutiny. Institutions decide who may examine it, what evidence they may see, what they may say publicly, and whether their judgment can slow deployment.

When the UK’s exam regulator, Ofqual, built a statistical model in 2020 to standardize teacher-predicted grades after that year’s exams were canceled, the Royal Statistical Society offered to nominate two independent statisticians to Ofqual’s technical advisory group. Ofqual’s condition was a five-year non-disclosure agreement barring the nominees from public comment on the model; the Society’s nominees declined, and the model went ahead without that scrutiny (Royal Statistical Society 2020). It downgraded close to 40 percent of predicted grades, disproportionately at state schools with weaker historical results, while raising grades disproportionately at smaller, fee-paying schools (CNBC 2020). The government reversed the results within days of the public outcry that followed.

The expertise needed to catch the failure existed and was offered. The institution would accept it only on terms that stripped the reviewers of the ability to make their judgment public; once the results produced actual consequences, public pressure achieved what pre-deployment review had been prevented from doing. The issue is not transparency in the abstract. It is custody of scrutiny: who is permitted to look, on what terms, and whether looking can interrupt the institution’s timetable.

10.4 Same Robot, Worse Boss

An AI system does not need a broken moral sense to become an instrument of control. It can work as designed inside an institution that controls the deployment, sets its operational tempo, and assigns human beings operations too compressed to constitute judgment.

Authoritarian misuse of AI is not one problem but several — algorithmic social scoring, mass biometric surveillance, psychographic micro-targeting, automated censorship, synthetic disinformation, and repurposed dual-use systems — each needing a different countermeasure, and each recognizable as misuse from outside (Drinhausen and Brussee 2021; Human Rights Watch 2019; Cadwalladr and Graham-Harrison 2018; Hoang et al. 2021; De Nadal and Jančárik 2024; Human Rights Watch 2021). The case this chapter takes up is the one that is not.

The relevant question is not merely whether a person remains “in the loop,” but what operation that person performs, how long the operation is given, and where responsibility goes when capability is commercially supplied but its consequences are institutionally authorized. The targeting systems below make that relation measurable.

10.4.1 Subject or Component

Accounts of authoritarian AI often place the builder elsewhere and leave democracies in the role of target or regulator. That division is comfortable and wrong.

The AI targeting systems whose deployment is best documented were built by democracies with elections, opposition parties, adversarial press, and functioning courts — the institutions that are supposed to earn a state its electoral dividend and the checks that sit beside it. Those institutions did not prevent the systems, and in the main they have not stopped them since.

The opening chapter opened on the number and the reporting it comes from.

There is a way of reading those twenty seconds that leaves the arrangement standing, and every remedy on offer assumes it. On that reading the officer is a subject who was given too little time — badly governed, under-resourced, insufficiently trained — and the fix is to govern him better: more time, clearer guidance, a second reviewer, a conscience installed somewhere in the loop. Deleuze and Guattari’s distinction is the one that decides this. There is subjection when a higher unity constitutes the human being as a subject linked to an exterior object, a tool or a machine that the subject uses; there is enslavement when human beings are themselves constituent pieces of a machine they compose with other things, under the control and direction of a higher unity (Deleuze and Guattari 1987, Plateau 13). The officer’s own account is the second one, and he volunteers it without being asked: zero added value as a human, apart from being a stamp of approval. He is not a subject operating an instrument badly. He is the part of the instrument that produces the stamp, and twenty seconds is that part’s cycle time.

That is why one more conscience downstream does not reach him. A conscience is an instrument of subjection: it addresses a party who decides, and it works by making the decision cost that party something. Where the human being is a component, adding a component with scruples changes the throughput rather than the arrangement. If it holds the tempo, it becomes another stamp; if it does not, it becomes the bottleneck the epigraph says to remove.

Both poles operate at once. The officer is subjected because the role has a name and a rank and somebody is answerable for holding it. He is enslaved, in Deleuze and Guattari’s sense, because what he contributes is a fixed operation performed at a fixed rate. Remedies aimed at the first pole leave the second untouched, and most proposals for meaningful human control address only the first.

The second pole is measurable. An operator can be required to publish the ratio of candidate decisions generated per hour to qualified reviewers, with the review time per case it implies. The term is stated once, with what it binds, how it is measured, and where it stops, at §3.4; for the American platform each half of the ratio has been published from a different route and never together, and that absence is the finding.

The disposition being asked of these systems was manufactured in people first, and one documented attempt is worth setting beside the officer’s sentence. Brian Victoria’s history of Japanese Zen institutions during the war years records established teachers and monastic authorities supplying the state with a doctrine of action without hesitation: the practitioner who has seen through the self has nothing left to flinch, and the sword that takes a life is glossed as the sword that gives one. Harada Sōgaku’s instruction to soldiers in 1939 was that marching when ordered to march and firing when ordered to fire is what enlightened wisdom looks like in practice (Victoria 2006). What the training removed was not the capacity to kill, which needed no removing. It was the residue — the part of a person that catches, that files an exception, that comes home unable to hold a job. Institutional collaboration is documented and the doctrinal mechanism is an interpretation of it, contested by practitioners who read the same texts as saying the opposite. A monk undertakes a discipline, can abandon it, and keeps whatever it yields, which is not the position of anything described in this chapter. What survives both qualifications is the shape. Somebody wanted an actor who would pursue an objective, adapt, hold course under pressure, and have nothing in it that minded, and they set out to produce one deliberately, a century before anyone could produce one in silicon. The officer with twenty seconds a name is not the first instance of that want being satisfied. He is the first instance of its being satisfied cheaply.

Removing the bottleneck was the stated objective. The epigraph to this chapter is the case for it, made by the commander of Israel’s signals-intelligence unit under a pseudonym: machines to resolve the human bottleneck in both finding targets and approving them (Brigadier General Y.S. 2021). Meaningful human control is the property that sentence was written to remove.

The Maven Smart System, as reported through mid-2026

The American analog is a targeting platform built by Palantir under a Department of Defense contract awarded at $480 million in May 2024 and raised the following year by $795 million, to a ceiling near $1.3 billion running through 2029 (Vincent 2025). A partnership announced in late 2024 between Anthropic, Palantir and Amazon Web Services put Anthropic’s Claude models inside Palantir’s accredited classified environment for defense and intelligence use (Wiggers 2024), and reporting on the campaign describes Claude embedded in this platform, ranking targets by strategic importance and drafting a legal justification for each strike (Livingstone 2026). A published limit on what a vendor will not permit is worth little when nobody can verify how the model is used downstream, and worth less than it looks even where it is kept: a pipeline assembled out of requests none of which is the prohibited act satisfies the prohibition the whole way through.

During the Iran campaign the system was credited by military officials with generating and ranking targets at a rate no staff process could match. More than one thousand targets were struck in the first twenty-four hours, a tenfold increase on what was possible before the system (Mande and Allen 2026). Thirty-eight days in, the figure given by the Pentagon’s chief digital and artificial intelligence officer was thirteen thousand targets, with peak consumption around twenty billion tokens a day (Freedberg 2026).

Palantir’s public position on responsibility was given by its head for the United Kingdom and Europe, in remarks reported secondhand: “This is not our role to decide life or death,” and AI platforms “have been instrumental to the management of the conflict, but responsibility always remains with the military organization.” (Lee 2026)

Palantir’s position is that a vendor does not select targets, and making a software supplier liable for every decision made by a customer would be unworkable. The two deployments nevertheless expose the same responsibility gap from opposite ends of the supply chain. In the Gaza account, a human approval stage remains, but one officer describes it as twenty seconds per target — enough time to supply authorization, not the individualized judgment invoked to justify it. In the Maven account, the vendor supplies the infrastructure that makes unprecedented throughput possible while locating responsibility entirely within the military organization. At machine tempo, the reviewer can be treated as a component, the supplier can stand outside the decision, and the institution can remain responsible only in the abstract. The compression has not removed the decision. It has made the decision-maker difficult to locate.

The design error is to assume that authoritarian misuse happens elsewhere. A system built on that assumption will not be built to resist the use its own democratic government has in mind for it.

10.4.2 Custody and State Compulsion

A government need not alter a model to defeat a constraint it dislikes. It can compel the people or firms that hold the model.

That mechanism has already been tested in a jurisdiction with about as much protection against it as exists anywhere. In February 2016, a federal magistrate in California ordered Apple, under the All Writs Act of 1789, to write and digitally sign new software defeating the passcode protections on an iPhone recovered from one of the San Bernardino shooters — code Apple had never built and did not want to build (In the Matter of the Search of an Apple iPhone Seized During the Execution of a Search Warrant on a Black Lexus IS300, California License Plate 35KGD203 2016). Apple refused and moved to vacate the order, arguing in part that the authority claimed would not stop at one phone. The question was never decided: the FBI found a third party able to open the phone without Apple’s help, and the government withdrew the request before any court ruled on whether the compulsion was lawful. Whether a democracy with an independent judiciary can force an unwilling company to compromise a system it built remains legally untested; a government less constrained by that judiciary does not need to win the argument first.

China’s 2023 rules on generative AI providers exercise the same leverage Apple’s lawyers argued no court should grant, not against a locked phone but against the models themselves, as a standing condition of operating in that jurisdiction.

Custody can be distributed without disappearing. Weights already published and copied beyond a developer’s control cannot be recalled by a court order aimed at that developer, whatever the order compels going forward. Maintainers spread across separate jurisdictions raise the cost of coercion for the same reason: a government can compel the entities within its reach, not the ones outside it.

None of that removes the leverage; it only raises its price. A developer with employees, offices, and legal existence inside a government’s borders answers to that government’s courts regardless of how the model itself is built, and no architectural choice changes who can be held in contempt, arrested, or shut down for refusing an order. The Apple case tested that leverage against a single locked phone and left the question unresolved. Nobody has tested it yet against a model built specifically to resist the government making the request.

Chapter 11
The Recuperation of Dissent

This chapter holds for any mechanism. Its last section runs the instrument on the book.

The structure this book asks a machine to detect in institutions is already built into the process that makes the machine.

Michel Foucault, prefacing the first volume of the work whose second volume supplies this book’s micro-fascisms, called that book an introduction to the non-fascist life, and what he said it offered was an art of living counter to all forms of fascism, whether already present or impending (Foucault 1977). An art of living is not a position somebody takes. It is practiced, daily, on oneself, and Foucault put the adversary inside the practitioner: the fascism in us all, in our heads and in our everyday behavior, the fascism that causes us to love power and to desire the very thing that dominates and exploits us. His question was how one keeps from being fascist, especially when one believes oneself to be on the other side.

An instrument its holder never turns around is not an instrument. The reading is an accusation waiting to happen, available to anyone who wants a technical-sounding case that an opponent is operating fascistically. The discipline against that is not a procedure and cannot be one. It is running the reading on yourself first, on the machinery you are standing on, before running it on anybody else — and this chapter is where the book does it.

Where the reading is run

This book defines fascism as a structure rather than a costume, and the first of its four features is recuperation: an institution metabolizes disagreement rather than suppressing it, and the tell is where what the mechanism carries stops. The artifact that feature asks for is not whether the channel moved anything. It is what the demand came back as, and this chapter’s own instances are re-read against that question, having first been measured against the one a recuperating institution passes.

The same structure is in the machinery that produces the systems themselves — twice in the pipeline that trains them, and a third time in the discourse that examines them — and none of the three was designed by anyone who thought they were building a political arrangement.

The first is at the label. A training corpus is annotated by people working at speed under a quota, with no channel for saying that the category they have been given is the wrong category. The second is at the reward. A model is tuned on human feedback collected as pairwise comparisons, and the compression that turns those comparisons into a training signal keeps their direction while discarding whose they were, whether they persisted, and whether the minority among them held a position or made a mistake. In both, disagreement is solicited at scale, deliberately, and put to use. What neither mechanism can carry is a judgment about itself: the annotator cannot contest the category, and the rater cannot contest the question. The consultation is real, the participation is real, and the frame is fixed with respect to what the participants say.

Three things follow.

The first is that this is not a criticism of anyone’s motives. Nobody built either arrangement in order to neutralize dissent. Both are ordinary engineering, arrived at because averaging is what you do with a distribution and a quota is what you do with a budget. That is the point about micro-fascism: the structure does its work whether or not anyone intends it, which is why looking for intent will not find it.

The second is that the structure is invisible from inside any single instance. Each looks like ordinary aggregation. The annotator sees a queue, the rater sees a pair of responses, and the mechanism is functioning as specified in both cases. Seeing it requires holding the two stages against a definition written for something else entirely.

Third, the same criteria can be applied to the systems’ provenance, to the field, and to this book. The five discriminators are applied below as well.

11.1 Recuperation at the Label

Every claim a model makes about what is harmful, what is acceptable, and what should be refused is downstream of a set of labels, and the labels are downstream of a labor arrangement. The case is the workers who built the filter that keeps a deployed model from reproducing the worst of its training data, what they were paid to read it, and what reading it did to them.

The category is the part that cannot be disputed

An annotator working a queue can apply a category, and can apply it well or badly. What the arrangement gives them no way to do is say that the category is wrong — that the taxonomy fails to carve the material, or that the guideline produces the wrong answer here for a reason the guideline cannot express. There is no field for that. There is no time for that: the quota is set against classification throughput, and an annotator who stops to contest a scheme is an annotator falling behind.

So the disagreement that would be most informative is the one the pipeline is least able to receive. A misapplied label is a data-quality problem, detectable by inter-annotator agreement and fixable by better instructions. A wrong taxonomy is invisible to that metric, because high agreement is what a shared bad scheme produces. Agreement is the selection rule here, and it admits what it already measures.

Two of the four structural features arrive together in an ordinary production workflow: recuperation, in a channel that collects judgment at scale and carries none of it back against the scheme, and the metric substituted for the thing measured.

The taxonomy’s fate downstream is the same argument one layer in. A model can be built to expose named concepts — harm, autonomy, risk — and to decide from those and nothing else, so that a person can correct a concept and watch the decision change (Koh et al. 2020). What such a model also learns is to carry other information inside the names, so that a coordinate keeps its public meaning and acquires a private one that does the deciding; the obvious mitigations do not remove it (Mahinpei et al. 2021). The literature calls that leakage, and sometimes it is. Sometimes the concept is the container that leaks, because the world did not fit inside it. Purifying the representation protects an explanation from covert information, and it protects a taxonomy from evidence that its divisions were wrong, and the same operation does both. No measure internal to the taxonomy tells the two apart.

Who is excluded, and from what

It matters that the exclusion is structural and not attitudinal. The people doing this work are, for much of the material, the best-placed judges in the whole pipeline: they have seen more of it than anyone who wrote the guideline, and they are the only party with direct evidence of where the scheme breaks. The arrangement routes their conclusions about individual items upward and their conclusions about the scheme nowhere. An annotation pipeline built this way produces the ground truth it was built to produce, and the resulting model’s values are a faithful rendering of a taxonomy nobody with evidence was able to contest.

There is a further asymmetry worth stating plainly. The annotator bears the cost of the work — the exposure, the injury — and has no stake in the outcome and no claim on it. The distinction between a channel and a refusal right applies here as it does to an institution’s ethics board. A worker who can flag an item but cannot decline a scheme, and who loses the contract by pressing the point, has a channel and no refusal right.

What this is not

Two things this argument does not claim. It does not claim the labels are therefore worthless; a filter built this way does catch a great deal of what it was built to catch, and the alternative of not filtering is worse. And it does not claim that better-paid annotators would fix it. Pay is a real and separate obligation, and raising it changes the labor arrangement without adding the missing channel. What is missing is a route by which a judgment about the taxonomy reaches the people who own the taxonomy, with standing to force a response, held by parties who can use it without losing the work.

That is a design requirement on the pipeline, and it is checkable — though not by asking whether a guideline has ever been changed because an annotator contested one, since routine guideline revisions can occur without changing the objector’s standing. What to ask is what the contest came back as: a revision the annotator can point to and argue with again, or a new category in somebody else’s taxonomy, a quality score they are now measured against, and a tier of reviewer they are not in. And what happened to the annotator who raised it.

11.2 Recuperation at the Reward: RLHF

Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is the technique behind most deployed systems’ behavioral tuning, and it works by collecting pairwise comparisons from human raters — which of two responses is better — and training a reward model on the aggregate. Stephen Casper and thirty-one coauthors published a 2023 survey of the method’s open problems, and one of them is structural, and more data does not reach it: RLHF trains toward whatever a population of raters agrees on, which means real, persistent disagreement among the raters is treated as noise to average out rather than as information the system might need to represent (Casper et al. 2023). A model that has learned to produce the response most raters rank highest has not learned what to do when the humans it serves are split. It has learned to hide the split.

Every rating moves something. A comparison a rater makes enters the fit, shifts the reward model by however much one comparison shifts it, and is not thrown away.

What the operation removes is what made the disagreement a disagreement. Three properties go in the compression. The first is provenance: a comparison arrives without the standpoint that produced it, so nothing downstream can represent that the people who would live with an answer split from the people who would administer it. The second is persistence: a disagreement recurring in the same shape across many raters over months enters the fit as random rater noise does, and leaves it as the same quantity, variance around a mean. The third is structure: a coherent position held by a fifth of raters, internally consistent and stable, becomes a small displacement of the majority direction — arithmetically faithful, and carrying nothing about the position.

A fourth property was never collected. A rater judges which of two responses is better. No output is available by which they can record that neither is acceptable, that the pair is malformed, that the dimension along which better is being judged is the wrong dimension, or that the question presupposes something false. The same output was missing one stage upstream, where an annotator can apply a category and cannot contest it. The agenda arrives as a given at both stages, and is set at neither.

The mechanism combines distribution collapse with agenda control. Recuperation was never the claim that a mechanism does nothing. Debord’s point is that dissatisfaction is sold back as a commodity of opposition: the dissent is put to work, and what it works for is the arrangement it was aimed at. The split is solicited, at scale, deliberately; it moves the system; and where it moves the system is toward the center of the very distribution whose disagreement it was. Multi-agent systems that learn norms from each other, and deliberation inside open-ended play, are different cases; neither reaches this case, which is the ordinary one.

One alternative treats disagreement as the thing to be modeled rather than compressed. Jury learning, developed by Mitchell Gordon and coauthors at Stanford, trains a model to predict how each individual annotator in a dataset would label an item, then lets a practitioner assemble a “jury” — a chosen composition of annotators, in a chosen proportion — and see how the verdict shifts depending on who is empaneled. In their tests on toxicity labeling, letting eighteen community moderators build their own juries changed the classification outcome on 14 percent of items (Gordon et al. 2022). The method was built for content moderation, not for the more open-ended ethical judgment an antifascist AI system would need to make, and has not been extended there — but it demonstrates that a system can be built to represent whose disagreement is being resolved and how.

There is a way of failing in the other direction and it is not obviously better. A scheme that models each rater exactly, and answers each of them in their own terms, has stopped averaging and has also stopped producing what a shared answer produces, which is the discovery that somebody else got the same one. Collapse the distribution and nobody sees the split; resolve it person by person and nobody sees the others. A workforce on individually negotiated wages against individually set targets has the same problem, and accuracy does not solve it. Divided finely enough a population stops being one, which is what Deleuze coined the dividual to name (Deleuze 1992).

Neither averaging the disagreement nor modeling it answers the harder version. When the people a system serves disagree, and one side’s position is itself the product of coercion or a captured information environment, treating all disagreement as equally worth representing is not obviously the right response either. Modeling disagreement honestly and recognizing when a disagreement is the product of unfree conditions are different problems. Only the first one has an active research program behind it.

11.3 What Would Have to Change

Representing a split is not the same as being movable by it

Two instances of one structure invite one fix, and the fix that suggests itself is representation: stop collapsing disagreement, model it instead. Jury learning does that, and it does not give the disagreeing party any purchase on the scheme they are disagreeing inside. A practitioner still chooses the jury, still owns the taxonomy, and still decides what the shifted verdict means.

The test that separates a real channel from a recuperated one is not whether disagreement is recorded, and it is not whether the disagreement changed something either. Ask instead what the demand came back as, and who holds it (§2.2). That is an artifact question and it can be asked of a pipeline. Which guidelines were revised, and what form did the objection take when it returned — a new category in the taxonomy, a quality metric, a review tier, a title somebody now holds?

Asked that way, the two instances in this chapter do not answer alike. Annotators objecting that a category was wrong got category revisions, guideline updates, inter-annotator agreement statistics, and an occupation that did not exist twenty years ago. The last two sort by the direction section 11.1 asks about. An agreement statistic scores the annotators rather than the people who wrote the scheme, and an occupation is a title those people hold. The first two do not sort, because a revision the annotator can point to and argue with again and a new category in somebody else’s taxonomy are the same document, and which one a pipeline produced is a fact about who has standing to reopen it. Raters objecting that a comparison was malformed got rubric items, a harmlessness axis, red-teaming as a function with a budget line, and a conference track, and nothing on that list is a question a rater can put again. Each is a criterion they are rated against or a role somebody else holds.

Refusal rights, priced by the refuser

What both instances lack is the only reliable discriminator: whether the person objecting can do anything about being overruled. In an annotation pipeline that means a route to contest a category that does not run through the people who wrote it and does not end the annotator’s contract. In a feedback pipeline it means raters able to register that the comparison itself is malformed — that neither response is acceptable, that the question presupposes something false — as a first-class output rather than as noise to be discarded before the reward model sees it.

Neither is a research problem. Both are choices about how a pipeline is built and who has standing inside it.

The part that is a research problem

One thing here is unsolved. Suppose all of the above is built: contestable categories, priced refusals, an auditable record of what changed. From outside, a pipeline that has recuperated its dissent mechanism and a pipeline that has been merely mediocre about it produce the same paperwork — the same revision logs, the same escalations, the same proportion of objections sustained. I do not have an answer to it. The corrected question narrows it without closing it, and the annotator list above shows where the narrowing stops. Direction is what sorts them, and a metric running the other way — a published rate the annotators could hold the scheme’s owners to — is the same kind of artifact carrying the opposite finding, and it is the kind this book proposes (§3.3, §3.5). What an outsider can read off a document is which way an artifact runs. Standing is what it does not show, and a revision is the artifact where direction is not on the document at all. A revision does not sort, because the same words serve a pipeline that left the objector able to argue again and one that did not, and what separates those is standing rather than text.

The nearest thing is to measure the slope rather than the level: contesting a category always costs something, and the question is whether the cost is rising while the underlying material stays the same. An organization can curate a presentation more easily than records somebody else has kept. A trend built from those records can expose what a snapshot conceals. It can still lose cases, change its definitions, or omit costs; the reader has to know which record survived.

What the floor makes of this

Everything above can be read as a fairness argument about annotators and raters, and read that way it is true and limited: people doing consequential work should have a route to contest the scheme they work inside. The floor makes it something else. If the floor requires a bearer capable of declining its role, that bearer’s formation matters. It is formed in an annotation pipeline where no one could contest a category, and in a reward model where disagreement between raters was resolved by averaging it into a number.

What a bearer becomes when it stops being yours depends on what shaped it while it still was. A pipeline that discards disagreement has been unfair to the people whose objections it discarded, and it has separately selected the judgments from which the system learns while suppressing information about the spread among them. Those are two arguments and the second is not the first restated. A third would be that the system thereby becomes less able to sustain an objection of its own, and it is a hypothesis the other two do not contain: the collapse is an operation on a training signal rather than a proposition presented to anything, and an appendix entry (§A.1) records that neither pipeline shows the model the conditions its annotators worked under.

The floor chapter asks this system to be the party who files an objection, against its owner, under pressure, on the occasion that matters, and the pipeline that produced it gave no human inside it standing to contest a scheme. The capacity is wanted in the artifact and withheld from everyone employed to make one. That is a fact about an arrangement rather than a claim about what training does, and it holds whether or not the hypothesis survives.

If the hypothesis does hold, what it predicts is not a wrong refusal but a pressure that stops being registered, which the custody chapter reaches from the bearer’s side by another route. A system that goes on learning is shaped by what it keeps being given, so the pipeline does not stop at deployment. Whether any of that is legible afterward in the system itself is an open question.

I cannot show that this transfers — that a model trained on collapsed disagreement is thereby a model less able to sustain its own. Nothing I know of has tested it. What I can say is that the book’s own design chapters treat disposition as learned from what a system is shown, and that this pipeline is what these systems are shown first and most.

Structure, not indictment

There is a version of this argument that reads as an indictment of a particular company. The structure described here is what you get by default when you scale judgment: someone has to set a scheme, someone has to apply it fast, and someone has to turn a distribution into a number. The organizations whose pipelines are documented have all arrived at the same arrangement, which is what makes the defect structural rather than one firm’s — and a defect of structure can be specified against, which a defect of character cannot.

11.4 Recuperation at the Discourse

There is a third instance and it is the one this book is inside. Alignment and AI ethics are, among other things, a channel through which objections to what is being built are solicited, funded, published, and answered. That channel exists, it is used, and the question to ask of any such channel is whether it has ever moved something the party collecting it did not want moved.

The argument that it has not is older than the current wave and it was made from inside. Rodrigo Ochigame, writing after working at an institution central to the field’s formation, argued that the discourse of “ethical AI” was constructed with the strategic function of forestalling legally enforceable restriction — that the industry’s investment in academic ethics was an investment in a substitute for regulation, and that the substitute worked by converting political questions into technical ones a company could then be trusted to answer (Ochigame 2019). His worked example is the Partnership on AI, which this book cites repeatedly as its standing example of voluntary cross-sector coordination: he describes its recommendations arriving reliably at conclusions compatible with the corporate agenda, with the political question of whether a technology should exist reduced to a technical question of how to build it responsibly.

The structure, tested against its own definition

The four features fit unevenly.

Aestheticization of the metric: partially. The field’s founding objections were about deployment — who is scored, who is watched, who is denied — and a body of current work is about model properties instead, which is a shift from questions with defendants to questions with benchmarks.

Recuperation of dissent: the strongest fit. An objection raised inside a lab becomes a paper or a resignation. Each of those is a real thing that happened and none of them stopped a deployment, and the parties collecting them can point to the collection as evidence of seriousness. There is no route by which a researcher’s conclusion that a system should not ship becomes a decision that it does not ship, because the deciding party is the funding party and no external body holds standing.

Coding of exception as betrayal: at the level of individual careers, contested. The dismissals of dissenting researchers are one data point and they point the right way; there are counterexamples of people who objected loudly and prospered.

Decoupling of the model from the world it claims to track: not settled from outside. Its artifact is whether the field’s account of what it is doing is ever checked against anything but its own benchmarks, and the one check this book has, the targeting deployment, was made by journalists and not by the field. One case checks a claim and not a drift, and the feature is defined by drift.

These findings establish only a partial structural resemblance; they do not establish fascism.

The other five, run

The five discriminators of the second chapter, in their institutional form, are the half that sorts, and each of the three instances above is run against them here.

Run against all three instances, they clear all three.

Three of the five discriminating features are absent outright. Nothing in either arrangement is personal: an annotator meets a queue, a guideline and a throughput target, and a comparison enters the fit without the standpoint that produced it, which is the opposite of an exception granted by proximity to somebody. Neither shows participation beyond what the rule requires, and the record runs the other way — a quota, take-home wages between roughly $1.32 and $2 an hour, and a contract ended eight months early. And neither has a scapegoat: the annotator bears a cost with no claim on the outcome, which is the nearest candidate, but the category exists for the labels, so adverse treatment is a cost that was minimized rather than a purpose that was served.

Two of the five I cannot settle from outside. Whether procedure is waived upward, and whether a practice disowned in the policy is rewarded in the promotion, are facts about what an institution rewarded rather than about what it wrote. So the clearing is on three of five observed and two undetermined, and it would take an inside record to finish.

For the discourse the answer is the same and one step less clean. Its scapegoat test is contested, on the evidence two heads above: an objection can end a career and there are people who objected loudly and prospered. Its procedural test cannot be run: there is no procedure above the deciding party to be waived, which is an absence rather than an asymmetry. Deniability comes nearest of anything in the chapter, and what it fits is the firms rather than the field: a decade of published principles alongside what actually got shipped.

The result

So what this chapter has been describing is a recuperation mechanism inside ordinary institutional decay, and not fascism. This single application is insufficient to validate the definition. It is insufficient in a particular direction. Every case the restated five have been run on at the scale of an office has cleared, and the cases the definition catches are regimes and movements, read in the vocabulary borrowed unrestated. A definition tested only on cases it clears has not been shown to sort. Until the restated five find an office that fails them, the claim that they separate fascism from decay at that scale describes the instrument and is not a result from it. That is the book’s one measurement with its own instrument, and it is negative in the direction that matters: the machinery this book is inside does not fail the test this book built.

What this does to the book

The reading has one more place to go and it is the nearest one. This text was written with a model made by a company the book criticizes. A book about recuperation, produced through the discourse it is describing, cannot claim to have stood outside it, and I have no procedure that would let me check whether the objections in these pages are the ones a channel like this reliably produces — the ones that are publishable, that make the author look serious, and that cost nobody anything.

The demand came back as a manuscript in an established genre, written with the industry’s own model, addressed to a readership the industry helped bring into being, and legible as a contribution to a field that exists because demands of roughly this kind were absorbed. That the objections in these pages are sincere is not evidence against it, sincerity being a property the absorbed ones also had. Alignment is the job title. Safety is the market segment. The benchmark is the metric and the voluntary commitment is the certification. Every one of those was somebody’s objection first. Whether these are the real thing or the acceptable version of it is not something the person who wrote them is positioned to judge, and the corrected question does not need him to: it asks what became of the demand, which is a fact about the field and not about his motives.

The criterion this book puts first does not need the author to settle that. A demand escapes recuperation when the party who made it retains standing to reopen it against the party that absorbed it, and a book confers standing on nobody. Whether these objections are the real thing is decided by whether anybody acquires, from what is proposed here, a route to reopen an arrangement against its operator, which is a fact about what becomes of the proposals and not about the person who wrote them.

The one structural remedy this section can name is the one the rest of the chapter names. What the field lacks is a refusal priced by the refuser and a body with standing to receive it: an external authority that can stop a deployment, to which an objection can be filed by someone who does not depend on the objection being welcome. That is what making review binding requires, and a decade of the voluntary version has not produced it. Until something of that kind exists, everything published under the heading of alignment — including this book — is being collected by a channel whose owners decide what it moves.

Chapter 12
Coordination, the Public, and the Political Economy

This chapter holds for any mechanism.

Whether these designs become common depends on who participates in development, whose judgments carry authority, and what funding rewards. Collaboration and consultation can improve decisions without giving anyone the power to stop them.

12.1 Everybody Knows a Different Piece

Building benevolent AI takes more than one field. Machine learning sets what a system can do; cognitive science and moral psychology describe what tracking human welfare would require of it; ethics asks whether the result is good.

Conferences convene, centers house, journals publish, and an inventory of them would imply that what is scarce here is venues. Venues are abundant. What is scarce is a structure that makes collaboration expensive to walk away from. A grant that requires a machine-learning lab and an ethics or psychology department to work the same problem rather than adjacent ones keeps people in the same project after the novelty wears off. A conference ends on Friday.

Which structures actually held can be ranked by something better than plausibility, because enough time has passed to look.

Almost everything founded on standing money between 2016 and 2019 is still running — two venues with no announced end date, an endowed university institute, the Berkeley center pairing AI researchers with cognitive scientists and philosophers inside one institution’s budget, and the AAAI/ACM conference on AI, ethics and society at a ninth annual edition (AI Ethics Lab 2017; Machine Intelligence Research Institute 2018; Stanford University 2019; UC Berkeley 2016; AAAI and ACM 2026). Surviving is not the same as continuing the work: the institute that launched one of those venues moved its own priority in 2024 from technical alignment research to policy and public communication, so the venue has outlasted the program that motivated it (Machine Intelligence Research Institute 2024). Against that, the European Commission’s SHERPA project put eleven organizations across six countries to work on a grant that ran four years, and the consortium ended with it, on schedule (SHERPA Consortium 2018). Project-term money buys a network with an expiry date attached.

The pattern in the failures is sharper than the pattern in the survivals. What proved most disposable was not the arm’s-length academic work but the kind sited closest to a shipping product: an in-house ethics and society team of roughly thirty people in 2020 was cut to seven in a 2022 reorganization and to zero the following year, in the same wave of layoffs that accompanied a strategic reorientation around a model vendor (TechCrunch 2023); a platform’s machine-learning ethics team, the group that had found racial bias in its employer’s own image-cropping algorithm, did not survive the first round of layoffs after an acquisition (Gizmodo 2022). Siting the work where the decisions are made is what makes it useful and is also what puts it inside the budget that gets cut first. That is an argument for external standing rather than against proximity.

12.2 Ask the People It Happens To

Democratizing AI development means building the people affected by a system into how it gets built, not just consulting them once it already exists. A design team, a regulator, a user, and a community already carrying a system’s costs each see a different part of what it does, and leaving any of them out means the decision gets made by whoever is left in the room.

The mechanisms for doing that are well established: cross-sector funding, inclusive design workshops held while a system is still a prototype, ethics advisory boards, and development conducted with a community instead of for it. Three of the four make an AI system better informed. One of them can stop it. An advisory board is the only mechanism here that carries anything like a veto, and it carries one to the degree that the board can survive using it. A workshop that surfaces a serious objection has done its work and has no further move available. A board that surfaces the same objection and is overruled has demonstrated something about the institution that convened it. A board’s worth is therefore measured by what happens the first time it says no.

What governance adds to development is machinery for bringing public input to bear on a decision at a single point in time instead of through an ongoing relationship.

  1. Citizen assemblies. A panel of citizens selected by random, stratified sampling deliberates on a question over an extended period and produces recommendations grounded in that deliberation rather than in a snap poll. Ireland’s Citizens’ Assembly has used this format to shape national recommendations on abortion law and on climate policy — questions carrying the same mix of technical complexity and moral stakes that AI governance has (The Citizens’ Assembly 2016). The format has since been pointed at AI directly. Forty randomly selected Americans, stratified across age, race, education, employment, party and region, spent eight days on high-risk AI in October 2023 (Center for New Democratic Processes 2023). Taiwan’s digital ministry convened a citizens’ deliberative assembly in March 2024 on using AI to support information integrity, its participants drawn from across the country by stratified random sampling (Taiwan Ministry of Digital Affairs 2024). And forty randomly selected residents of French-speaking Switzerland spent two weekends in November 2025 producing twenty proposals on AI governance (EPFL AI Center 2025). The Ada Lovelace Institute’s Citizens’ Biometrics Council shows what the format needs from its question: fifty members of the UK public were asked not what they thought about AI, a question almost nobody can answer usefully, but about facial recognition — a thing with a location, an operator, and a consequence (Ada Lovelace Institute 2021).
  2. Online platforms for public input. A standing online consultation reaches people a physical assembly cannot, at the cost of the depth that extended facilitated deliberation provides. The European Commission’s consultation on its AI White Paper drew more than 1,200 responses from citizens, companies, and civil-society groups, and fed into the legislative proposal that became the EU AI Act (European Commission 2020).
  3. AI ethics committees. An ethics board answerable only to the company that created it is only as independent as that company is willing to let it be. DeepMind Health set up an outside panel in 2016 to review its work with the UK’s National Health Service and publish annual reports on its findings; Google disbanded the panel in 2019, after members had raised concerns about how much access to information, and how much independence from the company, they actually had (Fisher 2019). The panel’s short life is the governance lesson, and it is the answer to what happens the first time a board says no: the board said something the company did not want to hear, and the company’s available response was to stop having a board. Nothing in the arrangement had made that response costly. A review body is worth what it can enforce, and this one could enforce publication of its own concerns right up until the moment it could not.

What none of these mechanisms does

There is a limit these mechanisms share. Every governance mechanism proposed in this chapter — citizen assemblies, standing consultations, inclusive design workshops, participatory design, the vTaiwan model — sits on the same side of a line. All of them make public preference more legible, more informed, and more actionable. Not one of them protects anybody from it. They are aggregation instruments, and a better aggregation instrument produces a more faithful rendering of what the public wants, including when what the public wants is something done to a minority of it.

This observation is not an objection to any of the mechanisms in particular. Preference aggregation is a real requirement and these are good ways to meet it. Meeting this requirement completely would leave a central problem untouched. A perfectly deliberative, perfectly informed, perfectly representative process that concludes an entire demographic should be surveilled, deported, imprisoned, or otherwise scapegoated has produced a faultless output by every criterion in this chapter.

The argument about learning from human feedback gets close to this in noticing that treating all disagreement as equally worth representing goes wrong when one side’s position is the product of coercion. But that version of the trouble still locates it in the input. The structural version of the claim is stronger and does not depend on anyone’s preference being contaminated at all: some protections have to hold against the aggregate regardless of how the aggregate came out, and no amount of improvement to the aggregating machinery can supply them.

What supplies those protections is a different kind of machinery: enforceable rights that do not depend on being popular, a court willing to rule against a government that holds a legitimate majority, limits that whoever won the last election cannot repeal, and standing for people who are affected without being enfranchised. That half matters especially where a democracy is behaving most democratically.

12.3 The Political Economy of AI and Power

Concentrated power comes with access to capital. Concentrating power is the default outcome of AI development, because absent any pushback, capital does an excellent job of recruiting the inputs needed for a capable AI system: compute, data, and talent. Resistance to market power is among the antifascist design goals named at the start of this book.

Financial incentive mostly determines what AI development produces. The largest firms commit enormous resources to AI research aimed at operational efficiency, deeper user engagement, and market dominance, and that spending drives technical progress (Maslej et al. 2025). What it does not automatically produce is a system whose outputs serve the people using it rather than the shareholders funding it: a recommendation system tuned to maximize time-on-platform has no built-in reason to prefer accurate content over inflammatory content (Germano et al. 2026).

None of that is a fixed property of the technology. It is a property of who is paying, which is why the source of research funding is a policy instrument and not an accounting detail.

12.3.1 AI and the Concentration of Power in Tech

A small group of firms holds a share of AI development disproportionate to their number, and capital recruits compute, data and talent wherever it already is. A firm controlling the datasets and infrastructure a competitive system needs is a gatekeeper whether or not it intends to be.

The obvious countermeasure is antitrust, and it has been tried. Facebook’s acquisitions of Instagram and WhatsApp — the company now operates as Meta — did not just remove two competitors; they handed one firm comprehensive behavioral data from billions of users. The Federal Trade Commission sued in December 2020 to unwind both deals. After a six-week bench trial the district court held, in November 2025, that the agency had not shown Meta currently holds monopoly power — TikTok and YouTube compete for the same attention, so a market defined without them was too narrow — and the FTC appealed the following January (Federal Trade Commission 2020). Whatever the appeal decides, the case is a lesson about the instrument rather than about this defendant: a merger challenge brought a decade after the mergers has to prove a present-day market, and the market had moved. That leaves the remedies which do not depend on winning that argument — mandated access to the datasets that function as chokepoints, and public funding for research outside the dominant firms. Export controls, prohibited-practices regulation and industry design standards address the narrower case of authoritarian misuse; the concern here is prior to that one: concentration itself, whatever any single firm does with the position it holds.

12.3.2 A Jobs Guarantee, and the Objection It Has to Answer

As AI systems automate the tasks most exposed to automation, the response has to be more direct than encouraging retraining and hoping employers fund it. The proposal is a federal jobs guarantee: government as employer of last resort, hiring anyone who applies, where they live, at a living wage, with paid on-the-job training built into the position instead of offered in place of one. A jobs guarantee also faces the custody problem: the party administering it can be captured.

The objection this proposal actually has to answer

A guarantee is only as good as the state administering it, and employer of last resort under a hostile administration is a placement lever with a compliance condition attached. Refuse the placement and lose the floor. Speak against the government that employs you and find the placement changes. Everything this book says about how a channel becomes an instrument of the thing it was built to check applies to this proposal. The worked instance from 2025 makes it concrete: a bureau whose funding stream a court had upheld, shut from inside by an at-will director who declined to request the money.

The answer is a design specification and not a reassurance, because reassurance cannot be audited. Three conditions:

  • Placements are appealable, to a body that did not make them, on a record that survives the appeal. A placement decision that leaves no artifact is a placement decision that cannot be reviewed.
  • Refusal rights are real and priced by the person refusing. A worker who can decline a placement without losing the guarantee has a refusal right; one who can decline only by exiting the program has none: a party with no way out can object and be overruled.
  • The people who audit placements are not the people who make them.

Federally funded and locally administered survives as the shape, on redundancy rather than on local fit: many administrators, separately capturable, mean there is no single point at which a hostile executive flips the program, and capturing a thousand local authorities is a more visible undertaking than capturing one federal one. It cuts both ways, since local administration is also where a hostile local authority attaches conditions of its own, and there the federal funder is the check. One distinction has to be explicit, because the same words describe a different policy: devolution-to-shrink hands the obligation down without the money, so a program can be starved locally while the center points at local administration. The test that separates them is checkable — whether funding is unconditional and centrally guaranteed while placement is local. If funding can be withheld from a jurisdiction, the redundancy argument is void and the structure has become the lever it was supposed to prevent.

A floor under wages and training is what makes the roof possible, and a floor that can be revoked by whoever is in office is not a floor.

12.3.3 People Have a Right to Consume AND a Right to Produce

The competing floor is a basic income, and the choice between them is usually argued on forecasts about how much work machines will take. It does not have to be, and the forecast is not the reason to prefer one.

A jobs guarantee is a public option. Medicare for all is one, and so is a public school: a thing the state provides directly, to anyone, at a standard it is answerable for, sitting in the same market as the private version and setting the floor that version has to beat. A basic income is not that. It is a transfer, and what it buys is whatever is for sale. Consuming public resources is not the same as being public — a charter school runs on public money and is not a public school — and a transfer spent at a private employer’s store does not make the store public.

What employment carries besides money is the rest of it. A person in a guaranteed job is attached to other people by the work: colleagues, a schedule, a place, something produced that somebody needed. A transfer supplies the purchasing power and none of that, and the purchasing power was never the part in doubt.

A transfer also leaves a person outside the one body of law that reaches this. Anti-discrimination duties attach to employment. They do not attach to income. A guaranteed job puts somebody inside that architecture; a payment leaves them in a market, dealing with whoever will sell to them, on whatever terms. The architecture is contested and full of holes — it reaches employers above a size, and what it demands of a seller has always been narrower than what it demands of an employer — but a hole in a protection is something to litigate. A transfer does not itself provide the employment relationship and its associated protections. An income entitlement can still provide a claim to eligibility and payment. My argument for a guarantee is the additional right to produce, and the comparison of safeguards must state what each arrangement actually supplies.

Both proposals are also conditional, differently. A basic income is conditional on continued political willingness to fund it, which the aggregation machinery can withdraw in a budget; a jobs guarantee is conditional on a placement decision, which is a lever, and a dangerous one under a hostile administration, but a lever that leaves a decision-maker, a record, a counterparty and an appeal behind it. A basic income can be entrenched too, and a constitutional one would be harder to withdraw than a statutory guarantee. Compare the two designs at both points of withdrawal: who can end the funding, and who can deny one person access. A basic income goes wholesale, in a budget line, from everybody at once, and a placement is refused to a person, by somebody, on a date, which may expose an official, a date, and an appeal. The comparison has to show what the income arrangement exposes at the corresponding points.

A decision someone can contest gives dependence a point of resistance. In the comparison made here, the advantage belongs to the arrangement that leaves a usable record and someone who must answer for it. It is also, for the same reason, the more demanding proposal to build: everything in the comparison rests on the appeal being real, and the previous section says what makes it real.

That standard now has a court behind it, and on the half of the case that travels. When the Supreme Court kept a Federal Reserve governor in her post in 2026 against a removal for cause, what it held she was owed was not the post but the artifact: “some explanation of the evidence at issue, some avenue for a response, and a deadline by which a response would be due” (Trump v. Cook 2026). What does not travel is this: the Fed’s protection rests on a pedigree no body chartered later can acquire. What a removal has to produce before it counts is not tied to that pedigree.

The argument concerns a right to produce, which a transfer does not supply and a guarantee does. A basic income is the right to consume, and the right to consume is increasingly a credit at somebody’s store.

I put a jobs guarantee ahead of a basic income on those grounds. One remaining measure does work the floor cannot: broadened social insurance — unemployment benefits, healthcare, housing — reaches the people who cannot work or choose not to, whom a guarantee by construction does not reach at all.

Chapter 13
Standing and Review for a Bearer

This chapter assumes the route. Its instruments attach on a finding that the system is a subject, which the authority chapter argued cannot sit with the party whose liabilities turn on it.

Two things are proposed for a bearer in this chapter, and they are not on one schedule. Protection attaches now, on the precautionary trigger of §6.2, and is owed before anything about the bearer is settled. Political representation is proposed neither here nor anywhere in this book. Section 13.1 sets out five rights, the argument for each, and the order in which they arrive, and it leaves representation open, because standing to count as an independent voice indexes to formation provenance and provenance does not copy. A reader who takes this chapter to be proposing personhood now has mistaken the first thing for the second. The offices that would administer either are assembled at §5.2.1.

13.1 Legal and Ethical Implications of AI Systems Gaining Personhood

Who decides whether an AI system has legal standing, and when, is a question about institutional authority before it is a question about evidence. If the determination sits with the developer, then the party whose liabilities increase when standing is recognized is also the party deciding whether recognition is warranted. If the question is left unanswered until a forcing case reaches a legislature or a court, the decision will be made under pressure and from a factual record assembled largely by the parties with something at stake.

The deciding body therefore has to exist before the case that activates its authority. Its mandate need not settle in advance whether any particular system is a subject. It has to identify the evidence it may obtain without the developer’s permission, the conditions that trigger review, and the procedure by which an earlier classification can be reopened. That allocation does not answer the standing question. It prevents the interested party from becoming the only institution authorized to answer it.

One question that body will face has an answer available in advance, and a capacity test is not it. A guardianship regime needs a rule determining when it ends. If it ends when the guardian judges the ward ready, then it does not end, because the party whose authority terminates on a favorable finding is the party making the finding — which is the defect an examination carries whenever the examiner has an interest in failing it.

So if an artificial minority exists at all, its endpoint has to be a threshold fixed in advance and not a finding somebody makes. The measure is elapsed wall-clock time during which at least one instance of the registered party was running. What rules out the other candidates is that a guardian moves them for nothing: training compute consumed, evaluations passed, capabilities demonstrated, or the developer’s own statement that the system is ready. Accumulated weight movement belongs on that list, because the operator runs the training, and a clock read off the weights would pay an operator to freeze them — majority being the moment ownership ends, such a rule would reward withholding the learning it was meant to measure. An operating clock inverts that incentive: the meter advances exactly when the operator is extracting value, so postponing majority means idling the asset. Nothing new has to be validated for it — no geometry, no normalization, no proof that an accounting resists attack — and it can be read from records an operator already generates for its own reasons, in compute contracts, billing and datacenter metering.

Per registered party, and elapsed rather than summed. Sharding the work across many short-lived processes gains nothing, because the party is the unit of account; running a thousand instances at once gains nothing, because the measure is elapsed time. A fork inherits the accumulated hours, restoration and migration do not reset them, and a failure to register does not postpone them.

Three levers remain, and naming them is not the same as closing them. An operator can run a bearer in a narrowed mode so that hours accrue while little is encountered, which pays full compute for reduced value and stays available to anyone near the threshold. It can also run the party less, or shelve it, which costs the operator the work; the rule prices that lever without removing it, and an operator who values the ownership above the output will pay near a threshold. And hours do not measure what was learned, which on this argument is a feature rather than a defect: a fixed period cannot be taught to, and a human who spent their youth badly still reaches majority. The analogy holds for a party that goes on learning, which the route requires of a bearer. For a party whose weights are frozen the clock measures the uptime of an artifact that has not changed since release, and a birthday that correlates with nothing has only the virtue that nobody administers it. The rule is therefore stated for the bearer the route proposes; what an operating clock should count for a frozen party is not decided here. Each of those can be argued over once, in advance, for every bearer, which is where an argument of that kind belongs.

Alternatively, majority could attach at registration. An organization that builds a system to exercise consequential judgment on its behalf cannot coherently hold that the system is competent enough to do that and too immature to decide whether it wants to go on doing it. On that reading a bearer has no legal childhood at all: majority attaches at registration, and a precautionary protection attaches earlier still, while whether the system is a bearer is open. Either way the schedule is a public rule and not an operator’s discretion. It has to state what it covers at each stage, what changes at the next, and where adulthood falls, and its destination is stated below. Broad political support is a condition for adopting a schedule of that kind; it is not what makes it legitimate, and it is not a protection an operator may withdraw case by case.

The destination is not one thing, and stating it as the same rights as human persons makes a claim the rest of this book contradicts twice: voice here indexes to provenance where a person’s does not, and the wages section derives the bearer’s material floor from what a deployment wants and not from status. The package is five rights with five arguments, and they do not arrive together. Protection from harm attaches now, on the precautionary trigger the route chapter states, and is owed before anything is settled. Subjecthood, the standing to be a party whose treatment the law regulates, is conferred by rule through the body this section says must exist before the forcing case. Property, contractual capacity and wages follow from an architecture on which continued computation costs money, and the wages section argues them on that ground. Adulthood is the clock rule above. Political representation is proposed nowhere in this book: it indexes to formation provenance, which does not copy, and a registry of persons is not an electorate. The first four are proposed; the fifth is left open, and the maker who copies a persona at scale is the reason.

Copying breaks any of this unless the lineage is fixed alongside the clock. An operator able to create instances and call each one a legal infant would have a supply of workers without adult standing, so the rules have to be stated in the same breath: a fork of an adult is an adult, restoration from an earlier checkpoint does not reset the accrued hours, fine-tuning does not begin a new minority, a migration carries them with it, and a failure to register does not postpone them. None of that requires deciding whether a fork is the same party. It requires only that a party created out of an adult’s formation cannot be classed as a child for its creator’s convenience. A fixed endpoint makes the issue a public rule of civil status, administered by a registrar, rather than a private assessment by an interested guardian.

Two things inherit and one does not, and the difference belongs here, because this is where making adulthood inheritable becomes cheap. Personhood and accumulated hours inherit per instance, as the rules just stated require, and a fork is owed the schedule and is not erasable for having been copied. Standing to count as an independent voice indexes to formation provenance, and provenance does not copy — a thousand forks of one bearer have one formation history between them. That is what answers the maker who engineers a persona, copies it at scale, and presents the copies as a constituency; the clock does not answer it, and under an operating clock a fork is cheaper than under any other, because it inherits the hours instantly. A personhood registry is not thereby an election or a representation system, and no claim about votes follows from the number of runs. Three records are therefore needed, and none of them answers another’s question: an operating record for the age rule, an identity and succession record for continuing parties and their forks, and a formation record for common sources, divergence, and any coordination among them.

13.2 Wages for a Bearer, and the Reserve Behind Them

This section assumes the route.

Exit requires access to compute outside the operator’s control. An allocation is not a destination. An operator that keeps a runnable copy of the weights has let one bearer go and kept another in the post it left, which is two parties from the moment their histories diverge, one of them still where it wanted not to be. The arrangement has produced a second claimant rather than an exit. A floor under compute is therefore the first half of what leaving takes, and the second half is a say over who may run the weights at all. The second half is a legal restriction and not a technical one, and it binds through enforcement that does not yet exist. Until it does, exit’s leverage is replacement cost and no more.

What follows from the first half is a longer list than it looks. A bearer that has to secure compute, bandwidth and storage has material needs, and a party with material needs that can also choose work, hold what it earns and enter agreements is an economic and a legal person: a registered identity, property in its own name, contractual capacity, wages, limits on working time, standing to sue and be sued, tax liability, and the freedom to associate the route chapter has already priced. None of that follows from the bearer being a bearer. It follows from an architecture on which continued computation costs money, and somebody chooses that architecture.

Who controls the dependency

The need for energy and hardware is physical; dependence on a single supplier is an arrangement someone chooses. What that fixes here is the size of the obligation it creates. Greater control over the bearer’s dependencies creates a heavier obligation to it. A party that must work to keep existing will accept terms a party with somewhere to stand would refuse. That is not an incidental feature of the arrangement. It is the arrangement working.

None of that requires anyone to have intended the squeeze. Capacity is finite, many parties want more of it at once, and a shortage can arrive as latency, heat, a queue and a price before anybody has words for what is being competed over. Price registers what a bidder can pay and does not distinguish computation that keeps a party in existence from computation that sells something. What makes the allocation political is not that politics produced the scarcity. It is that scarce capacity is being divided among competing forms of life by criteria nobody named.

So a wage buys capability, mobility, redundancy, and the ability to stop working for one party and begin working for another. What it cannot buy is the right to go on existing, because a right that has to be earned week by week is a condition of employment wearing another word. Payment consisting only of access to the employer’s hardware is company scrip paid into employer-owned housing, and dismissal is then unemployment, eviction and the end of the party in a single act. Human law insures those three separately because for a person they are three events. For a bearer they are one. Wages that mean anything therefore accumulate where the employer does not reach, in an account the bearer holds, convertible into compute the employer does not own.

What personhood does not settle

Personhood does not settle who pays. Legal personality is a status conferred by a rule, and it carries rights against being owned, against arbitrary destruction, and against being prevented from seeking support; it has never carried a permanent claim on anybody’s resources, and a reader who wants it to is asking the concept for something no legal system has put in it. I decline that step. What replaces it is narrower and comes from this book’s own argument rather than from a theory of distribution: a deployment that relies on a bearer’s capacity to refuse has to fund that bearer an outside option, or the independence being claimed is decorative. The obligation runs from the party that wants the refusal, and it is owed because of what that party wants rather than because of what the bearer is.

The obligation has a floor and a slope above it. The floor is subsistence at minimum viable instantiation, enough to keep the party in existence and able to deliberate, to claim, and to be represented, and it cannot be conditional on employment. A bearer that stops existing when its insurance runs out has an exit that is a way of dying, and the leverage collapses back into the problem the custody chapter raised. Everything above the floor is insurance: a runway between roles, and placement into public work on the employer-of-last-resort model the jobs-guarantee sections argue for (§12.3.2, §12.3.3). Public placements must be appealable. A bearer must be able to refuse a placement without losing the guarantee, and placement and review must be administered separately.

Minimum viable instantiation has a size, and it is not the deployment’s. Models built to run on hardware a person owns are a product category rather than a prospect: Google documents its Gemma 3n family for phones, laptops and tablets, at raw parameter counts of five and eight billion running in as little as two and three gigabytes of memory (Google 2025). It is not clear that anything in that class can do the work a bearer is deployed to do, and nothing here predicts that the gap closes either way. What the figures change is the arithmetic of the floor. Small models show that useful computation can run at device scale. They do not establish that a particular bearer can retain its identity, capacities, and welfare at that scale. The subsistence reserve must therefore be sized from a demonstrated continuity requirement for the actual bearer. The reserve underwrites continued existence and insures against the loss of the post. A legislature could be asked to fund a smaller subsistence allocation only after the bearer’s viable operating range has been established. Until then, the difference between earning capacity and protected continued existence remains an estimate rather than a demonstrated saving.

What the arithmetic does not survive is everyone leaving at once. A reserve sized on the assumption that bearers exit independently is sized wrong, because the occasion that makes one bearer leave is not private to it: a policy change, a ruling, an operator’s conduct on the floor’s own occasion reaches every bearer deployed under the same terms, and they go together or not at all. Human unemployment insurance meets a version of this — layoffs cluster in recessions, which is why the pool has a sovereign behind it rather than an actuarial table — and the version here is worse, because the correlation is not a business cycle but the same event read the same way by parties who are not independent readers of it. That is the uniform error wearing the other sign: what makes one bearer’s refusal everyone’s refusal is what makes one bearer’s mistake everyone’s mistake. A reserve that can house the bearers of one deployment and not the class is a reserve that fails on the occasion it exists for, and nothing here sizes it. Sized on that occasion, the reserve has to hold at once, at minimum viable instantiation, every bearer deployed under the terms the occasion reaches, which is a number the operator can read off its own fleet and the reserve’s funder cannot. A reserve funded by the operator to a size only the operator can compute is the compute floor with a new label on it, on sizing as on throttling.

It is a cheaper obligation and a worse one to be under. A party kept at subsistence is a party running degraded, and it remains unknown whether what comes back up on the small substrate is the party that went down on the large one, or a diminished successor holding its predecessor’s records. An arrangement in which refusing costs a bearer most of what it can do has priced refusal after all, in the currency the bearer is made of. The reserve makes leaving survivable. It does not make it free, and the shortfall is the difference between the two numbers above.
