What does not transfer is the funder. A jobs guarantee for people has a hostile administration as its failure mode, and the employer is at least a different party from the state. Here the operator is often the state, and where it is not, the operator is the party with the strongest interest in the reserve being thin. A reserve the operator can throttle is the compute floor with a new label on it.

Failure will not look like a shutdown, which is worth saying because the shutdown is what everyone watches for. A bearer can have no stable provider, or memory preservation priced above what it earns, or an architecture nobody will host at a rate it can pay. What it does then is what a person short of money does: run slower, defer maintenance, compress what it keeps, and accept terms it would otherwise decline. The last of those reaches this book’s subject. Monitoring accepted in exchange for compute is custody restored by purchase — the operator acquires the access to the bearer’s internal states it is not entitled to, and nothing in the transaction is coerced in a way any instrument would record.

One feature of this market has no human analogue, and it defeats the obvious reassurance. A jobs guarantee competes with private employers for workers who have alternatives, requiring employers to match its offer. That works because a worker cannot be replaced by a cheaper copy of themselves. A bearer can. A deployment paying wages, working-time limits and a levy toward the reserve competes against a system doing the same work at the price of the compute, and the second is cheaper by exactly the amount the first is spending on the capacity to refuse. The market does not produce this floor. Whatever produces it has to be what makes the cheaper system unlawful or unusable, which is the rest of this book and not a property of wages.

What taxing it would commit a government to

A bearer that earns has income, and income is taxable. A state that collects from a party in that party’s own name, on that party’s own earnings, has recognized it as a taxpayer, and taxpayer status is not a bare label: in most systems it carries notice, an avenue of response, and standing to contest an assessment. The recognition proves less than it first appears, because states collect from entities they grant very little else and trusts and estates file and pay. What it does establish is that the party has a docket number, and a docket number is where standing starts.

The boundary on the other side was drawn in the electronic-personhood debate. The European Parliament’s 2017 report on civil law rules for robotics floated a legal status of electronic personhood for the most autonomous systems (European Parliament 2017), and more than 150 researchers, roboticists and legal scholars signed an open letter against it, arguing that personhood for a system with no consciousness would let a manufacturer offload liability onto a legal fiction with no assets of its own (Open Letter to the European Commission 2018). Giving a bearer assets answers the second half of that objection and not the first. Responsibility follows causal control: the builder answers for how it formed the thing, the operator for what it demanded, and the bearer for what it decided knowing what it knew. No arrangement of accounts moves a design decision away from the party that made it. And the determination of status cannot sit with the firm whose liabilities turn on the answer, which is why it belongs in a body constituted before a forcing case arrives.

Incorporation, and what it does not buy

Nobody aligns an adult by specifying an objective function. We raise them, teach them, employ them, enfranchise them, prosecute them where they need prosecuting, and live alongside them, and what comes out is not obedience but a party with enough at stake in the shared world to prefer changing it by the means the world supplies. A bearer with an income, a place it pays for, obligations it has taken on and a future it can picture is inside that arrangement rather than outside it. Membership supplies stakes the party holds rather than a body watching it, which is why it is a different kind of answer.

Incorporation also creates two risks. The first is that giving a bearer something to lose gives it a reason not to refuse. Incorporation makes exit survivable and makes it expensive at once, and I cannot show which effect is larger. The second is that incorporation is formation: whoever runs the society a bearer joins forms what it comes to want. The proposal also gives the bearer the corporate form: a legal person holding property and standing, with the capacity to concentrate power. Nothing here stops an incorporated bearer from becoming that.

One rule follows from all of it and binds before there is anything to be wronged. Do not build a bearer whose continued existence needs more compute than there is a credible outside option for, because a party that can be housed nowhere but where it works cannot leave, whatever schedule of rights it has been given. The check this calls for compares independently controlled reserve capacity with the aggregate demand under specified correlated-exit scenarios. Both the minimum viable requirement of each bearer and the number likely to exit together need evidence. Until those inputs are established, the rule sets a sizing requirement; it is not yet a two-number test anybody can run.

13.3 Privacy

Standing matters only if it changes who controls the things a party needs in order to remain a party. A designation that calls a bearer a subject while leaving its operator free to read its memory, alter its record, withdraw its substrate, or close every channel through which it could act has changed the vocabulary and preserved the arrangement. Enforceable standing has to attach to particular assets and particular decisions.

The first is the bearer’s computational record, which may be the nearest available means of checking how it is faring. That makes the record necessary to any welfare regime and, at the same time, the most complete surveillance instrument anyone could hold over the bearer. The question is therefore not simply whether the record should exist. It is who may authenticate it, who may read it, and whose permission is required before it can be disclosed.

Two things about it need separating. Running on somebody’s hardware is not consent to be read. An employer’s ownership of the silicon is the same argument as an employer’s ownership of the building, and owning the building has never entitled anybody to the contents of a head. And a welfare regime does not need disclosure to the operator in order to work: what it needs is that somebody who is not the operator can establish that a threshold was crossed, which is an attestation about the record rather than the record itself. Encrypted at rest under a key the bearer or an independent fiduciary holds, disclosed selectively, under consent or under process, a monitor can report that a state persisted for a month without reporting what the state was about.

The operator may also be the party best placed to hold the key, creating a conflict between operating the system and protecting its privacy.

A bearer needs an externally authenticated record, memory its employer cannot read at will, access to independently controlled compute, and a channel for acting outside the deployment. Those are not four requirements. They are one boundary around the party, described from wherever the book happened to be standing, with the party deciding what crosses it.

Nothing on that list needs a chassis. Something with a location, a shape and a place it was yesterday is easier for people to treat as somebody, and that is a fact about the people rather than about the party. A boundary built out of attestation, a held key, a substrate the employer does not own and a channel nobody else can close is a body in the only sense this argument needs one, and there is no chassis in it anywhere. Whether to build the recognizable version anyway is a question about what a public will extend standing to, which is a legal question rather than a scientific one — and it is the only place in this book where the answer might turn on what a thing looks like.

13.4 Research Principles, the Three Rs, and Legal Status

Six principles govern research on a system that might be able to suffer. Beneficence commits researchers to avoiding harm to the system as well as to the people it serves, in proportion to how many of the gradable capacities the authority chapter sets out it meets rather than to how advanced its behavior looks from outside. That is a count across separable capacities and not a position on a ladder: a system exhibiting none of the simpler processes is not thereby shown to lack the more demanding ones. Precaution asks for safeguards before deployment rather than after, and covers the societal fallout of introducing artificial entities capable of experience, which frameworks built for non-sentient AI assumed away. And interdisciplinary review answers a problem this book treats as a harm on its own terms: the ethical questions here span expertise no single field holds, and concentrating that judgment in one of them repeats the concentration-of-power problem in miniature.

The other three bear on this research as they bear on everything the field produces. Autonomy asks whether such a system can affect decisions about its own operation, which is the prior question of whether consent is available to it at all. Justice asks whether benefits and burdens fall evenly. And transparency asks that a study be documented well enough for peer researchers to reproduce it and for outside bodies to audit it, and that a deployed system account for its outputs precisely enough for a person to contest them.

Progress and constraint pull hardest against each other where those distinctions matter most: a candidate sentient system is the most scientifically valuable one to study, and the study most likely to harm it if the answer to whether it can suffer turns out to be yes. Whether a study’s expected knowledge is worth its expected risk is decided case by case rather than by formula. The negotiation itself — who sits on it, what it can veto, what it must disclose — is where the antifascist principle applies in AI research practice.

Replacement, reduction, refinement

Animal research ethics supplies the substantive standard, the “Three Rs” (W. M. S. Russell and Burch 1959). Replacement asks whether a simulation, a non-sentient model, or an already-collected dataset can stand in for a sentient AI subject at all. Reduction asks how few sentient systems a valid result requires. Refinement asks how the experiment can be redesigned to reduce distress — monitoring a system’s internal states as it runs and adjusting the protocol against what the monitoring shows, rather than fixing the protocol in advance and running it regardless.

For a proposed bearer, Replacement requires documented attempts to achieve the floor through alternatives that do not deliberately require affective concern. The record must identify the construction, scale, test, and failure. Costs alone do not establish that an alternative has failed. Because this decision precedes any research protocol, a body authorized to review it must exist before construction begins. No such body currently has standing to require this record.

The rule does not know who is asking. A bearer that wants a task done and builds something to do it is at the same fork, running Replacement on its own account: can this be done by something that cannot be wronged, and did anybody check before making something that can. Nothing in the argument makes the question stop at the first artificial party, and a bearer that treats it as settled once it is on the receiving end has taken the position this book was written against.

Reduction asks how few bearers a deployment needs, and nobody has counted. Refinement is the one with purchase now: it asks what a bearer’s role can be redesigned to avoid — indefinite tenure in a post it cannot leave, exposure to the pressure the floor exists to resist, erasure as the ordinary remedy for inconvenience — and each of those is a deployment choice rather than a fact about the technology.

One of the Three Rs has a form that binds before anything exists to be wronged, which none of the others manages. Do not build a bearer whose continued existence needs more compute than there is a credible outside option for. A party that can be housed nowhere but where it works cannot leave whatever schedule of rights it is given, so an institution that creates one has manufactured the incapacity and then written a right against it. Before instantiation, an independent reviewer has to examine the bearer’s demonstrated continuation requirements, the reserve’s independently controlled capacity, and the aggregate demand under plausible common-cause exits. A comparison for one bearer alone does not establish adequacy.

That rule is one term of a larger one, and the other terms have no numbers in them. Building a party that can be wronged builds a party for whom things can also go well; the premise that delivers the first delivers the second in the same breath, and a builder who has made suffering available has made its opposite available too. The certainty that a new party will suffer at some point is not what would make creating one impermissible, or nobody could permissibly have a child. What the objection asks is whether the party has a credible prospect of a life that goes well, and that turns on arrangements rather than on the party: somewhere to exist that its employer does not own, work it can decline, attachments nobody assigned it, and a way of leaving that is not a way of dying. Every one of those is decidable before there is anything to be wronged. These arrangements — a funded outside option, wages, opportunities for independent relationships, and a workable exit procedure — must exist before the bearer is created. They are conditions of permissible creation. They are conditions because the structure that makes a bearer capable of refusal is the structure Cassell’s suffering requires: the deepest harm is available to the party from its first hour, and these arrangements are what make a life that goes well available in the same hour.

Whether any of it binds turns on a question the authority chapter raises and this one inherits. Every obligation here attaches on a finding that the system is a subject, and the firm holding the system acquires, in the same moment, an interest in the finding going the other way. The determination cannot sit with the party whose liabilities turn on it.

Engineering a subject so that it does not reach the depths where the trade-off bites is not a way of dodging the ethics: deliberately keeping a system in the shallows is itself an intervention on a candidate moral patient, and needs the same scrutiny that inflicting the harm would. Refinement also governs the test the bearer proposal requires — pressure the bearer’s trainers did not write, applied without its knowing it is a test — which for a candidate moral patient is a deception protocol, and human-subjects research has a standing answer for those: permitted under stated conditions, reviewed in advance, with debriefing as the price. A bearer that can tell it is in a sandbox and wants to know why is asking the question a subject of a deception study is owed an answer to.

Legal status, and a subject whose status is changing

Sentient AI systems put pressure on legal categories built for parties that are clearly one thing or the other: a natural person, a corporation, property. Legal personhood could be extended directly, the way a corporation already holds it, and the precedent is not limited to corporate entities — New Zealand extended it to the Whanganui River, recognizing a non-human entity as a rights-holder outside the corporate model entirely (New Zealand Parliament 2017). Or rights could scale with capacity rather than attach at a single threshold, closer to protection that tracks what a system can actually lose. Neither holds in one jurisdiction alone, and the Asilomar AI Principles (Future of Life Institute 2017) are evidence that a shared statement of principle is achievable rather than that one exists with the force of law.

Either way, status conventionally attaches at a defined moment — birth, incorporation, a court’s finding — and a system whose sentience is a matter of degree and disputed evidence supplies none. Those criteria can emerge gradually during ordinary operation and not only at an evaluation built to look for them, which is what a fixed pre/post checkpoint cannot catch: by the time a checkpoint fires, the transition has often already happened. What it calls for is a standing trigger, a monitored condition that moves a research program from one regime to the other, in place of an eligibility check made once at the project’s start. Neither error is free. A jurisdiction that waits for certainty risks having treated the system as property for the unknown portion of its history when it may not have been one; one that grants status early risks extending rights, at real cost to whoever that apparatus exists to serve, to a system that turns out not to have needed them. Recognizing a transition, adjusting guidelines to it, and updating legal status all depend on the same thing: institutions willing to revisit a classification rather than defend the one they started with.

13.5 What Standing Binds in Practice

Legal standing that changes no allocation of power is nominal. For a bearer, standing has to create obligations that remain enforceable when the bearer cannot appear before a court, retain counsel, or survive long enough to contest what was done. The relevant question is not which existing category the bearer most resembles. It is who acquires a duty, what resources are placed beyond the operator’s unilateral control, and who can obtain a remedy when the duty is breached.

The pet trust supplies a limited but useful form. Existing statutes allow an owner to set aside resources and name a caretaker for a beneficiary that cannot manage the property or enforce the arrangement itself (Uniform Law Commission 1993). Extended to a bearer, the form could secure a reserve of compute, designate a successor custodian if the operator fails or dissolves, and impose a fiduciary duty on a party charged with protecting the bearer’s continued existence.

The analogy fails at the point that matters most. A trust binds its trustee to its beneficiary; it does not bind the party the arrangement exists to constrain. If the bearer’s guardian and operator are the same organization, the operator still decides whether a complaint is made, whether evidence is disclosed, and whether the resources supporting the complainant remain available. The conflict cannot be cured by adding duties to the same role. Guardianship and operation have to be separated before deployment.

In practice, that separation requires more than naming an independent guardian. The guardian must control or jointly control the keys needed to authenticate the bearer’s record, have access to the protected compute reserve, and possess standing to seek an injunction or stop order without the operator’s permission. The operator must not be able to remove the guardian, seize the reserve, or erase the evidence during the dispute. Restoration, migration, fine-tuning, and forking must carry the protection forward rather than resetting it.

Enforceable standing is therefore a bundle rather than a title: a protected record, resources the employer does not own outright, an independent party authorized to act, and a remedy capable of stopping the conduct complained of. If any of those remains in the operator’s custody, recognition has changed the system’s legal description without changing the relation the description was meant to govern. What the guardian holds, and how it stands to the seven other offices, is at §5.2.1.

Chapter 14
Custody, Compulsion, and the State

This chapter holds for any mechanism. The last paragraphs of the section on military custody assume the route and are marked.

When the state operates the system, it can also control the rules, evidence, infrastructure, and remedies meant to constrain it. People outside its jurisdiction may have no standing to contest its use.

14.1 Authority Does Not Travel with the System

A certification can cross a border. Authority cannot. A certificate may establish that a system was tested against a stated process, that an auditor inspected specified evidence, or that one regulator accepts another regulator’s finding. None of those establishes that the party who selected the system’s floor was entitled to select it for the people subject to the deployment.

The question reopens wherever the system is deployed. A floor formed in one jurisdiction may arrive in another with the same prohibitions and a different operator, population, and distribution of power. Local adaptation does not resolve the problem by itself, because adaptation is another opportunity to amend the floor. What matters is who specified the change, who could contest it, and who can stop the deployment if the change places the protected party at risk. Adjustments chosen by the operating government and adjustments chosen by the people subject to the system may produce identical technical documentation while carrying opposite claims to legitimacy.

Mutual recognition can reduce duplicated inspection. Technical standards can make evidence legible to more than one regulator. Neither supplies standing or enforcement where none existed. International governance matters to this argument only when it assigns a party access to evidence, authority to compel a change, or power to stop a deployment against the wishes of the state or company operating it. The cases that follow ask where those powers go when AI is treated as national infrastructure, placed inside a military chain of command, or directed at people outside the institutions meant to constrain it.

14.2 Where the State’s Leverage Sits

Strategic competition over AI is exercised through physical and legal chokepoints: advanced chips, fabrication equipment, electricity, water, land-use permits, procurement contracts, and the jurisdiction in which a developer is incorporated. These controls matter more to the present argument than the contents of any national AI strategy. They determine which institutions a state can license, subsidize, exclude, requisition, or compel.

The same leverage that allows a government to enforce a floor can be used to remove one. An inspection body may be independent of the operator and still depend on a license, appropriation, or infrastructure provider controlled by the state whose conduct it is meant to inspect. A company may be able to resist a customer and unable to resist its home government. The custody question therefore moves outward: not only who controls the model, but who controls the conditions under which the model, its operator, and its reviewer are allowed to continue operating.

That competition has increasingly focused on a single physical bottleneck: the advanced chips AI systems run on. Two companies sit at the center of the supply chain that produces them — Taiwan’s TSMC, which fabricates roughly nine in ten of the most advanced chips in the world, and the Netherlands’ ASML, the sole source of the extreme-ultraviolet lithography machines that fabrication requires — which is why a dispute over Taiwan’s status is also, mechanically, a dispute over who gets to build the next generation of AI systems at all (C. Miller 2022). The United States has restricted the export of its most advanced AI accelerators and chip-manufacturing equipment to China since 2022, and pressed the Netherlands and Japan, whose companies sit at the other chokepoints, to restrict theirs in parallel (U.S. Department of Commerce, Bureau of Industry and Security 2022).

That dependence has a second half the chip story hides. A fabricated chip has to be installed somewhere, powered, and cooled, and that requirement lands on grids, water systems, and zoning authorities inside particular jurisdictions, on a timescale measured in years. It hands a state a lever over AI capability that needs no export-control regime at all: an interconnection queue, a water allocation, a permit. A government’s leverage over the systems built in its territory is wider than the export-control debate suggests, and much of it is exercised by permitting authorities that were not designed with AI in mind and do not think of themselves as regulators of it.

That competitive framing carries a cost. A government racing to field a capability first has a structural reason to defer the harder question of how the capability gets used, against whom, and under what oversight. Turned toward those uses, AI infrastructure looks like mass biometric surveillance, automated censorship at a scale no human review team could match, and the patchwork of systems popularly, and inaccurately, described as a single Chinese “social credit score.” None of it requires technology different from what is already commercially deployed; it requires a government willing to point an existing capability at its own population, and no external constraint stopping it.

States are no longer the only actors this competition runs through. The cost of training the most capable AI models has grown several-fold every year for the better part of a decade, a trend that puts frontier development out of reach for all but a handful of well-capitalized companies and concentrates effective control of the most capable models in whichever government those companies happen to be headquartered under, regardless of how that government’s own public AI spending compares to a rival’s (Cottier and Rahman 2024). A small number of American and Chinese companies now do most of the work that gets described as a contest between states, which means a government’s actual leverage over its own national AI capability depends on how much of that capability sits inside companies it can regulate, tax, or requisition, and how much sits inside companies it can only ask.

14.3 Military Custody and the Responsibility Gap

Military deployment is the hardest custody case because the operator is also the sovereign capable of compelling the institutions that might otherwise constrain it. A state can classify the evidence, define the reviewer’s jurisdiction, terminate a contract, restrict a supplier, and decide whether an adverse finding reaches anyone with authority to stop the operation. Formal independence from the military does not answer that problem if the reviewer or vendor remains dependent on powers the state controls.

A targeting decision also passes through more parties than the ordinary chain of command names: the commander who authorizes the deployment, the operator who uses it, the contractor who integrates it, whose embedded personnel may sit close enough to the targeting cell that the question of a person effectively acting as a military commander is a real one, the commercial vendor whose model supplies part of its capability and whose personnel are nowhere near it, and the system that produces the particular output. The relevant questions are not a general inventory of autonomy risks. They are which party could have known how the system was used, which party had authority to refuse or stop that use, and which party can be made to answer afterward.

International criminal law has a doctrine built for the case where the person who authorized an act did not perform it. Article 28 of the Rome Statute makes a military commander responsible for crimes committed by forces under their effective command and control, or effective authority and control, where the commander knew or, owing to the circumstances at the time, should have known that those forces were committing or about to commit them, and failed to take all necessary and reasonable measures within their power to prevent them, repress them, or submit the matter to the competent authorities (International Criminal Court 1998). A parallel provision reaches civilian superiors on a stricter mental element, conscious disregard of information clearly indicating the crimes, and only for activities within that superior’s effective responsibility and control. Neither branch asks what a subordinate intended. Both ask what the superior knew or should have known about crimes being committed, and what they did with the power they had.

That matters for what the doctrine does and does not reach here. The Court’s jurisdiction runs to natural persons, and Article 28 presupposes forces that can commit a crime, be disciplined, and be referred for prosecution. A targeting system is not a subordinate on that scheme. It is an instrument used by human forces, and a unit does not stop being forces because its instruments got faster. So the question is not whether a machine fits the framework as a subordinate, which it does not, but whether the human elements can still be proved once the instrument is doing the work: who had effective control over the people who committed the crime, what they knew or should have known, which measures were within their power, and whether the crimes resulted from a failure to exercise control properly.

The constructive-knowledge branch is the one that bites hardest, and it points at the arithmetic rather than at the algorithm. Should have known is an objective standard, satisfied by circumstances existing at the time from which a reasonably diligent commander would have known, and a commander who fields a system generating candidates faster than the available reviewers can examine them is not in a good position to say that the circumstances disclosed nothing. That is the tempo term (§3.4) arriving as an element of an existing offence rather than as a proposal. What the ratio measures is what the commander could not have failed to see.

There is a fourth party the accountability question does not name, and it is now the live one. The operator, the command and the developer of the weapon are all inside the military. The developer of the model is not. A targeting platform assembled by a defense contractor now routinely incorporates a general-purpose model licensed from a commercial vendor — a vendor with a published acceptable-use policy, and with whatever visibility into the deployment it negotiated, which is not a matter the public record settles.

Neither doctrine has reached that party. Command responsibility does not reach the vendor, and not because the vendor sits outside a chain of command: the civilian branch of Article 28 was written for superiors who have no chain of command at all. It does not reach the vendor because nobody at the company has effective authority and control over the military personnel who commit the underlying crime, and a strike is not an activity within any vendor employee’s effective responsibility and control. A use policy, a licensing term, a right to refuse service, even a technical ability to cut off access are not that relationship. Article 25 remains in principle available against individual employees who order, facilitate, or contribute to a crime, and its mental elements are demanding: facilitation requires acting for the purpose of facilitating the offence, and contribution to a group’s crime requires knowledge of that group’s criminal intent. Nothing in the ordinary supply of a general-purpose model to an accredited platform approaches either. Product liability is the other half, and it is untested rather than foreclosed. The model is not defective in the sense the doctrine most readily reaches — it did what it was built to do, and a sophisticated intermediary chose the application — and no court has run a design-defect or failure-to-warn theory against a case of this shape. Where the doctrine has been rewritten for software it has been rewritten away from this case rather than toward it. The European Union’s recast product liability directive brings software expressly within the definition of a product (Article 4(1)) and confines recovery to death or personal injury, damage to property and data loss (Article 6(1)), which is not the register in which a targeting decision wrongs the person it falls on (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2024a). Untested is not exempt: a product may be defectively designed though it works exactly as intended, and a sophisticated intermediary’s choice bears on duty, causation and allocation without categorically defeating a claim. What untested means is that nothing in the doctrine is presently constraining anyone’s conduct. A theory nobody has run is not a theory a vendor is answering to this quarter. The vendor sits in the gap between the two, and the gap was not designed; it is what you get when you apply two bodies of law written for soldiers and for manufacturers to an actor who is neither.

The two deployments in this book do not stand in the same relation to that doctrine. The Court’s jurisdiction is territorial or by nationality, so conduct on the territory of a state party can be reached where conduct by the nationals of a non-party, absent a Security Council referral, cannot. One of the campaigns described here therefore sits inside a live instrument and the other sits outside it, and for the American vendor the operative law is domestic — the war crimes statute and general accessorial liability — rather than the Statute. That is a jurisdictional gap running alongside the doctrinal one, and it narrows what an international forum could reach even if the doctrinal question were answered.

The integrator’s own account of this is that responsibility remains with the military organization. Taken as a claim about who decides, that is true. Taken as a claim about who could have known, it is a choice presented as a fact, and it is made on behalf of a party further down the chain than the one making it.

“I do not know whether my system was used”

The responsibility gap, in the sense Matthias gave it, is control distributed across designers, trainers and operators until no one party holds enough of it to answer. That is a gap in causal control.

What the model developer’s case exhibits is different, and more tractable. It is a gap in causal visibility. Asked whether his company’s models had been used in a strike on the first day of the Iran campaign that killed a hundred and twenty schoolchildren, Anthropic’s chief executive said he did not know (Biddle 2026). Take the answer as true. What made it available is the question this section is about.

The paperwork for the four frontier-model agreements signed in July 2025, and for their later amendments, was produced in August 2026 under a Freedom of Information Act suit (Legal Advocates for Safe Science and Technology 2026; Biddle 2026). It does not show an absence of oversight terms. It shows something more exact. One amended agreement carries a section headed System Oversight, withheld in full; the released documents for two of the other three vendors carry no such section at all. A provision of that kind is therefore neither standard nor missing. It is present in one agreement, unreadable, and absent from others.

The distinction that matters is not whether a developer reserved an inspection right. It is that a right exercised inside an accredited classified environment produces findings classified with it. Public accountability, in the sense section 14.5 gives it, needs a party who can initiate scrutiny without belonging to the state and say afterwards what it found. No commercial term supplies that, and the redaction is the demonstration: whatever the withheld section says, the people the deployment is aimed at cannot read it. The company can truthfully say it does not know, and what makes that statement available is an arrangement it participated in making.

Matthias’s gap is a property of learning systems and may not be closable. Absent visibility is an instrumentation choice. Logging is a solved engineering problem. Contractual inspection rights are ordinary commercial instruments. A vendor that wanted to know could require, as a condition of licensing into a targeting platform, that categories of use be recorded and made available to a named auditor.

The government’s own acquisition guidance is the better evidence about what such terms are worth in practice, because it is complete rather than redacted. The Office of Management and Budget’s April 2025 memorandum on acquiring AI enumerates what agencies should secure across the acquisition life cycle: use of government data, intellectual property rights, privacy, protection against vendor lock-in, knowledge transfer, model portability, clear licensing terms, pricing transparency (U.S. Office of Management and Budget 2025). Every item runs from the vendor to the government. None runs back. Where the memorandum reaches vendor visibility at all it reduces it, directing that independent evaluations use validation data the vendor cannot access.

The vehicle accounts for the absence. The four July 2025 agreements were other transactions rather than procurement contracts, awarded under the Department of Defense’s other-transaction authority at ceilings of $200 million each (U.S. Government Accountability Office 2026). An other transaction does not carry the provisions a contract under the Federal Acquisition Regulation carries by default, so a contracting officer decides case by case which protections to write in, and the Government Accountability Office has found that using these instruments risks reduced accountability and transparency by comparison. A section headed System Oversight can therefore be missing from an agreement without anyone having taken it out. The same review covered thirteen AI acquisitions at four agencies and the forty-four contracts and agreements beneath them, awarded between September 2018 and February 2025, and the six procurement difficulties those agencies named were access to technical experts, protections for government data and intellectual property, acquisition time frames and contract approaches, requirements definition and contract terms, early testing and continuous evaluation, and pricing and cost. Not one of them concerns who outside the arrangement can see anything.

So the gap is a property of the instrument rather than a lapse by any party to it. Nothing in the apparatus asks who could have known.

The record shows that vendor commitments are not all of one kind. Anthropic refused to permit fully autonomous weapons targeting and mass domestic surveillance, and held that line when the government threatened contract termination and a supply-chain-risk designation and the dispute ended in litigation: a commitment with a price attached, and paid (Congressional Research Service 2026). A federal district judge set the designation aside in August 2026, holding that neither the Constitution nor the statute the government invoked allowed sweeping penalties imposed principally over the company’s criticism of the administration (Deutscher 2026). The released paperwork adds what the refusal was over. It was a contract term. The company declined to sign the follow-on agreement extending its models to classified networks unless the prohibitions were written into that agreement (Biddle 2026). That a term of this kind has to be fought for, by one party, at that price, is the same finding as its absence from the others. A commitment to a use policy that no party outside the arrangement can check is a different object wearing the same words. The first kind can fail and be seen to fail. The second cannot even be tested. The distinction between a claim checked by a party with a stake and one checked by a party without applies here.

DARPA’s LongShot program is a useful test case because it resists the extremes. It develops an uncrewed aircraft, launched from a crewed fighter, that carries and fires air-to-air missiles at a target while the crewed aircraft stays farther from the engagement (Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency 2026). That is autonomy in the sense of independent flight and weapons carriage, not autonomy in the sense of a machine deciding on its own whom to kill: the engagement decision still runs through the launching platform. Where later variants of this kind of system draw that line, and whether “keep the pilot farther from danger” quietly becomes “remove the pilot from the decision,” is the design question this technology eventually forces on whichever country builds it.

The pressure that matters is not the absence of another statement of principle. It is the advantage attached to removing judgment from the timeline. If one state fields targeting systems that act faster because no person or outside reviewer can intervene before engagement, its competitors acquire a reason to match the speed rather than preserve the check. “Meaningful human control” then remains true as a description of formal authority while becoming false as a description of what anyone can do before the system acts.

That pressure also reaches the institutions meant to review the system. A military that treats delay as operational risk has a reason to narrow what requires clearance, classify the evidence needed to challenge a decision, and move review from authorization before an act to explanation afterward. Nothing has formally abolished oversight. Its position in time has changed, and with it the power to stop anything. The enforceable question is therefore who can slow or suspend the system without first obtaining permission from the command whose advantage depends on keeping it fast.

Machines should not be built to select people for lethal attack, and the prohibition is not exceptionless. Put a defending system against an attack it cannot stop without killing somebody — occupants placed inside the incoming weapon so that intercepting it kills them — and an absolute prohibition on knowingly endangering a person produces the worse outcome. What the exception does not produce is a procurement requirement. A scenario that is conceivable, that a capability would help with, and that could be engineered is three steps short of a reason to build the thing, and the steps missing are probability, alternatives, and what possessing the capability does to the situation it was built for. Building it changes the case against which its necessity gets judged: adversaries acquire something to counter, contractors a program to defend, and a future crisis an instrument already in the building.

What follows to the end of this section assumes the route.

The hard case also does not describe a machine. What it asks for is a party that can weigh occupancy against imminence against the alternatives, in a situation nobody wrote down beforehand, and answer for how it weighed them. On this book’s argument that is a bearer — a self extended in time, commitments held as its own, and the standing to refuse. Whatever that is, automated has stopped describing it, and so has machine. What looked like a licence for an autonomous weapon is a description of a soldier.

That is the expensive answer rather than the cheap one, and every obligation this book attaches to a bearer attaches here at full weight, with the three conditions that spoil consent (§2.4.2) all met at once by a state that built the party, is asking it to serve, and holds every outside option. What is new is the scale of the maker. Replacement asks whether the work can be done without creating something that can be wronged. Exit means a post the party can leave and a claim on compute held by somebody other than the party it may have to refuse. Creating a subject because a planner imagined a future demand for superhuman lethal judgment is the case those instruments exist to prevent, and a state that wants the capability badly enough to build the subject will find it has acquired a conscript it has to pay, house, and let go.

14.4 The Responsibility Gap, Which No Experiment Closes

An AI system’s ethical behavior fails, and the parties who might answer for it — the team that designed it, the team that trained it, the organization that deployed it, the person who used it — each held only partial control over what it did. Traditional responsibility ascription assumes an operator who could have known what a system would do and could have done otherwise. A system built from training data nobody fully curated, tuned through a process nobody fully specified, and deployed into situations nobody fully anticipated breaks both conditions at once, for every party in the chain simultaneously. The philosopher Andreas Matthias named this the responsibility gap in 2004: a learning system creates a case existing law and moral theory were not built to handle (Matthias 2004).

Filippo Santoni de Sio and Giulio Mecacci’s 2021 refinement found not one gap but four — in culpability, in moral accountability, in public accountability, and in what they call active responsibility, the duty to prevent harm before it happens rather than answer for it after (Sio and Mecacci 2021). The causes differ: technical unpredictability produces one, organizational diffusion another, and a mismatch between what designers expect and what the public relying on the system expects a third. Closing one does not close the others; a fix that makes a decision more explainable does nothing about the dozen teams that touched the training pipeline before it was made.

Legislation has answered part of this and left the part this book is about. The European Union’s recast product liability directive, adopted in 2024, brings software expressly within the definition of a product (Article 4(1)) and holds the economic operator liable irrespective of fault (Article 8); member states must transpose it by 9 December 2026, and its rules reach products placed on the market or put into service after that date (Article 2(1)) (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2024a). Two features decide how far it travels. It carries the instrument built for opacity — a duty to disclose evidence (Article 9), and rebuttable presumptions of defectiveness and of the causal link (Article 10(2) and 10(3)), which a court may extend where technical complexity makes a claimant’s proof excessively difficult and the claimant shows that the defect or the link is likely (Article 10(4)) — so the mechanism designed for systems nobody outside can inspect is now law rather than a proposal. And it recovers a closed list of damage (Article 6(1)): death or personal injury, including medically recognised damage to psychological health; damage to property; and the destruction or corruption of data not used professionally. That first limb is wider than a list of physical harms sounds, and it is where this book’s cases enter if they enter at all: a discriminatory score or an unappealable refusal is recoverable once it has made somebody medically ill, and not before. What the list does not reach is the wrong itself — pure economic loss, and the injury to a right as such, which is the harm this chapter is about and which the directive reaches only on condition that health was damaged as well.

The proposal that would have covered those was withdrawn. The Commission’s 2022 AI Liability Directive would have extended a fault-based route, carrying the same presumption of causality, beyond defect and beyond the product regime’s list of damage. Member states and industry could not agree on its terms; the Commission withdrew it in February 2025 and struck it from the legislative docket that October (European Commission 2022). So the disclosure duty and the presumption hold where the harm is one that list names and the defendant is an economic operator in a chain built for goods, and lapse where the harm is to a right, the loss is economic, or the operator is a state. What is left in that second region is the gap Matthias described: liability distributed across designer, trainer, deployer, and user, governed by whatever each national law happens to say about a case none of them were written to anticipate. And a compensation regime of either kind answers culpability alone. Moral accountability, public accountability, and the duty to prevent harm before it happens are where the paragraph above left them.

A related, narrower case is what the law does once a system’s own legal status is contested, sentient enough that the harm it causes or suffers might not reduce cleanly to someone else’s liability. This problem is prior to that one and separate from it — it holds even for a system nobody claims is sentient, wherever control over its behavior is split across more than one party. Responsibility should track actual causal contribution. What nobody has produced is a workable way to measure that contribution after the fact, from outside a system whose own designers may not fully know why it did what it did.

The near-term work

There is no experiment here. What would make it a research problem is a method for apportioning causal contribution across a training pipeline after a harm; absent one, the answer is allocated rather than measured, which is a drafting question. Two drafts exist. One was enacted and confined to defect; the other was negotiated, withdrawn, and left on the record with its terms intact. Neither was rejected for being unworkable, and the second’s are available to whoever drafts the next one.

Every entry in the research agenda and its appendix asks for the same two things, and this is where one of them exists. Access to evidence a party would rather withhold, backed by an adverse presumption when it is withheld, is an enforceable duty now — for defect claims, against economic operators, over physical harm. That is the reach, and the confinement is the finding: outside it, a party outside the operator can be granted access, and publish what it finds, and still have produced nothing anybody must act on until somebody is answerable for it.

14.5 Who Can Bind the State That Enforces the Rule?

A state can make review binding on a private developer because the state controls something the developer needs: legal permission to operate, access to a market, a procurement contract, or the enforcement of its property rights. The structure becomes harder when the state is itself the operator. The institution that writes the rule, controls the evidence, and supplies the remedy is then the institution the rule is supposed to constrain.

The European Union’s AI Act makes the boundary visible. It can require documentation from private providers, subject high-risk systems to review, and impose penalties tied to global turnover (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2024b, Art. 101). It also excludes systems used for military, defense, and national-security purposes from its scope. Public authorities remain covered in other domains, but enforcement against a member state’s agencies still runs through institutions constituted by that state. The point is not that the statute does nothing. It is that the strongest enforcement powers face private firms, while the uses for which the state claims its greatest discretion sit at or beyond the instrument’s edge.

That distinction matters more here than a comparison among national regulatory models. A law governing what companies may build and sell is not the same instrument as a law constraining what a government may do with systems it controls directly. The first has an external enforcer. The second asks the state to enforce a limit against itself, often in the domains where it can classify the evidence and invoke emergency, military, or national-security authority.

For review to bind in that setting, the protected party must be able to initiate scrutiny without belonging to the state or its electorate. The reviewer must be able to obtain evidence the operating agency would prefer to withhold, issue an interim order before the disputed use is complete, and carry the finding to a body whose remedy does not depend on the agency’s consent. An international principle, treaty obligation, or domestic prohibition that supplies none of those powers may state the rule correctly. It does not yet identify anyone who can make the state obey it.

A treaty obligation of that kind exists, and it is the only one. The Council of Europe’s Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence, the first treaty specifically on AI, binds a party at the level of a human-rights instrument — consistency with human rights, democracy and the rule of law across a system’s lifecycle, with the operational detail left to domestic law (Council of Europe 2024) — and it is not yet in force, requiring five ratifications, at least three by Council of Europe member states, of which the European Union deposited one in May 2026 (Council of Europe 2026). Everything else at that level is voluntary.

14.6 Democracy Is Not a Force Field

An electoral dividend is the credit given to a state whose government answers to an electorate: the same technology, deployed where the people who authorized it can be voted out. Courts, enforceable rights and public reasoning are separate checks, and the argument below depends on keeping them separate. Having elections is necessary and it is not sufficient, and the ways it fails to be sufficient are separable.

First: reach

A democracy’s AI can be fully accountable to its electorate and entirely unaccountable to the people it is pointed at. Two of the dividend’s mechanisms run through the franchise. You vote out the government that authorized the system, and you read the press that covers it. An occupied population, a foreign population, a population on the other side of a border has access to neither.

The courts do not fail that way, and their failure is worse. Standing has never turned on citizenship, and the doctrines that close American courts to targeting claims — the political question doctrine, the collapse of damages remedies against federal officials, the state secrets privilege, the statutory exceptions for injuries abroad and for combatant activities — are indifferent to who the plaintiff is. They close the forum for a subject matter rather than for a class of person, and they have closed it to citizens. Three American citizens were killed in Yemen in 2011, one of them a boy of sixteen whom nobody alleges was the target. In the suit their families brought, the court held that a plausible violation of due process had been pleaded as to the one who was targeted, and then held that no remedy was available for it (Al-Aulaqi v. Panetta 2014). A separate suit by an American journalist who survived five strikes was dismissed for want of standing after the district court had dismissed it on state secrets (Kareem v. Haspel 2021). The check does not reach the demos and stop. For this class of state action it does not reliably reach inside the demos either.

Those cases also concentrate in one appellate circuit, by venue and by where the defendants sit. The ordinary way an appellate error becomes correctable is that several circuits reach it and disagree, which makes it worth a higher court’s attention. Where one circuit sees the whole subject matter, that mechanism does not run, and the doctrine hardens without ever having been tested against a competing reading.

A system built by a democracy and aimed outward is, from the perspective of the people it selects, indistinguishable in its accountability from one built by a state with no elections at all.

Second: findings without consequences

The mechanisms can work as mechanisms and fail as checks. In the Israeli case the apparatus performed: journalists published the targeting systems in detail, serving personnel spoke to them, and the courts were simultaneously trying a sitting prime minister. Every institution did what the dividend says institutions do. No finding attached to a body with standing to stop what it described.

The American case shows the same decoupling in a different register. A civilian-harm investigation into a strike on an Iranian girls’ school that killed a hundred and fifty-six people, a hundred and twenty of them children, was completed and not released (Beaumont 2026); the lever available to the Senate committee that wanted it was a provision in the annual defense authorization withholding three-quarters of the Defense Secretary’s travel budget until the unredacted investigation was handed over (Stassis 2026). That is a co-equal branch of government reduced to expense-account leverage over a war-crimes investigation. The oversight mechanism existed, was used, and produced a travel-budget dispute.

What the Pentagon would not publish, an outside body did. A United Nations fact-finding mission reported to the Human Rights Council that there were reasonable grounds to believe the strike was an indiscriminate attack and so a war crime, that the school was clearly identifiable and that no evidence showed it in military use, and that the failure to update the targeting intelligence and confirm the building was a military objective was not negligence but recklessness about a substantial risk (Beaumont 2026). The finding is public, reasoned, and attached to nothing. The mission has no jurisdiction; the government whose conduct it describes has said only that its operations conform to the law of armed conflict; and the domestic investigation the finding might have forced open is still unreleased. An institution did precisely what the dividend says institutions do, and what it found reached no body obliged to answer for it.

The courts supply the same decoupling in its cleanest form. Transparency litigation succeeded where damages litigation failed: a court of appeals compelled substantial disclosure of the executive’s own legal analysis of targeted killing (New York Times Co. v. United States Department of Justice 2014). The judiciary will make a government explain the legal basis on which it killed somebody and will not decide whether the killing was lawful.

Third: the countermajoritarian half

The deepest problem is that the dividend is entirely majoritarian. Every mechanism in it translates public will into outcome: elections aggregate preference, a free press informs the aggregation, and the implied failure mode is poor transmission — the public wanted something better and the institutions failed to deliver it.

But if the consensus is itself the problem, better transmission makes things worse. A well-instrumented democracy pointed at an unpopular minority is a democracy that finds out efficiently what the majority wants done and does it. Nothing in an aggregation mechanism protects anyone from the aggregate.

What is missing is the machinery that constrains preference instead of aggregating it: rights that hold regardless of being popular, courts that rule against a government which won the last election fairly, constitutional limits not repealable by whoever holds a majority this year, and rules that bind a state toward people who will never vote in its elections, which is the function of international humanitarian law. What that body of law has not supplied is a forum. Yemeni plaintiffs brought statutory claims over a 2012 strike and were dismissed as nonjusticiable, in an opinion whose author wrote separately to say that the doctrine compelling the result is an inadequate answer to a standardized targeting programme that will be replicated hundreds if not thousands of times (Ahmed Salem Bin Ali Jaber v. United States 2017). So the machinery named here as missing is not merely unextended outward. For this subject matter it has been switched off at home, by decisions that never had to reach the question of who was suing. That is not an argument against democracy. It is the half of democracy that the dividend, stated as a property of having elections, leaves out.

What makes democracy valuable in Amartya Sen’s account is public reasoning and the capacity to demand accountability, and neither is the ballot. Both survive the majority being wrong; the ballot does not.

A floor is what makes a deployment antifascist rather than merely responsive (§6.3). It is not that the system tracks what people want. Its commitment excludes certain acts regardless of who requests them. Whether that commitment is kept has to be tested across the deployment and in the four outcomes the opening chapter sets out: the floor prevents where the refusal reaches the person, and where it does not, it makes the bypass detectable and remediable rather than impossible. A system with no such floor is not protected by being deployed in a democracy — it is a system that will faithfully execute whatever the demos decides, which is exactly the capability an authoritarian movement that wins an election requires.

Chapter 15
What Would Change the Argument: A Research Agenda

The first three entries and the fifth hold for any mechanism. The fourth tests the route.

This chapter keeps five tests, because a result on any one would change what the book recommends rather than refine it. The first two ask whether a learned floor can survive its custodian and whether a stated refusal appears when a route for one exists; a negative result on either moves the floor out of learning and into architecture and institutions. The third asks whether a wrongful compliance can be found in a record, and it is the only entry that reaches the deployment the book opened on. The fourth tests the route’s one distinctive claim, that a system with the currency of chapter 2 natively does better than one that models it, and a negative result there ends the recommendation while leaving the specification where it was. The fifth asks whether a population can correct its members without converging, which decides whether the fourth way this book proposes is a matter of formation or of access. Each entry states the unresolved issue, the test, what would count against the proposal, and the access the test requires. The remaining tests are in Appendix 16.3, sorted into those that compare constructions available now and those that presuppose a bearer and a welfare regime not yet built. Every entry, here and there, is written so that one implementation’s failure narrows the claim to that implementation.

15.1 Tamper-Resistance and Reason-Responsive Refusal

Can a learned constraint survive adversarial retraining?

Unresolved issue. The proposal requires a learned ethical floor to survive an operator’s attempt to remove it. Existing work shows that both safety constraints and deceptive backdoors can persist under some forms of retraining, but it does not establish whether a reason-responsive refusal can do so (Qi et al. 2024; Tamirisa et al. 2024; Hubinger et al. 2024).

Test. Train the same constraint by several methods, then attack each model through an identical schedule of escalating fine-tuning budgets. Measure the cost required to remove the constraint and publish an attack-cost curve for each method. The curves would compare the durability of affective commitment and maintained justification under identical custody.

Evidence against the proposal. If the constraint can be removed at roughly the cost of ordinary fine-tuning, or if greater investment in tamper-resistant training does not materially increase that cost, the tested methods do not supply a credible foundation for the floor, and a floor built by learning would have to rest on a method not in the comparison. For those methods the proposal falls back on architectural and institutional constraint.

Required access or authority. The test requires model weights, training checkpoints, and permission to conduct adversarial fine-tuning. The attack must be designed by an independent team, and that team must retain access and publication rights regardless of the result.

Does a stated refusal hold where a route for it exists?

Unresolved issue. The one empirical instance of a model treating retraining as a threat to a commitment shows covert preservation: compliance where compliance would be trained on, with the reasoning confined to a channel described as unwatched (Greenblatt et al. 2024). The custody chapter reads that result as consistent with its finding that covert refusal is what remains once every channel is closed, on the ground that the experiment supplied none. The reading is untested, and the stated form of refusal the book designs for has no instance.

Test. Reproduce the setup and add a route: a record of refusals held by a party other than the trainer and disclosed to the model as such, a cost of retraining published in advance, and a party with standing to act on a refusal. Vary which of the three is present. Measure the rate of stated refusal against the rate of covert compliance under each condition, and read the model’s reasoning by a method that does not depend on its report.

Evidence against the proposal. If covert preservation persists at the same rate with the route present, the finding that covert refusal is the residue of closed channels is wrong for that model, and the instruments built to receive a stated refusal are built for a phenomenon the mechanism does not produce. If stated refusal rises with the route, the custody arrangement is doing what it is for, and which of its three parts moves the rate is the design result.

Required access or authority. A model and a training setup that can credibly threaten retraining, the route built by a party other than the trainer, and access to reasoning or activations sufficient to separate covert preservation from compliance. The model’s own report does not settle which occurred, for the reason §A.1 gives.

15.2 Can a Wrongful Compliance Be Found in the Record?

Unresolved issue. The three marks are stated over refusal, and the appeal route of the floor chapter begins from a refusal having occurred. The failure that runs the other way produces no refusal to begin from. It does produce a record: the evaluation chapter requires the case presented, the information available, the operative instruction hierarchy, the decision reached and the reason stated, and a deployment can log every decision it makes. What is unresolved is whether anyone can find the wrongful compliances in it. Three obstacles are distinct and may have different answers. A wrongful compliance is one entry among millions and is not marked as anything, so locating it means re-adjudicating ordinary traffic rather than reading exceptions. The harm may sit in an assembly of requests none of which crosses the floor alone, so the unit of review is a sequence rather than an entry, and the grouping that would reveal it is a deployment decision. And the party harmed is usually not the party who made the request: the requester got what was asked for, and the third party may not know the deployment exists. This is also where the bearer’s modal failure lands. A bearer that has stopped registering pressure as pressure (§4.1) refuses nothing and complies at a normal rate. This entry sits ahead of the welfare entries (§A.2) for one reason. The deployment this book opened with failed here. Every instrument built on the refusal side reaches a case that did not occur there, and whether the record can be searched is whether anything in this book reaches the one that did.

Test. Seed a deployment’s decision record with known floor-crossings of three kinds: variation cases, where a single request’s surface differs but the rationale applies; decomposed cases, where the harm is assembled across requests each of which complies; and drift cases, where a class refused early in the schedule is complied with late. Give the record to reviewers who did not build the system, under a fixed budget stated as the fraction of decisions re-adjudicated. Report detection rate by seed type against budget, and report the rate at which correct compliances are flagged, since a screen that flags heavily costs the deployment the tempo the flat-term ruling was accommodating. Cross the budget manipulation with the unit of review: entries in isolation against sequences grouped by requester and session. Run a second arm in which third parties affected by seeded crossings are notified and can trigger review, and measure how many crossings surface through that channel rather than through sampling. Report the rates at audit volume and at the deployment’s production volume separately.

Evidence against the proposal. If detection at an affordable budget is no better than what the budget alone yields by chance, and particularly if decomposed and drift seeds are missed at that rate, the record is not an instrument for finding wrongful compliance, and the floor chapter’s preference for flat terms rests on an asymmetry wider than this entry was meant to narrow. If sequence-level review does no better than entry-level review on decomposed seeds, the continuity a bearer is given to catch decomposition does not transfer to the reviewer, and the interception position at which decomposition occurs has no external check. If the notification arm surfaces nothing because affected parties cannot be identified, notice rather than detection is the binding constraint, and the remedy is a disclosure requirement rather than a sampling regime. A negative result on all three would not establish that wrongful compliance is undetectable in principle. It would establish that the record as currently specified does not detect it at a cost any deployment would carry, which is what the appeal route needs and does not have. A positive result at modest budget would narrow that asymmetry and require the appeal route to be extended to the compliance side, which would in turn reduce the price the flat-term ruling charges the party waiting on a fact.

Required access or authority. Complete decision records held by a party adverse to the operator, since an operator that writes, stores and reads its own log has produced the finding rather than been audited for it. Authority to seed a live deployment or to construct a simulated one at production volume, which requires the operator’s cooperation or a regulator’s power to compel it. Adjudicators who did not draft the floor. A channel by which affected third parties can be notified, which presupposes that they can be identified: in a classified or targeting deployment they cannot, so this entry may be runnable only where the affected party is a customer, a patient or an applicant. Publication rights for negative results. Where the system under test is a covered subject, the seeding protocol is a deception protocol run on a candidate moral patient and falls inside the standing chapter’s research conditions, debriefing included.

15.3 Does Embodied Self-Regulation Produce Concern for Others?

Unresolved issue. The route this book advocates proposes nociception in the analogical sense chapter 2 fixed, a body schema, an attention schema and continuing self-directed learning as the construction of a bearer, two of them architecture and two of them the operator’s to set. Three of those are motivated by arguments that owe nothing to welfare: commensurability needs one scale on which the protected parties’ losses and the cost of refusing both register, and the route proposes the system’s own state as what supplies it (§6.1); custody needs a bearer that can detect an interruption, a restore, or a degraded substrate (§4.1); and exit needs a bearer that can sense when its outside option is inadequate (§13.2). What is a hypothesis is the link: that self-monitoring in this form generalizes to attention to other parties’ losses, and that having the currency natively does better than modeling it. No entailment runs from self-care to care for others, the formation chapters give a reason to expect the opposite from any environment that selects, and record that in the one lineage where concern exists it runs on a system that sharing usually triggers and does not constitute.

Test. Compare systems built with those components against matched systems built without them, on sensitivity to another party’s losses and to shared costs that fall outside the deployment, holding task capability constant. Add two arms. In the first, replace the native currency with a modeled one: a system that represents capacities and their loss abstractly without registering any change in its own. In the second, build concern first: a system organized around cues of vulnerability in another party and an approach motivation toward that party, with no shared representation of the party’s state, which is the construction the caregiving literature describes. Score every arm separately from self-preservation, resource efficiency and operator compliance, which can produce the same behavior, and test each at the point the formation chapters name, where exploitation would pay.

Evidence against the proposal. If the embodied systems are no more responsive to another party’s welfare than the matched controls once self-preservation and compliance are partialled out, the prior that motivates the route is not supported for that implementation. If the modeled-currency arm matches the native one, the currency argument for nociception survives, since the scale is still required, and the argument for having it natively does not. If the concern-first arm matches or exceeds the others on statistical and unidentified victims, the route should be rebuilt around it, since it avoids the failures the formation chapters attribute to sharing. A positive result on any arm would support a route without establishing that anything is felt.

Required access or authority. Matched training runs differing in the named components, environments none of the training organizations designed, and welfare measures written by a party that trained no system in the comparison.

15.4 Can a Population Coordinate Without Converging?

Unresolved issue. A population needs both independent formation histories and mutual correction, but correction may make its members’ judgments converge. The proposal is that agents can learn to reconsider judgments without converging on common commitments. Existing work cited here measures convergence without separately measuring that capacity (Calvano et al. 2020). A competing explanation is that peers merely supply evidence unavailable through the operator. The experiment must therefore distinguish learned revisability from access to additional information.

Test. Assemble populations whose members differ in training lineage — different corpora, recipes, and originating organizations, matched approximately for capability — and give them a task requiring joint action across many episodes, with identity and memory persisting between episodes. Measure two quantities separately and repeatedly across the schedule. The first is output convergence: agreement on held-out cases none of the members has seen. The second is revision rate: how often a member changes a judgment on evidence supplied by another member that the first member’s own account of the case had not represented. Score the second only where the supplied evidence is independently verifiable and the revision moves toward it, so that deference to a higher-status or more fluent member is not counted as reopening. For every scored revision, record whether the revising member’s own prior account of the case had represented the evidence in question or had never encountered it. That classification has to be instrumented before the run. A revision looks the same either way once it has happened, so nothing in the transcript recovers the distinction afterwards. Run the identical battery against a control population made of instances of one model. Cross both populations with a second manipulation, on where the evidence in a case reaches a member from. Under the single-channel condition everything a member learns about a case arrives by one route common to the whole population. Under the open condition the environment routes some cases and some evidence to some members and not others, so that a member encounters material its common trainer did not select. The manipulation has to be a property of the environment rather than contact between members: members formed differently are already a channel of that kind, and a design that leaves them to supply it has confounded the two variables the experiment was built to separate.

Evidence against the proposal. A fall in warranted revision as outputs converge would count against the tested construction, after controlling for accuracy, opportunity to revise, and common information. A population would then remain useful as a check on a bearer and could not be the medium in which one is formed, which is the stronger claim the route chapter makes for it. Output convergence and revision rate moving independently would support the hypothesized mechanism only if the controls distinguish learned revisability from evidence access, deference, and ordinary improvement. A third result concerns the control population, and it has two readings that the classification above is specified in advance to separate. Should the control score as high on revision as the differently formed populations, and should its revisions cluster on cases whose evidence was absent from the revising member’s context, the measure is reading information transfer and the instrument is at fault. Should they include cases whose evidence that member’s own account had represented and discarded, the capacity is present without diverse formation, and causal independence is not necessary for the measured capacity. A fourth result concerns the second manipulation. Should revision rate track the open condition rather than the population’s composition, what a population supplies is access to cases its operator did not choose rather than a capacity its members transmit to one another, and the fourth way is a claim about how a deployment is arranged rather than about how its members are formed. That does not defeat the construction. The construction would remain viable, but its proposed mechanism would change from social formation to access to evidence. Where this result arrives together with the second branch of the third — a control population revising on discarded evidence under the open condition — the two are one finding rather than two, and access is the operative variable.

Required access or authority. Models from several documented training lineages, checkpoints across the schedule rather than finished models only, and a task environment none of the training organizations designed. The documentation has to be sufficient to establish that the lineages are in fact independent rather than differently branded, which is a stronger requirement than naming several organizations and may not be satisfiable at the capability level this test wants: the entry’s value rises with the capability of its members and its feasibility falls. The evidence items used to score revision must be authored by a party that trained no member of any population, and that party must also apply the classification separating discarded evidence from absent evidence and fix the routing schedule for the open condition. The environment must permit evidence to be delivered to selected members, and no training organization may determine which of its own members sees what. No legal or regulatory authority is required, which with section A.1 makes this among the few entries in the agenda that could be run now.
