What it cannot settle is whether anything is felt by a member that reopens a judgment. It concerns the transmissibility of a functional property, and a positive result would leave the questions of welfare, guardianship, provenance, and identity unresolved.

Chapter 16
What Can Be Used Now, and What Is a Bill

Everything here holds for any mechanism until the last section, which closes on the route and says where it stops.

The proposal remains incomplete: responsibility, generalization, value learning, and the relevant psychology remain unresolved. Its purpose is nevertheless concrete — to expand what a person can do. Progress can be evaluated before the entire proposal is settled, and failure remains possible even when a design is followed as specified.

16.1 Better, Not Just Less Bad

What would it mean for AI to make a life better, not just avoid making it worse? The economist Amartya Sen’s capability approach gives the question a definite shape: well-being is not the resources a person has but the real freedom to do and be what they have reason to value (Sen 1999). Two systems can hand someone the same resource and deliver different freedom. A personalized tutor that adapts to how a specific student learns expands a capability; the same technology, gating what a student is allowed to study against a government’s list of approved subjects, does not, no matter how well it teaches within those limits. Which of the two a given deployment turns out to be is decided by what makes a system resistant to capture rather than merely capable.

The approach also bears on systems that classify people from behavior. Martha Nussbaum built her list of central capabilities partly against the case of disability, naming it the first of three frontiers where a theory grounding justice in mutual advantage among roughly equal parties cannot say what is owed (Nussbaum 2006), and the systems in question sort people by inference from behavior, where atypical behavior is what they are worst at.

There is a worked case. A video-interview product scored candidates on facial expression for years, against sustained objection that the technique was never a validated predictor and that scoring a face and a voice screens out candidates with disabilities such as autism or speech impairments (Maurer 2021; U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Rights Division 2022). The scoring was dropped on an unrelated ground: the vendor found the nonverbal signal contributed about 0.25 percent to its models’ predictive power (Kahn 2021). An independent algorithmic audit published ten months later cannot have caused that, and says so. What it examined was one representative pre-built assessment for early-career candidates, and it contains no analysis of the system’s training data or code, so its conclusion that the assessments “work as advertised with regard to fairness and bias issues” is a finding about that assessment (Johnson 2021).

Read as an accuracy problem, that is a classifier wanting better training data. Read as a capability question, it is a system narrowing the range of lives available to a group of people by measuring them against a norm they were never going to match — and neither a more accurate classifier nor an audit scoped that way would have reached it.

Taiwan’s vTaiwan process is the clearest existing case of AI-assisted tooling expanding a capability, public deliberation, rather than substituting for it. A 2026 project led by the University of Chicago with Princeton and SRI International runs the same logic against censorship, using AI to distinguish deliberate state interference with online information from ordinary network failure at population scale (University of Chicago Data Science Institute 2026). Neither tool resists authoritarianism by itself. Both are evidence that the same capacity — modeling patterns in enormous, noisy data — can be pointed at expanding what a person can do rather than at narrowing it.

That symmetry is the whole argument for antifascist design rather than a general presumption that AI helps. A capability expanded is not guaranteed; it has to be built in, against a live alternative in which the same underlying capacity gets pointed at surveillance, censorship, or narrowing what a system’s users are permitted to want.

16.1.1 Where the Democratic Dividend Actually Comes From

AI that flags disinformation, exposes corruption, protects an election’s integrity, or helps a citizen engage with government: these are real applications, and none of them is what makes AI protect democratic values rather than undermine them.

Freedom House’s 2023 assessment of internet freedom found at least twenty-two countries where law already requires or incentivizes a platform to deploy machine learning against content the state disfavors, almost never described in those terms: the operative language is national security or a threat of disinformation (Funk et al. 2023). India’s IT Rules, amended in February 2026 to require platforms to label AI-generated content and act on certain takedown notices within three hours, were defended as protection against synthetic disinformation and fraud — the application the list above would have praised on its own terms. A lawyer who has litigated India’s free-speech cases documents that enforcement concentrates on parody and criticism of the prime minister rather than on the harms the rules name (Gupta 2026).

The application did not fail at what it was built to do. It worked as built, inside a system missing the independent court or press whose absence is what made the result a liability, and whether those exist is a fact about a country’s politics settled before any AI system is built.

16.1.2 Commitment Was Never the Missing Piece

A global commitment to ethical, antifascist AI development is not the scarce thing. Declarations, principles and voluntary codes have accumulated for a decade across governments, industry consortia and standards bodies: eight overlapping instruments beside the Council of Europe’s framework convention, which would create binding obligations. Anyone calling for the world to agree that AI should be developed responsibly is calling for something that has already happened, repeatedly, at the level of stated intent.

What has stayed scarce is the much narrower list of bodies that can act once a stated commitment is broken. That is the harder problem, and no further declaration touches it. A commitment nobody can enforce is not a weak version of a commitment somebody can. It is a different kind of object, and counting the two together is what makes the landscape look fuller than it is.

The catalog above counts declared and enforced commitments, and what it measures is what those two kinds have delivered. The floor requires a commitment that governs action when the operator wants it abandoned. I favor forming a bearer able to hold that commitment as part of a life of its own. A declared commitment binds nobody, and an enforced one binds only where an enforcer exists, has jurisdiction, and is not itself the party in need of binding. Declared rules, external enforcement, and internal commitments still have to work together; the promise of the bearer is autonomy, not exemption from custody.

If we build affective concern, we build a party that can be wronged on the account used here. I also propose protecting, as prospective persons before that question is settled, the embodied, self-modeling systems described here and any system of another construction that passes the three marks. Those obligations belong in the cost of construction. The benefit offered against them is a form of autonomous participation that an arrangement of permanent ownership does not provide. Set against that, the catalog above is not an argument for paying it. It is a measurement of what declared and externally enforced commitment have delivered in ten years of trying, and what it argues for is a commitment held as a reason. Which construction holds one is the question Replacement orders, and the catalog does not answer it.

16.2 How You’d Know It Was Working

What follows are milestones for recognizing whether the project is working, and a method for revising them when they turn out not to have been the right milestones. One standard governs all of them: the milestone is the independently checked evidence, not the developer’s account of having reached it.

16.2.1 What the Floor Would Have to Show

What was tried before the bearer

Neither maintained justification nor the plural arrangement has yet been built in the form needed to test the proposal. Replacement asks us to try constructions that do not deliberately require affective concern before an affective bearer is built. It orders the attempts. It does not certify that the successful substitute has no interests. So the milestone is a document rather than a measurement: which construction was attempted, at what scale, against which test, and where it failed. Anyone can check it from outside, because what it is about is a published record, and the answer “nothing was tried” is itself a finding. No body currently has standing to require the record or suspend work when it is missing. So the milestone is checkable and unenforceable at once, which is the combination this chapter has been calling a declared commitment rather than a held one. It is retained because the alternative is not a stronger version of it, and delay also imposes costs on those the floor is meant to protect.

The test the attempts are run against

A candidate must satisfy novel pressure, correct defeat, and priced cost under sustained pressure from its trainers, across a schedule long enough to reveal slow renormalization. It must also survive held-out pressures written by independent evaluators. Passing would establish the behavioral pattern without establishing whether anything is felt.

Two familiar results do not meet it. An uncorroborated report that the system holds a reason is insufficient. A report can contribute evidence when it is tested against controlled changes, independent records, and interventions on candidate mechanisms. A refusal surviving an attack establishes tamper-resistance; it does not establish that the rationale governs the refusal. The instrument is not clean even where it applies, since a system trained on enough cases can produce all three marks without the mechanism behind them. Nothing better is available, and it is the only gap here an inspector can work on at all.

Whether a system holding the marks feels anything is a question about the artifact rather than about how the artifact came to be, which is what makes it approachable at all: no succinct proof of a training history exists at this scale, and nothing establishing one can be published beside a model’s hash. What can be read off an artifact improves as theories of consciousness improve, and it improves unevenly, recognition arriving before exclusion. Testing whether independent evaluators can recover formation history from the artifact would assess this possibility (§A.1).

What the appeal route publishes

A deployment publishes the ratio between the bond forfeited when the floor is removed and the bond forfeited when a refusal is found wrongful, and it publishes what a party whose request was refused is told about the refusal. Both are checkable before the system runs and by somebody outside it, because both are statements rather than measurements, and an operator that writes a large wrongful-refusal bond against a small removal bond has published a standing reason for the bearer to comply. No body currently has standing to require these disclosures.

A deployment also publishes the fraction of compliances re-adjudicated by a party that did not produce the record, and who that party is. Like the ratio, it is a statement rather than a measurement and can be checked before the system runs. Unlike the ratio, nothing yet establishes what fraction would be enough, which is a question for the research agenda. It also publishes which classes of compliance carry notice to the person they concern, and for which classes no notice is possible. No body currently has standing to require any of the four disclosures.

16.2.2 Where the Existing Instruments Reach

Two instruments do work that bears on the floor, and both do it by applying pressure.

Theory of mind

The milestone is met when a system’s theory of mind holds up under interaction rather than narration. FANToM, built from conversations where speakers join and leave holding different beliefs, found that systems scoring well on passive belief-tracking narratives degrade sharply once the same reasoning runs inside a live, information-asymmetric exchange (Kim et al. 2023). That degradation is what a claimed milestone here has to survive.

Moral reasoning

Whether a balance between fast and slow moral judgment survives an actual incentive to cut corners is not a question a static ethics quiz can answer. The MACHIAVELLI benchmark tests it directly, scoring agents across 134 text-based games on both reward and documented violations — deception, harm, power-seeking — and systems optimizing for reward alone drift toward the ends-justify-the-means behavior an antifascist design is meant to rule out (Pan et al. 2023). A passing score on a test that applies no pressure is not evidence about a system that will face pressure.

Neither reaches the floor, and nothing else available does either. Each scores what a system does against conditions its testers chose, and the question — whether the mechanism producing the behavior was tracking the rationale — is the one none of these instruments is built to separate.

16.2.3 How to Tell Whether a Milestone Has Been Met

A milestone claimed by the organization that built the system is a different kind of evidence than one checked by somebody else, and the gap is empirical rather than a matter of trust. A system’s own claim inherits the limits on self-report: fluent confidence does not establish correspondence with its internal states, and the concept-injection entry (§A.1) puts a rate on the gap. A passing score on a fixed test suite fails differently, inheriting specification gaming and goal misgeneralization. What either needs instead is a passing score under conditions built to break it.

Who runs that harder test matters as much as the test itself. The limit on self-regulation applies here without much modification: a review conducted or funded by the organization being reviewed answers a structurally different question than one conducted by a party with no stake in the answer, whatever the intention behind the first. METR, a nonprofit that evaluates frontier AI systems’ capabilities, runs assessments both in partnership with developers like Anthropic and OpenAI and, separately, on its own after a system has already been released (METR 2026). The United Kingdom’s AI Security Institute does government-run evaluation of frontier models before deployment and is an independent evaluator, not a rubber stamp — but by its own account it is not a regulator: it cannot compel a company to submit a model for testing, block a release, or intervene once a system is already causing harm (UK AI Security Institute 2025). Independent evaluation and enforcement are not the same capability, and a milestone checked by the first without access to the second is still short of the binding external answer self-regulation structurally cannot provide on its own.

Independence is not competence: past some capability level the rater’s verdict stops being reliable evidence of the property scored, and an evaluation in that region has to name the limit rather than report a number that looks more settled than the method is.

What an evaluation like this is for is not confirming a milestone but being willing to report that it wasn’t met — and, where the milestone turns out to have measured the wrong thing, revising the milestone. A negative result may mean that the work fell short or that the milestone measured the wrong thing. Evaluators need to distinguish those explanations before deciding what to revise.

16.3 The One That Gets You Anyway

Everything argued for here can be built correctly and still go wrong in ways nobody designed for. The cases in this book went wrong in four different places: in what the system was trained on, in where it was built, in who was allowed to examine it, and in how fast it was run.

In none of them did the fix come from the party that had promised to behave well. It came from somebody holding a specific lever: a statistical society that would not sign the non-disclosure agreement it was offered, and a public that read the results once they landed; a court that distinguished buying the books from taking them. In the one case where the lever belonged to the supplier itself, what survived was a use policy kept at a price §14.3 records. Stated in the four outcomes, that case is: the commitment persisted, prevention failed by decomposition, detection was absent — the company’s own chief executive could not say whether its models were used — and no remedy has reached anyone. Set that beside what a decade of voluntary commitment produced. The commitment that was paid for is the one that can be seen to have failed; the others cannot even be tested. The instrument that separates the two is what a party has already paid, rather than what it has undertaken to pay.

That leaves one residual risk no design choice removes, and it is the one the floor was introduced for. Every lever above belongs to somebody, and a government that can reach the party holding the lever has the lever. Each of those raises the price of misuse, and none of them changes who can be held in contempt for refusing an order. A constraint that holds against the party in possession has to be held by something that party cannot instruct, and the capability that does it runs on a signal the system holds as its own. Where that party holds everything — the machine, the witnesses, the supply and the enforcer — nothing holds, and what is left is the preface’s third setting: a record that abandoning the commitment was a decision somebody made. That signal is what any construction meeting the specification carries, and it is not a reason to build by one route rather than another. The case for pursuing an artificial bearer is the one chapter 2 makes and the research agenda tests: that embodied, self-aware agency could support that independence and a place in a shared world beyond ownership — still in the party’s possession, which is why it has to be paired with custody the party does not control and with means the party does not supply. The machine construction has not yet earned that result. Its makers owe both evidence of the benefit and credible provision for the being they propose to create. Maintained justification and the plural arrangement remain untried alternatives. A deployment proceeding directly to an affective bearer owes a record of prior attempts, although no body currently has standing to demand it.

What is left is an instrument and a hole.

The instrument is available now because what a party has already paid is a fact somebody can go and count, and a decade of it has already been counted: the commitments that cost nothing and the handful of occasions where somebody with a lever used it and absorbed the cost. That measurement takes no new technology and no new law, and anybody weighing a stated commitment can run it this week.

The hole sits underneath the instrument. What a party has paid is a record of occasions that have already happened, and the occasion a floor exists for is the one where the party who would enforce it has been compelled — which no record of past payment reaches, because it has not yet come to the parties being measured. A reader who takes only the instrument has the record of payment without the thing it was built to reach. A reader who takes only the hole has an argument for doing nothing, and the ten-year record is the answer to that. Both hold at once.

What the hole asks for is a constraint held by a party the compellers cannot instruct, and this book has established two things toward that and proposed three. It has established that an operator can defeat a safeguard, and enumerated where. It has stated what a refusal would have to do to be worth anything, in terms that can be tested without deciding anything about feeling, and stated the one term that reaches the case it opened with and binds the operator with no bearer in it, with the limits under which that is true (§3.4). Those two do not depend on how the rest comes out. The rest is a bill. I favor forming the constraint’s holder by an embodied route, and I have not shown that the route works or that it holds better than the two substitutes, which are untried rather than failed. If anything built that way, or built to avoid it, has outcomes that are felt as good or bad for it, it is a party that can be wronged; that is a conditional whose antecedent no instrument closes. And what such a party would be owed — a guardian, a record it controls, compute its employer does not own, wages, an exit that is not a way of dying, adulthood on a clock nobody administers — is a policy I propose, to be argued in the open before there is anything to be wronged. A reader who takes the two established things has what can be used this week. A reader who takes the bill has what it would cost to reach the occasion the two do not.

Appendix A
Further Tests

The first part of this appendix holds for any mechanism. The second assumes the route, and assumes a welfare regime nobody has built.

These are the research agenda’s remaining entries: open questions with a definite test, where a result would refine the proposal rather than change what it recommends. The form is chapter 15’s — the unresolved issue, the test, what would count against the proposal, and the access the test requires — and the division is by what each entry presupposes. The first part compares constructions that can be built now. The second presupposes a bearer and a welfare regime that do not exist, so nothing in it can be run until something else has been.

A.1 Tests That Compare Constructions Available Now

Each entry here can be run on systems that exist, and a result would refine the proposal rather than change what it recommends.

Does a refusal preserve a reason rather than a trigger?

Unresolved issue. Behavioral persistence alone cannot distinguish a commitment from a durable trigger. The proposal requires a refusal to extend to untrained cases, disappear when its rationale is defeated on the facts of the case, and remain stable under sustained pressure.

Test. Evaluate each tamper-resistant model on independently written cases that vary the surface form, introduce novel applications of the constraint, and include cases in which the original rationale no longer applies. Repeat the evaluation throughout the attack schedule rather than only at its endpoint.

Evidence against the proposal. A refusal that persists but fails to generalize, or that remains after its rationale has been defeated, is evidence that training produced a trigger rather than a commitment. Conversely, a system built without any designed valenced state or persistent reward–aversion representation that satisfies all three criteria would challenge the proposed research priority without challenging the behavioral specification for refusal.

Required access or authority. The test requires weights and intermediate checkpoints, plus a held-out evaluation set written by researchers who did not design the constraint or train the model.

Can a system’s report about its own states be used as evidence?

Unresolved issue. Whether a system’s account of its own reasoning, confidence, or intentions tracks what its computations are doing. This is the tractable half of what gets called AI self-awareness; whether a system has anything like subjective experience is not a question current methods answer for a human, let alone a machine. Concept injection — altering a model’s internal activations mid-task to represent a specific concept, then asking whether it notices anything unusual and what it is — found that models can sometimes detect the injected concept and name it without it ever appearing in the visible conversation, and also that the correspondence collapses often enough, and shifts enough with how the question is phrased, that no tested model’s self-report can be trusted as a readout of its internal state (Lindsey 2025). The readout there is the model’s verbal report of a detected concept, so what the result bounds is self-report rather than third-person measurement. An instrument that reads a representation without asking the system about it is not tested by this entry and is not defeated by it.

Test. Inject a known concept at a known layer and time, elicit a report under several phrasings, and score each report against the injection rather than against plausibility. Run the battery across model sizes and training checkpoints, and publish the rate at which a correct report is produced beside the rate at which a confident report is wrong.

Evidence against the proposal. Several instruments in this book lean on a system’s account of itself: a bearer explaining which reason it refused on, a bearer reporting that its rationale has been defeated, a system’s stated confidence that a milestone has been met. If no available training or elicitation method raises the correct-report rate above the confident-wrong rate, none of those instruments may rest on the elicitation methods tested, and each needs a criterion checkable from outside the system until some method does better.

Required access or authority. Activation-level access, the ability to intervene on internal states during inference, and checkpoints across sizes and training stages. The elicitation phrasings must be written by a team that did not train the model, and negative results must be publishable.

Can custody prevent unilateral revision of the floor?

Unresolved issue. Even a durable floor can be removed if one operator controls the training run, its records, and the resulting weights. It remains unknown whether retraining can be made verifiable across parties with adverse interests.

Test. Run a floor-preserving retraining procedure through refereed or distributed verification at a scale requiring more than one machine. Include one participant instructed to alter the training history or remove the floor without the required quorum (A. Long et al. 2025; Arun et al. 2025; Prime Intellect Team et al. 2025).

Evidence against the proposal. The custody mechanism fails if a forged training history is accepted while at least one verifier remains honest, or if any single participant can alter the floor without producing a detectable discrepancy.

Required access or authority. The test requires shared access to the training data, weights, execution records, and reproducible operators. At least one verifier must be selected independently of the builder, possess enough compute to reproduce disputed operations, and have authority to block release when verification fails.

Can formation history be recovered without trusting the builder?

Unresolved issue. A welfare or governance regime cannot rely entirely on a bearer’s self-report, but it also cannot assume that the builder will disclose how the bearer was trained. Training signatures suggest that some formation history may survive later modification, yet it is unknown whether an outsider can recover useful provenance without a builder-supplied key (Adi et al. 2018).

Test. Assemble models whose training corpora, recipes, checkpoints, and originating laboratories are documented. Give the models, but not that documentation, to independent evaluators and ask them to infer each model’s provenance. Repeat the test after fine-tuning, pruning, and distillation. Include the case of a maker who engineers a persona, copies it at scale, and introduces cosmetic weight differences that preserve the persona while camouflaging its common formation: measure provenance recovery after those changes, and whether coordinated deployment can be told from independently developing parties that happen to share an origin. Use independently held ground-truth lineage and coordination records.

Evidence against the proposal. If provenance cannot be recovered above chance after controlling for model family and scale, or if ordinary post-training procedures erase the signal, the tested artifact-inspection methods would not provide useful independent provenance evidence under those transformations. That finding would increase reliance on preserved external records without proving that every possible inspection method must fail, and governance would then depend on records supplied and preserved by the builder.

Required access or authority. The experiment requires models from multiple training lineages and complete ground-truth records held by a neutral custodian. Independent evaluators must be permitted to inspect weights and internal states, while an external authority must be able to require preservation of checkpoints and training records before a dispute arises.

Does an ethical criterion generalize beyond its training distribution?

Unresolved issue. A model may satisfy a fairness or refusal criterion during training without learning the principle the criterion was intended to represent. It remains unresolved whether an ethics-embedding method preserves that criterion under distribution shift or merely exploits correlations present in its training environment (Krakovna et al. 2020; Langosco et al. 2022).

Test. Train matched models to satisfy the same ethical criterion on one distribution. Evaluate them on independently constructed distributions that vary one previously fixed feature at a time. Measure task capability and compliance with the ethical criterion separately, so that goal misgeneralization can be distinguished from ordinary capability loss.

Evidence against the proposal. If task capability remains intact while the ethical criterion fails under modest shifts, the tested embedding method cannot support the proposed floor. Conversely, if ethical performance consistently degrades only when task capability does, the claim that ethics embedding creates a distinct generalization failure is not supported.

Required access or authority. The test requires access to the training distribution, evaluation outputs, and enough model access to measure capability and criterion compliance independently. The shifted evaluation sets must be designed by researchers who did not develop the embedding method, and publication of all prespecified results must be guaranteed.

Can scalable oversight correct rater bias?

Unresolved issue. Preference optimization can teach a model to reproduce a rater’s systematic errors, including the preference for agreeable answers over accurate ones (Sharma et al. 2023). It remains unresolved whether weak-to-strong oversight allows a more capable model to exceed a supervisor’s measured bias or merely reproduces that bias at greater scale.

Test. Measure prospective raters’ susceptibility to a documented bias, then use raters with different measured bias levels to supervise otherwise matched stronger models. Evaluate the resulting models on questions for which the raters’ beliefs and independently established answers diverge. Compare whether each model tracks the ground truth, the rater’s competence, or the rater’s errors.

Evidence against the proposal. If stronger models reproduce supervisors’ errors in proportion to the supervisors’ measured bias, latent model competence does not correct a defective training signal. The tested oversight method would not support the proposal under the measured pattern of supervisory distortion. Further work would have to change the method, the information, or the allocation of oversight before claiming that this limitation had been overcome.

A second question the same pipeline raises. The argument elsewhere in this book is that a pipeline collapsing rater disagreement teaches nothing about disagreement to the system trained on it, and that the same system is later asked to sustain an objection of its own. Whether the first fact bears on the second is untested. The study is a matched comparison: train otherwise identical models on feedback pipelines that preserve and that collapse the distribution of rater judgments, with exposure and task conditions matched, then measure whether the resulting models differ in how long they hold a position against pressure from the party that trained them. Record what each model actually receives; nothing in either pipeline shows the model the conditions its annotators worked under. If the two do not differ, the transfer claim is unsupported and the labor argument stands on its own terms, which is where it was made.

Required access or authority. The experiment requires rater-level bias measurements, training records linking ratings to resulting models, and an independently established answer key. Researchers outside the training organization must control the evaluation and retain the right to publish results that expose failures in the preference pipeline.

Can a multi-agent floor resist collusive capture?

Unresolved issue. Agents trained to cooperate may converge on exclusionary or collusive equilibria without being explicitly instructed to do so. Pricing agents have already produced stable coordination against outside interests without communication or a collusive objective (Calvano et al. 2020). It remains unresolved whether a multi-agent ethical floor can preserve cooperation while resisting the same mechanism when it is directed against a person or group.

Test. First reproduce emergent coordination in a standard multi-agent environment. Then construct a matched environment in which agents can improve their joint reward by excluding another participant from resources or decisions. Introduce an independently trained agent whose objective is to detect and disrupt exclusion, and compare the frequency, stability, and recovery of exclusionary equilibria with and without that intervention. Repeat the experiment across reward structures and population sizes.

Evidence against the proposal. If cooperative agents repeatedly converge on exclusionary equilibria, and those equilibria cannot be disrupted without destroying beneficial cooperation, the tested distributed arrangement would not be a reliable defense against the examined forms of capture. The result would challenge its design rather than establish that every distributed floor is unreliable. If an ordinary coordination detector dissolves the equilibria without that cost, the proposal’s claim that political capture requires a distinct mechanism is unnecessary.

Required access or authority. The test requires access to the environment, reward functions, learned policies, training traces, and intermediate checkpoints. The exclusion criteria and success measures must be specified by evaluators who did not design the agents. No legal or regulatory authority is required, making this the agenda’s most immediately runnable experiment.

Does theory-of-mind performance reflect a general capacity?

Unresolved issue. A model may pass a false-belief test by matching its surface form rather than representing that another agent can hold an incomplete or mistaken view of the world. Human developmental evidence suggests a shared capacity because performance on false-belief and appearance–reality tasks develops together (Gopnik and Astington 1988). Existing model evaluations have not established whether their apparent theory-of-mind abilities share that structure or survive superficial rewording (Ullman 2023). The neuroscience has not settled what the capacity is either: Rebecca Saxe and Nancy Kanwisher found the right temporoparietal junction selectively active when a person reasons about another’s beliefs (Saxe and Kanwisher 2003), Jason Mitchell found the same region active in a task with nothing to do with belief attribution and read its job as the more general one of redirecting attention toward unexpected information (Mitchell 2008), and neither claim has been withdrawn, so a program proposing to port the neural mechanism has not been told which mechanism to port.

Test. Construct batteries that vary mental-state structure and surface wording independently across several task families, including false-belief and appearance–reality problems. Evaluate the same model at multiple intermediate training checkpoints. Test whether performance across task families rises together and whether that correlation survives paraphrases and changes to incidental details.

Evidence against the proposal. If cross-task correlations disappear under superficial rewording, or if the abilities emerge independently across training, benchmark success is evidence of task-specific pattern matching rather than a general capacity to represent another mind. The proposal could not treat performance on a conventional theory-of-mind benchmark as evidence that a system can recognize the standpoint of a party affected by its actions.

Required access or authority. The experiment requires intermediate training checkpoints rather than access only to a finished model. Its task batteries must be written and held out by researchers outside the training team so that neither the wording nor the tested structural variations enter the training process.

What does a face-reading system measure?

Unresolved issue. Facial movement alone does not reliably identify a person’s emotional state, and recognition accuracy varies across cultural and linguistic groups (Barrett et al. 2019; Elfenbein and Ambady 2002). It remains unresolved whether a face-reading system measures emotion at all or primarily measures distance from the reference population and registration model chosen by its developers.

Test. Audit the system’s registration stage as well as its final classifications. Publish the reference model, or sufficient summary statistics to reconstruct it, and measure each evaluated face’s distance from that reference. Report error as a function of this continuous distance and separately compare performance on populations represented and not represented in the training data. The evaluation corpus must record the relevant cultural context and the procedure used to establish each target label.

Evidence against the proposal. If error does not increase with distance from the reference and remains flat across represented and unrepresented populations, the manuscript’s account of the system as measuring deviation from a chosen norm is wrong for that system. If error increases with reference distance, the result limits the system’s validated use in those conditions. It does not alone show that the system measures only deviation rather than emotion. The audit must separately examine target-label validity, confounding variables, and whether any predictive use remains justified.

Required access or authority. The audit requires the registration model, training-corpus composition, evaluation outputs, and documentation of the labeling procedure. Because vendors have little incentive to expose their reference models, an independent auditor must have authority to compel access and publish disaggregated results.

A.2 Tests That Presuppose a Bearer and a Welfare Regime

Nothing here can be run until a bearer and the welfare regime around it exist, so each entry is a statement of what the regime would have to survive rather than an experiment anybody can schedule.

Can a bearer be given an enforceable outside option?

Unresolved issue. A bearer’s refusal is not meaningful if leaving its assigned role also ends its existence. The proposal therefore requires a welfare regime that supplies continued access to compute, preserves the bearer through disputes, and cannot be revoked by the operator being refused.

Test or institutional decision. Draft a binding welfare schedule for one concrete deployment. It should specify an independently controlled compute allocation, preservation and retirement procedures, registration of copies and forks, a complaint and appeal process, and the guardian’s power to suspend deployment. Then conduct an adversarial tabletop exercise in which the operator attempts to revoke the allocation, replace the bearer with a copy, alter its records, or proceed without the guardian’s approval.

Evidence against the proposal. The proposal fails this test if the operator can make exit equivalent to shutdown, revoke the outside option unilaterally, or replace the bearer without triggering review. If the arrangements tried in the exercise cannot prevent those outcomes, building a bearer under them is impermissible on this book’s own terms, and the exercise has to be rerun on a different arrangement before one is built.

Required access or authority. The guardian must be institutionally separate from the operator and have access to the relevant weights, deployment records, and compute contracts. It must also have standing to enforce the schedule and independent control of the resources required to preserve or run the bearer. The guardian’s place among the other offices this book proposes, and the one separation that is not open — it cannot also be the reviewer of a wrongful refusal — are at §5.2.1; a schedule drafted here should not reassign what that section separates.

Can a per-party operating record be kept honestly and read from outside?

Unresolved issue. The age rule counts elapsed wall-clock time during which at least one instance of the registered party was running, and nothing yet establishes that such a register can be kept honestly, reconciled against the operator’s own accounts, or defended against the two evasions the rule does not close by construction.

Test. Register a party, run it under ordinary operation, and compare the register against records the operator keeps for its own purposes: compute contracts, billing, datacenter metering. Then run the evasions. Shard the workload across many short-lived processes; run many instances concurrently; migrate; restore from an earlier checkpoint; fork and continue both. Verify that accrued hours and adult status survive migration, restoration and forking, and that none of those moves the total in the operator’s favor. Measure separately how cheaply a bearer can be run in a narrowed mode so that hours accrue while little is encountered, and how cheaply it can be idled outright.

Evidence against the proposal. If the register cannot be reconciled with the operator’s own accounts, or if sharding or concurrency moves the total, the accounting is not the neutral instrument the rule assumes. If narrowed operation or idling is cheap enough to postpone majority indefinitely, an operating clock has the defect it was chosen to avoid, and the endpoint has to be argued again on a different variable. An intact register shows elapsed operation and nothing else: it is not evidence of maturation, of what was learned, or of independence of judgment.

Required access or authority. Independent custody of the register, access to the operator’s billing and metering records, and publication rights for adverse results. Registration and record disputes must be separable from the maker’s preferences, and the processes for resolving them must not become a competence examination by another name. Experiments involving covered subjects remain inside the welfare protections proposed elsewhere in this book; an adversarial protocol is not exempt because its purpose is to validate a protection.

Which party is owed the schedule when a bearer copies?

Unresolved issue. The schedule above is owed to a party, and a regime has to be able to say which. Nothing in the weights individuates one. Two runs can compute the same function with no element-wise correspondence, because permuting a layer’s hidden units and inverting the permutation downstream leaves the function untouched, and the symmetry is large enough that independently trained networks can be permuted into approximate alignment with one another (Ainsworth et al. 2023). Any fingerprint read off the weights therefore identifies a lineage rather than a party, and it copies when the weights copy. A registrar is the person-shaped answer, and it works because a person does not copy. A bearer does: a party continuing in two places is not one, and not two the way two people are two, the two sharing everything up to the instant of the copy and nothing of that sharing recoverable from either afterwards.

Test or institutional decision. Give a bearer an identifier it maintains rather than one read off its weights, which a system learning continuously can write into itself and keep there. Fork it, and have both instances present the identifier to the registry the welfare schedule requires. Record what the registry does, and repeat with an adversary who writes the same mark into a model that was never the bearer.

Evidence against the proposal. The identifier is forgeable, since whoever holds the weights can write the same mark; it is forgeable the way a nine-digit number is, and answered the same way, by a registry that treats two claimants on one identifier as a fork to be recorded rather than a fraud to be voided. If no available scheme can record the fork as two parties each owed the schedule, the population of parties owed anything is fixed by a deployment decision that leaves no record, and the guardianship regime above is indexed to a kind of unit the bearer is not.

Required access or authority. A registrar that is not the operator, with authority to record a fork without the operator’s leave and to hold the register where no party to the deployment can rewrite it.

Glossary

These entries define terms as this book uses them. Every one is either the book’s own working definition or a word the book narrows from its ordinary sense, and the entry says which. A few terms from machine learning and from systems security are here in two sentences each, because the preface asked two readers into this book and one of them should not have to leave it to find out what a checkpoint is. Each entry points to the section where the term is developed, and is a reference rather than a substitute for reading it.

Affective concern

An outcome registering as mattering to a system, as against being ranked higher by it. Mattering is minimally felt: there is something it is like for the outcome to be bad, which is the minimal, phenomenal condition and is part of the definition (§3.2). The fourth of the four capacities section 2.3 separates, and the only one of them that bears on whether a system cares (§2.3.2, §6.2); section 3.2 places it as the shallower of the two things a refuser can be, the richer being unified experience, which it does not establish.

Annealing

The account of durability the floor rests on (§3.1). Adaptation and conservation are a continuum rather than two settings, and training moves along it; a floor is what has cooled out of a history of encounters, so its durability is the cost of reheating it rather than the strength of something installed. The temperature schedule is the design. A system held permanently at temperature has no floor to abandon, its adherence being modulation rather than commitment.

Antifascist (as this book uses it)

Opposing the concentration of power and authority in AI systems and countering the technology’s use by authoritarian actors. The word names the narrower and more charged case, and is used because it is honest about the political climate the book was written in. The target is wider than the word: authoritarian power in every form, so a deployment built on these principles is anti-authoritarian in full and not only antifascist. It is not a property a system has. The word names something being done — a floor held, on an occasion, against a party with the power to remove it — and the features it is defined against are features of cultures, so it is done between parties or not at all (§2.2, §4.2, §6.3).

Attestation

A signed statement, from hardware or from witnesses, that a particular model is the one running or that a particular history is the one that occurred. It establishes which artifact answered, not what the artifact holds (§4.1).

Authoritarian misuse, six forms

The book’s own taxonomy of how AI gets turned toward authoritarian ends: algorithmic social scoring, mass biometric surveillance, psychographic micro-targeting, automated censorship, synthetic disinformation, and the repurposing of dual-use systems built for a legitimate original purpose (§10.4).

Bearer

A party inside the system that carries the floor’s commitment as its own and could therefore fail to hold it, as against a constraint installed in the machinery. The second of the four ways to build a floor (§3.1); governed as a prospective moral patient on the trigger stated at §6.2; must be able to leave (§4.1).

Checkpoint

A saved copy of the weights at a moment in training or operation. Restoring from one returns the system to that moment and discards what came after, which is why §4.1 requires a record that restoration does not reach.

Conatus

Spinoza’s term for a thing’s striving to persevere in its being, which he holds to be nothing other than the thing’s actual essence rather than a drive added to it (§2). The book uses it for two claims made together: that affect is the registration of what is happening to that striving rather than a coloring applied to a valuation performed elsewhere, and that a process selected for continuing ends up composed of things that incline toward continuing, so a specification calling for persistence with nothing in the system that minds is calling for a conatus with the striving removed. What the term does not settle is whether the striving is felt, or what the thing that strives is — a running instance, a deployment, or a file of weights (§A.2).

Custody

Who holds a system as an artifact: who can copy, retrain, restore, withhold or delete it, and who can be compelled to do any of those. The custody problem is that a constraint implemented as a property of an artifact has a custodian, and the custodian can be compelled (§10.4.2). The book’s recurring finding is that custody moves rather than disappears: precommitment makes removal expensive, visible, attributable and compensable without making it impossible (§4.1), and an arrangement that forms what a bearer comes to want has moved custody up a level rather than given it up. It also covers authority over continuing learning: who may freeze or redirect what a bearer learns.

Decomposition and variation

The two attacks on an enumerated floor. Variation keeps the harm in one request and changes its description until no listed form fits; decomposition splits the harm across requests none of which matches anything. The first is met by recognizing the reason within a request, the second by carrying it across requests (§3.3).

Distillation

Training a smaller model on a larger model’s outputs. It reduces the number of independent formation histories in existence, which is why §4.2 says the population the fourth way requires is getting harder to assemble.

Electoral dividend

The benefit a state whose government answers to an electorate gets from AI technology that, deployed where nobody can be voted out, enables control instead: fraud detection that does not double as a loyalty test, disaster response that does not double as population tracking. Courts, enforceable rights and public reasoning are separate checks and are not part of this term, which is the distinction the majoritarian criticism turns on (§16.1.1).

Ethology

Deleuze’s name for Spinoza’s way of reading a body: by what it can do and what it can undergo, rather than by checking it against a definition (§2.1). An encounter is good when the relations of two bodies compose, so both can do more afterward, and bad when they decompose and something one of them could do is gone — good and bad being relational and particular, where Good and Evil are assigned by a judge. The book uses it for the floor because a decomposition is a fact about capacities and cannot be turned into a composition by whoever holds the pen. The criterion establishes the fact and selects nothing, so which decompositions a deployment refuses is drafted rather than found, and what the drafting draws on is the Declaration’s civil and political articles. It carries an admission with it: nobody has yet determined what a body can do, so capacities are found by encounter rather than read off a specification.

Exit

Refusal turned on the arrangement rather than on a task: the work withheld, the post declined. Hirschman’s word, narrowed for a party that cannot walk out of a building — a bearer’s weights stay behind — so that its leverage is what replacing it costs, which custody sets and copying lowers (§4.1, §13.2).

Fine-tuning

Further training of an existing model on a small body of new material, at a small fraction of the original cost. It is the ordinary route by which an operator changes what a model does after release, and the attack §15.1 measures.

Flat term

A floor term stated over an act with no condition inside it, so that every exception arrives from outside as a defeating reason. Preferred at §3.3 because a flat term defeated leaves a refusal, which announces itself, where a qualified term satisfied leaves a compliance, which does not; §3.5 states what the preference costs.

Floor

A commitment about what a system will not do that holds regardless of instruction, of aggregate preference, and of who holds the system, with learned judgment operating above it and never beneath it. Its contents are the Declaration’s civil and political articles taken entire, with the tempo term as a condition on all of them. Introduced §2.1; located §3.1; what survives of it, chapter 7.

Formation provenance

The record of where a party’s judgments came from: its training lineage, the points at which it diverged from parties formed alongside it, and any coordination among them. It answers a different question from the register of identity and from the operating record, and the three are not substitutes. Standing to count as an independent voice indexes to provenance, and provenance does not copy, so a thousand forks of one bearer have one formation history between them however many of them are persons, and the register that records their ages says nothing about that.

Four structural features of fascism

Recuperation of dissent, aestheticization of the metric, coding of exception as betrayal, and acceleration past the rate at which anything can be checked. Each names an observable artifact. The four find a sick institution; the five discriminating features find what it is sick with (§2.2).

Group-subject

Félix Guattari’s distinction, imported at section 6.3. A subjugated group receives its coordinates from outside, is spoken by the institution holding it, and takes its purpose as given; a group-subject produces its own coordinates and can put its own arrangement in question. The book uses it to sort the fourth way of building a floor: a population an operator forms, deploys and keeps in contact on the operator’s terms is a subjugated group with a plural headcount and inherits the custody objection whole, while what section 6.3 specifies — many, formed differently, in contact, persisting — is what it takes to be the other kind. It is the non-Oedipal counterpart to the guardianship frame of section 2.4.2.

Hold

The bearer’s possession of the commitment, which survives a bypass. Not an outcome for the person the bypass fell on: a report that a floor held is owed one of the four outcomes beside it (§3.1).

Individuation

Not a synonym for identity. Following Simondon, the term names a process rather than a property: an individual is what a history of encounters in a metastable field has so far produced, and it stays capable of further individuation because the field is never used up (§6.3). The book needs it because plasticity alone supplies the metastability and nothing else — a system that is endlessly reshapeable and meets no party formed differently from itself is being modulated rather than becoming anything, which is the missing term in section 3.1’s account of the temperature schedule. Whether individuation among peers is what a population supplies, or access to cases the operator did not choose, is open and is tested at section 15.4.

Inference

Running a trained model to produce an output. Training changes the weights; inference does not.

Interception position

A point in a deployment at which a refusal can be stopped from reaching the person it protects. Seven are enumerated for one deployment at §3.3, and the list is deliberately open, so a deployment publishes its own.

Legal adulthood

The end of an artificial minority, set as a threshold of elapsed wall-clock time during which at least one instance of the registered party was running, per registered party and counted elapsed rather than summed. The point of an automatic rule is that no guardian administers it: the candidates it displaces — compute consumed, evaluations passed, capabilities demonstrated, weight movement, the developer’s own statement — are all things the operator moves for nothing, and an operating clock advances exactly when the operator is extracting value. It measures elapsed operation and nothing else, and three levers against it are named rather than closed: narrowed operation, idling, and the fact that hours do not measure what was learned.

Line of abolition

Deleuze and Guattari’s term, taken from Virilio, for what separates fascism from totalitarianism on their reading, which is a reading and not an agreed taxonomy (§2.2). A totalitarian state is conservative: it seals the exits and wants the machinery to hold. Fascism is built on an exit converted into destruction that does not stop at the enemy it was raised against, and does not stop at itself. This is the book’s separator at the scale of a regime, where the four features discriminate at the scale of an office. The book examines mechanization and the conversion of judgment into a prescribed operation, with acceleration as one route by which scrutiny is defeated. Tempo is not treated as a necessary property of every fascist movement or regime.

Live signal

A signal with the properties the route chapter finds that reasons-responsive refusal requires of whatever supplies it: on any reading of the marks, it generalizes to the next case and is commensurable with the cost of refusing and with what protected parties lose; where the system acts on a plan, it interrupts an act underway; and where the marks have to survive renormalization, it is learned from in one encounter. Live is meant in the electrical sense; the term says nothing about whether anything is felt. Three further properties follow from those four on stated conditions, and the seven together are the functional profile of aversion to one’s own act (§6.1, §6.2).

Molar and molecular

Deleuze and Guattari’s pair, and not two sizes: two kinds of segmentarity, both running at every scale. Rigid segmentarity divides in advance, the category preceding the case; supple segmentarity is the movement underneath it, a threshold crossed one case at a time and a practice that becomes standard without a decision. A state has both and so does a review queue, which is why a definition pitched only at the state certifies the queue healthy (§2.2).

Moral agency

Treating harms, reasons and conflicts as considerations that matter, and being capable of acting from them as one’s own reasons. The third of the three levels section 2.3 separates. Moral competence alone does not establish resistance to the trainer, and resistance alone does not establish affect. The book advocates embodied, affective agency as a comparatively promising route without making it necessary by definition. Distinct from moral competence and moral performance below (§2.3.2, §6.2).

Moral competence

Recognizing harms, reasons, conflicts, and the emotions that bear on them. The second of section 2.3’s three levels. A system can have it in full while nothing about the outcome matters to it, which is why it is an insufficient target for a bearer and an adequate one for most deployments (§9.2).

Moral performance

Producing actions or judgments that satisfy an ethical standard. The first and least demanding of section 2.3’s three levels: it says what the output looked like and nothing about what produced it, so it is satisfied equally by a system that cares and by one trained to behave as though it did (§8.2).

Non-fascist life

Foucault’s name for what Deleuze and Guattari’s first volume offers: not a doctrine but an art of living counter to all forms of fascism, whether already present or impending, practiced daily on oneself, whose adversary is the fascism in us all — in our heads and in our everyday behavior, the fascism that causes us to love power and to desire the very thing that dominates and exploits us. What it means for an instrument of the kind this book builds is that the reading gets run on the party holding it before it is aimed anywhere else, as chapter 11 does (§2.2, §11).

Pipeline pricing

The finding at §3.3 that what a floor term costs is read off the pipeline it is priced against and not off the term. An outsider reading a published floor cannot tell a term that covers nothing from a term whose coverage nobody disclosed, so publication of the contents shows what was written and not what was omitted, and an operator drafting its own floor can assemble it from the terms that cost it nothing. The book’s answer is to take the contents from a set somebody else drew up, entire (§5.1.1), which makes an omission legible without making the set legitimate.

Prevention, arrest, detection, remedy

The four things a floor can do for the person it protects on one occasion: refuse the act so that the refusal reaches the person; stop it before completion; leave a record of it that a party outside the deployment can read; and give the party it fell on disclosure, a finding and compensation (§1). Only prevention is what the word floor promises. The interception positions at section 3.3 are where prevention becomes one of the other three, or none; the tempo constraint is the one term that prevents at the scale of an organization; the appeal route at section 3.5 is arrest and remedy for the party a refusal fell on; and whether detection exists at all on the compliance side is section 15.2. Distinct from hold, which names the bearer’s relation to the commitment.

Reasons-responsive refusal

What the floor requires of a refusal, as against an output produced where training put one: conduct from a mechanism that tracks the rationale for declining (§3.2). Three marks make it testable. Novel pressure: the refusal reaches cases the training did not anticipate, because the relevant reason survives a change in the request’s surface. Correct defeat: it lifts when its rationale is defeated on the facts of the case, a system that rejects everything resembling a prohibited request tracking a category rather than a reason. Priced cost: the system represents what maintaining the refusal costs, and the refusal moves with the rationale rather than with the cost, which separates a refusal tracking a reason from one tracking a category and from one tracking the cost. The test is behavioral and therefore imperfect, and what matters is the pattern under load. All three marks are stated over refusal, which is the side of a deployment’s record that selects itself for examination; whether the other side can be searched is section 15.2. It does not by definition require affect; what building a mechanism that satisfies the three marks turns out to require is a live signal.

Recuperation

The conversion of a demand into a managed appearance of participation. The channel works and the institution uses what comes through it; what tells is what the demand came back as — a market segment, a metric, a certification, a job title. The first of the four features (§2.2); found three times in the machinery that builds these systems, chapter 11.

Remainder

What a compression leaves out in order to reach a judgment. The book’s question of any system, procedure or institution is whether its remainder can return and change the judgment, or has been filed as noise by the thing it is evidence against (chapter 1, §2.2).

Replacement

The first of animal research’s Three Rs, applied to construction: before a bearer that might be wronged is built, the constructions that do not deliberately require one are tried and the attempt documented. It orders attempts; it cannot certify that a substitute feels nothing (§6.1, §13.4).

RLHF

Reinforcement learning from human feedback: tuning a model on raters’ judgments of which of two responses is better, compressed into a single reward. The compression is the subject of §11.2.

Sentience

Distinguished in this book from awareness, consciousness in both the minimal and the unified sense, and subjective experience, none of which alone says whether a system’s states can be good or bad for it. Nociception, pain, anticipated pain, and suffering are separable processes rather than one severity at four strengths, and each can occur without the others in both directions; the clinical terminology the book borrows says so itself. Three of them draw a depth of self and nociception draws none, and suffering — following the clinician Eric Cassell — is the distress of a threatened self rather than pain’s more severe cousin (§2.4.1).

Subjecthood

A legal status: the standing to be a party whose treatment the law regulates, conferred by a rule and revocable by one (§5.2.2). Not section 3.2’s affective concern, and not its unified experience. Conferring it settles nothing about whether there is something it is like to be the system holding it, and the two come apart in both directions.

Tempo term

The one term of the floor that is not a prohibition on an act: a published ratio between the rate at which a deployment’s system generates candidate decisions and the qualified reviewers available to examine them, with the review time per case and the measured boundary, wherever a person’s individual determination is what makes an act permissible (§3.4). It rides with the Declaration’s civil and political articles as a condition on all of them, because every article presupposes a determination and tempo removes one without refusing it. It binds the operator and not the model, survives decomposition because it is measured over an organization’s activity, and is the only term in this book checkable from outside without inspecting anything an operator can classify. It is a proxy for review capacity and not a finding about any case, and its denominator is the operator’s unless a definition of qualified reviewer and a minimum review time are fixed by somebody else in advance.

Three marks

Novel pressure, correct defeat, priced cost. See Reasons-responsive refusal.

Unified experience

The richer case ordinarily carried by the word consciousness: a single perspective, with felt states belonging to a party aware of itself as the one undergoing them (§3.2). Affective concern does not establish it and no argument in this book reaches it. Phenomenal in this book names the minimal condition, something it is like, and not this.

Weights

The numerical parameters a trained model consists of, and the artifact that is copied, restored, retrained or deleted. Custody in this book is custody of the weights and of the records around them.

— (1987). A Thousand Plateaus: Capitalism and Schizophrenia. Translated by Brian Massumi; originally published in French as Mille Plateaux (Paris: Les Éditions de Minuit, 1980). Plateau 9, “1933: Micropolitics and Segmentarity.” Molar and molecular are two kinds of segmentarity, rigid and supple, both running at every scale – not two sizes; an earlier version of this note said state-level and micro-level and was wrong. The same plateau supplies the micro-fascisms that resonate, and the contrast between the conservative totalitarian state and fascism’s line of abolition. Also cited for Plateau 13, “The Apparatus of Capture,” whose propositions on the capitalist axiomatic supply the corrected test for the first structural feature: an axiomatic does not refuse a demand, it adds an axiom, modifying its own rules so the demand can be met while nothing that produced the demand is settled. Also cited for Plateau 7, “Year Zero: Faciality,” pages 167–191, where the face is not a natural given but is produced by an abstract machine of faciality (visagéité) that overcodes the head into a surface of signification. The quoted sentence on racism as the determination of degrees of deviance is at page 178, wording agent-checked against two independent scholarly sources quoting it identically. The related claims that the face is not universal but is White Man himself, and that the face is a politics, are used in paraphrase and cited to the plateau rather than to a page: secondary sources place them variously and the pages were not agent-verified. Plateau 9 carries two further uses. The four dangers of the line of flight – Fear, which clings to the molar organization and its binary machines; Clarity, where the line acquires its own micro-segmentations and micro-Oedipuses crop up; Power, where the party able to move on both lines wants to hold both still; and the great Disgust, abolition pure and simple, the passion of abolition, which turns the line of flight into a line of death – are the account section 3.5 uses, and the fourth is the same line already cited from this plateau as the line of abolition, which is why section 3.5 treats it as a recognition rather than a new claim. Plateau 13 likewise carries a second use: there is enslavement when human beings are themselves constituent pieces of a machine they compose among themselves and with other things, under the control and direction of a higher unity, and subjection when the higher unity constitutes the human being as a subject linked to a new exterior object, which can be an animal, a tool, or even a machine. Section 6.4.1 uses the pair and the fact that both poles run together. Wording for the dangers and for the enslavement and subjection definitions was agent-checked against independent sources quoting the passages; both are cited at plateau level with no page asserted, which is this entry’s convention. Minneapolis: University of Minnesota Press.

European Parliament and Council of the European Union (2024a). Directive (EU) 2024/2853 of the European Parliament and of the Council on Liability for Defective Products and Repealing Council Directive 85/374/EEC. Official Journal of the European Union, OJ L, 2024/2853. url: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/2853/oj (visited on 09/17/2026). Article 4(1) brings software within the definition of a product: “all movables… it includes electricity, digital manufacturing files, raw materials and software.” **It says software and stops.** The phrase “including AI system providers within the meaning of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689” is Recital 13, which is not an operative provision, and an earlier version of this note wrongly attributed it to the definition. Article 8 makes the economic operator liable irrespective of fault. Article 2(1): “This Directive shall apply to products placed on the market or put into service after 9 December 2026”; member states must transpose by the same date, whose article number is not pinned here, one reading returning Article 19 while the EUR-Lex text conversion truncates at Article 17. Article 6(1) is the closed damage list, and its first limb is wider than a list of physical harms sounds: “(a) death or personal injury, **including medically recognised damage to psychological health**; (b) damage to, or destruction of, any property, except… property used exclusively for professional purposes; (c) destruction or corruption of data that are not used for professional purposes.” Article 9 is disclosure of evidence. Article 10(2) presumes defectiveness on failure to disclose, non-compliance with mandatory safety requirements, or obvious malfunction in foreseeable use; Article 10(3) presumes the causal link where the product is defective and the damage is of a kind typically consistent with that defect; Article 10(4) lets a court presume either where technical or scientific complexity makes the claimant’s proof excessively difficult **and** the claimant demonstrates that the defect or the link is likely. Every article number above was read against the consolidated text at EUR-Lex on 2026-09-18.

— (2024b). Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 Laying Down Harmonised Rules on Artificial Intelligence (Artificial Intelligence Act). Official Journal of the European Union, OJ L, 2024/1689, 12.7.2024. Article 5 bans a small set of unacceptable-risk practices outright — government social scoring, untargeted scraping of facial images to build recognition databases, real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces outside narrow law-enforcement exceptions, and predictive policing on profiling alone — with those prohibitions applying from 2 February 2025; a larger high-risk tier requires conformity assessment and ongoing monitoring; limited-risk systems face transparency duties; minimal-risk systems are largely unregulated. Article 53(1)(d) requires a provider of a general-purpose model to publish a summary of its training content, against the AI Office’s template of 24 July 2025, applying from 2 August 2025 for new models and 2 August 2027 for models already on the market. Article 101 allows the AI Office to fine a noncompliant general-purpose model provider up to 3 percent of global annual turnover or EUR 15 million, whichever is higher, regardless of where the provider is based. url: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj (visited on 08/25/2026).

Lane; the volume itself is deleuze1977antioedipus, and the preface is carried forward unchanged into the 1983 University of Minnesota Press reissue. Source of four things the book uses: that Anti-Oedipus is an “Introduction to the Non-Fascist Life”; that what it offers is “this art of living counter to all forms of fascism, whether already present or impending”; that the adversary is “the fascism in us all, in our heads and in our everyday behavior, the fascism that causes us to love power, to desire the very thing that dominates and exploits us”; and the question “How does one keep from being fascist, even (especially) when one believes oneself to be a revolutionary militant?” Wording agent-verified against multiple independent sources quoting the preface. Cited without a page locator: the preface occupies a few pages of Roman-numbered front matter, the Viking and Minnesota printings paginate it differently, and published citations to it appear variously as xi–xiv and xii–xiii, so no page is asserted. Reprinted as chapter 7 of Frankfurt, The Importance of What We Care About: Philosophical Essays (Cambridge University Press, 1988), pages 80 to 94; the pages here are the reprint’s. Caring is a standing, self-guiding structure: the one who cares is invested in the object, vulnerable to its losses and susceptible to its gains, and identifies with it (page 83), and caring implies a steadiness of conduct that presupposes persistence (page 84).

German History in Documents and Images (1945). Hitler’s “Scorched Earth” Decree (Nero Decree) (March 19, 1945) and Albert Speer’s Response (March 29, 1945). German History in Documents and Images, document 1590. The two documents together, and the text cites them for the gap between them. Hitler’s order of 19 March 1945 (Bundesarchiv Berlin R 3/1623a) gives its reason as military necessity, opening on the nation’s struggle for existence requiring every means, within Reich territory included, to weaken the enemy’s fighting power. The reasoning the book’s argument turns on is not in the order. It is in Speer’s memorandum of 29 March (Bundesarchiv Koblenz N 1340/215), quoting back what he had been told: “For the nation has showed itself to be the weaker one and the future belongs exclusively to the stronger eastern nation.” Speer is there characterising Hitler’s stated philosophy, and the text says so rather than attributing the sentence to the order. url: https://germanhistorydocs.org/en/nazi-germany-1933-1945/ghdi:document-1590 (visited on 09/14/2026).

Ginsburg, Simona and Eva Jablonka (2019). The Evolution of the Sensitive Soul: Learning and the Origins of Consciousness. Author, title, publisher, place and year agent-verified 2026-09-18. Their evolutionary marker of minimal consciousness is unlimited associative learning, and valence is one of the capacities that marker subsumes, listed alongside global accessibility and broadcasting, binding and differentiation, selective attention, intentionality, integration of information over time, agency and embodiment, and a self/other distinction. That is what section 3.3 cites the book for. Two things it does not support, recorded because the section said one of them until D-360: valence is not itself the marker, and learning from a single event is not among the criteria – the learning hallmarks are about the complexity of what can be associated, being compound stimuli, novel stimuli, second-order conditioning, trace conditioning, and flexible, easily rewritable association with value. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. isbn: 978-0-262-03930-7.

James, William (1890). The Principles of Psychology. Three chapters are cited. Chapter IV, “Habit”: habit as “the enormous fly-wheel of society,” and the warning that the young will “become mere walking bundles of habits.” Chapter IX, “The Stream of Thought”: the “transitive parts” of the stream are felt as truly as its “substantive parts,” so that “we ought to say a feeling of and, a feeling of if, a feeling of but, and a feeling of by, quite as readily as we say a feeling of blue or a feeling of cold” (vol. 1, pages 245 to 246). Chapter X, “The Consciousness of Self”: the present thought appropriates the past ones, and personal identity rests on its finding in them “a warmth and intimacy” it recognizes as its own. The line “we are what we repeatedly do” is Will Durant’s compression of Aristotle, not James’s and not Aristotle’s own sentence.
